##### **EDITORS’ BIOGRAPHIES** 

**Ricardo Bassa** , Metallurgical Senior Engineer. 

Labor History Summary :  Presently he works for INCONSULT as a Project and Services Manager.  He has participated in several projects related to the area of copper smelters. Since 2012, he's formerly the President of Pyrometallurgy Commission of the IIMCH. He graduated from Universidad Tйcnica del Estado, Santiago, Chile (now known as USACH) as an Metallurgical Engineer in 1981. In 1997 he made a postgraduate in Management at the Adolfo Ibaсez University and in 1998 studied in Japan using a Scholarship by JICA. His first job was at CIMM (Mining and Metallurgical Center Research) in the position of Researcher until 1984. Afterward he worked at Las Ventanas Smelter (ENAMI), for eight years, as Process Engineer and Smelter Manager. In 1992 he returned to CIMM and held the position of Head of Projects and Head of the Environment and Metallurgy Units. To finish as a Manager of the South Central Zone of CIMM T & S, and North Zone after.  In 2007, he returned to ENAMI where he was Project Manager of Delta Plant, which was built under his direction. He also had worked at Schwager Energy and at White Moutain Titanium Corp., between 2011 and 2012. 

**Roberto Parra ,** Ph.D., Engineering and Material Science 

Professor, Researcher and Metallurgical Consultant 

##### Professional Summary 

Graduated from Universidad de Concepciуn as a Metallurgical Engineering in 1991. He obtained a D.E.A. (1992) and a Ph.D. (1998) in Engineering and Material Science, ~~at~~ from the National Polytechnic Institute of Grenoble (France) under the supervision of Drs. Michel Allibert and Lucien Coudurier from the former Laboratory of Thermodynamic a

nd Metallurgical Physical Chemistry (LTPCM). 

He joined the Department of Metallurgy at Universidad de Concepciуn in October 1992, where until today he is Professor on process metallurgy and pyrometallurgy for the undergraduate and postgraduate program. 

His main interes ~~ts~~ in R&D, is Physical Chemistry of High Temperature Processes with special emphasis in copper pyrometallurgy, design of new processes and reactors, optimization of metallurgical plants and environmental control. 

The valorization of residues of mining operations, as well as the control of minor elements in non ferrous processes, has been one of the subjects that he has developed under different national and international grants and direct contracts with the industry. The approach for the development of different R&D projects covers the analysis at laboratory scale, pilot plant tests and industrial campaigns. 

He is also adjunct professor at the Mining School of Oviedo in Spain, where he develops academic activities in the research group of Steelmaking, Metallurgy and Materials. In addition, he is associated as a researcher in the group Sustainability on Metallurgical and Steelmaking Processes at CENIM in Madrid (Spain). 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

##### **Antonio A. Luraschi ,** Ph.D., M.Sc., Chem. & Met. Engineer 

Process Manager and Metallurgical Consultant Professional Summary. 

Presently Dr. Luraschi works for AMEC International Ltd. as Metallurgical Consulting Manager. Previously he was Engineering Manager for five years and Head of Metallurgical Process in AMEC-Cade.  In this position and formerly as a partner of CADE-IDEPE, a Chilean engineering firm acquired by AMEC in 2007, he has been responsible for the process aspects of a multitude of studies and projects developed by this company in the mining and metallurgical area for the last 17 years, in Chile and abroad. Process design and analysis, particularly with the use of the METSIM Software as a process modeling tool, has been a strong component in his work during these years. 

His previous experience includes ten years as Research Director at CIMM, a position in which he was in charge of research and technological services, such as technical consulting, laboratory testing, piloting, field process optimization and conceptual engineering projects, delivered to the most important Chilean mining companies. 

He has developed more than sixty applied R&D and engineering projects in the fields of copper pyrometallurgy and electrometallurgy, extractive metallurgy of precious metals and special metals such as molybdenum, titanium, vanadium and germanium. 

Has eleven patents, among them: “Procedure to abate arsenic by confinement in Copper Smelter solid Slag”, "Process for removal of arsenic, antimony and other impurities from molten copper by flux injection", "Hydrometallurgical Process for recovering vanadium from vanadium containing slag and the like", and "Procedure to decrease copper losses

in copper smelting slag". 

He has more than forty publications in Chile and abroad.  Some of them are: "Modern Tendencies in Copper Pyrometallurgy", "Developments in Fire Refining of Copper - Flux Injection into Molten Copper", "A Study of the Smelting and Refining of Anode Slimes to Dore Metal", "CIMM's Experience in Industrial Property Protection", and "Slag-metal Equilibrium and a Study of the Thermodynamics and Phase Relationships of the Cu-Fe-S-O-SiO2 System at Copper Smelting Temperatures". 

He has participated in a number of technical meetings and symposia in Chile and abroad. Was a member of the organizing committee of the Copper '87, Copper ‘91 and Copper '99 international conferences and an editor of the Pyrometallurgy Proceedings in these meetings.

## **PREFACE** 

Copper 2013 International Conference is the 8<sup>th</sup> version of the most important global meeting that brings together leading scientists, researchers, academics, and executives from different companies and organizations devoted to the areas of economy, copper processing, metallurgical extraction techniques; environmental compatibility; copper applications, copper recovery, and waste management and recycling techniques. At the same time, the challenges faced by different mining projects will be addressed. We appreciate the work and collaboration from colleagues coming from over 30 countries and representing more than 300 companies and institutions. 

Copper 2013 Conferences find their origin in the joint work conducted between the Chilean Institute of Mining Engineers (IIMCh) and the Metallurgical Society of the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum (METSOC). Since 2007, when the Copper Conference was held in Toronto, new co-organizer institutions have helped disseminate the results achieved by the Conferences while granting th

ese a strong global character in terms of convening power, submittal of papers, and the generation of collaborative knowledge. We deeply appreciate the disinterested contribution from GDMB of Germany, MMIJ of Japan, and TMS and SME from USA. This time, the current global situation is not only a scenario where competitive prices are being realized but also where strong and serious uncertainties are being handled in connection with the global economy; energy and key resources prices. Globally, ore grades have declined to historically low levels and, therefore, the recycling and recovery of what used to be waste material, nowadays represent great opportunities for the overall development of new projects. Water uses in production processes and the solutions applied no doubt represent a source of knowledge for the community gathered at this venue. Likewise, new long-term and mid-term forecasts to be made in the future will certainly set their focus on eventual challenges and on mining and metallurgical development opportunities in the decades ahead. The total of 330 papers submitted in response to the original call will present the main changes to take place in metallurgical processes, as well as the state-of-theart techniques responsible for providing effective solutions to new challenges posed by metallurgical processes. The widespread interest generated by innovations, particularly in the area of pyrometallurgy will undoubtedly occupy a special place in the course of the Conference, thanks to the research and development of technological solutions conducted in countries like China, for example. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ The 2013 Conference has issued 7 volumes of Proceedings containing all the papers and management initiatives presented in each of the 10 symposiums hosted by the Conference. Our special gratitude to all authors and their papers presented during symposium sessions. Copper 2013 Organizing Committee. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ #### **FOREWORD** The Symposium has received 112 abstracts and 91 papers, for the Pyrometallurgy Symposium. This shows the historic interest of the participation of the professionals working in this area of extractive metallurgy of copper. In

this opportunity the papers have subdivided in the following concepts, including the presented papers for each of them: 

- Fundamental Physical Chemistry, Phase Diagrams and its Applications, 29 papers 

- Operation Analysis and Improvements, 38 papers 

- New Processes, 18 papers 

- Refractories, 6 papers 

In this Symposium we will pay tribute for the contribution made by Mr. Nickolas Themelis in the field of cooper pyrometallurgy and the engineering process of metallurgy. 

The aim of this Symposium is to bring together international experts to review the latest innovations in pyrometallurgy copper and its impact on the cooper industry. 

On behalf of the Institute of Mining Engineers of Chile, through the commission of pyrometallurgy, we appreciate the effort made by all authors, co-authors and anonymous people who have made this great event come possible.

### **OUTOTEC® COPPER PLANT SOLUTION** 

Primary copper smelting has long been the dominant processing route for copper production and in the past decade the proportion of global copper production derived from copper secondaries has been around 35% [1-2]. However, certain trends are already shaping the industry, thus some aspects needs to be taken into consideration, whilst trying to predict the future. 

In the following there are few industry shaping trends listed and also an example how to combine different technologies and process knowledge together in order to be able to answer these challenges. 

Economy of scale and increasing capacity of all the new operating smelters around the world can be seen. Only 20 years ago the largest smelters were producing just over 200 000 tpa copper, whereas today even 400 000 tpa single units are coming on stream [3]. Increase in production volume is very effective in means of decreasing unit costs and increasing cost efficiency. At the same time, however, should the relative emissions levels decrease and plant efficiency to increase. 

Rapid rise in electronic and metal containing waste generation is leading to prediction that secondary copper processing will gain an ever increasing importance within the global coppe

r industry [1]. In addition, reduced supply of copper raw materials has resulted into the low TC/RCs for custom smelters. So, additionally smelters need to be able to recover all the valuable metals passing through the value chain in smelting plants not only copper. 

Energy efficiency, environmental emissions and license to operate have gained a considerable amount of importance globally, especially in recent years. Total sulfur dioxide emissions from copper smelters have been reduced over the last ten years [3] even while the overall production has increased. In addition to sulfur currently and in very near future there is pressure for cathode producers to be able to show the environmental and carbon dioxide footprint of their copper production process starting from the beginning to end. 

The Kennecott-Outotec Flash Converting process has been described in several publications over the years and some of them compiled in the references [4-5].  Also, most recently continuous TSL converting has been commissioned (paper in this conference). The advantages for using a single vessel, continuous converting and/or direct blister, instead of several low intensity vessels to do the same job makes common sense. By optimizing the whole process flow chain with the combination of sealed, high intensity/capacity, continuously operating furnaces together with low volume, high SO2

content off-gases using heat recovery and latest gas treatment possibilities, provides the company the license to operate – meaning economical justification while also meeting the social responsibility towards the surrounding community. Environmental aspects and reasoning for using the integrated approach is more described in the next chapter. 

Valuable metals recovery is extremely important to the operations via bringing the additional value to primary copper production, with relatively low investment. The most successful application in the treatment of anode slimes has proven to be Kaldo process. The anode slimes contain mainly Cu, Pb, Ag, Au and Se. Slimes are first leached followed by smelting, converting and refining producing a Dore containing the Ag, Au and small amount of PGMs. Valuable products that can be retrieved include pure silver and gold ingots, crude selenium and Pt/Pd slime. Successful introduction of Kaldo based process into precious metals recovery leads into considerable improvements in recoveries, energy usage and emission levels. Results in Boliden operations have been published in ref [6]. 

The proportion of global copper production derived from copper secondaries is expected to increase in the future. The number of low-grade secondary materials as a byproduct coming from the modern society can include, but not limited to, slags, sludges, oxide residues, metallic scrap, electrical and electronic waste. Traditional treatment methods have been slowly replaced by newer bath smelting technologies such, Outotec

TSL Ausmelt, Kaldo and Troff applications. This aspect of paying more attention to possibilities for enhancing and adding value to existing operations by maximizing revenue from a wider range of valuable by-product metals can become a necessity in the future in order to stay competitive. Also, it makes economical and social sense to expand the existing industrial units instead of generating more individual and separate plants in remote locations, which might not have the reasonable infrastructure and/or critical know-how in the region. In addition to selecting a most suitable flow-sheet and smelting technology, handling and cleaning process off-gas can be considered critical part of the overall plant performance. Secondary copper materials are commonly associated with plastics and ceramics, which can contain elements that produce toxic/hazardous substances if processed under certain conditions.

The idea is that the intelligent control system is linked to process control system and based on sophisticated Heat and Material Balance model takes into account the real situation of the process and adjusts automatically. The monitoring is not limited to the one furnace only, but can also take into consideration different furnaces, the gas line and returning flows. Inside the overall expert system cooling monitoring can be conducted via Outotec® Sentinel intelligent furnace cooling monitoring system. Heat load from each circuit is calculated

Nowadays, all the sand cast cooling elements can be replaced by superior quality continuous cast cooling elements. Besides making modifications to the cooling elements to improve the conductivity, cost structure (new manufacturing solutions) also the design of the whole cooling set-up with the refractories has been revisited. Refractorory thickness and the contact between the element and bricks was improved by the new ICE(integrated Cooling Element design). These new design features enhances the thermal contact between the refractory and the cooling element, thus promoting protective solid layer formation and thereby also longer lifetime.

### **PNEUMATIC CONVEYING OVERVIEW** 

Pneumatic conveying is, generally, the most efficient and effective method of transporting granular and bulk solid materials to storage or to process within a production environment. The metals industries were amongst the first to adopt pneumatic conveying initially Lean Phase solutions. These solutions offered low cost, quick and simple installation and wide range of material application. 

The Lean Phase solutions however, move materials at high velocity 15-30 metres per second and therefore are not suitable for highly abrasive materials found in the metals industries. These systems are now being replaced by Dense Phase solutions which have much improved performance, delivering high availability, improved valve performance and reduced power consumption and wear.  Dense Phase solutions transfer the materials at much lower speeds 4-8m/s so reducing wear. 

This Dense Phase mode of conveying is a little more difficult to install, needing more headroom but results in minimal wear of pipelines and bends, it has less moving parts and a lower electrical power requirement.  Combined with the Schenck Process Dome Valve minimum maintenance and long life is delivered. This efficient conveying technology delivers process ready performance and exceptional performance which is trusted by major users.

Schenck Process focus on delivering Pneumatic Dense Phase conveying systems with high quality valving, high conveying density, engineered pipelines, with assured capacity and low air usage. Energy efficient, environmentally supportive, high availability and reliability delivered are all essential features of a process environment solution. 

A Schenck Process Dense Phase Pneumatic conveying system is shown in Figure 1, which consists of a pressure vessel and control valves, used to manage the flow of material fed into and out of the conveying vessel. Schenck Process’ Dense Phase systems can convey materials over significant distances and at high tonnage rates. Distances and tonnages are material dependant but Schenck Process have experience in moving materials in single steps over 2000m and at tonnage rates in excess of 250 tonnes per hour which covers most applications in the non-ferrous environment. 

Dense Phase Pneumatic conveying system  are used by many of the Worlds smelter sites for conveying ores, concentrates, additives and for recycling dusts. 100% environmentally safe enclosed conveying and high availability scored in the high 99% region, with single annual 1hour planned maintenance and low power consumption, these

### **SCHENCK PROCESS DOME VALVE** 

The valves used in pneumatic injection systems have often been its downfall. Many pyrometallurgical process users report the valve as its number one failure issue. Many valves have a short life of hours or days. Schenck Process’s Pneumatic Conveying and Pneumatic Injection solutions all use a valve known as the Dome Valve.  This valve delivers unrivalled performance allowing Schenck Process Pneumatic Injection Systems to work on an annual planned maintenance basis with high availability. 

The Schenck Process Dome Valve was originally designed and patented by Clyde Process in 1974 and has been used in a wide variety of materials handling applications; the valve has become an industry standard. The valve configuration, shown in Figure 2 & 3, comprises of a dome shaped closure mounted on half shafts that is moved through 90 degrees by means of a pneumatic cylinder. A rubber seal mounted at the entry to the valve is inflated by compressed air when the valve is in the closed position in order to obtain a gas tight closure. When the valve is opened, the seal is first deflated, causing it to retract away from the dome; the dome then moves to the open position. In this way there is no direct contact between the dome and seal while the dome is moving, hence the associated abrasive wear of the seal is avoided. 

A seal life of typically 500,000 operating cycles, equivalent to more than 2 years operation, is achieved. This valve is seen as the most reliable in the industry and is used by many operators in demanding environments as their chosen standard. The valve can be modified through cooling, seal types and finishes to suit a large range of materials. The resulting technology has resolved the valve problem for most applications used for pneumatic conveying and injection solutions. Valves are available with outlets from 50 to 650mm and versions are available up to 750C operating temperature.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Pyro-metallurgical industries are constantly affected by more rigorous environmental regulations and global lack of necessary resources, like energy and water for their processes. Plant owners look for new ways to operate their plants in an efficient and economical way. One possibility is the usage of waste heat boilers (WHB) to recover the energy potential of their plants. The WHB recovers the waste heat of the process to generate steam and cools down the gas. The produced steam can be used for power generation to improve the energy efficiency of the plant. By cooling down the waste gas, the requirement of additional cooling systems like water injection is not necessary. Water consumption is reduced. This work describes some existing furnace technologies and types of WHB which can be installed in non-ferrous industry plants. The main objectives are to show different possibilities to save natural resources (fuels, water, etc.) while producing electrical energy from the steam generated by these WHB. Furthermore, some mechanisms which improve the efficiency of the waste heat recovery are described and an example for using the recovered heat to generate electricity is shown. Finally, a preview on further developments for this subject is given.

### **FACTORS AFFECTING THE WASTE HEAT RECOVERY EFFICIENCY** 

The generated steam quantity can be described by Formula 1. In the following an explanation of the different parameters affecting the recovered waste heat and the enthalpies involved in the process is given. 

### **Enthalpy of the Saturated Steam and Feed Water** 

The enthalpies of the steam and the feed water (hfeedwater, hsteam) are thermodynamic properties, which depend on the parameters pressure and temperature. Both parameters can be controlled and are defined by the design of the WHB. 

The temperature of the waste gas decreases inside the WHB and can generate sulphuric acid condensation which can cause corrosion on the tubes. To protect the heating surfaces of the WHB from this kind of corrosion, the temperature of these surfaces has to be kept above the sulphuric acid dew point. Therefore the operational pressure of the cooling water/steam is chosen to ensure that the corresponding saturated water/steam temperature (boiling temperature) always remains above this dew point temperature, including also a certain security margin. One of the characteristics of the evaporative cooling technologies is that the wall temperature of the heating surfaces of the WHB remains constant and similar to the temperature of the saturated steam, which is thermodynamically defined by its pressure. If the temperature of the heating surfaces cannot be smaller than 275 °C (acid dew point plus security factor), then the pressure which corresponds to this temperature of saturated steam is approx. 5.95 MPa. This is the minimum operational pressure, and together with its corresponding saturated steam temperature determines the enthalpy of the saturated steam. 

The enthalpy of the feed water depends mainly on its temperature: The higher it is, the higher is its enthalpy. Then, for generating a maximum steam quantity, the feed water should have the highest temperat

ure possible. Besides, the water temperature is essential for degassing, which requires a minimum temperature of 105 °C under standard conditions. If the feed water temperature is not sufficiently high, heating is required. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

31 

### **Fouling of the Heating Surfaces** 

The enthalpies of the steam and the feed water are variables that can be controlled.  Therefore, as indicated in Formula 1, the main factor which determines the generated steam quantity is the amount of waste heat recovered by the WHB, Qinlet – Qoutlet. 

The geometrical dimensions of the WHB are designed for keeping the waste gas velocity in a certain range in order to obtain a homogeneous temperature profile for optimum cooling performance. The waste gas is loaded with dust, whose characteristics change inside the WHB due to two main factors. The first one is the variable waste gas temperature profile due to the cooling effect of the WHB and the second are reactions and metals condensation occurring inside the WHB. The dust can acquire a sticky behaviour before it transforms finally to a solid phase in the WHB and can form deposits on the boiler tubes, especially on the tubes of the evaporator screens and bundles. This phenomenon is known as fouling and the efficiency reduction described by the fouling factor. As a consequence of this deposition, the heat transfer to the water/steam circulation system is reduced and the gas temperature at the boiler outlet increases, thus reducing the waste heat recovery. How the fouling factor (Rd) affects the thermal efficiency is described in Formula 2. 



Ud denotes the thermal conductance of heat exchanger after fouling and U the thermal conductance of clean heating surfaces. 

To avoid fouling and an increasing fouling factor of the heating surfaces (i.e., a reduced overall heat transfer coefficient under operating conditions), the dust has to be removed and discharged continuously. A cleaning system is necessary. 

Oschatz has developed two different types of cleaning devices with different functional designs depending on the place of installation: 

- Mechanical hammering cleaning devices operated by electric motors. 

- Pneumatic hammering cleaning devices operated by pneumatic actuators. 

The quantity of hammering devices operated by one electric motor depends on the individual installation place at the boiler tube walls and heating surfaces [1]: 

- Single device (one motor, one shaft, one hammer) and/or multiple hammering cleaning devices (one motor, one shaft, two or three hammers). 

- Bundle hammering cleaning devices (one motor, one shaft, up to 20 hammers).

### **SUMMARY** 

The increasing cost of electrical energy, in connection with the worldwide stronger emission regulations makes power generation using WHB systems an interesting option in the non-ferrous industry. Nearly all WHB systems downstream of smelters or converters as suggested in the present paper work with steam pressures between 4.0 MPaa and 6.0 MPaa in order to avoid sulphuric acid corrosion. 

However, the steam used for drying and heating processes in the non-ferrous industries is mainly a low pressure steam (approx. 0.6 MPaa). Thus, the use of a condensing steam turbine with extraction downstream of the WHB system is the most feasible option. ### **ABSTRACT** 

In July 2011 a new copper ISASMELT™ furnace was commissioned at Kazzinc Ltd’s Metallurgical Complex in Ust-Kamenogorsk, Kazakhstan. It was part of a brownfield smelter project, situated inside an existing metallurgical complex. Kazzinc had up to that time been primarily a zinc and lead producer so the entire copper circuit was new, from feed blending through to cathode strapping. Within 14 months it was achieving its design production capacity. 

For the project to be brought to successful fruition, numerous challenges had to be met: new technology had to be brought into the Republic of Kazakhstan and the local operating team had to become competent to operate it; the complex polymetallic concentrates of the East Kazakhstan region had to be smelted without compromising the production rate or product quality; and the copper production circuit had to be integrated into the overall metallurgical complex to derive greatest economic benefit from the polymetallic nature of the raw materials. 

This paper describes how the copper ISASMELT™ furnace fitted into this strategy, and how the coordinated actions of Kazzinc and Xstrata Technology personnel brought this project to fruition.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Formerly part of the Soviet Union, the Republic of Kazakhstan has been an independent nation for more than 20 years. It is the world's largest landlocked country by land area, being larger than Western Europe. It has a wealth of mineral resources spread throughout the country. Kazzinc Ltd is a major, fully integrated, zinc producer established in 1997 through the merger of Eastern Kazakhstan's three main non-ferrous metals companies. In addition to zinc, the concentrates from Kazzinc’s mines contain significant amounts of lead, copper and precious metals. The capital of Eastern Kazakhstan province is Ust-Kamenogorsk, a city of about 350,000 people, which has been a hub for transporting and processing base metals concentrates for more than a century. Since 1943, Ust-Kamenogorsk has also been home to a multi-smelter metallurgical complex specialising in the production of zinc, lead, silver, gold, antimony, bismuth and various other by-products. The Ust-Kamenogorsk Metallurgical Complex (UKMC) is one of Kazzinc’s assets, and in 2005 when Kazzinc wished to add a copper smelter and refinery to UKMC it approached Xstrata Technology to provide the ISASMELT™ and ISA PROCESS™ technologies for the new copper plant. 

Despite UKMC’s rich smelting history, copper had not previously been a major product. About 5000 tonnes per an

num (tpa) of blister copper was produced as a byproduct of lead smelting.  A completely new plant was required for the copper smelter and refinery. The new plant would be akin to a greenfield project in scope, except that its location amid a major metallurgical complex had all of the complications associated with a brownfield expansion project. The concept of the new copper plant was that it should have a nominal production capacity of 70,000 tpa of cathode copper, be able to treat polymetallic copper concentrates and a range of by-products from zinc and lead refining, be tolerant of minor element fluctuations, and be readily expandable in the future. For the primary copper smelting furnace, an ISASMELT™ was a logical choice to meet these objectives. During the course of the next 6 years, many things changed in the process of evaluating, locating, designing, constructing and commissioning the copper plant, but the original project objectives remained unchanged. 

With a capacity of just 70,000 tpa of copper, the UKMC copper smelter was destined to be small by world standards, and subject to a high ratio of fixed:variable costs. For the project to make sense, the key performance characteristic would be that the smelter could run well on a fluctuating supply of polymetallic concentrates sourced locally from Kazzinc mines, recover the precious metals contained therein, and eliminate the transportation and penalty costs associated with sales of concentrate to third parties.

### **Plant Description** 

The copper smelter at UKMC has a conventional flowsheet. Concentrate smelting is performed in the copper ISASMELT™ furnace, matte is converted in one of two P-S Converters, and fire refining occurs in two anode furnaces, prior to anode casting. The sulphuric acid plant is able to accept gas from the ISASMELT™ furnace and one blowing P-S Converter. The flowsheet is shown schematically in Figure 1. 



**Figure 1** :  Schematic Diagram of Copper Smelter Flowsheet 

Within this flowsheet, impurity removal was to occur via a dedicated bleed of slag from the P-S Converter copper blow, and via dusts produced from the smelting furnaces. Direct recycle of dust streams was calculated to be impractical owing to the build-up of volatile impurity elements. Instead, an existing metallurgical facility was modified to perform dust leaching duties, thereby removing target elements and producing a clean copper cement that could be recycled to the smelter.

### **Plant Start-up** 

For a completely new copper smelter and refinery complex, especially one in a cold climate, a plant start-up is not a single event that takes place on a particular day. By necessity the activities span many weeks as various parts of the flowsheet are brought into production. Seasonal plant and equipment are brought into operation on schedules of their own, such as concentrate thawing sheds, building heaters or ventilators, steam heating plants and fuel supply equipment. Concentrate is delivered, stored and blended weeks in advance of its consumption. An inventory of anodes must accumulate in an electrolytic refinery before entire cell sections can be energised together. 

At UKMC the operations team implemented an astute practice of commissioning an entire sulphuric acid plant (designed by SNC Lavalin) ahead of the copper smelter. This was made possible by interconnecting ducts with existing non-ferrous smelting plants and the supply of SO2-rich gases for several months in advance of commissioning the copper smelter. Similarly the air separation unit (designed by Kryogenmash) was also commissioned and operating at full capacity well in advance of its required duty for the copper smelter. 

In part because of the care and planning that occurred during pre-commissioning, UKMC achieved 100% of the copper ISASMELT™ plant’s design smelting capacity, measured on an 8-hour shift basis, within a few days of first adding feed to the ISASMELT™ furnace. However, the job of ramping up a smelter to full production does not end there. The following year of operation was spent achieving both consistency and reliability across the whole copper smelter, qualities that are necessary for stable plant operation. Xstrata Technology personnel provided some assistance in this endeavour, whenever asked to do so. For the first few weeks after deciding to heat the ISASMELT™ furnace Xstrata Technology was able to assist all operations shift crews, with two specialists per shift, on a 24 hour basis. The required assistance diminished significantly as the operations team gained experience and competence in their tasks. Within a couple of months the UKMC team were “flying solo” with proficiency, and have continued to optimise and improve the smelter operation ever since.

The Ust-Kamenogorsk Metallurgical Complex has commissioned a new copper smelter and refinery, treating mostly feeds sourced from its own mines and metallurgical facilities. The new plant was conceived with a future vision of polymetallic concentrates being a major component of the feed material. 

Personnel from Kazzinc and Xstrata Technology worked together on an extensive programme of training and pre-commissioning activities to prepare the people and plant equipment for their respective roles in plant operation. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

Feed preparation plays a crucial role in having a smooth smelting operation and also the overall smelting economics in metal production. Drying is of significant importance for smelting economics as it is a very energy intensive process and it should not affect the availability of the smelter. Selection of the proper drying technology is the key factor herein, as it not only affects directly the economics in both drying and gas handling, but also gas emissions, safety issues, availability, maintenance and operational expenses. 

Non-ferrous metal concentrates can be dried using various techniques. Conventional drying, based on direct heating and use of fossil fuels as drying energy, has almost entirely been replaced by steam drying during the past 20 years. Steam drying, on the contrary, is based on indirect heating and it has become the most dominant drying technology for copper concentrates during the last decade with over 90% of the market share of all new dryer installations. 

Steam drying has been acknowledged to be the most user friendly technology and additionally several millions of euros can be saved yearly when using energy efficient steam drying technology. There are, however, significant differences between steam dryers, particularly regarding factors such as the availability (down time the dryer may cause to the smelting process), and the cost of maintenance. Because of these factors, the Kumera Steam Dryer is known to be a favourable technology for drying non-ferrous metals concentrates. 

### **BENEFITS OF FEEDING DRIED CONCENTRATE TO SMELTING** 

Removal of water from the concentrate is very energy intensive thus having a significant environmental impact. However, drying prior to smelting is always economically feasible and very often viable also from the perspective of process operations. 

Whether drying must be, or must not be, or may be applied prior to smelting depends primarily on the smelting technology. All flash furnaces and in-flight reactions strongly prefer or even necessitate the use of dry concentrates to allow instant oxidation reactions to take place within a few seconds. On th

e contrary, all TSL reactors prefer or even necessitate the use of wet concentrate in order to prevent excessive dust load from the TSL furnace. Also agglomeration, like pelletizing may therein be required. Other bath reactors, like Noranda and El Teniente can utilize dry concentrate, in injected, being thus more flexible with respect to moisture content of the concentrate. Main benefits in removing the water prior to smelting relate to sustainability, i.e. decreased energy consumption and decreased emission rates. The lower expenses relate to the fact that when water is removed down to 0.2 - 0.4% H2O prior to smelting, some 2,700 MJ/tH2O of energy is required for each tonne of water, as heating of the water in concentrate, evaporation of water and heating of the evaporated water vapor require approximately 380 MJ, 2,260 MJ and 50 MJ, respectively, as can be _Proceeding of Copper 2013_ _Santiago, Chile_ 51 seen in Figure 1. This is due to the fact that the hot gases from primary smelting must be cooled before directing them to the sulfuric acid plant During this process, the waste energy is captured in the form of steam and part of it is used in the drying process while the surplus of steam can be used for other purposes, e.g. heating or electric power generation. _Proceeding of Copper 2013_ _Santiago, Chile_ 54 A common controversy about steam drying includes the discussion of its benefits versus a possible loss of power generation in case that part of the steam would alternatively be used for drying. cts [5]: - Reduction of energy required for drying by 20 - 30% - Reduction of OPEX due to energy and maintenance costs by some 30 - 40% - Reduction of OPEX and CAPEX of gas cleaning by some 70 - 75% - Minimization/elimination of gas emissions - Reduction of problems in gas cleaning, like burning of filter bags - Efficiency increase of electric power generation to almost 100% due to utilization of latent heat (as comparison: conversion of surplus steam to electric power has a relatively low efficiency of less than 40%, as only mechanical energy is utilized) - Increased availability of drying (e.g., in case of the Kumera Steam Dryer, the dryer does not cause any smelter downtime) All these benefits, which are worth 4 MEUR/y in OPEX as an average for a mid-size smelter (150 t/h dry feed to furnace) have to be compared with the main drawback, i.e. the value of steam, which is no longer available for power generation. All the combined benefits of using steam drying easily overcomes the loss of possible power generation of about 3 - 6 MW, which could have a value of about 1-2 MEUR/y. Furthermore, also low pressure steam from other sources, like acid plant, can easily be used as a heating media for steam drying. Therefore, all high pressure steam could be used for power generation, if required. However, optimum use of steam should always be made on case by case basis taking into account the prevailing conditions, price and availability of steam, fuel and electricity, pressure of steam, and drying and smelting capacity with relevant OPEX, etc. ### **Gas Emission – CO2, SO2, NOx** The most important factor in determining the environmental footprint of drying is the drying technology itself, as it affects the amount of energy needed in drying, the type of fuel used in drying, and thus the quantity and type of gaseous emission[6]. ### Carbon Dioxide CO2 The use of steam is advantageous regarding gaseous emissions, as no carbon dioxide is generated. Consequently, there is a significant difference in CO2 emission between steam drying and conventional drying with emission rates of zero versus some 40,000 tonnes CO2/year, respectively, at an average-sized smelter which processes1 Mtpy concentrate. Consequently, the dryer off-gas can be directed to atmosphere with zero NOx emission. ### **Dust Emission** Dust emission depends primarily on the dryer technology, subsequent off-gas flow rate, as well as on the dust cleaning technology (e.g., bag house, ESP, scrubber). Conventional dryers have gas flow rates typically two to four times greater than steam dryers due to convection versus conduction (direct vs indirect heating). Due to the fact that dust emission is determined by the dust load in mg/Nm3 , the emission rate is practically a function of gas flow rates an

d not really dependent on the actual dust load entering the bag house filter [6]. 

The lowest overall dust emission (dust load in kg/year) can be achieved by steam dryer technology (low gas flow rate) together with a bag house filter (high dust capture rate). By such means dust emission rates of less than 3 mg/Nm<sup>3</sup> can easily be achieved under normal operational conditions. Furthermore, low emission means also better working environment and enhanced metal recovery with better capture of valuable metals. 

It is also worth noticing that due to the significantly smaller gas flow rates in steam drying, the gas cleaning device can be designed with a size three to four times smaller than for conventional dryers. Similar downsizing occurs also for the fan. This downsizing strongly affects the costs of gas cleaning and may decrease the associated direct costs by a factor of 2 to 4. 

With a combined use of steam drying and a bag house filter, the dust emission can easily be kept below all regulation limits, with typical emission rates being in the range of 1 - 3 mg/Nm<sup>3</sup> . 

### **Safety Issues** 

Steam drying is based on indirect heating by steam, which is generated in the waste heat boiler where an excessive amount of chemical energy from sulphide smelting is captured as waste energy. Part of this steam is further utilized as an optimum heating media for drying. 

Due to the nature of indirect heating, the temperature profile and the gas atmosphere inside the dryer can be properly controlled. This is important as the tendency for ignition of dry fine sulphide or even elemental sulphur particles can thus be significantly decreased or even fully eliminated as the gas temperature does not exceed 125 °C and the concentrate temperature remains below 120 °C at any point during the drying process. 

Conversely, the conventional dryers have very high combustion gas inlet temperatures (600 - 800 °C) when coming into contact with fine sulphide particle. This results in a much higher tendency for ignition and subsequent CO2, SO2 and NOx emissions, as well as problems in gas cleaning.

Enrique Herrera and Leopoldo Mariscal _SOUTHERN PERU Fundiciуn Ilo, Punta Tablones S/N Ilo, Peru eherrera@southernperu.com.pe / lmariscal@southernperu.com.pe_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

The Ilo Copper Smelter operates from 2007 with an ISASMELT™ furnace as a single smelting unit (1,200,000 tpy of copper concentrates), four PS converters (two blowing), two anode furnaces, a casting wheel and two acid plants. Depending on the operational conditions of the smelting furnace, sulfur trioxide (SO3) can be generated causing potential corrosion issues in the subsequent gas line and increasing the weak acid formation in the acid plants. This paper describes the modifications and improvements carried out at SPCC Ilo Smelter in order to control SO3 formation. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Southern Peru is one of the largest copper producers in America. Its production facilities include two mine-concentrator centers in Cuajone and Toquepala, and a primary copper

smelter and an electrolytic refinery located in Ilo, on the south part of Peru. 

The Ilo smelter plant started operations in 1960 and since then has been through a number of upgrades to increase its capacity and modernize its equipment. The latest modernization, implemented in 2007, was the incorporation of the ISASMELT™ technology to replace two reverberatory furnaces and a Teniente Converter. The new plant, with an installed processing capacity of 1,200,000 tpy of copper concentrate, consists of a single ISASMELT™ smelting unit, two rotary holding furnaces, four PS converters (two blowing), two anode furnaces, a casting wheel and two acid plants. Figure 1 shows the smelter flow diagram. 

The ISASMELT™ furnace carries out the function of smelting the SPCC copper concentrate feed which contains approximately 26% copper to produce a molten copper matte containing approximately 62% copper. This process is accomplished by injecting oxygen-enriched air (60 - 65% O2) into the molten slag bath using an ISASMELT™ top submerged lance. A turbulent bath ensures a fast reaction and high mixing allowing incorporation of the fresh feed into the molten phases. The generated molten copper matte and slag are batch tapped into the rotary holding furnaces for separation of the copper and slag phases. 

The ISASMELT™ furnace process off-gas with a relatively high SO2 content (flow rate: 100,000 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h; SO2 (28 vol-%, wet basis) is cooled down in a waste heat boiler to recover energy and then de-dusted in an electrostatic precipitator. The cooled gas is then mixed in a duct mixing chamber with process off-gases from the two blowing PS converters, and forwarded to the two acid plant facilities for further cleaning and sulfuric acid production. The weak acid from the gas cleaning system of the acid plants is neutralized by adding Ca(OH)2 in a conventional effluent treatment plant.

### **CONCEPTUAL AND THEORICAL CONSIDERATIONS** 

### **Waste Heat Boiler Description:** 

Figure 6 shows a schematic diagram of the WHB manufactured by Oschatz. The vertical radiation section of the WHB consists of a transition piece, and two radiation shafts. The convection section of the WHB consists of two evaporative screen bundles and six evaporative bundles. 

The design basis of the ISASMELT™ process considered an inlet off-gas temperature range to the WHB of 1050 – 1150 °C. The WHB design considered an outlet temperature of 650 ºC at the exit of the radiation section and finally at exit temperature of 350 ºC at the outlet of the convection section. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

67 











Figure 6 - Ilo Smelter ISASMELT™ Furnace’s WHB schematic diagram

To avoid acid corrosion risks on the WHB tubes, there are two aspects that need to be considered: 

- Minimize conversion of SO2 to SO3 

- Keeping heating surface walls in the WHB above the dew point. 

To ensure that these two criteria can be satisfied, the water/steam operating pressure was designed at 64 bar allowing a saturated steam temperature to be in the range of 280 °C. 

### **Dust Sulfation:** 

To achieve an optimum WHB operation across the convection section, it is recommendable to complete the dust sulfation within the WHB radiation section. If this is not achieved, dust particles may come into direct contact with the boiler surfaces (evaporator bundles) increasing the probability of forming sticky dust layers on these surfaces as particles get closer to their sintering temperature. This condition will negatively impact the heat transfer efficiency and increase the probability of blockages within the convection section causing severe operational problems. 

In the radiation section, on the other hand, the dust particles have the possibility to react in the gas suspension if the temperature is low enough and sufficient oxygen and turbulence is available for dust sulfations reactions. Therefore the off-gas temperature and oxygen concentration at the outlet of the radiation section must be carefully monitored and kept lower than the optimal sulfate formation to allow a proper sulfation to occur. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

68 

Supplying cold air or gases into the radiation section will also promote the dust sulfation reactions as lower temperatures and high oxygen concentration are favorable for these reactions to occur. 

### **SO3 formation:** 

It is important to keep SO3 formation controlled at lower levels across the off-gas line of the smelting process to minimize the probability of sulfuric acid formation that could cause corrosion issues in ducts and equipment as surface temperature drops below the dew acid point temperature. High SO3 formation also increases production of weak acid formation in the washing stage at the acid plants. 

The oxidation of SO2 to SO3 can progress by two different mechanisms<sup>(1)</sup> : by a homogenous gas phase reaction, involving oxygen radicals, or by a heterogeneous reaction with O2 on the surface of some catalyst materials. 

The formation of SO3 by homogenous reactions occurs primarily at high temperatures inside the smelting furnace, and this process is strongly dependent on the amount of free oxygen. On the other hand, the catalytic oxidation of SO2 to SO3 takes place at temperatures below 700°C, and it is strongly dependent on the accessibility of catalytic surfaces (like metal oxides contained in the flue dust or deposited over the boiler surfaces), off-gas temperature, off-gas oxygen content, and the off-gas residence time. Experimental work<sup>(2)</sup> reports that the conversion rate is higher in the temperature range of 570 – 640 °C, and this occurs when the

gas is diluted and cooled at this range of temperatures, and it is estimated that 1-3% SO2 is converted to SO3. 

Thermodynamically, both SO3 and sulfate formation are favored by low temperatures, but kinetically elevated temperatures generate high reaction rates. Although SO3 and sulfate formation are analogous phenomena, the optimal temperature is not the same for both reactions, since sulfate formation includes condensed phases as reactants and products. Thus, the temperature of maximum sulfation is higher than the optimal SO3 conversion temperature, but if the place where oxygen is supplied is too cold, SO3 may form but not be consumed by the sulfation reaction<sup>(2)</sup> . 

### **ACTIONS TO REDUCE SO3 FORMATION** 

### **Increasing ISASMELT™ furnace oxygen efficiency:** 

During the initial campaign of the ISASMELT™ furnace, higher oxygen consumptions were reported. This observation was corroborated with plant measurements that showed higher than expected oxygen and SO3 contents in the ISASMELT™ off-gas within the WHB. In order to reduce free oxygen content in the off-gases and subsequently increase the oxygen efficiency within the smelting process, the depth of the ISASMELT™ lance tip immersion was increased. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

69 

### **Control of accretions formation in the first shaft of the WHB radiation section:** 

In order to reduce and control the accretions formation in the first shaft of the radiation section the following actions were implemented: 

- Reduction and control of the magnetite content in the slag in order to decrease its viscosity and solidification temperature. 

- Installation of a new transition piece located at the inlet of the radiation section of the boiler, constructed with omega tubes that provide a flat surface on the heat side, and in order to reduce the accumulation of accretions on this boiler section. 

- Installation of new inspection windows on the first shaft of the radiation section, in order to manually clean the accretions formed on this part of the boiler, if required. This preventive cleaning takes place during furnace downtime as a measure to prevent further accumulations. 

- Installation of an enlarged splash block in the ISASMELT™ furnace. 

- Reduction of the amount of "post combustion" air that is injected to the furnace through the lance port during smelting, in order to avoid decreasing the off-gas temperature at the inlet of the boiler and to avoid oxidation from FeO to Fe3O4 within the slag that is projected by the lance from the molten bath . 

- Reduction of the fine coal addition to the furnace in order to avoid higher temperatures of the process off-gas and to reduce the requirement for oxygen in the process off-gas. 

- Reduction of the lance slag splashing by improvements to operating practices. 

### **Implementation of an additional air sulfation system:** 

A new air sulfation system was installed to ensure proper dust sulfation. The new system

allowed the addition of post combustion air through a boiler inspection window located in the middle part of the radiation section as shown in the right photo of Figure 7. The new installed air blower had the capacity to inject post-combustion air up to 6,000 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h.

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The main mechanism of formation of SO3 in the process off-gas of the ISASMELT™ furnace seems to be by a homogeneous gas phase reaction that occurs within the furnace mainly due to the presence of free oxygen that escapes from the molten bath when there is not enough lance tip immersion. In order to avoid high SO3 formation rates, the ISASMELT™ furnace is now running with high oxygen efficiency. This also prevents the formation of acid in the off-gas handling system as well as a high acidity of the weak acid generated in the gas cleaning section of the sulfuric acid plants. 

To prevent dust accretions in the boiler the following actions are in place: 

- Control oxygen content at the outlet of the WHB convection in the range of 2.0 - 2.5 % (vol.) adjusting the air flow injected through the radiation section. 

- Control temperature at the outlet of the WHB radiation section below 700 °C minimizing the accretion formation at the radiation section and also with the proper use of reverts, oxygen and coal. 

- Minimize accretion formation at the inlet of the WHB, lowering the magnetite content in the slag and also through a proper operational control.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Looking back at the history of copper smelters, it is noted that concern for environmental issues were practically non-existing about 100 years ago.  The first attempts to decrease the pollution in the area around the smelters were to build high stacks and to increase the dilution of the process gas. High stacks made the working environment at the smelter sites and in the area surrounding the smelters acceptable. Installations of high stacks were the environmental efforts done to make it possible to run the smelters without any gas and dust cleaning. 

As the years went by the production of copper increased.  In 1900 the copper production was only 0.5 million ton, today 2013 the copper production is about 16 million ton [1]. With the increased production there was a fast increase of emissions. The environment around the smelters was significantly impaired and the copper industry had to find new ways to handle the situation during the middle of the 20th century.  New environmental regulations were introduced in Europe, North America and Japan, which the copper industry had to follow, and it was also important to win back the approval of the public. Gas cleaning for dust capture was introduced and soon also sulphuric acid plants were built around the world. The first sulphuric acid plant at the Boliden Rцnnskдr smelter in Sweden was built in 1952 [2]. 

After instal

lation of sulphuric acid plants the cost for the smelters increased, due to high gas volumes with low sulphur dioxide, SO2, concentrations. Gas cleaning of large gas volumes is expensive and in order to reduce the costs, gas volume and SO2 concentration have to be improved.  Primary smelters changed technology from e.g. reverberatory furnaces to more energy- and environmental-efficient smelting units like Outotec FSF or TSL. When a high environmental and economical (power consumption and throughput) performance was reached for the primary smelters, focus has changed towards the tail gas of acid plants and the converter aisle. 

By converting single absorption sulphuric acid plants into double absorption, SO2 in acid plant tail gas is reduced.  As the next step (or at the same time) the environmental performance for the PS converters has to be increased. PS converter hoods with better environmental and economical performance are necessary to reach the environmental goals of the 21th century.

Later on, Boliden started a subsidiary called Boliden Contech, which continued the work with development of the PS converter hoods. ### **CONVERTER HOOD HISTORY** 

Gas capture around the old traditional air cooled PS converter hoods was poor. The converter hoods were assembled with a great distance from the converter mouth to prevent overheating. Large amount of dilution air was also needed. Before gas cleaning with sulphuric acid plants was used, a high amount of dilution air was not a problem and high dilution was an easy way to make the process gas less harmful. Later on, when sulphuric acid plants were built for gas cleaning, a large amount of dilution air lowered the performance and increased the cost for the gas cleaning, i.e. sulphuric acid plant. 

With the understanding that the PS converter hood had to be closer to the converter mouth, the only way to go has been water cooled hoods or water spraying in the hoods. The solution on the market for water cooling was water jackets, a solution where the hoods are built by water boxes. Water jackets hoods were built around the world, and thus a closer fit was possible and the amount of dilution air decreased. 

However, this solution did not satisfy the engineers at Boliden Rцnnskдr. They wanted closer fitting of the hood due to t

he need for lower dilution. Low dilution was needed both for the gas cleaning and to increase the efficiency on the new boiler. The boilers require the process gas to be as hot as possible in order to be effective and consequently the amount of dilution air has to be low. The engineers at the Boliden Rцnnskдr started to look for other solutions for the PS converter hoods in the late 1960s. A solution known at the Boliden Rцnnskдr smelters was water tubes used in boilers. 

Water tubes with high speed water flow solved the problem with local boiling and hoods with closer fit were now possible. The problem with intensive piping was also solved with tube-type panels, as the water could be introduced through headers into the tubes. But the drawback with the use of water tubes soon appeared. Build-ups were created rapidly and frequent cleaning was necessary. Sometimes very large pieces fell down without control and damaged the equipment. The build-ups created corrosion problems and the cleaning was wearing the tubes. The consequence of the corrosion and cleaning was of course water leaks. 

### **FINAL SOLUTION** 

The engineers at Boliden Rцnnskдr were looking for a new and better solution. The new solution had the following requirements:

### **Pushing the flame backwards** 

To avoid gas leaks around the door, the PS converter flame has to be directed away from the front door.  The flame can be pushed backwards in two ways, either by tilting the PS converter or by closing the PS converter on the back side. By closing the converter on the back side with a hydraulic operated flap, the flame will be pushed backwards and the

gas leaks in the front are minimized. Most of the dilution air enters under the front door and almost no gas will leak out around the door. The dilution air protects the door and reduces the heat load against the door; hence water cooling of the door is not necessary. As most of the dilution air is entering from the front, charging with boat during blowing without too large gas emissions is possible. The hood door can be

The good door solution is one other key factor to reduce and avoid gas leaks to the converter aisle. The best way to avoid gas leaks is to have a door with a tight fit against the primary hood, especially in the top. The Outotec door has a sealing device in the top of the door, which slides against a stiff water-cooled box that has a smooth surface. The tight fit in the top prevents emissions when the door is opened and it makes it possible to charge cooling scrap by boat during blowing without large emissions.

### **Water quality** 

From each project the know-how about the importance of good water quality for the primary hood cooling has increased. PS converter hoods installed at the Boliden Rцnnskдr smelter have always used water of boiler feed quality. However, the first time the impact of bad cooling water quality became obvious was in a project where the client had an existing water system of “open” type providing water of lower quality. The problems emerged after a couple of years.  Good water quality is necessary to avoid build-ups inside the water tubes and corrosion due to low pH and high levels of halogens. The PS converter hood water cooling system should be a closed system, where the water is of boiler feed quality and pH regulated to 9.5-10.5. An open water circuit is detrimental for the oxygen level and the water easily gets contaminated with impurities. Around the smelters there are a lot of impurities all over, especially metal sulphides.

Improved welding techniques have been adopted. Different projects have improved the knowhow and the welding technique has been changed from simple butt welding to double butt welding with double fillet welding. See Figure 8 to the left.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Reliable and accurate furnace level information for blister, matte and slag during smelting and converting processes is invaluable for decision making and process optimization. 

AGELLIS Group AB had previously identified inherent problems with gauging levels accurately in furnaces. We had successfully installed our EMLI-ELP systems on Submerged Arc and other electric furnaces in order to solve measurement problems. In flash furnaces the problems appeared to be the same, with sounding bars operated from the furnace roof area being used to take measurements. As a result, the results are often inaccurate. It was therefore decided to test the ELP system on a flash smelter. 

This paper shows how the AGELLIS EMLI-ELP system was successfully trialled at Kennecott Utah Copper (KUC) on both their Flash Smelting (FSF) and Flash Converting (FCF) furnaces. The results were used to compare the consistency and reliability of Kennecott’s current measuring methods with that of the AGELLIS system. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

In the production of copper the pyrometallurgical process has, in recent years, made many advances with more efficient furnace design coupled with modern comprehensive control systems. With all of the advances made so far, none has yet been applied to the current inadequate methods for recording material levels using sounding bar systems. 

As reliable and accurate data about blister, matte and slag levels during the melting process is invaluable for good decision making and furnace process optimization, a modern and safe method of obtaining this data is a priority. In order to bring this part of the furnace in line with all the other advances, AGELLIS Group AB of Sweden have used their knowledge and years of experience in the field of electromagnetics to produce a system capable of recording the working material levels in a furnace reliably, accurately, rapidly and above all safely, at any time during the melting process. 

### **BACKGROUND** 

Contact was made with Kennecott Copper explaining the benefits to be obtained by using an automated/semi-automated system in smelting furnaces. Kennecott Copper uses two flash furnaces, a Flash Smelting Furnace (FSF) and a Flash Converting Furnace (FCF), to produce copper from copper concentrate. In the furnaces it is important to know the depth of the interface layer between slag and matte/blister to be able to run

the furnaces efficiently. 

Kennecott believed that this measurement technology, if proven at their plant, would be of significant benefit to them and so decided to move forward to trial the proposed solution. 

### **Current Measurement of Material Levels in the Furnaces** 

The top levels in the furnaces are today measured with a Vega radar system. This radar works well when the access ports are clear. Two measuring stations are also used on the furnaces. Typically, the south measuring station next to each Reaction Shaft is used to determine immersion temperatures and take immersion samples, while the north station is used to determine level measurements and obtain slag bar samples. Measuring holes are cleaned regularly to ensure that they remain open and free from obstruction. 

To measure the layers, a measuring rod/sounding bar is lowered down into the furnace until it contacts the bottom build-up. With a new measuring rod and no build-up in the furnace, there will be 9145 mm of rod protruding above the furnace floor. If the rod won’t go all the way down, the distance remaining is noted. This provides a figure for the amount of bottom build-up. The rod is placed into the furnace for approximately 30 seconds, twisted back and forth several times through approx. 90° before being quickly withdrawn. The rod is placed against the measuring bracket to cool. As the metal will cool first, a break line will develop at the matte-slag interface. The levels of matte and slag on the bar are then measured manually.

The accuracy of the measurement of slag and bottom build-up are reasonably accurate but matte measurement with the current practice has an accuracy of ± 25 mm with low repeatability due to difficulty identifying the matte/slag interface on the measuring bar. 

Temperature measurements are taken every hour by probe half way into the slag. As a result of uncertainty with regards to the slag layer thickness, some amount of uncertainty in the temperature measurement is introduced. 

### **Flash Smelting Furnace (FSF)** 

The FSF feed consists of dry concentrate and recycled dust. The FSF receives blended, dried concentrate via a gravity fed flow system. Normal levels in the FSF are: 

**Slag:** 810 mm – 1070 mm **Matte:** 530 mm – 690 mm

### **Reason for Conducting the Trial** 

The main reason

for installing an EMLI-ELP system is to obtain: 

- Consistent and objective levels: Level readings will be independent of the operators’ personal interpretations. This will allow Kennecott Copper to run the furnace in a more optimal way and in the end increase the throughput and decrease costs. 

### **Trial History** 

Initially, a trial was performed using an AGELLIS EMLI Control Unit and an Electronic Level Profiling (ELP) lance. As a result of that trial it was determined that the AGELLIS system could systematically measure the levels of blister and slag in the FCF and matte in the FSF. However, no reference sounding bar measurements were available to confirm the ELP determined matte levels in the FSF during this trial due to a broken sounding bar cable. 

Therefore a second trial was performed using the same type of AGELLIS EMLI Control Unit and ELP lance. The purpose was to verify the matte detection levels in the FSF against a working sounding bar. This paper details the results and conclusions of both these trials. 

### **LEVEL MEASUREMENT TRIALS** 

The AGELLIS EMLI-ELP System is designed to be used in combination with a full lance carriage mechanism which provides an easy to operate, accurate and very reliable delivery system for any furnace measurement probe. Further benefits can be obtained when using a lance carriage mechanism to deliver the AGELLIS EMLI-ELP level probe. Slag thickness, bottom build up, temperature and the ability to take metal samples are all possible. 

However for simplicity reasons, the trial system consisted of a lance, complete with a sensor probe, which can directly replace any sounding bar system. ### **Calculation of Matte and Slag Level** 

In the following sections the matte and slag levels are calculated as follows: 

Buildup = Virtual Depth + Zero Position – Maximum Depth. 

Slag Level = Virtual Depth + Zero Position – Slag Entry + Sensor Offset – Buildup. Matte Level = Virtual Depth + Zero Position – Matte Entry + Sensor Offset – Buildup. 

The individual components used to calculate the Matte Level are described below: 

- Buildup 

- Virtual Depth 

- Zero Position 

- Maximum Depth 

- Slag Entry 

   - The thickness of buildup at the bottom of the furnace. The furnace depth relative to the Zero Position. A fixed reference controlled before each dip. 

   - The maximum Draw-Wire position encoder depth. The draw-wire reading at the point of slag detection. 

- Matte Entry The draw-wire reading at the point of metal detection. 

- Sensor Offset Position of sensor in lance. 

   - (~50 mm from tip + 100 mm additional compensation). 

The slag thickness can be determined by the difference in slag and matte levels.

### **Precision and Accuracy Consid

erations** 

The precision of the measurements is subject to several environmental factors including: 

- The precision of the height measurement system. 

- How constant the dipping speed is. 

- How much the lance is allowed to deviate off the vertical during a dip. 

- How even the bottom of the furnace/build-up is. 

Improved precision is possible by: 

- Changing to a motorized (constant speed) delivery system. 

- Employing a (low deviation) lance guide-rail. 

- Using a higher precision height measurement meter. 

Note that these improvements are all available when using a lance carriage delivery system. The accuracy of the system is dependent on other factors such as: 

- Ensuring that an installed system is correctly calibrated. 

- Ensuring that operators use the system correctly. 

- Ensuring that system components are regularly serviced and maintained. 

- Ensuring that the system is recalibrated when physical changes to the furnace environment occur. 

KUC and AGELLIS both see the potential benefits of installing full lance carriage EMLI-ELP systems on flash smelters. In production the accuracy and reliability of the measurement data will greatly assist flash furnace process optimization. 

### **Maintenance Considerations** 

Since the EMLI-ELP system uses light and affordable disposable shields for the sensor and lance body, the measuring equipment itself is protected from the high temperatures in the furnace environment. This provides a long life for the lance and sensor components of the equipment.

Since an automated lance delivery system performs an identical operation every dip, the results are precise accurate and objective. The added precision can be used to

### **ABSTRACT** 

The “O-SR” Process, which is an innovative combination of a newly installed Mitsubishi-Process S-furnace(SF) with the existing reverberatory furnaces (RFs) followed by PS-converters (PSC), has been operated since December 2007.  The project of the O-SR process had aimed to increase the treatment of copper concentrates in the S- furnace while enhancing the treatment of combustible wastes such as shredder residue (SR) and successively corresponded the intention.  The original facilities of the O-SR process have recently modified to establish an optimum operation, as follows: 

- Launder between the S-furnace and RFs was redesigned to increase the availability at S-furnace 

- A new coal combustion system and a compact hot-blast stove were adopted for RFs. 

- The operation of PSCs including the number of working converters was changed to treat high grade matte. 

As a results, the operation cost and carbon footprint due to the consumption of fossil fuel have decreased dramatically.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Onahama smelter and refinery had been operated as custom smelting of copper concentrates since 1965. Smelting facilities were subsequently expanded to two reververatory furnace(RFs) and five PS-converters(PSCs) in 1973. Since RF is a typical old-fashioned smelting hearth which consumes a huge amount of fuel to smelt copper concentrates, saving fuel cost has been the most important item to be developed. In early 1980’s bunker oil combustion was changed to the pulverized coal combustion, which was followed by the utilization of waste tires. 

Furthermore, in 1990’s, treatment of combustible waste such as shredder residue(SR),  which is generated from scrapped automobiles and vending machines, have started, in RFs while the dried concentrates have injected through tuyeres into PSCs to reduce the amount of treated concent

rates in RFs. These modifications have enabled to reduce the amount of the pulverized coal combustion and to increase SR treatment. SR treatment capacity have enhanced to 12,000T/M by social request originating from the enforcement of vehicles recycling law[1,2]. 

As a result, RFs have changed to waste materials combustion furnace from copper concentrates smelting furnace which was accompanied a huge consumption of fossil fuel. Accordingly, thermo-materials recycling system of SR has been established. 

However, the operation had to be optimized further against severe copper business circumstance. The reduction of energy cost at RFs and the enhancement of concentrates injection into PSCs were limited as far as existing facilities were utilized. In order to overcome the limitation, Mitsubishi Process S-furnace(SF) was installed at the upstream of the  RFs (the O-SR process) in December, 2007. These modifications have achieved noticeable cost reduction and the enhancement of copper concentrates treatment. Profitable operation after the introduction of SF is attributed to the optimization of the O-SR process  as described in the present paper. 

### **OUTLINE OF THE O-SR PROCESS** 

Before the introduction of SF, the concentrates and SR, which is substitution of fossil fuel, were treated in two RFs. When the amount of SR treatment was increased, the combustion of  pulverized coal had to be decreased and the amount of concentrate treatment in RF was decreased, because heat input into RF was always operated at maximum. Therefore SR and concentrates treatment was contrarily operated. 

The O-SR process has enabled the simultaneous increase of concentrate and SR treatment. At the SF the concentrate is injected into melt through lance pipes with oxygen en-riched air continuously, and then oxidized and smelted in a moment. Although small amount of concentrates are still melted in RF in order to protect furnace wall and inhibit the formation of dioxin, the main function of RF was changed to separation of

This has allowed to reduce the number of hot converters to 2 blowing and 3 hot from the previous strategy of 3 blowing and 4 hot. ### **ABSTRACT** 

In the nearest future, development of Udokan deposit, one of the world´s largest complex oxide-sulphide copper ore deposits, located in Chita Region (Russia) is to be started. The characteristic feature of copper sulphide concentrates produced by ore beneficiation process is low Fe grade (3-4 wt%) at high silicon oxide level (35-45 wt%). In this work, two methods of pyrometallurgical processing are discussed: 

   - smelting to blister copper in  Two-Zone Vaniukov Furnace; 

- concentrate roasting in a fluidized bed furnace followed by calcine’ reduction 

- smelting in a DC furnace. 

The laboratory-scale and pilot test-work results are presented including the proposed process flow-sheets’ comparative analysis and discussion of the said flowsheets’ advantages and drawbacks.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Udokan deposit mainly contains oxide-sulphide copper ores. The said ore type treatment by the combined hydrometallurgical and concentration methods results in the production of sulphide concentrates containing (wt%): 24-30 Cu; 4.0-6.0 Fe; 7-11 S; 3542 SiO2; 8-9 Al2O3; 0.8-1.6 CaO; 0.4-0.8 MgO; 0.5-2.5 K2O; 0.5-2.0 Na2O; 0.005-0.015 Zn; 0.01-0.03 Pb; 0.004-0.006 As; 0.002-0.004 Sb; 220-240 g/t Ag; 0.05-0.07 g/t Au. 

Low sulphur and iron and high silicon dioxide levels are the characteristic features of the concentrate. According to the concentrate phase composition studies, chalcocite (Cu2S) and bornite (Cu5FeS4) are the principal sulphide copper-containing minerals, while  areantlerite (Cu3(SO4)(OH)4) and malachite (Cu2CO3(OH)2) make up the principal oxide copper-containing minerals. The major rock-forming minerals are as follows: quartz (SiO2); alb

ite (Na,Ca)[AlSi3O8]; potassium feldspar (Na,K)[AlSi3O8]; anorthite Ca[Al2Si2O8]. Chalcopyrite, covellite, biotite, chlorite, hematite, rutile, and ilmenite are tributary minerals. 

Different process flow-sheets are considered for the said concentrate treatment including two pyrometallurgical methods: 

- concentrate’ complete oxidising roasting in fluidised bed furnaces; calcine smelting in DC electric furnaces to semi-blister copper followed by refining to copper anodes; 

- concentrate smelting in Vaniukov Furnace (VF) to blister copper followed by refining to copper anodes . 

Fig. 1 and 2 give the pyrometallurgical process flow-sheets. 

The current investigation’ objective was as follows: experimental verification of both process flow-sheets; calculation of the principal process indices, as well as energy carriers’ cost and flux consumption rates, based on the results produced; comparative analysis of the processes and selection of the most efficient one for commercial scale implementation. The results of both process flow-sheets’ study are given below. 

### **Sulphide concentrate smelting in Two-Zone Vaniukov Furnace** 

Smelting of copper sulphide concentrates in Two-Zone Vaniukov Furnace is widely practiced in Russia and CIS. At present, about 710 kt copper are annually produced using this processing method. However, Vanukov Furnaces are currently used for smelting of copper concentrates with high sulphur and iron content to produce copper mates of various grade [1]. Udokan sulphide concentrates’ special feature is low iron content, which makes it possible to consider a direct smelting to blister copper as the possible scenario. The assumption is supported by the practical experience of Glogow (Poland) [2-5], Olympic Dam (Australia) [6,7], and Konkola Copper Mines’ Nchanga (Zambia) [8-10] operations where flesh smelting is used for  processing of concentrates with a relatively low iron content (5-20%) to blister and semi-blister copper. 

The Udokan ore concentrate differs from the above mentioned concentrates in substantially higher silicon dioxide content. The said type feed requires fundamental understanding of the process’ chemistry and the suitable process flow-sheet. A brand
