new method of oxidising smelting and slag reduction cleaning in a single unit, Two-Zone Vaniukov Furnace, is proposed. Fig. 1 shows the equipment lay-out and the process flow-sheet for the Two-Zone Vaniukov Furnace smelting. 

Wet concentrate, CaO-containing flux and coal are charged into the Furnace’ oxidising zone. The need for flux addition is determined by high SiO2 and Al2O3 content in the concentrate. Coal is charged into the oxidising zone to compensate for any heat deficiency, and coal derived gas is also injected. The coal derived gas is used due to the lack of natural gas in the Chita Region. The oxygen-enriched blast is fed in the amount required for blister copper production and for fuel firing

consumption. From the oxidising zone, copper-rich slag is delivered to the reduction zone where slag cleaning takes place by the coal derived gas injected via the lances together with the oxygen-air mixture. Coal is additionally dosed to create the required reduction potential ensuring substantial slag reduction in terms of its copper grade. Blister copper and slag discharged is performed in a continuous mode. Blister copper is delivered to the anode refining circuit, and slag is granulated and removed to the waste-dump. The oxidising zone’ gases containing SO2 are delivered to the Sulphuric Acid Plant. The reduction zone’ gases containing СО and Н2 are after-burnt in the Waste Heat Boiler, and after de-dusting are vent to the atmosphere. Preliminary limestone roasting is advisable as it decreases the VF’ fuel and oxygen consumption. Pulverised coal is used as a fuel for roasting in the Tubular Rotary Kiln.

### **_Choice of the optimum slag composition_** 

Selection of the optimum slag composition achieved by fluxing agents’ addition is among the most important technological issues in terms of processing concentrates with the increased silicon dioxide content. Fluxing conditions are important not only for the Vaniukov process but for any other pyrometallurgical method used for the Udokan concentrates treatment. Correctly selected slag composition ensures both high-performance process and safe operation of the Furnace (e.g. stable smelting without foamy melt). 

Slag composition should meet a number of requirements. It should have a relatively low liquidus temperature to prevent blister copper overheating in excess of liquidus temperature of the latter (~ 1100<sup>0</sup> С), which is caused by sharp increase of oxygen solubility in copper at copper temperature rise [11]. Slag must be of as low density as possible, and its crystal phase (magnetite or other spinels) must be in the minimum amount [12]. At the increase of slag’ spinel phase concentration, decrease of the surface and interphase tension takes place, while slag’ viscosity and density increase. All the above impinges the smelting process stability. Therefore, crystal phase concentration in slag should be under close control and must never exceed 10 %wt. Slag should have high surface tension since the dissolution rate of fluxing components, metals’ losses to slag, and slag melts sponging are dependent on the surface tension. According to [13], surface tension of 240-270 mN/m still is able to maintain the process stability. However, the above range must be considered as a nearboundary-type level. Surface tension of 240 mN/m can be assumed as a boundary level. Finally, slag should be

of low viscosity. According to the published data, viscosity limit should make 30-50 P. So, 30 P is the accepted boundary value. Also, it should be noted that when choosing the optimum slag composition, minimum consumption of fluxing components should be considered since fluxes raise smelting cost, increase slag throughput, and, correspondingly, metal losses. Moreover, flux addition usually leads to the decrease of SO2 concentration in the off-gases. Based on the available published data, results of the theoretical calculations of liquidus temperature and slag melts viscosity using FactSage software, and the experimental data, effect of SiO2/CaO concentration ratio on slag´s principal properties has been defined. The principal target of the process’ reduction stage is, on one hand, production of slag with the least possible copper content and, on the other hand, production of quality blister copper suitable for refining by a single-stage process, i.e. by reduction. 

For the concentrate of the said composition, S, Fe, O, As, Pb, Sb, and Zn are the principal blister copper’ impurities. Concentrations of Zn, Pb, and Sb found in blister copper (see Table 5) do not affect anode copper quality. The same is true for As, its concentration in copper being below 0.01%. At that, the level of these impurities remains very low regardless of Redox potential at both process stages. Iron concentration in blister copper shall be determined by the rate of slag cleaning in terms of copper content. Iron reduction is possible at substantially high reduction potential. However, the performed investigations show that even at rather low residual copper level in the slag, iron level in blister copper is extremely low (see Table 5). The result produced confirms the widely recognised fact of copper reduction selectivity as compared to that of iron in pyrometallurgical processes. Sulphur and oxygen contained in blister copper are distinctive impurities-antipodes at the oxidising stage of the process. The higher sulphur content is, the lower that of oxygen becomes, and vice versa. So, in order to realise the single-stage refining process, it would be reasonable to produce high oxidised copper. At that, some oxygen portion can be removed from copper simply by virtue of the VF reduction process. The experimental procedure was as follows. The pre-set temperature (850-950<sup>0</sup> С) having been achieved, air was injected into the reactor in the amount of up to 60% of that required for the bed standard boiling (~9.5 nm<sup>3</sup> /hr), and ~ 6 kg roasted calcine produced during the previous test was loaded as a bed. By increasing the blast consumption, the calcine was transformed into the boiling state. The selected blast rate within the layer was pre-set, and the feed charging was started under the control of the feed loading rate and gas consumption at the hearth. The following process parameters were registered: fluidised bed temperature; oscillation peaks at the mercury pressure gauge indicating the material volume in the reactor; boiling process quality; the flue gas

path’ depression rate. On the test completion the roasting products were discharged. Specific features of the roasting products structure were studied using SEM and EPMA methods. Considering the test-work results, the process temperature, the blast’ oxygen enrichment rate and the Furnace’ specific output based on the concentrate feed volume are of the most substantial effect on the calcine’ residual sulphur content and on other parameters. It was determined that 9000 С was the optimum roasting temperature. At higher temperature levels, the material sintering takes place, while at the lower ones substantial diffusion limitations resulting in the increase of the calcine’ sulphur concentration are observed. ### **Comparative analysis of principal process parameters and consumption rates for metho

ds based on Vaniukov smelting and on roasting followed by the calcine electric smelting** 

It is of interest to compare two methods of copper production based on the Udokan deposit ore’ copper sulphide concentrates. The concentrate composition used for the process parameters’ calculation was somewhat different from that used for the pilot tests (see above). Table 8 presents the principal results produced for the tested process flow-sheets. 

According to the data in Table 8, a Smelter’ facility needs less space in case of Vaniukov smelting process implementation since only one Roaster and one Vaniukov Furnace are required. If the process flow-sheet based on roasting is implemented, 4 fluidised bed furnaces are required, each having hearth area virtually equal to that of the two-zone Vaniukov Furnace, and 2 electric furnaces of 149.5 m<sup>2</sup> area each. Besides, the roasting process flow-sheet is of higher capital and operating cost since off-gases volume is 4.5 times higher and the generated gas volume is 6.5 times higher than in case of Vaniukov smeltingbased process. 

Moreover, Vaniukov smelting-based process looks more attractive when comparing utilities consumption per 1 t of anode copper production. Thus, oxygen consumption in the fluidised bed furnace process is 20% higher than in Vaniukov Furnace, which is due to low sulpur content in the concentrate. As a rule, roasting of conventional high-sulphur sulphide concentrates can be carried out in fluidised bed furnaces using air-blast, while for the discussed  concentrates composition, it is necessary to use not only blast enrichment with oxygen, but also fuel in the form of coal derived gas. The said gas consumption in fluidised bed furnaces 3 times exceeds that required for Vaniukov Furnace, since blast enrichment with oxygen is lower for the fluidised bed furnaces (30%) as compared to that used for Vaniukov Furnaces (80%). 

Coal is the only energy carrier that can be considered as the roasting process’ advantage in terms of its consumption rate that is 48% less. However, low coal consumption cannot be set off by higher electric power consumption required for Roasting – Electric Smelting process flow-sheet. First of all, the bulk of electric power is consumed by electric furnaces. In the Vaniukov smelting-based process, the said cost item is absent. Secondly, a significant portion of electric power is used for oxygen and compressed air production. Comparison of the said electric power cost shows that in the roasting-based process it is actually 2 times higher, while total electric power cost for the said process flow-sheet is 6 times higher. For the sake of objective assessment, electric power cost for both processes was transferred into the units of equivalent fuel. As seen in Table 8, the method based on Twozone Vaniukov Furnace Smelting is more preferable in terms of energy cost.

It can be explained by higher copper and silver losses to the electric furnace’ dump slag than to the slag produced in Vaniukov Furnace where more efficient cleaning with intensive slag melt agitation, as well as efficient coagulation of copper drops in bubbling zone followed by precipitation in the siphon and mixer, are used. 

Comparison of anode refining in both process flow-sheets also demonstrates advantages of the Vaniukov Smelting-based method. First of all, deeper sulphur removal during oxidising smelting, as compared to the oxidising roasting method, reduces anode refining operating costs owing to the absence of oxidising stage. Secondly, utilisation of sulphur dioxide formed at semi-blister copper oxidation will be either impossible at all or very expensive due to extremely low SO2 concentration in the off-gases. 

According to the discussed pilot test results, comparative analysis of the two process flow-sheets shows obvious advantages of the Two-zone Vaniukov Furnace-based process flow-sheet. Of course, it is not free from some drawbacks that need to be mentioned. One of the principal disadvantages is the fact that there are no industrial-scale Two-zone Vaniukov Furnaces currently operating, which creates certain risks and often frightens potential investors when the new process implementation is discussed. Also, roasting circuit required for limestone preparation, as well as the need for expensive titanium to manufacture wet gas cleaning units treating oxidising zone’ off-gases, should be listed as disadvantages. However, in spite of the above mentioned drawbacks, advantage of the Vaniukov Smelting-based process in terms of both capital and operating cost is quite obvious even without detailed economic calculations. 

In conclusion it should be mentioned that other modern oxidising smelting processe, such as Outotec Flash smelting, Ausmelt-Outotec, Isasmelt, Teniente, etc., will have clear advantages over the method based on sulphide concentrates roasting.

Typically the primary cooling water system consists of tank, pumps, heat exchangers, cooling elements, and cooling water piping as well as headers which distribute cooling water to cooling elements. The heat loss of the furnace will vary during the campaign life, and typically increase along with the wear of the refractory brick lining. The amount of circulating cooling water needs to be adjusted according to wearing and heat losses. Longer furnace campaigns can be achieved by promoting the formation of the protective freeze lining layer. This can be helped not only through cooling design but also through proper monitoring of the process and ensuring good operational conditions. The Outotec® Sentinel monitoring solution provides the means for the promotion of the freeze lining formation. SCOE+ is an innovative solution that gives daily support on the analysis of operations, evaluation of strategies for the mitigation of pollutants, and it also stands as a help to look up for sustaina

### **ABSTRACT** 

With the aim of reducing copper levels in converter slag and to further optimize converter performance, the Atlantic Copper smelter (Huelva smelter) undertook a project leading to optimisation of its converter aisle practices. This study consisted of a review of the current converter aisle operation, a full mapping of the slag chemistry and a modeling of the converter cycle through a new “blow-by blow” approach. The modelling approach and main variables influencing overall performance, slag chemistry, and copper losses are discussed in this paper. The impact of operational parameters (e.g. iron left in the white metal, oxygen enrichment, Fe/SiO2, etc.) and operational practices (e.g. air blowing, fluxing, reverts and scrap copper addition, copper slag recirculation, slag left in the vessel. slag skimming) are discussed in the context of overall heat and mass balance for the Peirce-Smith converters. Activities performed at the plant, leading to marked improvements in the converter aisle performance and slag quality are also discussed.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Atlantic Copper facility, a subsidiary of Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold Corp., is a custom smelter and refinery located in Huelva Spain [1]. The plant treats over 1 million tpy of concentrate to produce up to 285 ktpy of copper cathodes and 900 ktpy of sulfuric acid. Figure 1 shows a schematic flow sheet of the smelter and refinery. The smelting of copper concentrates is carried out in an Outokumpu Flash smelter (FSF) produc

ing a matte of 62 wt. % copper and an iron-silica slag, both of which are tapped periodically. The matte is converted to blister copper in conventional Peirce-Smith converters (PSC). The iron-silicate slags from both the FSF and the PSC are cleaned in an electric furnace (EF) before being discarded. The blister copper is fire-refined in a rotary anode furnace (RAF), then cast, with the anodes sent to the copper refinery. Gases are treated in a total of three double absorption acid plants, producing high grade sulphuric acid. 



Figure 1– Huelva Smelter and Refinery general flow-sheet [1] 

During the last 20 years, Atlantic Copper has significantly improved the matte conversion at Huelva [2]. Larger converters and an increase in blowing capacity allowed anode production to be increased from 150 ktpy to 300 ktpy. Gas treatment was improved with upgrading of the primary hoods; installation of a new system for scrap addition and enlargement of the electrostatic precipitators were also carried out. Recently, a better SO2 capture was achieved by installing secondary hoods combined with a dry Ca(OH)2 scrubbing system. These improvements were accompanied by training programs for operators, resulting in higher production along with superior environmental performance.

### **METSIM model for a PSC cycle: approach and assumptions** 

A heat and mass balance model, in steady state, was developed to simulate a typical (average) PSC cycle at Huelva, using METSIM<sup>TM</sup> software. Figure 3 shows a general outline of the model adopted. The converting cycle was divided into three main steps (three blows), each blow represented by an operational unit with specific chemistry, including a portion of the total heat losses for one converter. The formation of reverts was modeled with cooling units, solidifying a portion of the slag and matte from slag blows, and copper from the copper blow. Flow rate and feedback controllers were used to control operational variables (e.g. blowing rate, oxygen flow, silica flux addition, etc.), according to specific parameters (e.g. Fe% in white metal, oxygen enrichment, Fe/SiO2 in slag, etc.), also to adjust the extent of the chemical reactions, in this way obtaining the required stream composition and temperature. 

In order to develop a robust model that correctly mirrored the different stages of the average daily converter cycle in a given PSC vessel, information including tonnages, chemical composition of gas, matte, flux, reverts; scrap, anode copper, and recycled slags were reviewed. Any gaps in data were developed by appropriate thermodynamic computations, and/or based on the authors’ experience. The following assumptions were made: 

_Proceedin

gs of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 168 - A fixed amount of matte (average tonnes/cycle) was added to the converter in the 1st and 2nd blow. - The FSF matte was composed of molten FeS-Cu2S with about 2% Fe3O4 content. - The total air flow (Nm3 /cycle) injected in the 1st blow and the 2nd slag blow was controlled by a set point related to the percentage of Fe in the end matte/white metal, and this can be optimised. - The total air flow (Nm3 /cycle) in the copper blow was controlled by a set point related to the oxygen content in the blister copper, and this can be optimised. - The reference oxygen enrichment in the 1st and 2nd blow was set to 22.8%O2. - Fixed oxygen efficiency was adopted in the PSC cycle, it was assumed to be 90% to match plant oxygen consumption data. - The amount of silica flux in each blow was adjusted to obtain a set Fe/SiO2 ratio. - A fixed amount of molten slag from RAF was added in each blow for a given simulation. - A fixed amount of slag left in the vessel (remaining slag) after skimming slag from each blow. - A fixed proportion of each molten stream (slag, white metal, and copper) were solidified and assumed to form solid reverts. The proportions of these materials were adjusted to match the annual composition and amount of internal reverts. - A fixed amount of reverts, scrap, and spent anodes were added to each blow to adjust temperature of the liquid phases and to ensure that all reverts would be re-melted in the converter aisle. - The copper solubility in slag from the slag blow was expressed as a function of the iron level in matte, based on thermodynamic data and the authors’ experience. - The copper solubility (as Cu2O) in slag from the copper blow was considered as a fixed value based on the authors’ experience. - The amount of entrained matte in the slag for each blow was adjusted to fit the total copper and sulfur reported in actual PSC slag samples at Huelva. - A fixed amount of solid magnetite, according to PSC slag assays (by SatmaganTM ), in reasonable agreement with calculated values at an average nominal temperature and Fe/SiO2 ratio. - A fixed heat loss per cycle was assumed, distributed between the three blows. ag”, essentially one with a reasonable fraction of solid magnetite in the liquid slag from 1<sup>st</sup> and 2<sup>nd</sup> slag blows. This improvement was considered in Case 1 (Tables 2 and 3). Silica flux addition was then adjusted according to the following set-points: A Fe/SiO2 ratio of 2.1 in slag of the first blow; a Fe/SiO2 ratio of 1.7 in slag for the second blow and a Fe/SiO2 ratio of 1.9 in slag of the copper blow. The blowing rate was kept at the same value as in the base case. 

As a result, the flux addition decreased by 1 tonne in the 1st blow and increased by 1.6 tonnes in the second blow and decreased by 0.3 ton in the copper blow. Globally the flux consumption and the heat balance were not significantly impacted, but overall, slag quality should be better due to lower magnetite and copper contents in the slag. It was also expected to decrease revert generation. This was not observed in the model, since the fraction of slag and matte remaining in ladles and spills was kept constant. However, this could be verified with quantitative measurement of reverts generation at the plant. 

At Huelva smelter, the control of the silica flux addition was improved to operate close to the suggested Fe/SiO2 in PSC slags, with bath temperatures in the range of 1230  C to 1250  C. A weekly adjustment of silica flux per converter was implemented in 2012 in order to achieve a Fe/SiO2 of 2 in the 1<sup>st</sup> blow and 1.8 in the 2<sup>nd</sup> blow. As a result of this control of the Fe/SiO2 along with the change on flux material, lower magnetite content was observed in the mixed slags (See Table 4, data of 2012). Converter cycles are currently operating with variations in the range of 1.5 to 2.5, which can be considered as quite acceptable. 

### **Air blowing rate control in slag blows –Iron level in white metal** 

The air blowing rate in the slag blows is usually adjusted according to a set point of iron content in white metal. As result, the bath temperature is almost fixed, for a given composition of feed and cold material addition. A proper iron set point is key to produce acceptable quality slag during the matte conversion. 

An optimization of this parameter was considered in Case 2 (Tables 2 and 3). The %Fe in matte at the end of the first blow was raised from 4% to 4.5% and the %Fe level at the end of the second blow was raised from 0.8 to 1.5%. Consequently, the blowing time for the slag blows was reduced by 15 minutes and the copper blow increased by 10 minutes. A beneficial drop by 1% content of the soluble copper in slag from the second slag blow was noted (it is noted that the copper solubility data here was developed by the model and plant validation would be required). The temperature slightly decreased due a slightly lower blowing rate.

### **Amount of slag left in the vessel prior the copper blow** 

During the copper blow the equilibrium level of Cu2O in slag is nearly

50 wt%. Under these conditions, a tonne of slag left in the vessel can be assumed to form one additional tonne of Cu2O. Proper slag skimming is very important to avoid excessive slag formation during the copper blowing, which in turn increases the recirculation of material to the first slag blow. In Case 3, the slag left in the converter was reduced from 10 tons (in the base case) to 5 tons. As a result, the slag produced in the copper blow dropped by 50% and the slag returned to the slag blows was reduced by the same proportion. This allowed for processing of more solid reverts from the converter aisle. The resultant blowing time and natural gas consumption also decreased in the copper blow (no use of natural gas in the copper blow). Reverts to be re-melted in the EF and the FSF were also reduced by 50%. This case underlines the importance of a good skimming prior to the copper blow. ### **Air blowing rate control in the copper blow - Copper end point** The blister copper from Peirce-Smith converting commonly contains between 100 to 300 ppm of sulfur and 1,000 to 8,000 ppm Oxygen [7]. The actual blister end point at Huelva is nearly 7,000 ppm oxygen and 120 ppm sulfur and this leads to a high fraction of copper oxide in the slag (50-60% Cu content). This is good however for minor element control in the blister copper. It also allows the copper to arrive in the anode furnace with a suitably low sulphur level for casting, especially when there is a tight schedule with the anode furnaces. The close relationship observed between sulphur and copper content in the blister copper as developed in laboratory experiments [7-8] is shown in Figure 8. ### **Benefit of combined improvements and increasing capacity** 

A METSIM simulation-Case 5 was performed with the objective to maximize the benefit of improving fluxing in the slag blows and optimizing slag generation from the copper blow.  As result, the copper blowing time decreased and the copper oxide slag recirculation was reduced by 10 tonnes per cycle (20 ktpy). The above conditions allow decreasing the copper content in the slag that is to be treated in the electric furnace, hence increasing the overall plant metal recovery.

The feasibility of increasing the matte conversion capacity was also studied in Case 6, which also includes all the improvements from Case 5. Matte addition changed from a 4-2 cycle to a 5-2 cycle, leading to 30 tonnes of additional matte processed per cycle. The annual copper production was kept constant, but with fewer cycles per converter, hence the heat losses during a cycle were raised proportionally to the matte throughput. As result, the copper blowing time increased, but with less consumption of fossil fuel compared to Case 5. The amount of copper slag was kept low while copper production increased, while the consumption of air and oxygen increased in slag blows. The amount of reverts to be processed in FSF and EF decreased by about 50% which is a benefit (could allow a higher concentrate throughput – but this was not studied). 

### **Blowing performance and tuyere submergence** 

In this section, we present some comments regarding to the operation of the converter aisle at the Huelva smelter. 

The four converters at Huelva are sized nominally 4 m in diameter by 10 m in length, with normally 50 tuyeres in use. Typical blowing rates were 36,000 Nm<sup>3</sup> /hr (720 Nm<sup>3</sup> /hr/tuyere) for the slag blow and 39,000 Nm<sup>3</sup> /hr (780 Nm<sup>3</sup> /hr/tuyere) for the copper blow. A benchmarking review showed that the above blowing rates while good were slightly below the average value for the particular converter size [11]. The average volumetric ratio calculated as the vessel blowing rate (Nm<sup>3</sup> /hr) per internal vessel volume as m<sup>3</sup> was 468 hr<sup>-1</sup> , compared to benchmark values of 510 hr<sup>-1</sup> to 550 hr<sup>-1</sup> . 

It was thought that the use of a slightly larger punch bar head coupled with improved magnetite levels in converter slag anticipated as a result of the study would help blowing rates somewhat. The tuyuere submergence at Huelva, while slightly shallower (by an average of 57 mm) than that for example for the converter benchmark value at the former Gaspe converters was considered acceptable. 

### **Plant optimization activities** 

A number of recommendations from this study were developed, including, the use of a sligh

tly coarser silica flux to increase efficiency in fluxing (i.e. fewer fine particles can be entrained and carried out with the off gas (refer also Guo et al. [9]) during slag blows, and increasing the iron level in white metal (2nd slag blow end point), the experience at Huelva is described as follow. ### Use of a coarser silica flux in the converters A first attempt of changing the flux material was performed in the months of January and February, 2012. The silica sand (2-5mm) used as flux in the PSC converters was replaced by somewhat coarser silica (4-20mm) from a local provider. During this period, it was observed the Fe3O4 levels in slags dropped from 30% to about 23.5%. The Cu content however, did not decrease in this period. A decrease in reverts production _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 179 from 0.25 to 0.18 ton reverts/ton of treated matte was found. This test showed the priority of reduction of Fe3O4 to help reduce revert production. The feeding of the somewhat coarse silica flux material was found to be problematic in the existing feed system, due the slightly higher moisture content of the material, causing frequent blockage in the feed conveyor. A number of mixtures of coarse silica flux (somewhat wet) and silica sand (dry) were also tested. In 2013, it was decided to return to the former flux material. The %Fe3O4 content then increased from 23 to 26%, which is still acceptable. It is noted that weekly adjustment in the Fe/SiO2 was maintained at the same time, but more variation in daily cycles was observed when using the course silica flux. The smelter is planning another trial using coarser 4-10 mm silica flux at the end of the current year. ### Decreasing the Iron level in white metal- 2nd slag blow end point control The Fe in white metal from the 2nd slag blow was increased from 1 -1.5%, since November, 2012. A calibration of the Semtech equipment was required to obtain this level of accuracy, by adjustment of the graphs PbS-PbO to the new set-point. The calibration was made directly on the PI Active-view graphs, without changing the raw signal from Semtech OPC. The adjustment of blowing conditions according to this point, showed a good impact on the copper content in PSC slag, presumably due the reduced matte entrained with better slag quality. Figure 7 shows this tendency in monthly samples from slag blows. ### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A full mapping of the PSC converter slag chemistry was performed by using Factsage thermodynamic package and supported by analysis of plant data.  The impact of the iron to silica ratio and the iron level in the white metal on the converter slag was studied with the aim of defining optimal converter conditions for the slag blows. A strategy for fluxing was suggested to avoid excessive solid magnetite formation, which is usually related to an increase in the copper content in the slag and can impact negatively the slag cleaning process (electric furnace). 

A simple METSIM model (blow by blow, state steady) was built to represent the average operational conditions of the PSC converter at the Huelva smelter. Different case scenarios were considered to improve the matte conversion. The results showed that a few minor changes could lead to significant improvements, especially as regards to reducing the slag produced from the copper blow. The cycle modeling approach allows for comparison of the operation for any converter and on any shift; helping supervisors and operators in the evaluation of their own practice and t

esting of alternatives they deem to be promising, prior to plant trials. 

This study clearly indicates that controlling silica flux additions (and also flux granulometry) and the specific blowing rate is critical to maintain a good slag quality during matte conversion. The flux rate and the air (O2) blown per tonne of matte can be controlled to achieve a certain ratio, specific to an individual blow. This is important to avoiding over-oxidizing or under-fluxing the slag, while maintaining a reasonable solid fraction (to help protect the refractory). Once the iron level in white metal has been chosen, the amount of air required is defined by the mass balance (e.g. using the METSIM-cycle model). The silica flux is adjusted according to an optimal Fe/SiO2 ratio (as shown for example in Figures 3 and 4). The oxidation condition of converter slag can 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

182 

be evaluated using information on magnetite levels in actual converter samples for a given range of conditions (e.g. Fe/SiO2, bath temperature, etc.). 

One of the parameters also having an important impact on reducing the slag produced from the converter aisle is the slag skimming procedure. The better quality of slag from 2<sup>nd</sup> slag blow, and the cleaner the skimming of that slag, the less slag is then finally produced in the copper blow and recirculated back to the process; also less variability is expected in the converter slag amount and composition. Another good practice, not simulated in this study, is to skim the slag before the end of the copper blow (i.e. when 2/3 of the blowing is completed). This practice would allow producing most of the slag from this blow at 15-20% Cu rather than a slag a 50% copper. 

Further improvement of the current METSIM model would be considered in future simulations. As example, the magnetite solubility in the slag should be set as function of Fe in matte, Fe/SiO2 in slag and the temperature. In the present study, the magnetite content in slags was adjusted manually, in each case, based on plant data and from the authors’ experience. Oxygen efficiency determination at the plant, to validate the model assumptions and also the calculation of heat losses as function of temperature could be considered. All these improvements would allow better predictive capabilities of the PSC cycle model developed in this study. 

The main author (Nubia Cardona) and her colleagues in Canada invite collaboration from other smelters to experiment with and further improve the model concept developed in this study. This type of model can be used, online or off-line, as an expert system to advice operators regarding to the impact of process control changes on the converter operation, increasing the general understanding of the converter aisle dynamics.

### **ABSTRACT** 

During the last 25 years sustainability has become one of the major issues in our growing society. The fast development of the emerging countries and the still high level of consumption in the industrialized states require the further development of existing production processes. The future challenge for the copper industry is to treat more complex ores on the one hand and to increase the yield by reducing the copper losses and to keep the iron-silicate by-product marketable on the other hand. 

By applying a magnetic field crossing a DC field to a slag, stirring is improved and the settling of entrained copper droplets is thereby fostered. Based on this theoretical background and on the results of an intensive parameter study by CFD simulation, the results were subsequently verified in a 2-4 t/h pilot plant. During 10 test trials, each lasting one week in the pilot plant, the aim was to generate reliable results for an approximation of the economic feasibility of the new process. The results confirmed that a significant reduction of the Cu content in the iron-silicate-product obtained is feasible 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

186 

and economically interesting, depending on the incoming copper-slag content. Hence, the basics for the design of an industrial furnace were determined. 

### **INTRODUCTION AND TECHNICAL PRINCIPLE** 

Copper mining is a very complex process. In most cases the copper content in the ore is low, and there are only a few mines which extract copper ore, compared to the huge number of iron ore mines. But the required purity of the product is very high. The classic copper production arose from these marginal conditions. Processing the ore concentrate causes an increase in the copper content in the melt able raw materials. The flash smelter and the converter provide the starting product for electrolysis. This process delivers large quantities of slag. To clean these slags and to still take advantage of their copper content, the familiar technology of around 30 to 40 years ago was supplemented by submerged arc furnaces acting as slag cleaning furnaces and, which act as settling furnaces and perform partial rest reduction. Using this technique, copper levels in the end slag from approximately 0.8 - 1% can be achieved, depending on the input slag; sporadically also achieving values of up to 0.7%. The latter value relates mainly to rectangular furnaces, which became popular (again) in the last 10 years thanks to the initiative of SMS Siemag. Especially at high mass flows, the rectangular furnaces  offer fluid dynamic advantages as well as thermal benefits. Nevertheless, the residual copper content of slag still appears to be high; too high when one considers that ore containing significantly lower copper content is worthy of selling. [2] 

Two issues arise from the above: Firstly a lower final copper content in the slag means a reduction in the use of raw materials, i.e. resour

ce-efficiency and therefore secondly a lower specific production costs for copper, since larger amounts from the ore can be used. Resource efficiency is increasingly gaining importance in social politics. Among metals, which are of great importance in the field of power transmission and electronics, copper is by mass the most used and it is important to ensure careful use of the raw materials. So the stocks, being finite, last long enough for future generations and commodity prices remain moderate and the demand from many areas of industry can be covered. 

To answer these questions of our decade, SMS Siemag has developed a new type of furnace, which will be arranged behind SAF and will ensure a significant reduction of the final copper content in the slag. Proven, state-of-the-art SAF technology is combined with a known technical principle which nevertheless has not previously been used in furnace technology: the three-finger-rule. A wide magnetic field active in the slag crosses a DC field at right angles and ultimately exercises a stirring force on the metal particles contained in the slag. 

The background is that the given process conditions only allow copper particles to settle if they are above a certain minimum size. As a result, the smaller copper sulfide droplets included in the iron-silicate product (the real constituent of the slag) remain 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

187 

suspended, which means that the economic use of the valuable metal content becomes impeded or restrained. In the well-known slag cleaning furnace some retention times for removal of the copper particles are ensured, but after a certain amount of time the particles cease to grow and therefore only minimal further settling takes place. In addition a large residence time means fewer throughputs or a larger furnace sizing requirement, which in turn causes the danger of cold zones and frozen slag. 

How can the copper droplets therefore be enlarged to improve their settling behavior? A 2006 patent from SMS Siemag together with Professor Andrej Warczok, professor at the University of Santiago de Chile at the time, indicated a new way by stirring the slag to promote the coagulation of the small copper droplets into larger ones. The new process combination intends to separate the remaining metal phase from the slag. This combination envisages that a stirring reactor with induced magnetic, activated “washing” (stirring) will be installed downstream of the already established submerged arc furnace. [3] 



Figure 1 - Patent drawing SMS Siemag [1] 

Physically, the Lorenz force is used. This works on metal particles if they are in a DC electric field which is crossed at right angles by a magnetic field. The copper particles are put into a rotary motion, which leads to impact and agglomeration of the particles due to different velocities, whereby the particles can settle after acquiring greater mass.. Together the stirring and the cleaning actions generate

the nickname of “the washing machine”. These physical processes briefly described here require a new furnace technology, moving away from an AC - SAF to a DC - SAF, of which the shell is enclosed by an electromagnet with a force that permeates the bath width as well as the lining, necessitating that at least in the lining area the shell has to be  made from a nonmagnetizable stainless steel.

### **TECHNOLOGY BENEFITS - IMPROVEMENTS** 

As per usual pilot plant operations, the time between the test campaigns was used for adjustments, modifications or extensions. Some of these improvements will in future also be incorporated  into industrial scale stirring reactors. 

The pilot furnace was designed with two electrodes and a ground electrode. This concept was chosen because the reactor was comparatively long and required even slag heating.. The trials started with a 1:1 energy input, i.e. 50% via electrode 1 and 50% via electrode 2. But after a short time it could be observed that especially during times of constant operation and regular charging, a lower energy input via the rear electrode was sufficient and also caused higher depletion of copper from this mode. In addition the slag resistances  achieved were lower and the electrode currents were higher than simulated at 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

195 

project start for this new process, the electrical system was soon modified  to enable a total energy input via only one electrode, electrode 1 at the inlet. After this change to the electrical system, the process could be adapted better to the requirements of the operation. 

Therefore, industrial facilities will be equipped with two electrodes plus a ground electrode, but the majority of the energy input will take place via a single electrode. Nevertheless, a higher proportion of the energy input via the second electrode will be possible and appropriate during extended periods when heat is required to prevent incrustations in the case of less favorable movement and low heat transfers. 

As seen on some pictures and illustrations of the pilot plant, the Hamburg plant was constructed with a special type of the bottom electrode. From a carbon block in the furnace hearth, a graphite electrode was positioned through the side wall lining parallel to the upper electrodes upwards and connected in that position to the power supply via a contact clamp. This was a simple and space-saving solution for industrial operation, the classical type of bottom electrode will be chosen, so that oxidation effects at the top of the electrode will be avoided. These were namely to be observed during the trials. Among other things by reinforcing the cooling in the area of the contact jaws, these oxidation effects could be minimized, but just not quite be prevented. 

While the examples mentioned above describe mechanical and electrical parts, there were also changes made to the furnace control. This was crucial to the process system. In particular, the challenge was to obtain a constant tapping temperature, independent of changing charging rates and different temperatures of the incoming slag. Alt

hough manual measurement of slag temperatures using a pyrometer and a measuring lance system was envisaged and executed from the beginning, the data from these were only presented as “snapshots”, even when the measurements were made frequently. 

However, continuous temperature measurement of the incoming and outgoing slag by means of new high-temperature cameras, data transmission in the control system of the pilot plant, an integrated calculation program for the prediction of energy consumption and transmission of the mass of the full bucket of slag then enabled the pilot plant to become partially automated as per a "Level 2" automation through a combination of all elements. This type of heater control and automation will satisfy the requirements even at an industrial plant for efficient, energy-saving and resource-saving operation. It is not only for a pilot plant that this integrated system has been used to set standards.

### **SUSTAINABILITY AND ECONOMIC** 

The stirring reactor as a new unit in the copper production line  enables new dimensions of  industrial improvements obtainable with  iron silicate products.. With the copper content in the by-product slag reduced  by 30-50%, depending the starting raw materials, the raw material copper is better exploited. Furthermore, additional ironsilicate by-products, which are unwanted for re-use  are  significantly reduced.. This has both ecological and economic benefits. 

In order to evaluate the resource efficiency potential, an assessment of eligible types and masses of slag is of great importance. To perform this assessment, many parameters must be considered. These include: 

- Amount of fayalite slag currently produced in the primary and secondary copper industry in Europe. 

- Average copper content of these products. 

- Potential of use of old copper slags, which are currently located in landfill sites. 

- Transferability to other slag systems in relevant quantities in the copper industry (such as converter slags). 

- Investigation of the chemical bond in which the copper is present. 

The above list can be extended and demonstrates the potential of the entire project whilst recognizing the quantification difficulties  of the resource potential. To perform an initial assessment regarding resource efficiency, the following assumptions were made: 

- Annual amount of comparable fayalite slag e.g. in Europe: 3.5 million t. 

- Depletion of Cu content by 0.35 mass % through the described process optimization. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

197 

- Additional amount of 12,250 t copper per year (This is a result and not an assumption). 

This amount of copper is available to the world community as an extra usable resource. The corresponding ores must neither be mined, nor be transport

ed, nor also be smelted. 

In the conservative scenario described as an example above, the potential of this development becomes clear. It should be noted that the previous copper content in the iron-silicate slag, was considered to be irrevocably lost and, in terms of the conservation of resources and steadily falling concentrate quality, it also makes a contribution to the conservation of primary resources. In most cases the copper content in the ore is low, there are only a few mines which extract copper ore compared to the huge number of iron ore mines. But the required purity of the product is very high. To assess the financial potential, the currently traded copper price of € 5,545 per ton of copper (as at 07.06.2013) was multiplied by the amount of copper recovered. An annual copper value of approximately € 67 million can be therefore be attributed per year to the balance of the copper producers.. 

The economic calculations were based on a very conservative improvement of 0.35% mass % reduction of contained copper in iron-silicate slag and highlights the fact that even higher benefits could possibly be obtained with the installation of a stirring reactor. 

An economic factor not to be underestimated is the improvement of the ironsilicate product quality due to the higher purity. Besides copper, also other components are reduced, so that in many cases a better re-use option will become possible, not least because a much more uniform product quality is achieved. Thus, a potentially required re-use of cooled-down slag in the production process of melting is avoided, which not only saves energy costs but also frees up capacities for the production of copper. 

It is worth mentioning in this context that this technique on a laboratory scale has already been applied to other chemically similar slags (Pb, Ni, PGM slag systems) and that there is also great potential  for resource conservation.[6] 

### **SUMMARY** 

SMS Siemag has developed a new technology for the super–cleaning of metallurgical slags, especially copper slags. This stirring reactor system was installed in cooperation with Aurubis, Hamburg, at their copper plant and tested successfully. During ten test campaigns many correlations, conditions and parameters were tested and fully integrated into the industrial process. It was proven that the magnetically induced stirring improves the quality of the iron-silicate product by reducing the copper content in the final slag by 30 - 50%.

### **PROCESS DESCRIPTION AND MAIN FACILITIES** 

Process was described elsewhere<sup>(1)</sup> . But for emphasis of the characteristics of the processes the new smelter and refinery employs, more description is given here. Concentrates from domestic and overseas market are transported by ship or truck to the concentrate storage in the smelter. Concentrates, flux and recycling are reclaimed by grab cranes and belt-conveyed to the 18 blending bins. Concentrate mixture is dried by two steam dryers, to moisture below 0.3%. The dry charge is dense-phase conveyed to the dry-charge bin above the FSF. It is fed to the FSF through a single concentrate burner with its feed rate controlled by two loss-in-weight (LIW) feeders. Between the LIW feeders and the concentrate burner, there are 3 air-slide feeders which convey the feed to the concentrate burner. 

Dry charge is distributed into the high-temperature reaction shaft (RS) space, reacting rapidly with oxygen, producing high-grade matte of 68% to 70% copper, slag and SO2 gas. Matte and slag is collected in the settler and separate into separate layers. Matte is tapped and water granulated. Slag is tapped into ladle and sent to slow-cooling area, and then to the concentrator for flotation, producing slag concentrate and tailings. Slag concentrate is recycled to the FSF while the tailings are for sale. Gas carrying dust flows into gas line, cooled and cleaned in the waste heat boiler and hot ESP. Dust collected is conveyed by dense-phase conveyors to the dust bin above the FSF, fed to the RS with concentrate mixture. 

The granulated matte is reclaimed from the granulation pit by bucket elevators. It is then belt-conveyed to the dome storage.

A stacker-reclaimer in the storage which stacks matte from the FSF and reclaims it to the matte mill, ground and dried. Ground matte is then transported to the matte bin above the FCF, from where it is charged to a LIW feeder and fed to matte burner through an air-slide feeder. Blister, lime-base slag and SO2 gas with dust are produced in the RS and the settler. Slag, containing 20% copper is tapped and water-granulated, and then recycled to the FSF. Blister is tapped and flows into the anode furnace through launders. Gas flows through the waste heat boiler and hot ESP, cooled and cleaned. Gases from FSF, FCF combine and flow into gas cleaning section in the acid plant for acid production. SO2 strength in the combined gases could be over 30%. SO2 strength designed for the convertor could be as high as 18%. Blister is refined in two anode furnaces. Anode scrap from the tankhouse is remelted by a shaft furnace and casted into anode. Anode is sent to the refinery. “Taco” permanent cathode process is employed for the tankhouse. ### **PROCESS PROBLEMS ENCOUNTERED WITH FCF** 

FCF feed are high-grade matte, recycled dust and burnt lime. FCF products are lime-based slag, blister, dust and strong SO2 gas. Matte composition is much simpler and stabler than concentrates. So FCF operational control should be easier than FSF. However, lime-based slag is very aggressive to the brick-lining, and its solubility to Fe3O4 is much higher than silicate slag and it is hard to form accretion on the brick-ling surface of the settler, brick-lining wear is a big problem. Liquid blister is much penetrating and it is hard to get furnace integrated. It is very dangerous for liquid blister to contact copper element since it is very corrosive to copper element. So liquid blister is much more difficult to handle than matte. Generally, dust generation and off-gas SO2 strength from FCF are higher than FSF, and off-gas is more difficult to handle. Since start-up of FCF, we have encountered some problems with flash converting process, most of the problems are related with insufficient experience in the process. The problems encountered include: 

### **Metallurgical Chemistry of FCF:** 

One of the key parameters in control of FCF slag metallurgy is to control the silica content in FSF matte. If the silica level in FSF matte is greater than 1%, the silica level in FCF slag will increase to more than 5%. At this point, the slag viscosity significantly increases and results in tapping difficulties. Because of bad matte tapping practice and not good FSF process control, matte contamination of slag happened from time to time. To make matters worse, not much attention was taken to this practice. So silica content in matte to FCF is frequently over 0.8%. On end of May, the situation was worse. Matte silica content was as high as close to 2% and silica in slag was close to 7%. Slag tapping became extremely difficult. 

Fe3O4 content in slag could indicate reaction extent in the furnace. At high Fe3O4 content, it can be decided that reaction is no

t well completed. As information from Kennecott(2) , Fe3O4 in slag is normally between 20%~30%. In our operation, Fe3O4 in slag is normally over 30%. In May, Fe3O4 average content in slag is 37.5%，with 50.4% the highest. High Fe3O4 in slag brings about heavy build-up at blister taphole on the sidewall, which hinders blister tapping. Slag tapping also becomes difficult at high Fe3O4. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 209 In Kennecott(2) , at 20% copper in slag, S in blister is at 0.2%. But in our operation, in May when copper average content in slag is at 20.6%, sulphur in blister is at 0.08% in average, lower than that in Kennecott. ### **Impurities in anode:** Since FCF employs high oxygen-enrichment in process air and reaction time is as short as a tenth of second, it is expected that FCF capability in impurity removal is not as good as PS converting. The variations of As, Sb, Bi, Pb in anode are shown in figure 4. It is seen that, As, Sb and Pb content in anode is stable and in low level. ### **Furnace Refractory Wear:** 

FCF slag is of calcium ferrite containing Cu2O, Fe3O4, CaO. After start up on January 18, we found the side walls and end wall under the RS eroded very fast and seriously. In order to control refractory wearing on this area, we took some actions to control slag chemistry, i.e. increase SiO2 and Fe3O4 content, and decrease Cu and CaO content. And we changed the matte burner control parameters, increasing process air velocity while decreasing distribution air flow. But it seems we didn’t success in controlling refractory erosion on this area. On May 17 when we shut down the FCF for maintenance, we were astonished to find there was no refractory at all on some area of the walls. The wall vertical elements contact the melt directly without refractory. Very thin layer of slag accretion exist on the element surface. Since then, we have taken water temperature from the elements on this area under close monitoring. 

### **Anode furnace operation:** 

In PS converting, blister is discharged from PS converter to ladle and transported by crane to anode furnace. Slag contamination of blister could be controlled 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

211 

to a very low level by controllable blister skimming from the PS converter and by controllable charging from the ladle to the anode furnace. With ladle transportation by crane, it is very flexible for anode furnace to skim slag. However, in FCF process blister is charged to anode furnace by launder. When the FCF metallurgy is in disorder, it is very hard, or even impossible to control slag contamination of blister tapped. Sometime slag has to be tapped so as to get the taphole on flowing. Converting slag contains high level of magnetite. In anode furnace，magnetite will separate from the melt and adhere to the bottom and wall of the furnace, growing up as buildup and shrinking the size of the hearth. Slag floats on the surface of the blister hearth, insulating heat transfer to blister underneath and interrupting heating of the blister liquid. Unlike PS converting, there aren’t cranes for ladle transporting. It is not possible to skim slag to ladle and transport it by crane. So in FCF process slag skimming from anode furnace is very difficult. We are now getting some troubles with slag in anode furnace and are trying to find solutions to skim slag. 

In FCF process, anode scrap from the tankhouse is remelted by shaft furnace. But it is not possible to remelt the shell from anode casting launders and ladles by shaft furnace. In our practice, we cut the shell and charge it to the anode furnace. But it is hard to keep the balance.

ONS** 

As our budget for this year, we shut down the FSF and FCF for 10-days maintenance after a half year of operation so as to solve the problems with design and equipment. The FSF stopped feeding on May 10 and the shutdown lasted for 10 days. Since the FCF had already shutdown for 15 days in March by the blister taphole failure, we kept the FCF in operation till May 17 and the FCF maintenance outage lasted for 7 days. Outotec’s Integrated, Lifecycle Solution to Furnace Rebuild Projects is designed to provide smelters with reliable furnace rebuild project solutions and asset program lifecycle services. mance of the furnace over the smelter lifecycle. 

The Integrated, Lifecycle Solution to Furnace Rebuild Projects offers clients a number of benefits both at the project level and the asset management level, ultimately with the goal of enhancing the return on investment that copper smelters extract from their rebuild projects and from the furnace asset itself over the lifecycle of the furnace.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Furnace rebuilds are critical projects that typically occur several times over the lifecycle of a smelter.  The scopes of work will vary over the furnace lifecycle, from minor repairs to complete rebuilds.  Typically, these rebuilds are treated as discrete, independent projects and commonly follow the EPCM (Engineering, Procurement and Construction Management) model for execution.  Although this traditionally has been the execution approach of choice, our view is that it does not always provide optimal results for the rebuild project or the overall furnace asset lifecycle. 

This paper will present Outotec’s Integrated, Lifecycle Solution to Furnace Rebuild Projects.  It is an approach aimed at improving them on two levels.  First, at the project level, it provides a solution for executing individual furnace rebuilds to improve project results and better achieve the smelter’s objectives for these projects.  Second, at the asset program level, it provides a solution for lifecycle management of a furnace rebuild program, aimed at maintaining continuity between individual rebuild projects and improving the overall performance of the furnace over the smelter lifecycle. 

### **THE SOLUTION CONCEPT** 

### **Concept Overview** 

The concept of an _Integrated, Lifecycle Solution to Furnace Rebuild Projects_ is to take a program view to furnace rebuilds over the lifecycle of the furnace, from initial design of the furnace to the final decommissioning of the asset.  That is, in addition to each rebuild project being planned and executed as a discrete project, the series of rebuilds that a flash furnace will need to undergo during its life are strategically planned to derive maximum value from the furnace asset. 

At the project level, furnace rebuilds are complex projects that require close coordination and attention to detail throughout the project lifecycle, from concept design through to commissioning and start-up, in order to achieve optimal project results.  The brownfield, shutdown nature of furnace rebuilds presents a unique and demanding set of challenges.  In our experience, the sequential nature of the EPCM approach does not provide the proper framework to facilitate the level of coordination, cooperation and detailed planning required to adequately address the construction and shutdown complexity of a furnace rebuild project. 

The basic premise is for one service provider to manage and execute all aspects of the rebuild project cycle, from project scoping and concept design th

rough to construction, commissioning and start-up, taking into account the unique nature of shutdown projects.  It has the internal expertise to assign a single team to manage and execute all of the design, construction/shutdown, commissioning and post-start-up support functions in an integrated fashion aligned with meeting the smelter’s overall business objectives for the furnace rebuild.  Outotec is well positioned to deliver such an

integrated rebuild solution package.  Outotec is recognized for delivering proven furnace technology, including process design, engineering and furnace component supply. Outotec’s Shutdown Services’ team (formerly Auburn) has a proven track-record for delivering furnace rebuild construction solutions through to start-up.  Post start-up, Outotec can support the smelter with its process expertise. 

At the asset program level, the EPCM model is simply not structured to maintain continuity between rebuild projects.  Often, the project teams and project stakeholders change from project to project, especially for furnaces with longer campaign periods. The period between rebuilds is also not addressed in this approach.  The owners/clients do provide some of this continuity, but typically not to the level that can support a lifecycle program approach to the furnace asset.   Outotec’s vertically integrated capabilities at the process, design, construction, operation and maintenance levels allow smelter owners to extract the benefits of a lifecycle approach to the flash furnace asset. Outotec can provide the smelter with ongoing annual audits and program management services to maintain peak performance of the furnace throughout its campaign. ### **Phase 1 - Planning & Engineering** 

The integrated furnace rebuild solution offers several advantages for improved project results during the planning and engineering phase.  Scope development is the first step and includes both a design and construction perspective.  From the design perspective, scope development would address furnace performance improvements, capacity increases and technology upgrades.  From the construction perspective, the scope would be developed to a higher degree of detail than the typical engineering scope. This includes scope as a result of working in a brownfield site, contingency planning for unknown conditions and specific site characteristics.  It also allows for early constructability reviews to identify and mitigate construction interferences. This level of review and scoping provides the basis for detailed construction planning early in the project cycle and reduces the potential for unidentified work.  This minimizes the risk of schedule and cost overruns during the shutdown

. 

As construction planning occurs early during the design phase, design-for-service concepts can be incorporated into the furnace rebuild engineering.  These can be simple design additions, such as improved access points, strategic lifting points and special tools for ease of installation.  Such concepts can lead to safer and faster construction and installation. 

### **Phase 2 - Supply** 

Supply of the furnace components and materials as part of the integrated furnace rebuild solution provides owner/clients single point responsibility for sourcing, expediting, quality assurance and delivery.  Supply coordination from engineering through to construction is typically improved versus the traditional EPCM model. 

With the detailed construction schedule and planning being developed in the early design phases, a “bottom-up”, construction driven scheduling approach can be utilized. This means that planning the engineering and procurement functions are integrated into the master project schedule to help ensure that their deliverables and milestones support a successful construction/shutdown execution. ### **ABSTRACT** 

Algorithms have been implemented at the Altonorte Smelter (Northern Chile), to automatically schedule daily production.  The resulting schedules should respect all of the operational constraints, including maintenance plans and furnace productivity, as well as the availability of converters, off gas handling, fire refining and casting.  The algorithms are classified formally as _greedy_ , following the terminology from computer science.  Scheduling automation is the first step toward advanced optimization techniques.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper smelters commonly apply manual scheduling techniques for their shortterm (daily) operations [1].  All of the start and finishing times are entered into the main computer system, which then transmits the resulting schedule to the control rooms. 

There are two main problems with this approach.  Firstly, the schedules may not be optimal with respect to some particular objective.  Consequently, there is no rigorous way of posing and analyzing alternative objectives, therefore the resulting operational policies are unscientific, as there is only a vague distinction between the various modes of operation. 

Secondly, the scheduling logic is a critical component of process simulation [2], which is used to quantify potential changes in the smelting.  For instance, to evaluate an upgrade of the off gas treatment system, it results very helpful simulate several months of operation, taking into account daily random variations.  To avoid the task of manually scheduling hundreds of simulated days, the scheduling algorithms may be grafted into the simulations. If the scheduling practices are not automated, then it is difficult to justify plant upgrades, as it is not practical to simulate alternative designs of plants on large ranges of time; this favors the status quo, and leads to technological stagnation [3]. 

In December 2012, Altonorte smelter followed the example set by the Chuquicamata smelter [1], to carry on a combinatorial search through a restricted space of schedules. The Altonorte approach is a slight improvement with respect that of Chuquicamata, as it applies the principles of greedy programming [4], so that the search space is a function of the control parameters, for instance, the mode of operation.  This document presents the application of Greedy Programming, related to converting and refining practices at the Altonorte Smelter (Figure 1) to converting and refining practices at the Altonorte Smelter (Figure 1). 

The Altonorte process is comparable to that of other copper smelters [1,5].  Under normal operations, the Noranda Reactor can provide feed exceeding the immediate capacity of the downstream operations.

Subsequently, the converting aisle includes several Peirce-Smith converters, which operate in parallel to produce batches of blister copper.  That means Peirce-Smith Converters (PSC) sets the time for the remaining operations: refining and casting.  PSC is effectively the operational bottleneck of the Altonorte process [6]. 

Greedy programming is a paradigm that generalizes a no delay job/shop scheduling [7]. Job/shop algorithms are readily adapted to various material industries, including steelmaking [8], but they do not describe copper smelting operations. [1]. The steel industry applies the Basic Oxygen Process (BOP), which is similar to the PSC process. However, the BOP process is relatively simple to manage, because the feed chemical composition is essentially constant.  In contrast, PSC process is noted for its

This is a functional strength of PSC process, but it precludes the use of conventional job/shop algorithms [1].  Therefore, the Altonorte approach relies on the more general notions of greedy programming, from which many of the job/shop algorithms are derived.

Aside from the work done at Chuquicamata [1], and at Altonorte (current document), very little has been written about the scheduling of copper smelting operations.  This is especially surprising, considering that the profitability of a smelter is directly affected by its scheduling practice. 

### **PEIRCE-SMITH CONVERTING** 

Converting cycles are performed within individual converters. The cycles at the Altonorte Smelter generally include the following steps: 

- 1) Initial charging of the converter 

- 2) Blowing 

- 3) Charging an additional ladle of matte 

- 4) Blowing 

- 5) Charging an additional ladle of matte 

- 6) Blowing 

- 7) Final skimming and discharging 

Thus, a converting cycle begins and ends with an empty converter.  The Altonorte Smelter has a particularly high matte grade, above 73 % Cu.  Altonorte converting is therefore dominated by the copper-blowing reactions [9], and intermittent skimming is unnecessary. 

Step 1 involves the charging of 4 to 7 ladles of matte, depending on the converter. (The converters are not all the same size).  The duration of a converting cycle is dominated by the blowing action, which spansSteps 2, 4, and 6.  It has been observed at Altonorte that the total blowing time depends on several factors, including the age of the refractory lining; the interior geometry seems to have an impact on the mixing characteristics, hence the oxygen efficiency [3].

### **GREEDY PROGRAMMING OF CONVERTING** 

The Altonorte smelter has implemented a combinatorial search which maximizes the amount of blister production within a 12 period.  The search considers all possible orderings by which the reactoroutput can be distributed into the converters. 

For example, the ordering (2-1-4), implies a repeating sequence that a cycle should be performed in converter 2, followed by converter 1, followed by converter 4, followed by converter 2, etc. filling up the schedule for the given planning period.  More generally, an ordering ( _i_ - _j_ - _k_ ) implies a repeating sequence of the form { _i_ - _j_ - _k_ - _i_ - _j_ - _k_ -…}. There are usually three out of the four converters that are in operation, so that the search evaluates 27 possible orderings (3<sup>3</sup> = 27).  The algorithm remains functional if at least one converter is operational. 

Each distribution ordering corresponds to a schedule which is constructed according to the following fourrestrictions: 

- A) Initial conditions 

- B) Availability the converters 

- C) Availability of the Noranda Reactor 

- D) Availability of the off gas handling system 

Restriction A considers the converting cycles which have begun at the end of previous schedule, and carry over into the current schedule. ### **FUTURE ALGORITHM DEVELOPMENT** 

There have been two major contributions to the automated scheduling of copper smelters.  Firstly, combinatorial searches were developed at Chuquicamata [1], forming a heuristic approach that addresses the discrete aspects of operation schedule.  The second contribution has been presented within this paper, as greedy formulations which begin to address the continuous aspec

ts. 

For complex scheduling problems, such as the ones described in this document, advanced approaches are most often based on branch-and-bound techniques [10].  In general terms, a branch-and-bound searchcan be represented as a traversal along the various branches of a tree, which are connected by nodes.  The branches encapsulate the discrete aspects of the problem, as the nodes encapsulate the continuous aspects. 

The effectiveness of a branch-and-bound technique depends on the notion of pruning.  The algorithm should prioritize the branches that are more likely to provide the optimal result.  Branches that do not have any chance of providing an optimal solution should not be explored at all, i.e. these branches should be pruned.  For instance, the greedy converting algorithm can obtain a lower bound on the maximum production of blister copper; a branch-and-bound algorithm need only explore the branches that may outdo the greedy algorithm.  Thus the greedy approach provides an initial pruning for the branch-and-bound tree. 

Standard methods to develop branch-and-bound procedures include integer programming and constraint programming [10, 11].  These will be hybridized with the greedy algorithms presented in this document, leading to advanced optimization techniques for the scheduling of copper smelting operations.

### **ABSTRACT**

They provide substantial improvements especially in anode refining furnaces, where savings in process time and energy are obtained as well as refractory wear and buildups inside the furnace are minimized. A newly developed system enables purging plugs to be implemented for the first time in both stationary and tilting furnaces. An additional advantage in these vessels, above all other benefits, is the significantly improved melting rate. This innovative and patented gas purging system consists of a purging plug cooling device and slidable, cooled piping system. The novel development compensates for any thermal expansion in the furnace lining and minimizes the risk of undesirable copper infiltration.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The pressure for process optimization in the copper industry is still very high. Energy and time savings are required to increase the productivity of copper production and remain competitive in a challenging economic environment. The application of purging plug systems has demonstrated its advantages in many copper processing units for more than a decade [1–3], principally in anode furnaces and ladles. The main benefits are faster process steps and lower energy consumption due to the introduced nitrogen bubbles [4]. 

One development resulting from productivity improvements is the furnace dimensions have increased significantly in the last years. This has challenged both refractory design and purging system installation. For example, the common configurations are no longer suitable for the huge tilting and stationary furnaces. 

### **THE GAS PURGING SYSTEM** 

In a drum-type anode furnace, the purging plugs are changeable and can be removed from the outside. However, this system is notpossible for a tilting furnace because the plugs must be out of the bath during exchange otherwise liquid metal can run through the opening. In the case of a drum-type anode furnace, it can be rotated until the plugs are almost in a horizontal position and no longer in contact with the metal.However, this procedure is not possible with a tilting furnace, where the plugs remain covered with copper, even at the end of casting when the furnace has been tapped. As a result, extracting the plugs externally would be too dangerous, especially because the work has to be performed overhead. Therefore, only a nonchangeable system w

ith the piping integrated in the lining is possible.The plugs and piping arrangement inside a tilting furnace are shown in Figure 1. The pipes run longitudinallydown the mid section of the furnace bottom towards the end walls and through the steel shell to the outside. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

239 



Figure 1– Tilting furnace with gas purging system 

The main problem with implementing such a gas purging system in a tilting or stationary furnace is the difference between the thermal expansion of the wear lining and the permanent lining, which becomes more and more critical the larger the furnace. The bricks in the wear lining must be very tightly connected to each other to prevent metal penetration in-between the bricks. Therefore, the refractory layout in the furnace is designed to provide significantly higher thermal expansion in the wear lining than in the permanent lining during heat up and operation. Usually the bottom lining moves from centre of the furnace bottom towards the end walls, where the expansion is partially compensated. 

The purging plug and well block are installed in the wear lining whilst the system piping is located below in the permanent lining. Since the plug piping crosses the boundary layer between the wear and permanent lining, high tensions are introduced that can cause damage to the welding or even the pipes. In this case, a nitrogen leak would occur at this spot,subsequently resulting in the plug becoming infiltrated with copper. Therefore, the relative movement of the two lining layers has to be compensatedto prevent pipe damage. The patented solution to this problem is a slidable, air-cooled piping system (Figure 2). 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

240 



Figure 2– Conical purging plug with well block, supporting brick, and gas connections 

The angled pipe connection fromthe plug is insertedinto a protection pipe, which provides an air-tight seal and is affixed in the permanent lining. The space between the protection pipe and the surrounding brickwork is filled with ramming mix.Since the angled pipe from the plug can slide within the larger protection pipe, thiscompensates for any plug movementcaused by thermal expansion. The nitrogen supply is realized with a flexible metal hose. Additionally, the plugbottom is cooled to minimize the risk of copper leakage into the pipe system as a result of metal penetration between the bricks in this area. For this purpose, the purging plug is equipped with a double-layered steel bottom. Compressed air is connected to the plug using a second flexible metal hose and is blown between the two steel plates, cooling the lower plug area and surrounding region. The cooling effect has been visualized in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, as shown in Figure 3. In situations where the piping is long and the cooling air line could overheat, an additional compressed air line is incorporated within the protection pipe to facilitate coo

ling. Due to the overall cooling effect, the temperature underneath the plug falls below a critical value so if metal infiltration occurs, the copper freezes and a molten metal leak is avoided. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

241 





Figure 3– CFD simulation. Air-cooling of the plug bottom, surrounding region, and pipe 

Online thermocouples monitor temperatures at two positions in the system. The first measures the temperature inside the purging plug, which indicates plug wear, whilst the second records the bottom plate temperature, monitoring the air-cooling efficiency. 

### **Plug Exchange** 

The lifetime of purging plugs used for this application is between 18 months and 3 years. In some cases the furnace lining has a longer durability so plug replacement may be necessary. Due to the modular setup it is possible to replace a worn out or blocked plug without renewing a large area of the furnace hearth; only about one square metre has to be removed and rebuilt. Furthermore, the piping remains untouched in the permanent lining. This can be easily executed during periodic repair to the tuyere zone. 

### **FLOW PATTERN SIMULATION** 

Purging plugs have shown numerous positive effects on the anode furnace process [4] including: 

- improvement of the melting rate 

- faster and easier slag skimming 

- more efficient oxidation and reduction 

- prevention of buildups and accretions 

- homogenization of the chemical composition and temperature 

- time and energy savings 

To gain all benefits from installing a gas purging system, an optimal number and positioning of the purging plugs is essential. This optimization is performed with the aid of CFD simulations [5]. The positive effect of gas purging on the melting rate is an inherent result of the metal movement. However, the impact on oxidation and reduction processesrequires more detailed examination. Especially in tilting anode furnaces, with a high number of tuyeres in the sidewall, an interfering effect from the plugs has to be avoided.

In these areas almost no material exchange occurs, the poling effect is very poor, and a very long reduction time is necessary to get these areas to react with the tuyere gas.Therefore, these zones have to be minimized by appropriately positioning the purging plugs and adjusting thegas flow rate.
