### **RESULTS** 

The innovative gas purging system with a cooling device and slidable, cooled piping system has been installed in more than 10 stationary and tilting anode furnaces on 3 continents, and has generatedenergy savings of up to 30 % during smelting. The process time for oxidation and reduction can be shortened by betwe

en 10–18 %and the skimming time can be reduced by approximately half. If the anode furnace is the bottleneck in the production line, these time savings contribute directly to the productivity. In addition, the production rate is increasedbecause the plugs keep the furnace free from buildups so the furnace capacity remains at the maximum level. In contrast, if buildups are allowed to occur, the tonnage per heat can decrease dramatically over the furnace lifetime, depending on the charged material and temperature distribution.

The new cooled, slidable piping technology enables gas purging systems to also be installed in stationary and tilting furnaces. The system can withstand all expansioninduced tensions in the furnace lining andhas proven to be a safe and long lasting solution. It enables all the benefits of inert gas purging in anode furnaces to be realized and is providing process improvements and energy savings in multipleapplications worldwide.

### **DOC (Dilute Oxygen Combustion) Technology** 

Traditional oxy-fuel burners produce very intense high flame temperatures which can potentially cause hot spots leading to concern regarding refractory damage, oxidation (such as in aluminum melting) and volatilization (such as in glass melting). 

Dilute Oxygen Combustion (DOC) developed by Praxair is a low peak flame temperature and low NOx oxy-fuel combustion process using in-furnace recirculation of flue gas. The in-furnace recirculation technique or the aspirating burner demonstrated that the peak flame temperature of oxy-fuel flames could be reduced even below the ones promoted by conventional air-fuel burners (Figure 1). 

DOC technology design is based on deep staging using separate high-velocity fuel and oxygen jets to generate strong in-furnace gas recirculation, producing combustion between the fuel and a highly diluted oxygen and furnace-gas mixture (Figure 2). The rich primary zone stoichiometry produces high luminosity flame for high heat transfer efficiency and the separate secondary oxygen controlled injection provides the flame adjustability. Due to the flame adjustability feature, DOC technology promotes optimized flame coverage and heat transfer. DOC technology meets industry needs for productivity increase, low operating costs with minimal capital expense and low maintenance. 

Figure 3 shows comparative NOx emission measurements conducted by a third party. It is clear that Praxair DOC-JL burner promote the lowest emission amongst commercial oxy-fuel burners. The NOx emission measurements were conducted under controlled conditions (1650<sup>o</sup> C/3000<sup>o</sup> F and 1% O2 wet) for different nitrogen content in the furnace atmosphere. 

Praxair installed DOC technology in over 25 copper anode fire refining type furnace for both refining and scrap melting in Brazil, China and USA. Praxair also installed over 750 units based on DOC technology in other types of industrial melting and heating furnaces such as in glass, frit, steel reheat, soaking pit, ladle pre-heating stations. 

### **Drivers for anode furnace conversion to oxy-firing technology** 

Codelco’s program for energy consumption reduction selected the cooper refining furnace as a potential unit to have the oxy-fuel technology implemented. The main issues identified by Codelco as follows: 

- (a) High energy consumption via fossil fuel; 

- (b) High power consumption with the combustion air supply system (blower); 

- (c)

High noise level in the fire refining area. 

DOC-JL technology was selected due to the uniform flame temperature profile, uniform heat distribution, multiple fuel capability (heavy fuel oil, gaseous fuel and solid fuel) and low maintenance.

### **Anode Furnace Description and DOC System** 

The nominal holding capacity of Codelco’s anode furnace #2 is of 380 t of liquid metal with about 10.5 m internal length and 3.5 m internal diameter (Figure 4). The anode furnace original combustion system was a dual fuel air burner rated at 9 MWHHV (30 MM BtuHHV/h) nominal firing rate. The originally installed air-fuel system operated with oxygen enriched air at 35 % total oxygen content in the oxidant stream. 

Air-fuel burner was removed and a DOC-JL burner rated at 3 MW (10 MM Btu/h) nominal firing rate was installed in the same port at anode furnace #2 in June/2012, as shown in Figure N°4. Vertical orientation of the DOC-JL burner, fuel and oxygen injection velocities and degree of staging were determined to promote uniform heat distribution over the bath. 

Subsequently changes position of the burner, being definitively horizontal orientation, as shown in Figure 5. In this case improves the processing capacity of the furnace and eliminates the use of high alumina refractory block. 

A fully automatic oxy-fuel combustion system was designed and installed for the DOC technology operation. The control system designed for the DOC-JL allows adjustments of fuel to oxygen ratio as well as the degree of staging in such way the oxyfuel system can be operated at the stoichiometric ratio required to each phase throughout the heat. This feature promotes the combustion of partially oxidized gaseous phases coming out of the liquid bath minimizing pollutant emissions. 

The anode furnace #2 is charged with liquid blister. The DOC-JL burner firing rate is maintained steady throughout those phases. Firing rate is adjusted for the oxidizing phase and the stoichiometric ratio lowered to promote slight reducing atmosphere during tapping step. The firing rate, stoichiometric ratio and degree of staging is remotely adjusted from the control room based on the requirement of each step throughout the heat. 

### **DOC-JL System Performance** 

The DOC-JL burner is easy to use for refining furnace operators. 

From energy stand point, the process optimization carried out by Codelco with the same type of charge led to a reduction in specific fuel consumption by 47% from the base line (Figure 6). No impact on the quality of the anodes casted was observed with DOC technology. 

The implementation of the DOC technology also promoted power reduction around 100 kW in the combustion air generation system. 

Flow rates of oxidizing and reducing agents were kept unchanged. 

The noise level was considerably reduced in the area of the furnace #2 where DOC-JL burner was installed. Noise measurements were conducted in the furnace´s #2 a

rea, where furnace #1 (air-fuel combustion system) and furnace #2 (DOC-JL technology) are installed. The first measurement was 107,8 DbA between the furnace #1

M. Gous, B.A. Martinich, J.M. Moreno and P.A. Reyes _ANGLO AMERICAN Chagres Smelter Av. Pedro de Valdivia 291 Santiago, Chile CP 7500524 mia.gous@angloamerican.com_

### **ABSTRACT** 

During the latter part of 2012 and the early months of 2013, the Chagres Copper Smelter has experienced several incidents, varying in intensity, of self-heating of the dried concentrate feed in the flash furnace feed bin.  These events lead to small fires in the feed transport, air circulation and concentrate storage systems and in the worst cases, dust explosion i

ncidents within the dry concentrate feed bin. 

Self-heating is a term that defines spontaneous heating of sulphide concentrates under certain moisture and oxygen conditions.  No external heat source is required.  These types of events are not uncommon to copper smelters, although it was the first series of events of this magnitude experienced at Chagres in more than 50 years of operation. 

An investigation was launched to identify which of the concentrate characteristics had substantially changed to activate the self-heating reaction and special conditions that can promote explosions.  This investigation has allowed the identification of the required remedial actions to ensure safe, continued high performance operation of the smelter. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

254 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Chagres Smelter is located in the town of Catemu, 100km North of Santiago, the Chilean capital. The original foundry installation entered into operation in 1917, undergoing various technical upgrades during the years to modernize and grow capacity and has been operating with an Outokumpu Flash Smelting furnace since 1995. 

Copper concentrates from the El Soldado and Los Tortolas concentrators are blended (Los Tortolas 70-80% : El Soldado 20-30%) and smelted at Chagres. For many years, no self-heating or dust explosion events were experienced during the drying, dry storage, transport or smelting of the concentrates from these supplying mines up till the latter part of 2012 when several incidents, varying in intensity caused not only damage to equipment but also posed a serious safety risk to the operational personnel whilst restricting operating time and smelting rates. (In 2001 a minor event occurred that was associated with the smelting of a 3<sup>rd</sup> Party concentrate.) 

Self-heating of copper concentrates is not a foreign concept to the industry, but due to the non-existence of these types of events at Chagres, the following questions had to be raised in order to return to a safe and optimal operation mode: 

- i) Why do these events occur? ii) What changes had triggered the self-heating events after many years of operation without a single occurrence whilst smelting concentrates from the El Soldado and Los Tortolas concentrators? 

- iii) What remedial actions can be taken to prevent self-heating or associated dust explosions? 

The impact due to the frequency and severity of these self-heating events on the Chagres operation could potentially lead serious harm to personnel, damage to equipment, smelting rate restrictions and potential downtime of up to 250 hours per year if the frequency of events between March and June were maintained. It was therefore imperative to understand and costs effectively eliminate the problem in order to ensure safe and continued operation. 

### **DESCRIPTION AND LOCATION OF THE SELF-HEATING EVENTS** 

The wet concentrates received are blended and dried in one of two steam dryers

### **THE THEORY BEHIND SELF-HEATING OF COPPER CONCENTRATES** 

A short literature study was completed in order to understand the likely factors enhancing the probability of self-heating and dust explosion events of sulphide minerals/copper concentrates.  In summary it was found that: 

- i) Dust explosions are essentially a very rapid combustion of a suspension of fine particles, during which heat is generated at a higher rate than is dissipated to the surroundings. Enright [1] 

- ii) The content of Pyrite (FeS2) or Pyrrhotite (Fe1-xS) increases the risk to have self-heating.  Pyritic ores with sulphur content greater than 18% can support a dust explosion. Enright [1] 

- iii) Other minerals of concern are Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2), Sphalerite (ZnS), Arsenopyrite (FeAsS), Galena (PbS) and Pentlandite ((Fe, Ni)9S8 when contained in high proportions. Enright [1] 

- iv) The surrounding atmosphere contains more than 13% oxygen. Enright [1] 

- v) Reactive sulphide dust is dust that is less than 180 microns in size.  In general, all sulphide dusts of fineness below about 50 microns are flammable and can be ignited by thermal energies. Enright [1] 

- vi) Once the self-heating reaction increases the temperature of the minerals to temperatures higher than 320

°C, the ignition temperature of pyritic ores have been reached and a dust explosion can occur. Enright [1] - vii) The highly exothermic oxidation reactions that lead to self-heating of sulphide concentrates are affected by many factors, including chemical composition, environmental temperature, particle size distribution (surface area), mineral-pore structure, moisture content, storage size, partial pressure of oxygen, oxygen diffusion conditions through the storage etc. Yang et al [3] - viii) Self-heating increases inversely with particle size (increased specific surface area) and the fineness of the pyrite that governs the self-heating effect. ### **Minimum Feed Bin Level** 

The dried concentrate storage bin feeding the flash furnace has a 400t capacity and has been operated in the past without any level restrictions, between 0 and 400t. During the explosion event, the bin only contained 150t of material, leading to the suspicion that if a self-heating event occurs together with a low bin level, the dust containing hot chalcopyrite and pyrite in a large empty volume can explode according to typical dust explosion mechanisms as experienced in various industries, purely because of the dust concentration, fineness and available dust volume.  During the explosion the temperature monitor within the feed bin sharply increased to approximately 350°C confirming the presence of hot material within the near empty bin. 

### **Feed Bin and Transport System Design** 

After the first self-heating events, additional thermocouples were installed to establish the point of origin of the self-heating reactions and therefore the o

rigin of the ignition. It was found that the first indication of increased temperature was at the inlet of the secondary cyclone that classifies the dry concentrate to the feed bin. **CONCLUSIONS FROM EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS/ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFICATION** 

Taking into account the results from the particle size distributions, mineralogical analyses and temperature indications from the additional thermocouples that were installed, the following conclusions were made: 

- The combined effect of the increased presence of chalcopyrite and pyrite in both concentrates together with the presence of these minerals in the fines portion of the concentrate lead to the self-heating of the concentrate. 

- The separation of dried concentrate feed and transport air in the primary and secondary cyclone exacerbates the combined mineralogical and particles size affect as mentioned above due to the high presence of the fines with high pyrite and chalcopyrite compositions in the secondary cyclone. 

- The high-temperature material from the secondary cyclone then enters the feed bin where the presence of dust and oxygen makes for ideal dust explosion circumstances. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

263 

### **PREVENTATIVE ACTIONS** 

Due to the severity of the dust explosion event and the frequency of concentrate self-heating experienced during March and April of 2013, immediate actions had to be taken to firstly ensure safe operation whilst medium to longer term solutions were put in place. The following actions were taken: 

### **Actions taken directly after the events** 

- Confinement of the dried feed storage and transport area, coupled with strict access control 

- Reduced feed bin temperature control settings 

- Installation of additional thermocouples to firstly identify the point of origin of the ignition and to secondly act as an early warning system to indicate renewed self-heating. 

- Implementation of a minimum dried concentrate feed bin level of 200t 

### **Short and Medium Term actions** 

- Installation of pressure release valves to the dried concentrate feed bin to ensure controlled pressure release in the event of a dust explosion 

- Oxygen measurement of the internal dried concentrate feed bin atmosphere 

- Nitrogen purging of the dried feed transport system and increased purging of the dried concentrate feed bin to reduce the oxygen levels to less than 13% 

- Continued monitoring of concentrate particle size distribution and mineralogy. 

### **Long Term actions** 

- Upgrade of the dried concentrate feed transport system to an ultra-dense material feed system, although this will still be coupled with a continuous nitrogen purging system to ensure low oxygen presence.

### **FORTY YEARS OF OPERATION OF THE NORANDA REACTOR PROCESS** 

Yves Prйvost, Marc Bйdard, Charles Levac _Glencore, Horne Smelter 101, avenue Portelance Rouyn-Noranda, Quйbec, Canada yves.prevost@glencore-ca.com_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

The Noranda Continuous Smelting Process at Horne Smelter was commissioned in March 1973.  Since then, it has evolved to follow the trends of feed complexity, material recycling and international competition.  Process control was improved, new auxiliary equipments were tested, and blowing enrichment was increased. 

This paper presents an overview of the main Noranda Reactor improvements that have occurred since its commissioning and the effect they had on the capacity and control of the vessel. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

266 

The Horne smelter is located in Quebec, Canada, on the site of the gold deposit found by Edmund Horne in the 1920’s.  Originally using 2 reverberatory furnaces with multiple hearth roasters and 2 converters, the plant developed over the years.  Mainly based on the smelting of the Horne mine concentrates, the smelter also accepted some local custom feeds from the first years.  When the mine was depleted in 1976, the plant became a 100% custom smelter. 



The developpement of the Noranda Reactor started in 1964 at the Noranda Technology Center, in Pointe-Claire, Quebec, and was tested at the Horne Smelter.  The full scale Noranda Reactor, then named the Noranda Continuous Smelting Process, was commissioned in March 1973.  Its main purpose was then to produce metallic copper from concentrate, a task it performed for 2 full years. 

Driven in a large part by the low capacity of the Reactor to eliminate certain minor elements, the decision was made in 1975 to start producing matte in the reactor instead metallic copper.  It was also expected that the new operation would increase the campaign life of the reactor and decrease the copper content in the slag.  The reactor has operated in this mode ever since. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

267 

### **<u>General description of the process</u>** 



As described in previous papers, the reactor is a 5.2 m diameter by 21.3 m long refractory lined cylindrical vessel.  All solid charge is fed into the vessel using a high speed slinger while oxygen enriched air is blown into the liquid matte using a series of fifty-four submerged tuyeres. 

The relatively high blowing rate (50 000 to 55 000 Nm3/h) produces an excellent mixing of the liquid matte; several tests have demonstrated its homogeneity along the lenght of the vessel.  The effect of this high blowing rate combined with the spreading of the feed by

the slinger allows the feed to be rapidly absorbed and oxydised within the molten bath.  Most of the heat required to melt the feed is generated by the oxydation of the sulfur and iron.  Carbon can be added to improve the reactor capacity to melt inert material, but operation without carbon sources have been achived for days in many occasions without  negative influences over the metallurgy or the slag quality. 

A settling zone of 8.9 m in length between the last tuyere and the slag end of the reactor allows the separation between the matte and the slag.  The slag is tapped from a taphole located in the end plate opposite the feed end, while the matte is tapped from the side of the barrel.  The matte being homogenous, the taphole location was chosen for convenience rather than for metallurgy. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

268 

Horne’s Reactor slag typically contains 3 to 5% Cu.  This slag is sent to a concentrator along with the Noranda Convertor slag where a 38% Cu slag concentrate is produced.  The copper content of the reactor at the Horne plant is considered a acceptable value because the reactor is followed by a concentrator, but it was demonstrated that slag with copper content lower than 1% can be achived for a reactor operating with an electric furnace, by using higher operating temperatures. 

Tests were performed over the years with different matte grades.  Operation was maintained at levels as low as 55% copper in the matte and as high as 75% copper.  The matte grade is actually targeted at 3.5% iron, corresponding generally to 70% copper. 

Even though the reactor is designed to maintain a continuous operation, its cylindrical shape allows it to rotate 47 degrees, thus putting the tuyere line outside the matte and slag level.  Natural gas is then used to maintain the reactor hot until it starts blowing again.Tuyeres and tapping blocs can therefore be repaired without emptying the vessel. 

### **REACTOR FLEXIBILITY** 

One of the main features of the Noranda Reactor is its ability to handle a large range of feeds. 

At the Horne Smelter, the Reactor’s wet charge is fed through a feed port, via a slinger.  No dryer is needed, the slinger being able to handle any material that can be handled by the Reactor’s conveyor and bin system.  Only excessively dry material would have to be conditionned in order to avoid dust at the chute points, and excessively wet material that would flow over the conveyors. 

Material size can also be quite variable at the reactor.  Though the feed would normally be limited to particles smaller than 5 cm in diameter, the slinger regularly receives particles of 10 cm and occasionally as big as 20 cm in diameter.  As long as these particles are mixed with smaller particles, both the slinger and the reactor will easily handle them. 

The reactor was originally built with a pelletizer to feed pellets to the reactor.  It was later found to be useless for the process and was finally removed. 

Be

ing on the custom market, The Horne smelter receives a variety of materials from different sources.  Instead of using a bedding plant to mix all the materials together, the smelter has choosen to use multiple bins to mix the feed material.  Even though it adds to the manipulation of the feed, the series of 7 feed bins used at the Horne smelter allows it the flexibility to change rapidely the feed to optimise the operating window of the vessel. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

269 

Matte samples are taken either from a tuyere or from the matte taphole every hour. Slag samples are taken every hour, during slag tapping.  In both cases, the samples are sent to the plant laboratory via a pneumatic tube, to be analysed by a X-Ray analyser. Assays are available withing 15 minutes.  The operators can then ajust the proportion of the materials, either by modifying the speed of the conveyors below the bins or by changing the bin content.  With a capacity of about 2 hours of feed for each bin, ajustments can be performed several times withing a day. 

In addition to the concentrates, feed materials also include different by-products from other plants.  Some of these materials have the capacity to react together.  This type of reaction caused, in 1993, a hydrogen generation within one of the bins, leading to an explosion.  To avoid such occurences, standard reactivity tests have been developped by the smelter to test the capacity of the materials to be mixed together.  Reactive materials can still be accepted but must be kept separated from the other materials.  Explosimeters were also added to each of the bins and are linked to automated alarms, in the occurrence that an unexpected reaction would occur. 

### **DEVELOPMENTS** 

### **Matte grade** 

The reactor suffered a few short campaigns at the end of the 80’s.  After investigation, it was considered that episodes of copper making in the reactor, often coupled with high operating temperatures, decreased the durability of the brick at the tuyere line. 

An advisory control program was therefore installed in 1990 in order to help the operator control the matte grade.  In a smelter receving such a wide variety of materials and where the minor elements in the matte are sometimes higher than the iron in the matte, it was suggested that the iron would be a better indicator of the degree of oxydation of the matte than the copper.  Iron control in the matte was then implemented. 

The advisory program allowed a decrease of the standard deviation of the iron to less than 1%.  Considering that metallic copper formation would occur at iron levels lower than 1% in the matte, it was calculated that a target of 3.5% iron would essentially eliminate metallic copper episodes in the reactor.  The target has been maintained since then and tuyere brick erosion is no longer the limiting factor for the reactor campaign life. 

### **Oxygen** 

The next phase of control improvement involved the acid and oxyg

en plants. 

The smelter instantaneous capacity is driven by two main limitations: the oxygen availability and the acid plant capacity.  The Horne smelter receives oxygen from 3 different oxygen plants producing a total of 800 TPD of oxygen.  This oxygen is 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

270 

consumed by the Noranda reactor, Noranda Converter and Peirce-Smith converters.  The total oxygen demand from these vessels normally exceeds the oxygen plants capacity. 

The second limit of the smelter is the acid plant capacity.  The acid plant was designed to receive 23500 Nm3/h of SO2.  Depending of the feed, the combined SO2 production of the Noranda reactor and Noranda converter sometimes exceeds this limitation. 

An automated control was therefore implemented in order to continuously reach one of these two limits.  It was decided to let the Peirce-Smith and Noranda converters use whatever oxygen they need, the reactor being the vessel where the remaining available oxygen is used.  Oxygen levels will therefore increase and decrease in the reactor blast air, with the conveyors feed rate following the total blown oxygen.  With the three oxygen plants in operation, the variations are small and have little impact on the reactor stability, but allow an optimal use of the oxygen produced. 

### **Oxygen enrichment** 

The Noranda reactor always had air added at the surface of the bath, via the feed port, to improve combustion in the vessel.  Furthermore, it was determined that the oxygen from this air had the same efficiency in the reactor as air blown in the tuyeres. 

With the construction of the Noranda converter, in 1997, the 20 000  Nm3/h of air going through the combustion air fan was considered too high a volume to sent to the acid plant and the fan was shut down, keeping only 8500 Nm3/h of air at the feed port air curtain.  In order to keep oxygen for combustion above the bath, it was decided to enrich this remaining air with oxygen.  Tests at different enrichments, ranging from 21 to 56% oxygen, were performed.  Due to oxygen availability and heat generation, the actual enrichment is kept at 45% oxygen.  Tests were performed at the different levels of oxygen used and confirmed that in all cases, the oxygen efficiency was maintained at the same level as the oxygen blown through the tuyeres. 

At the tuyeres, tests were also performed to increase the enrichment.  Following the closure of the remaining reverberatory furnace, in 1989, and the commissioning of the Noranda converter in 1997 oxygen became available for the reactor and levels as high as 48% oxygen were not uncommon.  At the beginning of the years 2000, the Noranda converter was increasing its oxygen consumption at the same time as we started using enrichment at the reactor feed port, limiting the oxygen available for the tuyeres. Nowadays, for lack of oxygen and acid plant capacity, enrichment at the reactor tuyere line is maintained in the 40-42% range.

**Slag** The wide variety of feed also caused at times some problem with the slag control. Each plant had a different experience with flux addition, leading each of them to choose an iron/silica ratio appropriate for their specific feed, a value that is normally kept constant. At the Horne smelter, the variations of feed led to a variation of the appropriate ratio over the years, something that was at times difficult to follow, with target ratios varying from 1.80 in the 80’s down to 1.30 early in the 2000’s, back up to 1.50 today. The variations were caused by the presence of oxides other than the iron in the slag, sometimes in high concentrations, that also needed silica. A new value was then calculated with the help of professor Nagamori, named Excesil, for “excess of silica”. This value is calculated by using the silica concentration in the slag and substracting the amount of silica needed for the various oxides (iron, magnesium, sodium, lead, zinc and nickel). A positive value means that the slag contains an excess of silica, while a negative value indicates a lack of silica. Both values, the iron/silica ratio and Excesil, are now available to the operators. Concurrently, the Factstage modeling package was used to help the plant optimize slag chemistry. TPD of dusts.  From the beginning, most of this dust was recycled to the reactor.  In order to avoid dust in the air, the dust was sent to the disk pelletizer, used as a mixer, where it was mixed with the solid charge and some water, so the dust would stick to the feed. 

As mentioned, the disk pelletizer was considered an overkill considering the little need the reactor has for the material to be pre-mixed. It was therefore removed around 2005, creating a problem for the recycling of the ESPs dusts. 

After trying screw handling and conditioning of the dust, a simpler and more economical  method was devised.  The ESP dusts are now pneumatically conveyed directly to the reactor feed port and injected above the bath. 

The main concerns with this method was to know if the dust recirculation would increase and if the minor element distribution would be affected, since dust injected with air could have a different behavior than dust mixed with the solid charge.  Both concerns were checked and did not show any difference with the previous feeding method. 

### **Shell temperature control** 

Water cooling of the shell and brick is not a desired practice at the Horne smelter. Though some outside water cooling of the reactor shell was performed in  the 70’s, the practice was rapidly stopped.  All cooling shell is now done by air. 

In 2008, brick deterioration in a very precise spot under the reactor riding ring led to a revision of our cooling practices.  High wear zones were clearly identified and online thermographic cameras were installed so the operators have a continuous vision of the shell temperature in these critical zones at all time.  Alarms were added both for high temperatures as well as for rapid temperature increases.  Complete reactor shell thermographies are also done twice a week by the reactor technician.  This control was also extended to the other metallurgical vessels. 

In addition, a series of thermocouples were added between the brick and the shell to get advanced indications of the brick deterioration.  This network of thermocouples is also linked to alarms. 

Air cooling was highly improved.  Fans were added in order to help increase the heat flux.  In all areas considered critical, fins were added to further improve the air cooling efficiency.  The space around the riding ring was a particular problem since fans could hardly push air between the riding ring and the shell.  Air knives where then added to get an increased flow in this specific area.  These modifications have proven efficient to control the shell temperature and protect the brick.

### **Value stream mapping** 

For the last 20 years, the smelter has seen a lot of process changes: NCv commissioning (1997), reverberatory furnace closure (1990), concentrate injection in the converters, soda injection in the anode f

urnaces, VPSA oxygen plants construction. With a plant flowsheet that has been more stable for the last few years, it was decided to perform a value stream mapping in 2011 to point out the main limitations of the smelter. The feed variations inherent to a custom smelter as well as the huge flexibility of the plant made the bottlenecks difficult to evaluate in day to day operation. Especially significant is the ability of the plant to buffer the copper flow by accumulating copper pigs or reactor matte when the performance of some of the vessels is below expectation. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 275 The value stream mapping exercise consists in checking the time required by any of the plant process unit to process one tonne of copper. In a well designed plant, the time required at the exit should be shorter than the time requires at the entrance of the process, so the plant is on a “pull” mode. In such a process, there is no accumulation of material inside the process. The value stream mapping allow to check this point. It also gives an accurate view of the material recirculation within the process. The exercise showed the plant to be well designed in terms of vessel capacity, the limit of the smelter being the reactor capacity to smelt new material, this limit originating from both the oxygen and acid plant. Any accumulation in the plant is therefore linked to process reliability instead of process capacity, therefore supporting the actual focus put on reliability in the plant. Coherent jet technology provides a tool for pyrometallurgical processes. The fundamentals of coherent gas jets are described in detail elsewhere [9]. In brief, the technology combines an oxy-fuel burner with a high-velocity gas injection lance in a single device. This enables chemical and kinetic energy to be independently applied in pyrometallurgical reactors. The technology is installed on steelmaking furnaces [10] and copper furnaces [1,2,11]. Trials have been conducted on shaft and ladle furnaces and the technology has also been developed for vacuum metallurgy processes [12].

### <u>Coherent Jet Technology for Copper Pyrometallurgy</u> 

The application of coherent jet technology in copper pyrometallurgy required the development of new classes of coherent gas jets. These were required for the following reasons: 

- a) lower gases supply pressures at copper smelters require different jet designs; 

- b) the process energy balance requires (in some cases) mixed gases jets; 

- c) sulfur and oxygen removal required oxidation jets and reducing jets with jet oxygen partial pressures from pure oxygen to high concentrations of reductant; 

- d) burner modes required increased momentum in the main flame (vs. a bushy flame); 

- e) for fill and cast modes the fuel to oxygen ratio is controlled for the copper casting process. 

Coherent jet technology development in copper anode refining is the subject of two provisional patent applications (13,14).

Charging large quantities of scrap can lower the molten copper temperature while insufficient scrap addition during burner-on periods can increase bath temperature. The challenge is to maintain the temperature in a narrow range to prevent operating problems (e.g. low temperature) during tuyere operation, or high temperatures (e.g. refractory wear concerns). Routine infra red furnace thermography is conducted to monitor areas of potential concern, an example image is shown in Figure 12. The operating practice is to maintain the temperature above 2150 deg F, and below 2250deg F and to charge 10 ton scrap charges to maintain temperature in

this range. ### **ABSTRACT** 

Sumitomo Toyo Smelter and Refinery has achieved a concentrate feeding rate for a flash smelting furnace up to 4,000 TPD by developing the Sumitomo type concentrate burner. To improve the performance of the concentrate burner more “Side-blowing Oxyfuel concentrate burner in Flash Smelting process” (S.O.F.) which had been developed by using a pilot plant in the 1980s at the Niihama Research Laboratories, was applied to a commercial plant. In the S.O.F. process, reaction air is blown from the side nozzles at the flash furnace reaction shaft. In the commercial plant, several tests were carried out and the longest test continued successfully for one month, without serious troubles. The S.O.F. process also showed very high performance, as demonstrated by a low dusting ratio. This paper describes the details of those technical development referring test operation results in the commercial plant.

The Sumitomo burner has it’s own devices, oxy-fuel burner(2) , speed adjuster for reaction air, and so on. These devices were developed to carry out the following concept of development. - Mixure of the concentrate and reaction air uniformly - Acceleration of the concentrate ignition - Advancement of collision between excessively oxidized molten particles and other particles The smelting reaction inside the reaction shaft and the front view of Sumitomotype concentrate burner are shown in figure 2. The concentrate is charged into the burner port through the concentrate chute, and the reaction air is blown into the burner port through the speed adjuster. The concentrate and the reaction air should be premixed to contact and react quickly. The mixture of concentrate and reaction air should ignite at once so that oxidization of the concentrate begins quickly. The collision frequency between excessively oxidized molten particles and other particles should be increased in order to finish the smelting reaction completely at the upper part of the reaction shaft. Figure 2– Schematic diagram of the Sumitomo type concentrate burner _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 300 ### **Mechanis

m of side-blowing oxy-fuel concentrate burner in flash Smelting process** Based on the two-particle model as shown in Figure 3, a concentrate particle, that is easily oxidized, is excessively oxidized up to white metal, at the upper part of the reaction shaft. The oxidized concentrate particles melt owing to their oxidation heat and collide with less oxidized concentrate particles during the particles fall down in the reaction shaft. At that time, the solid concentrate particles melted due to the heat received from the molten ones, which are reduced by the solid ones according to the following reaction. Such circumstances would remain until the reactions between the molten and the solid concentrate particles are completed, and then the objective matte grade particles are produced. Therefore, the advancement of collision is important to finish the smelting reaction completely. Flux Copper concentrate particles

Figure 3– Two-particle model in the reaction shaft In order to further advance collisions between molten particles and other particles in the reaction shaft, extending the retention time in the reaction shaft and increasing the frequency of collisions are useful. Both of them are achieved by blowing some of reaction air horizontally through side nozzles installed at the reaction shaft. Reaction air blown through the side nozzles oxidizes particles in the outer zone of concentrate flow and gathers them into the center of the reaction shaft. At the same time the air makes gas flow in the reaction shaft more turbulent when changing its direction from horizontal to vertical. As a result, un-reacted particles would be decrease (reduction of dusting ratio) and then magnetite formation decrease because of collision between molten particles (excessively oxidized) and other particles (less oxidized) in the reaction shaft. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 301 To achieve such reaction, the new flash smelting furnace, namely “Side-blowing oxy-fuel concentrate burner in flash smelting process (S.O.F.)” was designed and has been developed since the 1980s(3) . However, it was difficult to continue operations and fully evaluate the S.O.F. process due to problems such as high internal pressure in the reaction shaft and stoppage of side nozzles by accretion. These problems make it difficult to apply the S.O.F. process to actual commercial flash furnace. Recently, a combustion simulation model that takes into account gas flow, collision of particles and smelting reaction in the reaction shaft was developed, which has been useful for improving the Sumitomo burrner(4-5) . So, these simulation model was applyed to the S.O.F. process and the variation of the internal pressure in the reaction shaft were calculated (as shown in Figure 5) in order to apply the S.O.F. process to commercial flash furnace. ts, the internal pressure of the upper part of reaction shaft increaces, in the case of: - the volume of top-blown air increase - the number of side nozzles increase (horizonal interception effect increase) _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 303 Therefore, it was realized that applying the S.O.F. process to commercial flash furnace is possible by adjusting the side-blown air conditions. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

TSL (Top Submerged Lance) reactors are state of the art in primary and secondary metallurgy of some nonferrous metals. Core of the reactor is an – into the slag phase reaching – steel lance which injects fuel, air, oxygen and/or slag forming agents. Actually, this lance is equipped with a consumed tip, which is replaced regularly and reduces the down time of the overall system by one hour for each replacement. The lifetime of the lance tip varies from some hours in the lead industry to a couple of days in well operated copper plants. TSL manufacturers promote the formation of a solid slag layer on the lance surface; however, the extraordinary strong turbulence at the reaction zone prevents a stable layer at the lance tip. 

METTOP developed a cooled lance tip in order to increase the lifetime significantly. Theoptimized CFD design shows two cooling systemthat allows a homogenous cooling of the surface. By the significant lower surface temperature of the lance, the accretion layer is more stable; however, main advantage is the higher mechanical stability and longer lifetime of the lance tip. 

As a cooling medium, water is absolutely unsuitable, as a leakage would result in an immediate explosion at this essential vessel of the metallurgical process chain. When using ionic liquids instead of water, an unlikely leakage will not result in any reaction between the cooling medium and the liquid metal or slag. 

### **IONIC LIQUID COOLING TECHNOLOGY** 

The ILTEC (“Ionic Liquid Cooling Technology”) is a solution in order to overcome the disadvantages of todays standard cooling medium water. 

The development is ISIS B, an ionic liquid  (IL), which is a salt with a wide liquidus range. Per definition, ionic liquids show a melting point below 100 °C; many of them are liquid even at room temperature, caused by their badly coordinated ions. As their name suggests, ILs consist only of ions. Dislocated charging and one ion based on an organic molecule avoid the formation of a stable crystal lattice, so that only a minor amount of thermal energy is required to conquer the lattice energy and break the crystal lattice [1]. Varying the cations and anions allows designing ILs with different properties (e.g. melting point, viscosity and solubility) [2]. 

Ionic liquids have a variety of properties which give them unique character; some of them make them suitable and perfect for the use as a cooling medium [3]: 

- Non flammable 

- High ionic conductivity 

- Wide temperature range for liquid phase 

- Larg

e electrochemical window 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

313 

- Practically no vapour pressure below decomposition temperature 

- Relatively low viscosity 

METTOP’s ISIS B is a special selection of anions and cations determining the characteristics of this specific ionic liquid. Furthermore, special additives influence these properties, for example lower the melting point in order to be liquid below room temperature. The ionic liquid ISIS B, which is perfectly suitable as a cooling medium in metallurgical furnaces shows the following basic properties: 

- Melting point: 14 °C 

- • Short term stability: 300 °C • Long term stability: 200 °C • Density: 1.28 g/dm<sup>3</sup> (20 °C); 1.25 g/dm<sup>3</sup> (65 °C) • Heat capacity: 1.5 – 1.6 J/gK (30 – 100 °C) • Viscosity: 50 mPas (20 °C); 8.5 mPas (90 °C) 

An essential property of ISIS B is its chemical composition. A special and patented production process ensures that this ionic liquid is free of chlorine. The possibility of using ISIS B with every conventional cooling element material and most of the common sealing materials is a result of this characteristic. 

Generally, ionic liquids are viscous compared to molecular solvents and also are higher density than water. The strength of their heteroatom-carbon bonds and their heteroatom-hydrogen bonds respectively, indicates their thermal stability. An exceptionally considerable character of ILs is the fact that they have no measureable vapour pressure (i.e. negligible values). The heat capacity of ILs only shows existing, but relatively weak temperature dependence over a temperature range between -50 and 300 °C. The thermal conductivity, which is an important property for heat transfer applications, is significantly affected by water contamination [2,4,5]. 

Using ISIS B as cooling medium allows higher inlet and outlet temperatures than with water. Furthermore, an adjustable intensity of cooling is possible, also during heating up. The high cooling element temperature prevents the condensation of water vapour and – as a result – minimizes the risk of refractory hydration during heating up or leakages. A sufficient high cooling element surface temperature avoids the formation of corrosive compounds, and dew point corrosion respectively. Furthermore, heat or energy recovery gets feasible if the cooling medium temperature is higher. Ionic liquids decompose above a certain temperature under formation of gaseous components. As a result of the aforementioned aspects, using ILs as a cooling medium is a save alternative to water and allows cooling new areas with the following economical and technical advantages: 

- No hydration due to strong cooling 

- No hydration due to leakage

### **COOLED TSL LANCE TIP** 

Cooled lances are well established in the iron and steel industry, especially at BOF converters. However, this lance technology significantly differs from TSL lances. First of all, BOF lances use a high velocity oxygen stream in order to enhance the bath agitation and to improve the metal-slag reaction. All reactions occur in front and at a certain distance of the lance tip. Furthermore, the lance does not reach into the slag phase, the tip is positioned slightly above this level. The tip shows a diameter of up to 400 mm and is made of copper with normally one to six openings for the oxygen stream. The tip is also equipped with the circuit for the cooling water, which is pumped through the lance. This copper lance tip is regularly replaced in order to maintain process safety; however, it is not consumed during operation [6]. 

The above mentioned characteristic process show that the lance of BOF converters is stressed only thermally, there is no chemical attack by liquid metal or slag and the reaction occurs not directly at the cooled tip. 

In contrast, a TSL lance is built of concentric steel tubes, where the different media are injected to the vessel. The lower part – the lance tip– isa simple tube made of black or heat resistant steel. The injections of reactants through the lance result in an intense bath agitation and spl

ashes up to the reactor shaft. Nevertheless, the lance tip reaches into the slag phase and is in permanent contact with the slag. The slag splashes form a certain protection layer at the lance surface and prolongs its lifetime [7]. However, the strong bath agitation at the lance tip prevents the formation of a stable layer at the lance tip. There is rather a constant growth and break away of this slag layer which results in a consumption of the lance tip and the necessity of replacing it regularly. In dependence of the exact process and product of the TSL reactor, the lance tip life time can be several hours up to a couple of weeks. While lifetime of lances in copper reactors is comperatively high, the aggressivity of lead oxide reduces the lifetime in the lead metallurgy to less than one day. 

Based on the characteristics of the TSL process described above, a potentially cooled lance tip can not be designed similar to BOF lances. TSL lance tips are stressed thermally by the liquid slag and by the reacten directly in front of the tip, chemically due 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

316 

to the contact with more or less aggressive slags, as well as mechanically as a result of a continuous growth and break away of a frozen slag layer. 

Copper as a material for cooled TSL lance is one alternative which seems to be feasible. As the heat transfer in case of copper cooling elements is high, the formation of a stable freeze lining is promoted. However, the thermal and mechanical stability is rather low. Especially when the frozen slag layer breaks away due to mechanical stress, wear of the copper lance tip is probable. 

Carbon steel or heat resistant steel are suitable, as they are commonly used for TSL lances in order to maintain a maximum lifetime. Especially in case of austenitic steels, the heat transfer will be significantly worse than in case of copper elements. This fact reduces the probability of a stable freeze lining. However, the higher thermal and mechanical stability are solid arguments for choosing steel as construction material for cooled lance tips. 

The cooling system design is relatively not dependent of the lance tip material and a result of CFD calculations in order to prevent areas without any convection and to ensure a homogenious surface temperature. Differences are necessary due to the unequal machinability of copper and steel. Basis of the following considerations is the use of steel and therefore welded constructions. 

Generally, two basic designs are possible: The cooled lance tip can be made of three concentrically tubes, which form an inner and an outer hollow space for inflow and return. Another possibility is to realize inflow and return next to each other; in this case there are two concentrically tubes necessary. In both designs, installations and guide plates are useful in order to ensure a homogeniuous cooling medium flow through the lance tip. 

CFD calculations shows a clear benefit when using t

he second possibility. Although the temperature distribution over the circunference is less homogenious, there are significantly less areas with a low fluid flow. This prevents local overheating and degradation of the ionic liquid and therefore increases the lifetime. Also the possibility of breakthroughs due to hot spots is minimized. The most critical area can be seen at the redirection of the fluid at the tip; this could be further reduced by adding further guide panels and keeping openings in the existing ones.

### **ILTEC SYSTEM** 

The ILTEC System for a TSL lance has special requirements respect to system availability and behaviour in case of incidents. Therefore, all critical components needs to be designed reduntantly and the system needs to be implemented into the reactor control system completely. Some essential control mechanisms are described in the following paragraphs. 

A failure of the frequency controlled pump results in an immediate increase of the cooling medium temperature at the lance tip. A decomposition of the ionic liquid at above 400 °C results in the formation of gaseous components anda gas pressure increase. The system is equipped with overpressure valves on various positions to limit the pressure to 6 bar. Furthermore, a damage and leakage of the lance tip is probable within a limited time. Although there is no safety risk involved with this incident, a loss of cooling medium and shutdown of the reactor is the result. The detection of a pump failure is easely possible by flow and pressure measurement. As soon as the system detects a drop in the medium flow after the circulation pump, it instantly switches to the standby pump. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

318 

The loss of the secondary cooling is a major incident. Within a very limited time the temperature in the cooling system raises dramatically and leads – in dependence of the duration of this incident – to a degradation of the ionic liquid, a decomposition and finally to a leakage and damage of the lance tip. A standby heat exchanger with separate cooling water supply is essential to eliminate the possibility of secondary cooling breakdown. 

In case of a leakage of the lance tip, a certain amount of ionic liquid is released into the reactor. As described above, this is no safety risk, but an economic deficit due to the costs of the ionic liquid. Therefore, the leakage detection needs to be fast and reliable and should effect an immediate stop of the cooling medium supply. An easy way is the installation of a flow detection at the inlet and back flow,

as well as a pressure measurement. 

### **HAZID ANALYSIS** 

A HAZID (Hazard Identification) analysis is used to identify the main hazards of a faciltiy, as well as to evaluate the existing safety measures and – if required – to complete these measures. Goal of the efforts is an acceptable and tolerable residual risk for operators, third parties, surroundings and for the environment. The HAZID analysis is a structured tool and needs to be worked out in close cooperation between the issuing agency and the manufacturers or operators of the facility. Generally, it can be done both for new concepts and for existing installations [8]. 

In case of the cooled TSL lance tip, the HAZID analysis was done to work out possible malfunction or safety risks which may occur during start up, operation, shut down or in case of a leakage. As the use of ionic liquid as cooling medium comprises no safety risk, main focus was detecting and responding to possible malfunctions, as well as preventing improper operation. The system needs to be implemented into the reactor control and automation and is an integrated part; the battery limit for consideration of the analysis has been set in accordance to this fact. 

### **CONCLUSION** 

The present paper describes a possibility to increase the availability of TSL reactors by cooling the lance tip.While cooling lances is state-of-the-art in BOF converters, and the iron and steel industry respectively, it is not used in the nonferrous industry – especially not at TSL lances. As the lance and lance tip respectively is the limiting factor for the furnace up time, this technology holds a significant availibility potential. 

Cooling medium for this application is METTOP’s ionic liquid ISIS B – as the use of water would be too risky. ISIS B will not react with the liquid slag or metal in case 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

319 

of a leakage or breakthrough and therefore contains no safety risk. The liquid decomposes above 300 °C under formation of gaseous components. During normal operation, a maximum temperature of 200 °C should not be exceeded. 

The lance tip itself was designed with the help of CFD calculations in order to achieve a homogenious cooling medium temperature, to avoid blind spots and a local overheating respectively, as well as to stay within the operation limits of the ionic liquid ISIS B. Two cooling circuits have been chosen for the TSL lance tip. 

The ILTEC system for keeping the ionic liquid in a closed circuit was optimized by using a HAZID analysis to evaluate the safety level and detect possible risks. All safety relevant components and instrumentation have been designed reduntantely; several measures for the programming have been defined in order to achieve a maximum possible lance lifetime while maintaining a safe operation.

The use of high levels of oxygen enrichment in the air flow through tuyeres in the Teniente Converter, historically is associated with high temperature in the end of the tuyeres and refractory wear. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Teniente Converter (TC) was conceived in the early 70s and the first unit was commissioned in 1977 [1]. This reactor has been crucial for the expansion needs of Codelco-Chile. A big number of improvements and operation changes have showed that the Teniente Converter is a fair alternative for smelting/converting operations. Currently seven operating units exist in Chile. Several studies, concerning thermodynamical and operational features have been carried out in order to understand and improve the melting process in the TC [2,3,4]. The Teniente Converter is a reactor with a technology of fusion very flexible, allows the treatment of various types of concentrates, giving the options of wet concentrate feed through Garr-Gun and the injection of dry concentrate through special tuyeres for this material. Both types of

feed may be used in varying proportions,thus the heat and mass balance can be adjusted within a wide range. 

Initially, the Teniente Converter used moderate levels of oxygen enrichment (app. 28%), limited due to wear of the refractory in the tuyeres zone.  With the operational improvements made in recent years, it has been possible to reach levels of enrichment close to 40%. 

The efficiency of the process leads to find the upper limit of this parameter to be able to respond to the current demands of Codelco Chile. 

An important aspect of the operation of the converters is the injection of air through blowing tuyeres, this gas enters at a temperature of about 100 °C, generating a cold zone in the region close to the line of tuyeres, which produces accretions on the end of the tuyeres.  The only time when the bath is in contact with the tip of the tuyere is when the bubble detachment occurs, the bath portion which contacts the tip of the tuyere corresponds to that comes from the center of the reactor to the process temperature of approximately 1250 ° C.

### **MATHEMATICAL MODEL** 

### **Unidimensional Model** 

The unidimensional model is a global model that describes the behavior of a bubble stuck to a tuyere. This kind of models has been used by several researchers [56], that include heat, mass and momentum transfer phenomena.  The results of the present model to predict the following variables as a function of time: 

- Bubble size 

- Oxygen consumption within the bubble. 

- Temperature of the gas in the bubble 

According to the results given by the model, it is hoped to develop relationships between these two variables and well-defined operational parameters such as: 

- Air flow 

- Oxygen enrichment blown air 

- Submergence of the tuyeres 

The oxygen efficiency in the bath is determined for different operation conditions of the Teniente Converter [6]. 

### <u>Hypothesis of the model</u> 

Hypotheses adopted in this development are: 

- The bubble has spherical form 

- All the oxygen that reaches the bubble surface reacts with the bath. 

- Capillarity effects are neglected 

- Gas kinetic energy is neglected 

- Bath kinetic energy is neglected, which implies not to take into account the fact that the bubble gives waving energy to the bath. 

A fundamental hypothesis is the one that defines the instant of time in which the bubble detaches from tuyere, which is assumed to be given as follows: 

"The bubble detaches from tuyere at the moment in which the distance from the bubble center to the superior border of the tuyere is the same as the bubble radius" 

Under these hypotheses, it is possible to outline the equations of energy, mass and quantity of movement conservation. These equations generate a system of ordinary differential equations that once resolved, al

low representing graphically existent relationships among the variables of interest.  The Figure 2 shows a schematic view of the growth bubble in the tip of the tuyere.

### <u>Equations during bubble formation</u> 

The global mass balance in the bubble during its formation can be expressed as: 



- _t_ : time 

- _R_ : universal gas constant 

- _n_ : total number of moles in the bubble 

- _Q0_ : volumetric flow for the tuyere 

- _P0_ : pressure at which _Q0_ is specified 

- _PO2_ : oxygen partial pressure in the bubble 

- _T_ : bubbles absolute temperature

### **ABSTRACT** 

The copper content in chalcosite-bornite concentrates produced by KGHM Polska Miedź SA is similar to that in chalcopyrite concentrates (20 - 30 wt %). However, the concentration of sulfur and iro

n is much lower, respectively by 9 - 12 and 3 - 6 wt %. Furthermore, a characteristic of Polish concentrates is the presence of carbon (6 - 9 wt %) and impurities: lead (1.5 - 3.0 wt %) and arsenic (0.05 - 0.4 wt %) . 

Due to the low sulfur and iron content and the presence of organic carbon, two types of technology were chosen for the melting of the kinds of concentrates encountered in Poland: the shaft smelting process (Głogуw I and Legnica) and the one-stage flash smelting process (Głogуw II). In both processes the organic carbon constitutes a fuel to provide the desired temperature of the products. 

The smelters in which the shaft process is used are characterized by a high degree of elimination of Pb and As in the copper production cycle when, in the first two pyrometallurgical operations (concentrates melting, copper matte converting) stable sulfide phases occur.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper content in chalcocite-bornite concentrates at KGHM Polska Miedź S.A. is at the same level as its content in chalcopyrite concentrates (20 – 30 wt %), while concentrations of sulfur and iron are several times lower, i.e. at the level of: 9 – 12 and 3 – 6 wt %, respectively. 

Additionally Polish copper concentrates are characterized by presence of organic carbon (6 – 9 wt %) and impurities: lead (1.5 – 3.0 wt %) and arsenic (0.05 – 0.4 wt %). 

Low contents of sulfur and iron as well as presence of organic carbon resulted in implementation of two technologies for smelting of such concentrates: shaft furnace process (HM Głogуw I and HM Legnica) and single-stage flash-smelting process (HM Głogуw II). 

In the smelters where shaft furnaces are operating copper matte is produced from the concentrates and then undergoes converting. In the

single-stage flash-smelting process blister copper, applicable for fire refining, is produced directly from the concentrates. 

In the shaft furnace and copper matte converting processes lead and arsenic are removed in high degree to dusts, which are used as materials for lead production. 

Significantly different conditions in the single-stage flash-smelting process result in concentration of Pb and As in the slag mostly (converter slag from treatment of CuPbFe alloy, anode slag from fire refining). Because of the high copper content the slags are subjected to other technological operations which are characterized by very low degree of elimination of those impurities from copper production cycle. 

Because of the mentioned above problems in the currently performed modernization of pyrometallurgical installations in KGHM Polska Miedź S.A., consisting in replacing shaft furnaces in HM Głogуw I and HM Legnica with one flashfurnace, it was necessary to develop a different than the currently used method for removal of lead and arsenic from the single-stage flash-smelting process.

In that technology almost 70 % of Pb goes to CuPbFe alloy while only about 15 % in each of the other products, i.e. dusts and with waste slag, is taken out from the copper production cycle. 

During converting of CuPbFe alloy about 90 % of Pb is transferred to the slag, which is recycled to electric furnace, and about  10 % to the gaseous-dust phase. 

Such a behavior of lead in pyrometallurgical operations of flash-smelting process results in circulation of huge mass of that element (over 1.5 times higher than the Pb load introduced to the smelter with concentrates) between electric furnace and converters in CuPbFe alloy and in the converter slag. 

Operation of large masses of by-products with high lead concentration brings a series of  unfavorable phenomena, and the most important are:

- limitation of flash-smelting slag capacity of electric furnace because of treatment of large amount of converter slag, 

- consumption of additional amounts of limestone and coke breeze, also electric energy consumption, 

- higher wear of refractory lining of electric furnace and converters operating in presence of liquid solution of high lead content (CuFePb alloy, converter slag), 

- generation of a large mass of dusts from electric furnace which are difficult in processing in lead production technology.

Development of a new technology for treatment of converter slag from treatment of CuPbFe alloy provides possibilities for removal of significant amounts of lead and arsenic from the cycle of copper production by single-stage flash-smelting process.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The largest commercial copper smelter using Outotec<sup>®</sup> Ausmelt Technology has been successfully commissioned and put into operation at the Daye Non-Ferrous Metals Company Ltd operations near Huangshi City, in Hubei Province, China. The plant was commissioned b

etween November 2010 and January 2011 following three years of design and construction works. The smelter is currently treating low grade copper sulphide concentrates to produce a matte containing 55% copper and a low copper content slag. Molten matte and slag flow continuously from the Ausmelt furnace via an underflow weir to an ESF for matte/slag separation. This paper provides details of the start-up and the staged increase in production to the design capacity, of this, the largest Ausmelt furnace to date.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

To expand capacity, improve process flexibility and modernise existing equipment and facilities, Daye Nonferrous Metals Company Limited (DNMC) decided in 2008 to invest RMB 1,680 million Yuan (US$250 million) in the upgrade of their copper smelting and refining operations near Daye City in Hubei, China. The project was cited as the ‘Energy Saving, Environmentally Efficient’ (ESEE) Copper Smelter, with modernisation of the plant centring around construction of an Outotec® Ausmelt TSL furnace and downstream Electrical Settling Furnace (ESF) to replace the existing Reverberatory and Noranda smelting furnaces. Ausmelt TSL technology was selected based on a comparison of all available advanced non-ferrous smelting technologies with regard to process flexibility, energy consumption, operating costs and environmental performance. 

The new smelter (Figure 1) was designed to achieve a rapid increase in copper capacity and production through the introduction of an Outotec® Ausmelt Smelting furnace. Additionally, capacity would be increased with new installed oxygen and acid plant capacity, along with an Outotec® Twin M18 Casting system to supplement existing casting equipment also installed as part of the plant upgrade. 



Figure 1 – Ausmelt Furnace Building 

The engineering design for the Ausmelt furnace and ESF was carried out in 2008 and the plant foundations officially laid on 18th July 2009. Following only 555 days of plant construction works, the two furnaces were heated up in November 2010

Critical to the design of such a high-capacity operation was the furnace underflow weir which provided for a continuous flow of matte and slag, transferred via launder to the ESF for separation (Figure 2 and Figure 3). On the 28th of December, the first concentrates were fed to the furnace and both copper matte and slag tapped to the ESF. A continuous flow of matte and slag from the furnace underflow weir was subsequently achieved on December 31. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 362 During the first month of operation, concentrate feedrates were constrained below 60t/h due to limited oxygen plant capacity. Installation of a ‘low-flow’ oxygen line within the Ausmelt furnace lance valve train was used to ensure stable operation at these feedrates as construction of the new oxygen plant was completed. Operation at only 25% of design capacity and a lance air oxygen enrichment of only 35 - 40% presented a number of issues, most notably with respect to the furnace energy balance and off gas system operation. Additionally, reduced matte and slag flow from the furnace weir necessitated increased supervision of the launder connecting the Ausmelt furnace and ESF. Despite these issues however, furnace operations remained stable and well controlled, highlighting the turndown capabilities, flexibility and robustness of Ausmelt TSL technology. Even at very low flow rates, lance integrity remained acceptable, with minor tip repairs typically being required after 2 days operation. Lance flow optimisation over the course of the commissioning combined with online assessment of the lance tip condition did however aid in extending the lance life along with more stable furnace operation. Following the hot commissioning, ramp-up of the smelter to design capacity took place in a number of stages over the course of 2011 as other areas of the modernisation project were completed. Decommissioning of the old reverberatory furnace began during the overall plant construction works; however the existing Noranda furnace remained operational during the four (4) weeks of the Ausmelt furnace hot commissioning. Once DNMC were satisfied with the stability of the new Ausmelt furnace operation, the Noranda furnace was shutdown, with its air and oxygen supplies re-routed to the Ausmelt furnace, enabling concentrate feedrates to be increased to 100t/h. Following the completion of construction works for the new oxygen plant in April, 2011, commissioning of the ‘high-flow’ oxygen line within the Ausmelt furnace lance valve train was completed by Outotec and DNMC. This provided for a large jump in

concentrate throughput to 160t/h and lance operation with enrichments up to 45%. A further increase in concentrate feedrates to 230t/h was achieved following construction of the new acid plant in September, 2011. This stage-wise increase in furnace production to design capacity over the first 9 months of operation is illustrated in Figure 3.

### **CURRENT PLANT OPERATION** 

Following completion of all phases of the DNMC plant modernisation, the plant has continued to operate at or above design capacity. Despite a small but gradual decrease in concentrate grade, the plant has continued to achieve its design production, operating at concentrate feedrates up to 230 t/h. The operation of the Ausmelt lance at enrichments exceeding 60% has not proven detrimental to lance life, with minor tip repairs being required only every 3 - 4 days. Smelting temperatures are well controlled via feedback from pyrometer measurements taken at the furnace weir outlet and are typically in the range 1185 ± 10°C. The system has also demonstrated the advantages of Ausmelt TSL technology with respect to low dust generation rates, with feed carryover typically being less than 0.5%.

Ongoing efforts by DNMC to optimise furnace operating practices so as to maintain temperatures in the furnace freeboard region have minimised downtime associated with the removal of accretions around the furnace roof and WHB uptake. This, along with more stable furnace operation and extended lance life has resulted in a furnace availability exceeding 90%. 

As part of the DNMC overall plant maintenance schedule, partial re-lining of the Ausmelt Furnace refractory is carried out annually, taking the furnace offline for a period of 2-3 weeks. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Outotec® Ausmelt Technology has been successfully applied by DNMC as part of modernisation of their existing operations near Huangshi City, China. Following hot commissioning of the Ausmelt furnace and ESF in December 2010, production has been ramped up via a number of phases as oxygen and acid plants upg

rades have been completed. The Ausmelt furnace is currently operating at design capacity with concentrate feedrates of 220 – 230t/h and more than 90% availability. Incorporation of an underflow weir into the furnace design has facilitated not only such high throughput, but also improved process stability and control. 

This project has successfully demonstrated the advantages of Ausmelt TSL technology for the treatment of variable and low-grade concentrates. The system has also shown superiority in high specific smelting capacity, stable operation and process flexibility. Replacement of the existing Noranda and Reverberatory furnace operations has provided superior environmental performance in line with Chinese National Emission Reduction Policies

### **COMING OF AGE - 21 YEARS COMMERCIAL OPERATION OF COPPER ISASMELT™ AT MOUNT ISA** 

J.S. Edwards _Xstrata Technology 160 Ann Street Brisbane, Australia 4000 jedwards@xstratatech.com_

### **ABSTRACT** 

Development of a new smelting technology, such as ISASMELT™, requires a significant investment of time as well as resources and capital.  In the case of the copper ISASMELT™ process developed in Mount Isa the commissioning of the commercial furnace in 1992 was the culmination of 14 years of bench, pilot and demonstration scale testwork.  The demonstration plant was operated from 1987 to 1992, initially at a feed rate of 12 t/h of concentrate increasing to a maximum of 50 t/h during trials performed to reduce the scale-up factor between demonstration plant and commercial plant. 

The commercial scale copper ISASMELT™ furnace in Mount Isa was commissioned in August 1992 with a capacity rated at 180 000 tonnes per year of copper anode.  In 2013 the copper ISASMELT™ has been operating for 21 years which is a Coming of Age birthday in Australia.  After two major smelter upgrades in 21 years the original furnace is still in service and routinely treats in excess of 1 000 000 tonnes per annum of copper containing feed and has a demonstrated campaign life, using uncooled refractory, approaching 4 years. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

368 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Mount Isa Mines was founded in 1924 to mine the lead-zinc-silver orebody that had been discovered the preceding year by John Campbell Miles.  Mining the lead-zincsilver orebody was the mainstay of the operations for the next 20 years and continues to be integral to metal production from the site.  Copper production commenced in Mount Isa in 1943 to provide copper for the war effort. 

The initial copper production was through the lead sinter plant and blast furnace, with copper production replacing lead.  This switch was reversed in 1946.  Both lead and copper production began in parallel in 1953 after construction of a copper smelter on the Mount Isa lease

issioned in 1992, an air preheater was included in the gas handling system.  Process air entering the smelter passed through the preheater to recover heat from the furnace offgas and return it to the process.  The preheater was a shell and tube heat exchanger and by 1999, it needed monthly cleaning to maintain draught on the ISASMELT™ furnace.  Over the period 1999 to 2000, the air preheater was removed from the gas train to reduce the pressure drop and restore the furnace draught. 

### **Upgrade 2** 

In 2003, Xstrata introduced a new operating philosophy to the copper smelter following the takeover of MIM Holdings Limited, the former the owner of Mount Isa Mines.  At various times, the copper smelter had been treated as a unit either in an integrated copper stream or as one of several extractive metallurgy plants.  The new philosophy was to consider the copper smelter as a toll smelter with supply agreements put in place with the Mount Isa and Ernest Henry concentrators. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

370 

An upgrade of the copper smelter was planned and executed from 2006 to 2007 and included installation of the following new equipment: 

- Revert crusher to increase the revert recovery to the Peirce-Smith converters and reduce the recycle to the ISASMELT™ furnace; 

- A second RHF to add surge capacity to the converter aisle and increase the time available for matte prills to settle from the slag. 

### **Availability and Throughput** 

Figure 1 shows the availability of the ISASMELT™ plant for all 21 years of operation.  The data has been adjusted for the Air Quality Control (AQC) downtime periods.  There has been a steady improvement over time in the overall plant availability. 

For approximately the first five years of operation, the boiler was a major cause of lost time with shutdowns lasting up to seven days to replace tube bundles that had worn and leaked.  The issue was rectified by armouring the tube bundles after a materials testing program lasting several years.  More recently, a concentrate shortage and the acid plant not being available have affected the plant availability.

The annual copper output from Mount Isa as anode or blister copper is shown in Figure 2.  Blister copper was produced at site until 1979 when anode furnaces were installed in the copper smelter.  After the copper ISASMELT™ furnace was installed in 1992 the throughput was constrained until 1997 by aisle interactions between the ISASMELT™ plant and the FSR and reverberatory furnace, followed by a commissioning period for Upgrade 1. 

The average annual lost time due to AQC downtime prior to 2000 was approximately 10%.  With the commissioning of a sulfuric acid plant the downtime was reduced.  The reduction is reflected in the improved copper smelter production figures after that time. 



Figure 2-Annual Copper Smelter Throughput 

### **Campaign L

ength** 

The copper ISASMELT™ furnace was initially justified on a 2 year campaign length.  Figure 3 shows that this target was not achieved for the first 6 campaigns from 1992 to 1998.  Efforts at managing the campaign length and predicting the rebrick date were unsuccessful. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

372 



Figure 3-Copper ISASMELT™ Campaign Life 

The refractory lining in the ISASMELT™ furnace is all brick, there is no freeze lining or forced cooling of the brick.  It is an insulated lining with the purpose of keeping the steel cool enough to avoid creep and minimizing heat losses.  Based on the results of Campaigns 1 to 6 it appeared that a refractory lining would not perform as required. 

In Campaign 7, a renewed focus was placed on process control.  Approximately 14 months into the campaign, analysis of the wear rate indicated that the rebrick could be delayed by several months to extend into another financial year.  Additional resources were allocated to a daily review of plant performance.  Based on the daily review plant operating set points were adjusted.  The result was an extension to the campaign length and a record of 105 weeks.  Management of the ISASMELT™ plant has continued to improve with a 4 year campaign life becoming the new standard for the operation. 

### **CONCLUSION** 

With 21 years of operating experience with the commercial ISASMELT™ plant and a decade of new knowhow in refractory management, a 4 year campaign life with uncooled refractory is the new standard.  The copper ISASMELT™ plant at Mount Isa has come of age.
