### **ON THE EFFECT OF REVERTS PARTICLE SIZE AND FLASH FURNACE REACTION SHAFT HEIGHT ON THE FURNACE PERFORMANCE: A SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS** 

M. Leуn, J. Larrondo and T. Gonzales _Hatch Ltd. El Bosque Norte 500, 12_<sup>_th_</sup> _Floor, Las Condes, Santiago, Chile maximo.leon@hatch.cl_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

The current trend in integrated or custom smelters is treating low Cu/S ratio concentrates. The additional heat load on the furnace and increase in off-gas volume negatively impacts the capacity of the furnace.  A practice in the smelting industry is to add low Sulfur and Iron feed materials (reverts) to minimize the negative impact on furnace capacity. 

The current paper provides a sensitivity analysis for a generic flash furnace. Two parameters are studied: 1) several mean particle sizes of reve

rts and 2) three furnace heights. For these factors, a relation is developed between the heat transferred to reverts, the cooling system of the furnace, and off-gas. 

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is used to model an axi-symmetric generic furnace model. 

It is found that only reverts particle size have a major influence in the following features of the furnace operation: First, heat transfer in the furnace is characterized by a non linear dependence between heat absorbed by reverts, walls and off-gas and reverts particle seize. Second, the chemical reactions can be delayed by decreasing reverts particle size. In contrast, increasing the reaction shaft height has a mild reduction of wall temperatures in the first half of the reaction shaft height.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Currently, many copper smelting operations in the world are treating low grade copper concentrate, which has presented several challenges to their operations. In particular, Flash Smelter operations which are autogenous in nature, due to their flash smelting process, have experienced a decrease in copper throughput from low Cu/S ratios in their feed concentrate. This promotes a higher heat load due to higher quantities of labile sulfur and iron in the feeding particles. In order to reduce the increasing heat load of low grade mineral in the flash reaction, reverts have been used as a heat sink to control the heat balance in existing Flash Furnaces that were not designed to operate with this low Cu/S ratios. 

Previous studies [1,2,3,4] have shown that smaller sized reverts have the necessary effect as a heat sink mechanisms. However, the increase of operational costs in the industry, especially in comminution, is pushing for the inclusion of coarser reverts into the process. Little is known about the effect of increasing reverts particle size and their behavior as a heat sink in the flash process. Thus, the motivation is to address a particle size that could be beneficial for the flash process and also reduce the cost of the grinding reverts to the optimal size. In view of this, the goal of this paper is to present a sensitivity analysis of the impact on: heat transfer phenomena and also its effect typical metallurgical reactions inside a generic flash furnace, for several reverts particle sizes and also the Reaction Shaft (RS) height. 

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) commercial package FLUENT is used to model the fluid flow and heat transfer in a two-dimensional axi-symmetric geometry. 

### **MODEL DEVELOPMENT** 

This section summarizes the characteristics of a simplified and generic flash furnace, physics models used, boundary conditions and numerical features of the CFD simulations, and definition of cases. 

Figure 1 shows the axi-symmetric geometry of a generic flash furnace considered for the CFD simulations. The burner is represented as two inlets where the process air, fuel-air mixture and injection of soli

ds feed are introduced into the model. In addition, existing water cooled walls commonly present in Flash Furnaces (FF) are represented in this model, such as the spray-cooled wall and the copper-block-cooled wall at the RS bottom. The outlet boundary condition represents the area between the slag bath surface and the settler roof where the gases exit from the RS. The geometry selected has been simplified to include only the reaction shaft mainly due to the negligible effect of reverts in the heat transfer and fluid flow structures at the settler region.

The fluid flow and scalar quantities (e.g. temperature, concentrations) are included in the model through the following equations: continuity, momentum, k-  turbulence model, transports of species (O2, N2, H2O, S2, SO2, CH4, CO2), the energy equation, and radiation through the Discrete Ordinates (DO) model (for details, see Fluent [4]). The solids feed into the furnace is a mixture of two types: 1) concentrate and 2) reverts particles only. Silica flux has been also left out as part of the solid feed for this simulation since its effect is to reduce the temperature of the gas inside the furnace through the formation of fayalite (Fe2SiO4). ### **RESULTS** 

### **Typical Fluid Flow Structures and Scalars Transport** 

Figure 2 shows the typical flow structures and distribution of temperature and species for the base case D1500H0. Flow inside the reaction shaft, shown in Figure 2a) is predominantly characterized by a recirculation zone in the vicinity of the process air and fuel inlets; a central jet-type flow which spreads at a half-angle of about 13 degrees, and a recirculation zone near the outlet to the settler. These features of the flow have been observed in other CFD modeling works laboratory experiments [3,4,5,6,7,8], and also in plant experiences. In this model the burner central lance has not been included, as it has only a near field influence in the fluid flow structures. Moreover, it has been previously tested by Hatch in 3D simulations of flash furnace burners, that the introduction of this geometrical feature results in a local relocation of some flow structures, but the overall characteristics (e.g. velocities, temperatures) remain slightly unchanged. 



Figure 2– Typical model results for the base case D1500H0: a) Contours of velocity magnitude in m/s.; b) Temperature contours in Celcius; c) Volume fraction of SO2; d) Volume fraction of S2.

Figure 2 b) shows the temperature distribution inside the reaction shaft. In the vicinity of the process air and fuel inlets two fronts are clearly observed. The central front corresponds to the high temperatures generated from natural gas combustion. The lateral fronts mark the start of the oxidizing and combusting fronts of the concentrate feed. These fronts extend approximately 2 m below the reaction shaft top. The central region of the reaction shaft has temperatures in the range 1500 to 1650 C, and between 1150 and 1300 C towards the walls. These temperatures and their distribution have been observed in other CFD studies [9,10,11] and in plant operations. Figure 2 d) show the oxidizing fronts of S2. The contours represent where the concentrate releases S2 and it is immediately transformed into SO2. The extent of this front is

related to the core zone where the concentrate has reached almost all of its conversion, according to the metallurgical reactions considered in the CFD models. In the base case D1500H0 the full conversion is reached at approximately 1 m below the injection surface, which represents roughly the first 20% of the height of the furnace from top to bottom. This is close to what it is observed in plant experiences with flash furnaces, where conversion occurs at approximately in the first one-third of the furnace. The reason for this deviation is the absence of the lance in the present CFD models. The burner central lance is imbedded typically 50 cm below the top of the reaction shaft, where concentrate starts to increase its temperature, thus lowering the height for full conversion. The SO2 volume fraction, shown in Figure 2 c), shows a high concentration in the center region of the RS, which is formed after concentrate combusting and convected downwards by the jet type of flow inside the RS. 

### **Effects of Reverts Particle Size and Reaction Shaft Height** 

This subsection describes typical trajectories of reverts particles, and its effects on Mean Height of Conversion (MHC, defined later) of concentrate particles, wall temperatures and heat transfer between reverts and walls of the reaction shaft. MHC is defined as the distance from the top surface where 99% of the compounds of CuFeS2 and FeS2 in the concentrate particle have been depleted. 

Figure 3 shows the profiles of mass fraction,  , of relevant components of a concentrate particle along with its temperature, as it travels from the injection surface towards the slag bath. From these profiles it is observed how particles interact in terms of metallurgical reactions taking place as they travel towards the slag bath. Furthermore, it is observed that the evolution of temperature is related to the chemical reactions of the particle. As an example the temperature drop after 0.015sec corresponds to endothermic reactions taking place, in particular the decomposition of CuFeS2.  The temperature increase that follows can be explained in part due to the high temperature flow surrounding the particle and that exothermic reactions are taking place (e.g. formation of

Particles with size 25 microns are expected to follow the flow structures in the furnace, as depicted in Figure 4 a). In the case D25H0, 25wt% of particles leave the domain, suggesting that these fine particles are being carried out by the turbulent flow and, that in real cases might reach the upta

Larger particle size trajectories (larger than 100 microns), like the ones shown in Figure 4 c) and d), follow trajectories into the bath not altered by flow structures inside the furnace.

Figure 5 shows the MHC value, as a function of reverts particle size. It is important to mention that similar profile is obtained for the MHC of FeS2. It is observed that reducing the reverts particle size to 10 microns shifts the MHC down an additional 20%with respect to the MHC obtained in the base case. The heat absorption properties of reverts as a function of their mean size and effects on the reaction shaft are discussed in what follows. 

Figure 6a) shows wall temperature profiles for reverts particle sizes of 25, 50, 100, 200, 400 and 1500 microns as a function of the height of the reaction shaft, measured from the top towards the end of the copper-block water cooled walls. Overall, it is observed that reducing the particle size from 1500 to 10 microns produces, at most, an overall 100°C decrease in the average wall temperature. In addition, all profiles are characterized by a first kink related to the boundary conditions at H=0.1 m, an inflection point at around H=1 m related to zone where conversion occurs, a second kink at H=3.5 where the transition between the spray- and copper-block-cooled walls. The kink observed at H=5.5 is related to the backflow temperature settings of the outlet boundary condition of the model. The decrease of the mean temperature over the wall is mainly influenced by reverts sizes ranging 100-200 microns. For larger rever

For smaller particles (below 50 microns), the profiles also do not show marked differences, since they are mainly carried by the turbulent flow into the settler. Figure 6 b) substantiates the above discussion, showing  the heat rate absorbed by spray cooled walls, copper-block-cooled walls, and the total heat absorbed by the cooled walls. It also includes the heat absorbed by reverts particle stream as a function of reverts particles size. There is a strong non linear dependence of the total heat rate absorbed with particle size, where the maximum heat rate is predicted to occur at 75 microns. For this reverts particle size, 96%wt of the particle stream absorb heat in the reaction shaft domain. This may be explained because particles of this size are light enough to be influenced by turbulence and have small enough surface area to allow rapid heating, until the melting point of the different components is reached. For larger reverts particle sizes the heat rate absorbed drops mainly because these particles only absorb sensible heat, and melting may occur only at the slag bath surface. Furthermore, the decay is observed to be non linear also for particle sizes larger than 400 microns. The reason for this is mainly due to an increase in surface area and weight, rather than an influence by the turbulence flow. For particles smaller than 75 microns in size, not all the total heat rate is absorbed by reverts as they tend to travel into the settler, carried by the turbulent flow. It is mainly because of this effect that the decay in the absorbed heat rate is much faster for smaller particles ranging 10 to 50 microns. 

The heat rate through the walls only shows a mild variation for reverts particle size below 100 microns. This effect happens mainly because of the choice of the boundary conditions at the walls. The assumption of an overall heat transfer coefficient does not acquire the changes in the transfer mechanism on the hot-side of the cooled walls. In spite of this, the CFD models suggest that both cooling systems have less thermal load as reverts particle size decrease.

### **CONCLUSIONS AND RECCOMENDATIONS** 

From CFD model of the considered generic flash furnace, the following conclusions are extracted: 

- Reducing the particle from 1500 to around 100 microns does not produce a change in the MHC which is about 1 m below the top of the reaction shaft. Only for fine reverts particle sizes (below 75 microns), the MCH 

- increases, indicating that the conversion is delayed. 

- The MCH i

s strongly related with the ability of reverts particles to absorb sensible and latent heat. Large particles (around 1500 microns) absorb sensible heat, but do not reach melting temperatures, leaving the MCH practically unchanged. Small particles (around 75 microns) tend to absorb sensible and latent heat, which starts to shift the conversion height downwards, since the location where the critical temperature for concentrate reaction is lowered. 

- The impact of particle size in the heat absorbed by the walls is mild. However, the CFD models suggest that reducing reverts particle size may reduce the 

- thermal load of cooling systems. This could be caused by the choice of a heat transfer boundary condition at the water cooled walls, which may impose a more strained case that it really occurs in plant operations. Thus, it is recommended to perform a more detailed study on the mechanisms of heat transfer at the 

- interior walls of the RS. 

- In contrast to the above, heat absorbed by the off-gas into the settler shows a major overall decrease. This effect suggest that small reverts particles may be used to control the temperature at the outlet at the up-take of the furnace. However, this may increase the dust load and accretion formation in the up-take. 

- Increasing the shaft height for large reverts particle sizes does not change the MHC and allows a decrease in wall temperature only in the first half of the reaction shaft. Furthermore, although not shown here, the heat absorbed by reverts particles, walls and off-gas do not present any significant variation.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The processing of copper bearing materials is becoming more challenging due to the increase in their mineralogical and compositional complexity. 

Smelting of polymetallic concentrates is becoming more common and this trend has led to the requirement that smelters modify their operating strategies to remain cost competitive, whilst meeting ever more stringent environmental regulations. In addition, a key aspect in the recycling of secondary materials, including electronic scrap, is the diverse range of elements that require recovery. 

The increased complexity of these primary and secondary raw materials requires the use of advanced technologies to maximize the recovery of the targeted metals whilst maintaining sustainable operating practices. 

Glencore Xstrata plc, one of the world’s largest global diversified natural resource companies, has developed a number of processes at its operations, including ISASMELT™, the Albion Process™, and IsaKidd™ technologies that, b

oth individually and when combined, provide a competitive solution that enables the production of copper and associated by products from these complex feed stocks.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

In recent years, processing of complex polymetallic sulfide concentrates and recycling of secondary copper and waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) scrap have become a focus of attention for numerous smelters world wide. 

Traditional smelters have generally been designed to treat “standard clean concentrates”. Processing of polymetallic copper concentrates, characterized by relatively high levels of minor elements (over 5% of elements such as arsenic, antimony, bismuth, lead and zinc) is more challenging. If the facilities have not been designed for these types of materials significant plant modifications may be required. Often the incorporation of new technologies to pre-treat or directly treat these materials needs to be considered. 

The range of complex components used in modern electrical and electronic equipment with a relatively short life cycle means that recycling of secondary copper and WEEE is increasing. This new type of “urban mining” raw material is challenging the traditional metallurgical industry while creating opportunities to create new metallurgical processes. New smelter concepts, such as the Aurubis Lьnen Smelter and Umicore Hoboken Smelter have been developed to process these materials to maximize the recovery of copper and the other valuable metals contained in these waste materials [12]. 

This paper describes how technologies developed by Glencore Xstrata companies such as ISASMELT™, IsaKidd™, and Albion Process™ have been combined in different ways to meet the challenge of processing complex polymetallic concentrates, secondary copper and WEEE materials. 

### **TECHNOLOGY DESCRIPTIONS** 

### **ISASMELT™** 

The ISASMELT™ technology is now well established as one of the standard technologies for primary copper smelting [3-8]. The ISASMELT™ process was developed by Mount Isa Mines Limited (MIM – now part of the Glencore Xstrata group of companies) in the 1970s and 1980s. It is based on the top-submerged Sirosmelt lance, developed by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO – an Australian government research organization) in early 1970s, and involves using a lance to inject air or oxygen-enriched air into a slag bath contained within a stationary, vertical furnace. The lance contains a device to impart a swirl on the air forcing it against the internal wall of the lance, increasing the heat transfer from the wall to the air. This cools the lance and allows the formation of a protective layer of frozen slag to form on the outer wall of the lance, thus protecting it from the rigours of the environment inside the furnace. The result of the injection of the air directly into the slag is an intense smelting process in a highly turbulent bath, allowing the construction of plants with relatively low capital costs and smaller footprints than other base-metal sulfide smelting approaches. These plants are generally lower cost than alternative approaches and highly energy efficient. They use the chemical energy contained in the sulfide concentrates as the major source of energy for the smelting process. In typical base metal sulfide smelting applications, the technology also avoids the necessity for drying of raw materials by permitting filtered concentrate and residues to be mixed with fluxes and dropped directly into the furnace rather than requiring bone dry feed for injection through burners, lances, tuyeres or injectors. 

### **IsaKidd™ Tank House** 

Permanent cathode technology was developed by MIM and first implemented at Copper Refineries Pty Ltd (CRL) in Townsville, Australia in 1978. The technology eliminated the need for starter sheet cathodes and led the way to a reusable, automated

solution for copper electro-refining and electro-winning operations. Following this development the technology, known as ISA PROCESS™, gained extensive acceptance in the global copper industry [9]. The KIDD PROCESS was developed by Falconbridge for their Kidd Creek refinery in Timmins, Canada in 1985. Both technologies use permanent stainless steel cathode plates and highly automated material handling of anodes and copper cathodes. 

Following Xstrata’s acquisition of both MIM Holdings and Falconbridge, in 2002 and 2006 respectively, the ISA PROCESS™ and KIDD PROCESS were consolidated and are now marketed globally by Xstrata Technology as IsaKidd™ Technology. 

IsaKidd™ cathode plates are permanent, reusable cathodes with exceptionally high flatness tolerances, upon which full deposits of cathode copper are grown.  By careful control of material selection, fabrication, and operating parameters, the bond between the cathode copper and the cathode plate is sufficient to allow normal handling of the cathode plate, while still allowing the copper deposits to be stripped in the automatic stripping machines. 

The sizing and choice of materials for the cathode plates have been engineered and designed to optimize reliability, durability, corrosion resistance and economy of manufacture. IsaKidd™ stainless steel plates have proven themselves in many operations around the world for over 30 years in a wide variety of operating conditions. Today, over 11.7 million tonnes of refined and electro-won copper is produced annually utilizing IsaKidd™ cathode plates and know-how. 

### **Albion Process™Dust Leaching** 

The Albion Process™ was developed for atmospheric leaching of Glencore Xstrata’s bulk lead-zinc concentrates [10]. The process was subsequently modified for copper smelter dust leaching. The dust leaching process is an

oxidative acid leach. Oxygen/air is injected into a sulfuric acid liquor to dissolve both oxide and sulfide copper, iron and arsenic species from the dust. After dissolution, arsenic is precipitated and the precipitate disposed to tailings. Copper remains in solution, and is recovered by cementation onto copper concentrate and returned to the smelter to be recovered as anode. A commercial scale Albion Process™ dust leaching plant has been in operation in Mount Isa since 2004 and treats dust from the copper ISASMELT™ plant off-gas system. ### **ABSTRACT** 

Inefficient combustion has been shown to be the principal cause of a number of operational problems in Outokumpu flash smelting. A considerable volume of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and physical study results have been published on particular problems; however, more general investigations of the behavior of the flash smelting process have been rare. A review of a number of modeling studies and plantdriven practical burner improvement studies published to date has identified important parameters that affect performance. These have been further investigated using a “burner geometry independent” CFD model of the flash-smelting process, taking place in a hypothetical reaction shaft. The study confirms that high oxygen enrichment and velocity control are strong levers in controlling dust rates and combustion efficiency, while burner diameter and combustion gas / feed injection angle are aspects of design with a strong impact on performance. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

414 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Outokumpu flash smelting is currently the predominant method of primary copper production [ (1)] and a significant method of production for nickel [ (2)] from sulfide ores. It is widely acknowledged that poor performance of the concentrate burner can be implicated as the direct cause of, or a major contributing factor in many of the operational problems which can plague flash smelters. These include: 

- High dust production 

- Uptake accretions 

- Burner accretions 

- Low oxygen efficiency 

- High metal losses to slag 

- High or non-uniform reaction shaft heat loads leading to accelerated wear of the lining 

- Process variability (i.e., difficu

lties in controlling matte grade, furnace draft, etc.) Over the years, considerable effort has been expended by flash furnace operators, research institutes and equipment suppliers in order to ameliorate the above problems. These efforts, ranging from operational design changes, to computational modeling, to elaborate physical prototyping and plant trial studies, have produced a wealth of information on a variety of problems. This information has been used by the authors to identify a number of parameters for further study using computational methods, in an effort to establish general principles for the design and operation of an improved concentrate burner and the associated feeding equipment. This paper provides a brief summary of the computational studies that have been conducted as part of the burner development effort. ### **INVESTIGATION METHODOLOGY** ### **Identification of Parameters for Further Study** A comprehensive review of the literature was conducted to identify candidate parameters for use in the study. (10)(12)| ### **Generic Reaction Shaft Computational Model** The objective of the present study was to investigate a broad range of potential operating and design parameters in order to gain an understanding of their relative impact on burner performanc

e. Based on the parameters which were identified, it was decided that a steady-state, two-dimensional axisymetric geometry with a detailed reaction model would provide the most efficient platform for the study. The model was made to be “burner geometry independent”, meaning that the same calculation domain could be easily reconfigured for different burner sizes, process velocities etc. without requiring remeshing. While this approach imposed some additional limitations (discussed below) it had the advantage of reducing the considerable effort required for model preparation. The multiphase CFD model used a Lagrangian-Eulerian formulation and the k-ω SST turbulence model. Both convective and radiative heat transfer between the phases and reaction shaft walls was modeled. Key chemical reactions pertaining to the smelting _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 416 of a blended copper sulfide concentrate feed material were modeled by suitably adapting the particle-surface reaction and eddy-dissipation models available in ANSYS FLUENT. For a more detailed description of the modeling approach, see [13]. Three particle size groups were used to approximate the particle size distribution of the feed material. This was seen as an important feature of the model because the ignition of the concentrate relies on a “kindling chain” in which the smaller particles heat up and ignite first, providing the necessary heat to ignite the larger particles. Initial trial runs showed significant performance differences between uniform and multi-sized particle distributions (having identical mass-averaged diameter). This finding is consistent with the results presented in [14]. The reaction space geometry selected for the study was modeled to represent a furnace with a relatively small reaction shaft and a high specific smelting rate. It was reasoned that because of the high process intensity, this type of reaction shaft would exhibit greater sensitivity to changes in smelting conditions. All walls are treated as capture surfaces, with the surfaces being separated into roof, upper side wall and lower sidewall. This allows particle impacts with the wall to be quantified, which is used as a conservative approximation for the likelihood of accretion formation. 

### **Model Limitations** 

The model of this study suffers from the usual limitations inherent in computational modeling work; however, in contrast to recent studies, the simplifications that have been made for the sake of expediency and model flexibility have additional implications which are addressed below: 

- **Absence of burner nozzle:** In making the model “burner geometry independent” the feed chute and disperser have been omitted. This largely eliminates the influence of the burner outlet geometry on the mixing between the combustion gas and feed material. 

- **Agglomeration neglected:** Particle agglomeration is a difficult phenomenon to model, although at least one study has investigated its impact on computational models [15]. Agglomeration has a significant effect on dust particle size distributions which inherently affects dust carry-over. In the late 1980’s [16] proposed the twoparticle model of the flash smelting mechanism, which identified particle-particle collisions as an important heat and species transfer mechanism in the flash-smelting plume. Although the mechanism has been disputed by other researchers [17] burner 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

418 

designs and operating practices which follow the conclusions implied by the model have been successful [18]. Necessarily, since the present study does not incorporate the effects of the two-particle model or particle agglomeration, the performance of burner configurations featuring a high velocity, compact plume could be underestimated, while the dust carry-over rate is expected to be over-estimated. 

- **Axisymmetric model / absence of settler:** The use of an 2-D axisymmetric model is a well-known approach for reducing computational effort. The flash-smelting problem is, however, inherently not axisymmetric, because the reaction shaft is typically located at the end of a rectangular settler. In this case, the use of axisymmetry could exaggerate re-circulation patterns andyield a larger, lower velocity, exiting gas stream. Because the present study is concerned with the relative impacts of different design and operating parameters, complete fidelity with

respect to the recirculation zones and gas exit path is not required. - **Chemically-generated dust:** Volatile oxides and metallic species which evaporate in the plume can condense downstream in the settler, forming chemically-generated dust [19]. This effect is neglected in the present study. As a result, the dust generation rates for conditions which favor chemical dust generation (i.e., high flame temperatures) will be under-estimated by the model. It therefore comes as no surprise that combustion gas velocity is

one of the strongest parameters determining burner performance. Dust carry-over is significantly improved with higher combustion gas velocities, as shown in industrial practice [6, 20], with attendant reduction in uptake throat accretions [6, 12]. Based on the results of this study, these improvements come at the expense of a reduction in oxygen efficiency. The improved carry-over performance can be understood by analogy to a dust cyclone: higher combustion gas velocities at the burner outlet produce a faster jet near the bath. As the jet impinges on the bath and is deflected horizontally towards the settler, the particles continue along their vertical trajectory and become trapped by the bath. The lower oxygen efficiency can be likely attributed to the shorter residence time of particles entrained in the high velocity jet at the centre of the reaction shaft. 

Of the swirl intensities considered in this study, neither the low or high swirl case was beneficial relative to the baseline case. Because of the strength of the recirculation zone formed below the burner outlet, larger particles were ejected from the oxygen-rich plume to the oxygen-depleted periphery of the reaction shaft, leading to lower oxygen efficiency. In the high swirl case, the increased turbulence caused a significant increase in oxygen efficiency, however, the particles were violently ejected and either reacted close to the reaction shaft wall or impinged directly on the lining (see Figure 4). This produced high reaction shaft heat fluxes and represents an industrially impractical mode of operation. It is possible that the geometric simplifications inherent in the axisymmetric

### **Design Factors** 

Feed injection angle was the design parameter with the greatest impact on the performance metrics. Injection of the feed towards the centre of the reaction shaft (i.e., a more compact plume) resulted in significant reductions in the dust carry over, and the percentage of particles impacting the reaction shaft walls. As can be expected, the more compact plume suffered from poorer heat transfer with the surroundings, leading to delayed ignition of the core, and thereby produced poorer oxygen efficiency. For the case where the feed was injected away from the centerline (i.e., a more diffuse plume) the dust carry over increased significantly. Interestingly, the combustion performance did not improve dramatically, as the particles exited the oxygen-rich plume into the oxygendepleted periphery of the reaction shaft. This suggests that optimal performance can be achieved with a more vertical injection angle of the feed into the reaction shaft. This is analogous to the reduced dispersion air velocities noted to give improved dusting performance in [11].

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 424 Concentrate injection velocity was found to have a small impact on oxygen efficiency and dust carry over. The added momentum reduced residence time, leading to lower oxygen efficiency values for increased velocities. Similarly, the higher particle velocities at the foot of the reaction shaft produced a greater tendency for particles to slip from the stagnation gas flow and impact the bath, leading to a reduction in the mass flow rate of particles leaving the settler. The opposite was true for reduced injection velocities. A larger diameter annular burner opening was positively correlated with higher oxygen efficiency. This is likely due to the improvement in ignition characteristics that can be expected as a result of the feed forming a thinner annular “sheet” as it enters the reaction shaft. This sheet has a larger surface area for radiative and convective heat transfer and thus reaches the decomposition and ignition temperature higher in the reaction shaft. Conversely, the resulting wider annular jet loses momentum to the surrounding gas more readily, and hence the velocities at the bottom of the reaction shaft are somewhat lower in magnitude than for the baseline case. As a result, the dust carryover is slightly increased for a larger diameter burner. ### **Noise Factors** Particle size has a strong impact on all of the performance metrics. Smaller particles reach the ignition temperature higher in the shaft, creating a more intense reaction zone close to the shaft roof. This improves oxygen efficiency while simultaneously elevating the heat fluxes in the upper portion of the reaction shaft. The smaller particles are more readily entrained in the gas stream, leading to generally higher carry over rates, and higher rate of particle impacts with the reaction shaft wall. Throughput was found, surprisingly, to have relatively little impact on performance. Increasing throughput up to 4x the nominal case only significantly elevated the dust carry-over rate. Heat fluxes and oxygen efficiency were affected, but not to a great extent. This is consistent with industrial experience, which shows that several-fold increases in throughput are possible within a given reaction shaft [11]. Because the current model assumes that feed and combustion g

as enter into the reaction space premixed, the effect of throughput on the mixing characteristics of existing burner geometries is not captured in this study. This, ultimately, is likely to be the factor which limits the maximum theoretical throughput of a given burner. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A multi-parameter CFD study was conducted to establish the relative impacts of a number of parameters on the combustion performance of a flash-smelting system. For the parameters which were investigated, the trends in performance were consistent with industrial observations. Based on the results of the study, oxygen enrichment and 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

425 

combustion gas velocity are potent levers for affecting both oxygen efficiency and dust carry-over rates. Swirl and turbulence intensity are potential levers, although their use requires a more detailed study to avoid deleterious modes of operation. 

Feed injection angle and burner aperture size are also strong determinants of combustion performance. Larger burner nozzle diameters favor ignition, while having a small negative impact on dust carry-over.  Vertical or near-vertical injection of the concentrate appears to avoid negative impacts on ignition (associated with injection towards the centerline) and dust carry-over (associated with injection away from the centerline). Feed injection velocity has an effect analogous to combustion gas injection velocity, although with a smaller magnitude. 

As identified elsewhere, the particle size distribution has a very significant effect on the dusting and ignition / combustion characteristics of the burner. 

Of the parameters which were identified but not covered in this study, eliminating combustion gas spatial non-uniformity and feed inlet spatial and temporal non-uniformity is thought to be a promising for continued burner performance improvement. The authors are currently investigating these aspects of burner design for presentation in a future paper.

r had been used for solidification and granulation of copper smelting slag and then discharged back to the bay. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

Tamano Smelter & Refinery of Hibi Kyodo Smelting Co., Ltd. is located in Okayama prefecture, western part of Japan, facing to the beautiful Seto Inland Sea. Hibi Kyodo Smelting is a subsidiary of Pan Pacific Copper Co., Ltd., Japan’s largest copper producer and a joint venture between JX Nippon Mining & Metals Corp. and Mitsui Mining & Smelting Co., Ltd., and is jointly owned by Nittetsu Mining Co., Ltd. and Furukawa Metals & Resources Co., Ltd. Since the temperature of the molten slag discharged from slag cleaning furnace is 1,230~1,260  C, the temperature of water after slag granulation goes up to 60~70  C. 

If this hot water is used again in the system without cooling, the risk of phreatic explosion increases during the slag granulation. The vapor layer formed between the granulation water and the liquid slag becomes thinner when the water temperature is high, as a result, the water layer could contact with the molten slag directly. Therefore, it is necessary to reduce the water temperature before granulation down to that of the seawater in the previous system. 

In general, a Cooling Tower (CT) or a Plate type Heat Exchanger (PHE) is used for temperature reduction of process water. In the area where Tamano is located, industrial water supply is rather limited unfortunately, so we have to use expensive city water as makeup for big evaporation loss in case of CT application.

Condensation of the heavy metals in the circulating water could deteriorate slag quality not to be suitable for industrial use, increasing the soluble heavy metals in the dissolution test. We consulted with the Saganoseki Smelter & Refinery of Pan Pacific Copper, who has been operating the similar slag system since 2001. The following information from their experience, to reduce the heavy metal concentration in the circulating water in the granulation system and to maintain the product slag quality suitable for industrial application, was received.1) - The cause of heavy metal dissolution is minute SS, containing the heavy metals, adhered to water-granulated slag _Proceeding of Copper 2013_ _Santiago, Chile_ 434 - As heavy metal concentration in the circulating water increases, SS precipitates on the slag exceeding solubility product - To prevent heavy metal (especially As) dissolution from the slag, its concentration in the circulating water should be controlled below a certain level - To minimize heavy metal dissolution, proper management of pH of the circulating water is essential Taking the above mentioned information into consideration, the original design of the renovated slag granulation system was made by Tamano. ### Preventing As Condensation in the Circulating Water In order to prevent accumulation of the heavy metals in the circulating water, it is effective to bleed off a certain amount of circulating water from the system. Commonly, similar type of bleed-off water in the copper industry is processed in general waste water treatment plant together with drainage and waste water from other processes to remove heavy metals, and cleaned water is discharged to the environ

ment. 

At the designing stage of the project, Tamano’s waste water treatment plant did not have enough capacity to process the bleed-off from the slag granulation. Instead of expanding the waste water plant, construction of a new plant exclusively for the bleed-off water treatment (PBWT) was decided, not only to remove heavy metals but also to recycle treated water to the slag granulation system. 

The As concentration in the treated water at PBWT was designed to be below 0.1 mg/L. Based on the results of slag dissolution test, determined in the Public Notice No.18 of the Ministry of Environment of Japan, and the simulation from the water balance shown in Table 1, the amount of bleed-off water was determined to be 40 m<sup>3</sup> /h, in order to maintain the As concentration in the circulating water below a certain required level.

### **Process Design of PBWT for Recycling Water** 

In order to recycle treated bleed-off water to the granulation system, a two stage treatment process; 1<sup>st</sup> process to remove heavy metals by hydroxide co-precipitation and 2<sup>nd</sup> process to modify the water quality from the 1<sup>st</sup> process not to cause scaling problem, was studied and designed jointly with Kurita Water Industries Ltd. 

### <u>Selection of Fe/As Molar Ratio and Neutralizing Reagent</u> 

For selecting optimum Fe/As molar ratio and neutralizing reagent for the 1<sup>st</sup> process, laboratory tests were conducted using actual process water sample from the slag granulation system of Saganoseki Smelter & Refinery. 

The test procedure is summarized as follows, and the test conditions and results are shown in Table 2. 

- Prepare 500 mL of sample water for each test 

- Add polyferric sulfate to each sample 

- Add neutralizing reagent  and firstly rapid agitation for 5 minutes (at 120 rpm) , secondly slow agitation  for 20 minutes (at 60 rpm) 

- Stop agitation and add anionic flocculant 

A series of test results indicated that the optimal Fe/As molar ratio to attain the heavy metal concentration target after treatment is 22.8, and Ca(OH)2 works better than NaOH as a neutralizing reagent. The reason for better As removal by Ca(OH)2 is assumed that the compound formed with Ca(OH)2 works as a core of Fe-As complex precipitate and its solubility is smaller than that with NaOH. 

### <u>Design of the 1</u><sup>st</sup> <u>Process for Heavy Metal Removal</u> 

Based on the above mentioned test results, the 1<sup>st</sup> process for heavy metal removal was designed and established.  A schematic flow diagram of the process is shown in Figure 3.  Configuration of the processes is similar to the coagulation sedimentation process adopted in general. However, it has an unique element that a part of alkaline sludge pulled out from the thickener is sent to the chemical reaction tank. In this tank, anhydrous gypsum is formed by precipitating the oxy-hydroxide on the sludge surface

to accelerate dehydrating condensation reaction. ### **ABSTRACT** 

Conventional alumina-chromia materials are characterized by a high resistance to acidic slags due to the formation of an Al2O3-Cr2O3 solid solution during brick firing. Typical application areas for such products are glass tanks, waste incinerators, and taphole areas of pyrometallurgical vessels. However, in other regions, where not only corrosion due to chemothermal load but also thermal shock predominates, these products suffer from discontinuous spalling and exhibit poor refractory service life. Therefore, research and development activities were focused on increasing the thermal shock resistance of shaped alumina-chromia products. Since physical investigations and pilot scale slag tests indicated the properties of these improved materials were at a sufficiently high level, a field trial was conducted at a copper smelter. The mineralogical and chemical analyses of postmortem bricks installed in the tuyere zone of a Peirce-Smith converter demonstrated that the material properties of a new alumina-chromia product met both the corrosion and thermal shock resistance required for this application.

452 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The main raw materials used in alumina-chromia products are fused or calcined, based on alumina, chromium oxide, and prereacted (Al,Cr)2O3 solid solution materials. During brick firing an (Al,Cr)2O3 solid solution is additionally formed from pure Cr2O3 and Al2O3 materials. Furthermore, the presence of Cr2O3 reduces the dissolution potential when in contact with acidic slags, as demonstrated in several studies [1–2]. 

Besides the most common application areas in the glass and chemical industry, there is an increasing demand for alumina-chromia materials in the base metal industry, for example in copper production processes. Compared to basic bricks, alumina-chromia products are resistant to hydration. However, during service in chemically and thermally stressed areas conventional alumina-chromia products suffer from discontinuous spalling as a result of high and frequent thermal loads. As a consequence, products with sufficient resistance to both corrosion and thermal shock are required for these operating conditions. 

To develop refractory products tailored to specific service conditions it is important to have a profound knowledge of the metallurgical processes and furnace conditions [3–4]. This enables the specific refractory consumption to be minimized and increases the overall operational efficiency. Economic considerations such as steadily increasing energy and resource costs have resulted in companies investing in recycling processes. In the base metal industry like copper, recycling operations involve modifications to the smelter feed,

process conditions, and the chemical composition of process slags. This adversely affects the performance of standard linings and drives refractory producers to search for material innovations. To achieve this goal, laboratory investigations enabling brick development and experimental testing in RHI’s Pilot Plant at the Technology Center Leoben were performed before evaluating the material under practical conditions in a customer field trial. 

### **LABORATORY INVESTIGATIONS** 

The laboratory investigations comprised development, production, and physical evaluation of alumina-chromia materials, including rotary kiln slag tests to examine the corrosion resistance. 

### **Product Development** 

During the alumina-chromia material development phase, the Cr2O3 content, fused grain content, content of thermal shock reducing components as well as grain size distribution and firing conditions were identified as key factors influencing performance. Since modification of each parameter affects both the corrosion and thermal shock resistance of the refractory material, an appropriate balance between these key factors is indispensable. By controlling the grain size distribution, space can be created to accommodate thermal expansion or prevent crack propagation. However, the resulting 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

453 

surface area increases the dissolution potential with infiltrating liquids and gases. Therefore, the addition of fused grain is necessary to increase corrosion resistance by minimizing the specific crystal surface area. Ceramization of the products is influenced by the firing intensity; however, increasing this process results in the formation of stronger sinter bridges between the coarse grains and reduces thermal shock resistance. To increase thermal shock resistance, zirconia-containing components can be added, for example synthetically produced zirconia mullite. The mechanism is based on the irregular thermal expansion behaviour of baddeleyite (ZrO2) with increasing temperature: At room temperature the monoclinic form has a density of 5.6 g/cm<sup>3</sup> and is stable up to 1000 °C. Between 1000 °C and 1150 °C baddeleyite undergoes a tetragonal modification resulting in a density increase to 6.1 g/cm<sup>3</sup> . The structural transformation is reversible and as a consequence of the thermal expansion mismatch, microcracking occurs in the material that can diminish crack propagation during abrupt temperature changes. 

Laboratory trials were conducted to find the most effective balance between the aforementioned key parameters. The ideal composition was found when the Cr2O3 content was between 10–30 wt.%  and the zirconia component exceeded 10 wt.%. In addition, > 20 wt.% fused alumina-chromia grain was added to maintain the corrosion resistance at an appropriate level.

Typically, the standard grades used in a copper converter are magnesiachromite bricks (19 wt.% Cr2O3), and a thermal shock resistant grade based on chrome ore and high purity sintered magnesia (26 wt.% Cr2O3) at the tuyere line, since refractory _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 456 bricks in tuyere zones have to withstand a highly oxidizing atmosphere combined with · considerable temperature changes and attack by fayalithic slag (2FeO SiO2). Therefore, a 30 wt.% Cr2O3 alumina-chromia grade with increased thermal shock resistance was chosen for the trial. The bricks were installed in the converter both directly at the tuyere line and in the region surrounding the tuyeres. ### Field Trial Results The first evaluation took place during the scheduled converter shutdown after 11 weeks in operation. Samples for further analysis were taken from both test areas, although bricks at the tuyere line were only examined macroscopically. In this region the SR alumina-chromia bricks had a residual thickness of 80 mm, compared to the high purity sintered magnesia-chromite grade (26 wt.% Cr2O3) with a residual thickness of 30 mm. The bricks installed above the tuyere line were analysed in detail [5]. In this region, the residual thickness of the SR alumina-chromia grade was significantly higher (175 mm) compared to the standard magnesia-chromite grade (19 wt.% Cr2O3) with 95 mm; namely 47% of the SR alumina-chromia grade remained relative to the initial thickness, whilst the standard magnesia chromite grade had retained only 25% of the original thickness. When the converter was stopped after 117 heats, a second evaluation was performed. The SR alumina-chromia grade from the area surrounding the tuyeres exhibited a residual thickness of 240–250 mm, representing 65% of the initial thickness. The cross section through the sample is provided in Figure 4. On visual inspection an infiltration depth of 70 mm was determined. Below the slag/metal coating, covering the immediate brick hot face, there was a 1–2 mm thin reaction seam. In this reaction zone the Cr-corundum rims were enriched with Fe-Ni-Cu-Zn-oxide. Whilst the materials were found to exhibit a decrease in bulk density as well as hot and cold modulus of rupture compared to the standard products, laboratory investigations demonstrated both improved corrosion and thermal shock resistance of these hydration-resistant materials. To evaluate this brick type in a highly oxidizing atmosphere combined with significant temperature changes and acidic slag, a 30% Cr2O3 alumina-chromite grade was installed in the tuyere zone of a copper converter. The field trial results, including detailed chemical and mineralogical investigations of postmortem samples, confirmed that the thermal shock resistant alumina-chromia products can be successfully applied in areas experiencing high thermal stress combined with chemical attack from acidic melts and sulphur. Therefore, these new products will also be suitable for a number of other application areas in pri

mary copper smelting, converting, and refining.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The processing routes in the base metals industry, especially in the copper smelters showed recently significant changes especially in terms of slag chemistries, process temperatures and raw material mix in the primary smelter feed. All these parameters significantly influence the performance of already approved refractory linings. This acknowledgement of process-changes with decreased brick life-times due to increased wear rate influenced by temperature and chemical attack of furnace linings- confirmed also through the results of the post mortem studies - were the signal for RHI AG to spend a certain priority on the development of so called high grade refractory bricks especially for installation in chemically highly stressed areas (slag lines, tap-holes, furnace end walls)of for example copper furnaces. In order to determine the most suitable refractory products and to improve the lining life of the latter innovative product development has to be performed. In addition to that the practical corrosion testing methods and facilities at RHI’s Technology Center such as for example induction furnace, rotary kiln, drip slag test and cup test allows the best possible understanding of the brick wear on the pilot scale. Testing has been performed with fayalithic and calcium-ferritic slag at different temperatures. A complete mineralogical investigation including thermodynamic calculations with FactSage has been performed. Based on the results after this test-work,the optimal refractory solution based on the detected main wear mechanism in the laboratory, can be recommended for a field trial directly at the customer on real process conditions on site.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

In order to improve the performance of furnace linings especially for non-ferrous metal industry, test procedures must be develo

ped to simulate the various demanding service conditions. The complexity of metallurgical processes in the extractive metallurgy of copper especially changes in the process conditions (temperature, slag chemistry, Red/Ox-conditions, etc.) in combination with diversity of metal processing furnaces [1] requires a precise knowledge of the system for the appropriate refractory product selection [2]. However, particular importance is still focused on the specific refractory consumption being as low as possible. The economical aspect should be also considered based on production losses influenced by possible furnace shut-downs using/installing non suitable brick grades in critical furnace areas. High grade refractory brands contain high purity raw materials with low secondary phases which lead to a significant higher price level compared to standard grades. Nevertheless the higher investment to install high grade refractories in copper furnaces is not comparable to the production benefit by an improved lining performance. Another important aspect is given by the global shortage of resources forcing companies to put more and more effort on recycling processes [3]. The raw material mix of primary smelters has also changed to a higher amount of secondary raw materials in the smelter feed. 

In order to determine the suitable refractory products and to improve the lining life especially for the copper processing furnaces innovative product development has to be performed. In addition to that, the practical corrosion testing methods and facilities within the RHI Technology Center Leoben such as an induction furnace, rotary kiln, cup test etc. together with mineralogical investigation enable a comprehensive understanding of brick wear following pilot scale trials [4-5]. Based on the results after testing the optimal refractory solution can be recommended for a field trial directly at the customer site. 

### **CORROSION TESTING FACILITIES** 

In order to  establish and to compare the corrosion resistance of the newly developed brick brands to already approved bricks rotary furnace- and induction furnace tests with processing slag of fayalithic- and calcium-ferritic type were carried out in the pilot plant of the RHI Technology Center Leoben, located in Austria. 

In the induction furnace up to 16 different grades with 4-5 different grades can be lined (Figure 1). The furnace diameter is 250 mm and the temperature range between 1500°C and 1750°C (1650°C in the present case). For the practical testing up to 60 kg metal and slag (1,5-2 kg/cycle) are used. The customer provided process slag is changed every 0,5-1,5 hour to achieve a constant high corrosive effect against installed refractory material.

### **WEAR PHENOMENA OF BASIC BRICK LININGS IN THE COPPER INDUSTRY** 

D. Gregurek and Ch. Majcenovic _RHI AG Technology Center Leoben Magnesitstrasse 2 A-8700 Leoben, Austria dean.gregurek@rhi-ag.com_

### **ABSTRACT** 

In the non ferrous metals industry particulary in the copper smelting furnaces the refractory lining made of magnesia-chromite bricks is exposed to several stresses rather complex in their interaction. These can be classified as chemical, thermal and mechanical stresses occurring as a single wear factor or in combination. The chemical factors include corrosion caused by acidic slag and gaseous SO2 diffusion, redox effects and in particular cases hydration. In most of the non-ferrous metallurgical processes the chemothermal load by Fe-silicatic slags of fayalithic type is a common wear mechanism of the magnesia-chromite bricks.

Nevertheless the extraordinary massive SiO2-supply caused by changes in the processing and the uncontrolled addition of silica sand results in a severe formation of forsterite respectively in a volume expansion due to “forsterite bursting”. Increased temperature level respectively changes in the temperature during the furnace operation as well as the copper metal infiltration into the brick microstructure are further wear factors on thermal side. The hot erosion is the dominant mechanical factor. Therefore understanding of wear mechanisms through “post mortem investigation” and praxis field trials are highly important to ensure product recommendation for industrial application.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Service stresses and wear phenomena on the working lining in the copper processing furnaces are neither constant nor easily understandable. In the non-ferrous metals industry, especially in copper smelting, there is a variety of different process routes, for example Outokumpu, Inco, Kivcet, Noranda, Teniente, Mitsubishi, TBRC, and Ausmelt [1]. Additionally, there are numerous furnace types; for instance in the case of copper production flash smelters, reverberatory furnaces, Isasmelters, TBRC converters, Pierce-Smith converters, six in line sub arc furnaces, and anode furnaces are used. The working lining in all these units mostly consists of magnesia and/or magnesiachromite bricks [2]. The complexity of metallurgical processes and diversity of copper processing furnaces requires a precise knowledge of each individual system for appropriate refractory product selection. Since particular importance is also placed on the specific refractory consumption being as low as possible, innovative product development is imperative to provide suitable refractory products that meet the diverse operating conditions. 

Moreover, the complex and mutual reactions which take place within the refractories in practical operations are many sided and complicated. With this contribution it is intended to present various factors which can affect the bricks in the copper processing furnaces and to show how magnesia-chromite bricks behave in this conditions. The latter is based not only on many years of experience through post mortem studies but also on additional laboratory work and experimental testing in the pilot plant of the RHI´s Technology Center Leoben [3-4]. 

To achieve this goal and improve the lining life, post mortem investigations are essential because they provide the best possible understanding of the brick wear mechanisms occurring during operation. Based on the research results combined with specific process operation knowledge, product development together with the marketing department recommend appropriate brick lining solutions for any metallurgical furnace. 

### **WEAR PHENOMENA** 

The observed wear phenomena can generally be subdivided into chemical, thermal, and mechanical stresses [4-6]. These c

an appear as a single stress factor; but as a rule combinations of these stresses occur and affect the lining. The most common chemothermal wear mechanisms influencing the basic brick lining in copper processing furnaces are corrosion by acidic slags, sulphate attack, redox effects and particulary hydration. Increased temperature level respectively changes in the temperature during the furnace operation as well as the copper metal infiltration into the brick microstructure are further wear factors on a thermal side. The hot erosion is the most dominant mechanical wear factor. In this publication the following wear mechanisms are presented in detail: Corrosion by Fe-silicatic (a fayalithic slag type) and Ca-ferritic slags, forsterite bursting, sulphate attack as well as hydration.

### - <u>Corrosion by Fe Silicatic (Fayalithic) Slag and Forsterite Bursting</u> 

The most common chemothermal wear in the copper processing furnaces is corrosion by acidic, Fe-rich (fayalithic) slag type. As a result of infiltration by the fayalithic slag, degeneration of the brick’s microstructure takes place. Within the infiltrated brick zone or at the interface between the infiltrated and original brick microstructure, cracks parallel but also vertical to the brick hot face can be observed macroscopically. In addition, short running cracks with rounded edges—softening cracks—can also be recognized. The immediate brick hot face is frequently covered with a slag/metallic-rich coating. 

At a microscopic level, several zones can be distinguished. Below the slag/metal coating, covering the immediate brick hot face, there is usually a thin reaction zone followed by an infiltrated and corroded brick microstructure. As can be seen in Figure 1 (left) , within the reaction zone there is severe dissolution of the magnesia brick component frequently leaving relics of chromite and primary and secondary chromite precipitations. 

In the infiltrated and corroded brick microstructure, due to corrosion of the brick inherent magnesia (coarse grains and matrix fines), the main reaction products are (calcium)-magnesium silicates of a forsterite (Mg2SiO4), merwinite (Ca3MgSi2O8) and monticellite (CaMgSiO4) type (Figure 1 (right)). Also the interstitial phase of the magnesia component, especially dicalcium silicate, is corroded. 

In general, the second main brick component chromite is not corroded compared to the magnesia but due to diffusion phenomena has a changed chemical composition. The reason for this is the fact that periclase (MgO) is more basic than chromite and therefore more susceptible to acidic corrosion.

<u>Sulfate attack</u> 

Another very common type of chemothermal attack is corrosion by sulfates. The penetration of gaseous SO2 from the oxidation of sulfidic matte creates the prerequisite for the SO3 to react below temperatures of approximately 1100°C with basic oxides of the magnesia-chromite brick leading to formation of earth alkaline sulfates (MgSO4 and CaSO4) (Figure 5). 

The intensity of a sulphate corrosion depends on the amount of supplied SO2. The surplus of acidic SO2 versus the basic components of the infiltrate such as alkalines, CaO, reaction temperature; reaction time but also brick properties such as porosity, bonding strength, kind of bonding, brick composition etc. For instance in case of overheated salt melts the solubility of CaO and MgO drastically increases and the corrosion can be much more severe. 

At further temperature increases the formed MgSO4 breaks down at temperatures of approximately >1000°C and forms fine crystalline MgO again.

### <u>Hydration</u> 

Generally hydration of basic bricks can occur in humid atmospheres preferably at temperatures between 40°-120°C. It is characterised by the transformation of periclase (MgO) into brucite (Mg(OH)2) according to the reaction: 

### MgO + H2O  Mg(OH)2 

This reaction is combined with an increase in volume of up to 115%. Additionally, the formation of brucite (Figure 6) is accompanied by an expansion of the crystal lattice because of the oriented growth of the hexahedral brucite on the cubic periclase. Therefore the space between the magnesium ions within the brucite is larger than in the periclase. Due to this reaction the periclase crystals are separated after the natural, crystallographical cleavage planes. The resulting “microcracks” represent new reaction surfaces, which show a high tendency towards hydration. This leads to a chain

### **CONCLUSION** 

Post mortem studies demonstrated

that as consequence of fayalithic and Caferritic slag attack, the infiltration and corrosion of the brick’s inherent components led to a softening of the bricks microstructure, loss of flexibility, and brick strength. This weakened microstructure was then susceptible to continuous wear by hot erosion. Additionally, due to the changed thermomechanical properties, thermal shock led to crack formation primarily at the interface between the infiltrated and non-infiltrated brick area and finally to discontinuous wear by spalling. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

482 

Compared to fayalithic slag attack, the consequence of corrosion by Ca-ferritic slag was a higher infiltration depth, and corrosion not only of the basic magnesia component but also the chromite and formation of low melting Mg-Fe-oxide (magnesiowustite). 

In magnesia-chromite bricks the chemothermal load caused by massive SiO2 supply resulted in the formation of forsterite, an associated volume expansion, and so called forsterite bursting. Such a wear phenomenon is very seldom experienced in nonferrous metal applications but is quite typical for regenerator chambers in the glass industry when there is extreme SiO2 carry-over. 

The consequence of the severe sulfate infiltration is corrosion of the brick inherent components (the CaO-containing secondary phase and MgO) which leads to a weakening of the bricks bonding strength, crack formation and discontinuous wear by spalling. The second brick component, chromite is not affected by sulfate attack. 

The detailed investigation of wear mechanisms is an important prerequisite for the refractory producer, since it provides the basis for both customer recommendations and innovative product development. It can clearly highlight which specific stresses affect refractory products in the various copper processing furnaces, and this is imperative since all these wear mechanisms can lead to a severe degeneration of the brick microstructure and a decreased lining life. 

On the basis of the investigation results, combined with long-term service experience, the most appropriate choice for the furnace wear lining can be made. This is frequently enhanced through active collaborations with the customer. Moreover, due to the variety of copper processes and steadily improving process technologies, the stresses on the brick lining are changing. Therefore, it is absolutely necessary for the refractory producer to develop innovative products with improved performance to meet future operating conditions.

### **THE EFFECT OF IN-SITU PHASE FORMATION ON THE INFILTRATION AND CHEMICAL DEGRADATION OF MAGNESIA-CHROMITE BRICKS IN CONTACT WITH A SYNTHETIC NON-FERROUS SLAG** 

L. Scheunis, P.T. Jones, B. Blanpain and A. Malfliet _Department Metallurgy and Materials Engineering KU Leuven Kasteelpark Arenberg 44, Box 2450 3001 Heverlee, Belgium lennart.scheunis@mtm.kuleuven.be_

### **ABSTRACT** 

To have a robust smelting process it is essential to be able to rely on a long refractory life. In case of Cu-smelters, life times of two and more years can be obtained. In these processes a fayalite slag is used. However, in processes operated with a PbO slag, the refractory life time is often lower. A major difference between both slags lies in the infiltration behavior of the slag; PbO slags can infiltrate the porous lining much deeper, attacking a larger part of the lining. In this paper the chemical degradation of magnesia-chromite refractory material in contact with a deeply infiltrating synthetic PbO-SiO2-Al2O3-“Fe2O3“ based slag is investigated. The results indicate the formation of two new phases inside the refractory sample: (1) a new spinel phase, rich in aluminum and iron, forming near the contact surface with the bath and (2) a forsterite (Mg2SiO4) phase forming deeper inside the sample. Unlike forsterite, the new spinel phase forms a dense protective layer, limiting the dissolution of the MgO into the liquid slag. The main dissolution of the lining does therefore not occur at the first contact area between the refractory lining and the unsaturated slag but deeper inside the sample when the protective layer is no longer formed. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

486 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Magnesia-chromite refractory bricks are used in the linings of several industrial pyrometallurgical furnaces, including those for copper production, because of their high melting point, good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures and their ability to withstand the aggressive conditions inside the furnace. Despite these properties, lining wear still occurs due to the combination of chemical, mechanical and thermal stresses, eventually requiring a relining, leading to significant material costs as well as production shutdown episodes. 

The chemical attack is often the primary driver for degradation and strongly af

fects the final failure. It consists of: (1) the dissolution of the refractory components into the liquid slag [1], (2) the diffusion of slag components into the refractory phases [14] and (3) the in-situ formation of new phases [3, 5]. In the infiltrated part of the brick the chemical reaction can lead to a weakening of the microstructure by either dissolving the bonds between the different phases or by the formation of new phases, leading to a volume expansion and internal stresses, either during reaction or during temperature variations of the furnace. The weakened structure is no longer able to withstand the thermal and mechanical stresses, aggravating the mechanical and thermal wear in the infiltrated part of the brick and significantly accelerating the overall wear rate. 

The formation of new phases can, however, also be positive if the new phase forms a protective layer between the refractory phases and the slag, causing the dissolution of the lining to slow down as the refractory components have to diffuse through the new solid layer. This effect is called indirect dissolution [6]. Examples are the formation of forsterite (Mg2SiO4) [2, 7] (for silica containing systems) and spinel (Mg(Al,Fe,Cr)2O4) phases (for alumina [6] and iron oxide [8] containing systems). 

In the primary pyrometallurgical production of copper less noble elements present in the ores are oxidized to the slag. The main components being removed are S and Fe, the iron forms a fayalite slag together with the silica fluxed to lower its liquidus temperature. The interaction between a fayalite slag and a magnesia-chromite brick is well known [9, 10]. The MgO from the refractory dissolves into the slag, while the slag reacts with the lining forming, olivine phases, a new spinel phase and a MgO-FeO solid solution [2], thereby removing the iron from the slag as it infiltrates and reacts further with the refractory lining. As a result the silica content of the slag increases deeper in the lining. With the silica content also the viscosity of the slag increases, slowing down the infiltration. In addition the liquidus temperature also increases, eventually freezing the slag inside the lining, stopping further infiltration and reactions. 

Beside iron also other impurities present in the ores are oxidized to the slag and can significantly influence the degradation of the lining. One such example is PbO. In a PbO-SiO2 system it will not react directly with the refractory lining but will lower the 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

487 

viscosity and the liquidus temperature of the slag, leading to a much deeper infiltration. When the reactive components are removed from the liquid by forming new phases and solid solutions with the refractory phases, the PbO concentration of the slag increases in the lining. So an even limited amount of PbO in the slag can significantly affect the refractory degradation deep inside the lining. 

Slags with an even higher PbO content c

an be formed during the production of copper from secondary resources. For example when recycling dross from decoppering of lead bullion, which contains both copper and lead. A typical secondary copper smelter recycles multiple smelting and refining residues. For example the first step of Umicore’s Hoboken plant consists of separating the feed into a PbO containing slag and a Cu bullion [11]. 

To investigate the effect that a fast infiltrating slag has on the chemical degradation of a refractory lining, a PbO based slag is used in this paper. “Fe2O3” and SiO2 are fluxed in order to investigate the formation of spinel and forsterite phases. Al2O3 is added in addition to “Fe2O3” to stimulate the formation of spinel phases which can form a protective layer on the MgO containing phases. 

### **EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE** 

The experimental procedure consists of a standard static finger test at constant temperature (see Figure 1). The materials used consist of a commercially available fused grain rebounded magnesia-chromite brick and a synthetic PbO-SiO2-Al2O3-“Fe2O3”-CaO slag. Prior to the experiment the refractory sample is cut in a bar shape (20x15x100 mm³). The slag is produced by mixing different pure oxide powders in the desired ratio. The composition of the bath at the start of the experiment is 47.5 wt% PbO, 11.9 wt% SiO2, 21.2 wt% Fe2O3, 16.3 wt% Al2O3 and 0.8 wt% CaO, as, determined by standardized XRF. The total weight of the mixture is 1.5 kg. It is heated in open air at a rate of 600 °C/hour in a 1 liter Al2O3 crucible using an induction furnace until a temperature of 1300 °C is reached. At the desired temperature, the refractory finger, which is heated together with the crucible, is partially submerged into the liquid slag bath. After a reaction time of 1 hour the sample is taken out of the bath and quenched in water in order to preserve the high temperature microstructure in the best possible way. 

After the test the finger is cut using a diamond saw. The section is made parallel with and 1 cm below the slag bath line (see Figure 1). To analyze this section, it is embedded in an epoxy resin and polished. After coating the sample with a conducting carbon layer, both its microstructure and the composition of the different phases are analyzed using a full quantitative EPMA-WDS (JEOL JXA-8530F) system. It was operated using an acceleration voltage of 15 kV and a probe current of 15 nA. The oxygen content is not measured directly; instead the oxidation state of the element was selected a priori. Although both Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> can be present in the sample under consideration here, only “Fe2O3” was selected for presentation purposes.

### **Reaction mechanisms** 

Combining the results of the microstructure and the slag composition, it is possible to determine the reaction mechanisms controlling the chemical degradation. According to Figure 3 the new spinel phase forms at the hot face. In Figure 4 there is a drop in the Al2O3 and “Fe2O3” content of the infiltrating slag at this position. The reaction forming these new spinel phases will therefore be:

The formation mechanism of the new spinel phase at the hot face on both the fused grains and the original primary chromite grains is investigated in more detail using compositional line scans. 

To facilitate the analysis of the results, the iron oxide inside the spinel phases in Figure 5 is separated into FeO and Fe2O3 based on the principle that only Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>2+</sup> can occupy the A position in the AB2O4 spinel structure. The sum of FeO and MgO thus has to account for 50 mol%, the remainder of the iron oxide being present as Fe2O3. A similar analysis could not be performed for the liquid slag or the fused grains. The iron present in these phases will be a mixture of FeO and Fe2O3 but is depicted as “Fe2O3” for representation purposes only. 

The spinel phase growing on top of the fused grain shows a constant concentration in Al2O3 and Fe2O3. The concentration in MgO shows a gradient decreasing from the fused grain to the liquid bath while FeO shows the opposite trend. The growth rate of the spinel phase thus appears to be controlled by the counter diffusion of MgO and FeO. Once the MgO diffuses through the newly formed spinel phase, it reacts with the liquid slag to form additional spinel. 

The same behavior for MgO and FeO can be seen for the new spinel forming on top of the original primary chromite grain. The main difference is that the Fe2O3 and Al2O3 concentrations do not remain constant but decrease towards the primary chomite grain. The reason for this can be seen in the Cr2O3 diffusion profile. This component is present inside the chromite and will thus diffuse into the newly formed spinel layer, taking the place of Al2O3 and Fe2O3. 

Due to the formation of new spinel phases, the concentration of spinel forming components decreases with infiltrati

on distance (see Figure 4) until the formation of these phases is no longer possible. At this point forsterite becomes the dominant new phase. The formation of this phase requires the removal of silica from the bath, explaining the decrease in this component seen in Figure 4 in zone b. 



The dissolution of the refractory into the liquid bath is closely related to these phase formations. The spinel phases act as a protective layer slowing down the dissolution of the magnesia into the liquid slag. This can be seen in the diffusion profile in Figure 5 where the MgO has to diffuse through the solid spinel phase before it can be dissolved in the liquid bath. When the new spinel phase no longer forms a continuous layer (see Figure 3c), the dissolution of MgO in the slag increases significantly (Figure 4). The subsequent decrease in MgO concentration with depth is due to the removal of SiO2 (by forsterite formation), causing the MgO solubility to decrease [14].
