### **CONCLUSIONS** 

This paper discusses the interaction between a fused grain magnesia-chromite brick and a synthetic PbO-SiO2-“Fe2O3”-Al2O3 in order to investigate the effect of deep slag infiltration on the lining degradation. The results show that the reaction between the infiltrating slag and the refractory lining causes the composition of the slag to change with position. As a result the local microstructure, which is controlled by the local slag composition, will also change throughout the sample. In the investigated sample new spinel phases form near the liquid slag bath, while deeper inside the sample forsterite was the dominant new phase formed. This also directly influences the chemical degradation of the lining. The new spinel phase acts as a protective layer, slowing down the MgO dissolution into the slag. Deeper inside the sample the spinel layer is no longer formed and the MgO from the refractory can dissolve unhindered into the liquid slag.

# **THE USE OF ALUMINA-CHROME REFRACTORIES IN THE HIGH WEAR AREAS OF ANODE REFINING VESSELS** 

A. J. Rigby 

_Harbison Walker Refractories, Cherrington Corporate Center, 400 Fairway Drive Moon Township, Pittsburgh, PA U.S.A._ 

Keywords: _Anode refining, alumina-c

hrome refractories, tuyeres, skim mouth, tapholes, charging mouth, copper oxide_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Refractory lining designs based on products containing direct-bonded or rebonded fused grain magnesia-chrome have been the industry-wide standard for anode refining vessels in all primary copper smelters. These linings are usually zoned with the denser rebonded fused grain material at the severe wear areas at the tuyeres, taphole, skimming ports and charging mouth. This zoning aids to improve the lining performance in these areas but commonly the vessels must be taken out of service every 4-6 months for maintenance. It has been shown in the past that wear mechanisms leading to severe joint penetration at the skimming ports and significant spalling of the brick in the tuyere areas are a result of copper oxide penetration and reaction. 

Early trials of alumina-chrome monolithics and bricks containing 30% chromic oxide have shown remarkable resistance to copper oxide slags. Chemical analysis and microscopical examination of laboratory test samples and refractory products recovered from the field illustrate that the matrix of the refractory rich in chromic oxide reacts with the penetrating copper oxide slag to form a refractory reaction layer that prevents further ingress of the slag. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

498 

### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

Over the past several decades, there has been a determined attempt to optimize the microstructural, chemical, and fracture properties of the magnesia-chrome refractories used in non-ferrous pyrometallurgical vessels. Furthermore, lining design concepts involving larger and longer brick and the extent and positioning of expansion allowance have been extensively trialled. Some benefits have been achieved by increasing the heat flux through the lining by removing any insulation at the shell/working lining interface. All these efforts have provided some significant, but not startling, improvements<sup>1</sup> . The simple fact is that a vessel lining composed of bricks with an optimized microstructure and chemical inertness, even when installed with a well-conceived design, can rapidly deteriorate if the process parameters are not sensibly controlled. 

It is the intent of this paper to emphasize that alumina-chrome linings can better withstand even the most severe environments within an anode vessel. These environments are present locally above the tuyeres, at the slag skimming mouth and the taphole areas. When the commonly experienced severe wear at these specific areas is avoided this will result in both exceptional extensive vessel integrity and reduced processing costs. In summary, alumina-chrome monolithic and shaped fired refractories can withstand corrosion and penetration by overheated slags rich in copper oxide. 

### **2. REFRACTORY QUALITY** 

Molten copper has little if no affinity for refractory oxide furnace linings. Channel induction furnaces used to melt cathode copper are line

d with inexpensive fireclay products and operate continuously without repair for up to four years.  However, these furnaces utilize a layer of charcoal or low sulphur coke to eliminate any possibility of forming copper oxide slag by contact of the molten bath with oxygen in the atmosphere. 

Converting and anode refining are conducted by injecting air into the molten matte and blister copper for the very purpose of generating iron and copper oxide slags. These slags must be contained by a refractory that, by its mineralogical formulation, is optimized for chemical inertness. 

Magnesia-chrome bricks with approx. 60% MgO have been found to have this chemical inertness in part due to the fact that by high-temperature firing (~1720ºC) the MgO portion of the product has been pre-reacted and saturated with iron and chromic oxide. Copper with over 0.1% O2 can penetrate magnesia-chrome bricks readily and lead to severe bloating and spalling as in-situ oxidation takes place. This copper penetration can occur to a depth of 25-30 cm. if the lining is insulated with SDFB brick or insulating paper or blanket. The magnesia component of the refractory brick lining at the hot face reacts with the copper oxide to form an expansile solid solution CuO-MgO phase called 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

499 

guggenite (2CuO.MgO). This expansion will often lead to spalling of the hot face in 4-5 cm. thick layers. (see fig.1) 

Typical magnesia-chrome product suitable for the bottom and roof areas of anode vessels need not be especially formulated for environments where penetration and corrosion by copper oxide rich slag is expected. 

However, in the areas of anode vessels where copper oxide penetration resistance takes precedence, the bricks must be formulated to provide for the highest chemical passivity and lowest permeability and porosity. The one key feature of alumina-chrome refractories containing 30% chromic oxide is the very significant resistance to penetration by copper oxide containing slags.

### **3. LINING DESIGN CONCEPTS** 

A well-engineered design for an anode vessel will effectively zone the high wear areas with suitably resistant products and ensure the lining is in excellent thermal contact with the vessel steel shell.  Maximizing the thermal contact aids in producing a steep thermal profile, which minimizes penetration of slag into the hot face of the lining, subsequently reducing the corrosion rate of the brick.  In some cases, a graphitecontaining mastic should be employed to safeguard against air gaps between the cold face of the brick and the steel shell. 

However, in many areas of these processing vessels, the localized heat loss will be sufficient to produce a build-up of frozen slag/matte and/or copper metal, which lowers the effective

working volume of the vessel.  The lining in this instance should be effectively insulated to allow the working hot face of the lining to operate at a higher temperature.  Microporous insulation has been shown to alleviate frozen slag/metal deposition in several areas of anode vessels.<sup>2</sup> 

### 3.1 <u>Anode Vessel Lining Design History</u> 

The original concept of using chromic oxide containing refractories was developed in a copper smelter that was using siliceous slags to remove contaminating lead values from the anode copper. The skimming lip of the anode vessel mouth was normally lined with rebonded fused magnesia-chrome bricks installed in place with a standard magnesia-chrome mortar. After three months the skimming lip would regularly require gunning maintenance to continue in operation. It was found that when the typical magnesia-chrome mortar was replaced with a phosphate-bonded alumina-chrome mortar a significant improvement in life was achieved. (see fig. 2). This success spurred a trial of alumina-chrome brick and subsequent trials showed that the skimming mouth life could be extended to over nine months without repair or gunning maintenance if the chromic oxide content of the mouth bricks was in the order of 30%.

The copper oxide was placed in slag cup samples at temperatures of 1400<sup>o</sup> C  which is far in excess of the typical working temperatures. ### **4.  SUMMARY** 

It is certainly quite apparent that any improvement to the overall refractory life of an anode refining vessel requires zoning of the most severe localized wear areas with particularly corrosion resistant materials. In the areas of the lining where frequent contact with turbulent high temperature copper oxide slag occurs there is little doubt that the use of alumina-chrome brick is warranted. Indeed these results illustrate a much more important over-arching indication as to further use in other areas of non-ferrous smelters. It has been reported<sup>3</sup> that alumina-chrome linings in an Ausmelt furnace at China Copper Ltd. have performed far better than previous magnesia-chrome linings. During slag penetration into the brick matrix the FeO within the slag and Cr2O3 and Al2O3 from the brick matrix reacted and formed a relatively impenetrable FeO.Cr2O3.Al2O3 spinel layer at the working surface of the lining. 

Alumina-chrome refractories were initially developed to withstand the extreme rigours of use in applications such as coal gasifiers, soda-lime glass furnaces and high wear areas of steel reheat furnaces where high temperature fluid iron oxide and siliceous slags are

present. There is a very high probability that extending the application of this class of chromic oxide containing refractories into other specific high wear areas of the smelting and converting vessels of copper, nickel and lead smelters will yield similarly remarkable improvements in lining life.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Improvements to industrial copper production can be made through informed decisions on the selection of slag compositions, fluxing strategies, and operating conditions for a given feed and product requirement. This can be facilitated through thermodynamic modelling in which phase equilibrium, partitioning of major and minor elements between phases, activities, vapour pressure, and other thermodynamic properties of the relevant systems can be accurately predicted over a wide range of process conditions. The “Cu2O”-Al2O3-CaO-FeO-Fe2O3-MgO-SiO2-S system is of importance for copper smelting, converting, and slag-cleaning processes. New experimental data of the systems for various compositions and conditions relevant to copper production process have been generated and improvement of the existing chemical thermodynamic FactSage<sup>TM</sup> database for the cuprous oxide-containing system has been carried out as part of the overall integrated research program on complex copper-containing slag-matte-metal-solids system. All cuprous oxide-containing binaries, ternaries, and multi-components systems are optimized simultaneously to obtain one self-consistent set of model parameters for Gibbs energies of stoichiometric phases, solid solutions, and liquid solution as functions of temperature and composition. Details of the recent optimization of the thermodynamic database and examples of industrial application of the database for the high-temperature copper making processes are pr

esented.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The “Cu2O”-Al2O3-CaO-FeO-Fe2O3-MgO-SiO2-S system is important for copper smelting, converting, and slag cleaning processes. An accurate evaluation and optimization of the system has been hindered by previously lack of reliable data, especially in the conditions of equilibrium with metallic copper. New experimental data of the systems for various compositions and conditions relevant to copper production process have been generated as part of the overall research program on complex copper system in PYROSEARCH-UQ combining experimental and thermodynamic modeling studies. 

In this article, further improvement of the previously existing chemical thermodynamic FactSage<sup>TM</sup> database for the system is outlined. The previously available data and new experimental data of the system are critically evaluated and then used to obtain a set of model parameters for Gibbs free energies of molten slag phase as functions of temperature and composition. Industrial application of the database for the copper metallurgical process is discussed. 

### **PHASES AND THERMODYNAMIC MODELS** 

Thermodynamic databases are developed through thermodynamic optimization that involves selection of proper thermodynamic models for all phases in a system, critical simultaneous evaluation of all available thermodynamic and phase equilibrium data and optimization of thermodynamic model parameters to obtain one self-consistent set of model equations for the Gibbs energies of all phases best reproducing the experimental data as functions of temperature and composition. From these equations, the thermodynamic properties and the phase diagrams can be back-calculated.  Thermodynamic property data, such as activity data, can aid in the evaluation of the phase diagrams, and phase diagram measurements can be used to deduce thermodynamic properties. Discrepancies in the available data can be identified during the development of the model.  These discrepancies can then be resolved through new experimental studies that, if possible, are undertaken in areas essential for further thermodynamic optimizations. Multi-component data, if available, are used to derive low-order (binary and ternary) model parameters, and if multi-component data for a system are lacking, the low-order parameters are extrapolated. In this way, the thermodynamic databases are developed and all the data are rendered self-consistent and in concordance with thermodynamic principles. The FactSage<sup>TM</sup> thermodynamic software package [1] was used to perform the thermodynamic optimization in the present study. 

No significant concentration of Al, Ca, Mg or Si was found in the liquid copper alloy and matte; as a result their presence in the solutions was neglected. The recently

improved modified quasi-chemical model was found to be adequate to reproduce available experimental

Quartz, tridymite, and cristobalite (SiO2) were treated as stoichiometric compounds; their non-stoichiometry was assumed to be negligibly small. The solubilities of Al2O3 in hematite and Fe2O3 in corundum were described in the corundum solution [1]. The olivine solution was described by considering two octahedral sites and the mixing of cations on three sublatices was taken into account for melilite and pyroxenes [3]. The monoxide and spinel solutions were modeled [4-6] using polynomial solution and compound-energy formalism models, respectively. The later takes into account the crystal structure and physical nature of the spinel solution which comprises of cations and vacancies distributed over tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sites: (Al<sup>3+</sup> , Cu<sup>2+</sup> , Fe<sup>2+</sup> , Fe<sup>3+</sup> , O Mg<sup>2+</sup> )<sup>T</sup> [Al<sup>3+</sup> , Ca<sup>2+</sup> , Cu<sup>2+</sup> ,Fe<sup>2+</sup> , Fe<sup>3+</sup> , Mg<sup>2+</sup> , Va]2 O4. 

The modified quasi-chemical model [7], which takes into account short-range ordering of second-nearest-neighbor cations in the ionic melt, has been used to model the interactions between most of the oxides in the molten slag phase. Cu<sup>1+</sup> was considered to be the only copper species present in the slag, since over the range of copper-smelting/converting/cleaning the conditions were assumed to be reducing to have negligible Cu<sup>2+</sup> in the system. The Bragg-Williams [7] model has been used in the present study to model the interactions between several oxides in the slag. The use of Bragg-Williams model results in a greater flexibility in fitting the experimental data of the slag solutions with strongly positive excess properties.

### **INDUSTRIAL APPLICATION** 

With the depletion of clean concentrate resources, operations are moving generally to slag systems containing more complex slag system affecting the amount of flux required and the outputs of the processes. An example of analysis on the effects of additional components on the phase equilibria of the iron-silicate slag using the current thermodynamic database is given below. Figure 8 provides O2-isobars and liquidus in the “Cu2O”-FeO-Fe2O3- SiO2 system in equilibrium with pure copper at 1275<sup>o</sup> C from the current model. The effects of additions of 8.4 wt pct CaO and 4.0 wt pct MgO on the O2-isobars and liquidus are also calculated using the current model; the calculation results are projected onto the Cu2O-Fe2O3-SiO2 ternary plane and plotted in Figure 8.  The calculation results show that the additions of CaO and MgO slightly shift the O2-isobars toward lower copper concentration in the slag. It can also be observed that the additions of the CaO and MgO result in a wider operating window and a shift of the fully liquid area towards higher SiO2 concentrations. This indicates that if the operation was carried out in the spinel primary phase field appropriate adjustments to the SiO2/Fe ratio in the slag, and corresponding SiO2 flux additions, have to be introduced to avoid excessive solids formation. Moyano _et al_ [26] performed an industrial test in Codelco continuous converting process with slag having the same CaO and MgO concentrations; the bulk composition of their slag in terms of the Cu2O-Fe2O3-SiO2 proportions is plotted in Figure 8. The industrial-test slag sample is located within the liquid + spinel region having a significant solid to liquid proportion; this can been confirmed by the micrograph of sample presented by Moyano _et al_ [26] where significant amount of spinel crystals is observed in the slag sample (see Figure 8). The results provide an important basis for trend analysis of sl

ag behavior for a copper smelting/converting slag to assist with the selection of fluxing and prediction of copper loss in the slag. Later, the new thermodynamic database can also be

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Thermodynamic optimizations of the “Cu2O”-Al2O3-CaO-FeO-Fe2O3-MgO-SiO2-S system at conditions of equilibrium with metallic copper, or copper alloy, has been carried out. The previously available data and new experimental data on the system were critically evaluated and used to obtain a self-consistent set of model parameters for all binary, ternary and higher order sub-systems. The model reproduces all experimental data within experimental error limits and permits good estimations of the thermodynamic properties of multi-component solution to be made. Industrial applications of the database for the copper metallurgical process presented in the paper demonstrate examples of approach to the use of this powerful thermodynamic modelling tool in practical processes.

# **CALCIUM FERRITE SLAG PHASE CHEMISTRY CONTROL USED IN CONTINUOUS FLASH CONVERTING** 

E. Jak and P.C. Hayes _PYROSEARCH, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia, e.jak@uq.edu.au_

### **ABSTRACT** 

Calcium ferrite slags with “Cu2O”, "Fe2O3" and CaO as major components are used in the continuous flash copper-converting process developed at Rio Tinto-Kennecott Utah Copper LLC (KUC). A number of other impurities including SiO2, S, MgO, Al2O3, As and others are also present in the slag. Knowledge of the phase equilibria in this slag system is important for optimal control of the furnace performance including melting temperatures and side wall accretion deposit control. Extensive investigations have been undertaken a) to characterise the phase chemistry of deposits taken from various parts of the smelter, in parallel with b) comprehensive laboratory-based liquidus and sub-liquidus phase equilibria studies in the multi-component system using synthetic slag samples. Major findings related to the phase chemistry control of the Ca-ferrite slags, constitution and possible mechanisms of deposits formation in the converter, including protective freezelining, have been summarised. The role of major and selected minor elements, includ

ing SiO2, S, and As, is discussed. The combination of systematic collaborative research into the plant deposits and fundamental phase equilibria studies have provided better understanding of the melting and solidification behaviour of the complex calcium ferrite slags. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 520 ### **INTRODUCTION** The Kennecott Utah Copper Smelter utilizes Outokumpu Flash Smelting (FSF) in conjunction with Kennecott-Outokumpu Flash Converting (FCF) to process over 1.0 million tonnes of copper concentrate per year, while achieving the lowest emission rate of any copper smelter [1]. The smelter commenced commercial operation in June of 1995 and is now operating above the original design capacity. The copper concentrate feedstock originates entirely from the Kennecott Bingham Canyon Mine. Tanaka [2] reported that accretions formed above the slag surface in the copper converting furnace of the Mitsubishi process contain calcium sulphate, CaSO4, and calcium arsenate in addition to the spinel (Fe3O4), calcium-ferrite and delafossite (Cu2Fe2O4) phases. Clearly knowledge of the liquidus temperatures and phase equilibria in the system is essential to provide guidance in optimising the chemistry of the operation and in avoiding the operational issues outlined above. The role of the major elements (Cu-Fe-Ca-O) has been relatively well understood. The CaO flux is added to reduce the liquidus of the iron oxide-rich spinel phase and the CaO/Fe ratio is one of the key operational parameters used in practice. The oxygen to feed ratio determines the copper oxide concentration in slag; the higher oxygen partial pressure the higher the copper oxide concentration in slag – the lower the liquidus. On the other hand, the greater the copper oxide in slag - the lower the first pass copper recovery; over oxidation is to be avoided to reduce recycling and therefore increase throughput. The effects of minor slag elements, such as, Si, As and S have not been fully characterised, and have not been understood. Prior to the present study there had been a number of observations and general trends in KUC plant operations. For example, high silica slag had to be avoided as it resulted in the formation of the dicalcium silicate. In relation to the arsenic - plant experience suggested that the appearance of the accretions in the form of “bridges” probably coincided with periods of high arsenic and possibly high-silica in converter feed. However, no quantitative relationships between these observations were established at that earlier stage before this study. E

### **RESULTS OF FURTHER STUDIES** 

The results presented in the present study come from the characterisation and analysis of plant samples obtained from Kennecott Flash Converter Furnace (FCF) and laboratory-based studies of synthetic slags produced under controlled conditions. 

### **Plant Samples** 

Two types of slag samples were taken from the Flash Converter Furnace for characterisation. The bulk compositions of the sampled materials are given in Table 3 [17]. First type – quenched samples of the converter slag that were obtained from the furnace during operation through the insertion of cold 2.5cm diameter steel bars directly into the converter slag, at the interface between slag and gas or area just above the slag. In this way quenched slag “live accretion” samples were obtained from material frozen on the surface of the steel bar. It was found that the slag on the live accretion samples contained principally entrained copper metal and Ca-Fe-Cu oxide phases. 

Second type samples of materials were taken from the converter blister and slag launders; these materials were either formed earlier inside the furnace and were “washed out” during tapping or were deposited on the launders during the tapping the furnace. Some launder accretions consisted of two distinct types of materials, which appear as (dark) and (light) materials (Figure 3, top- macro image); examination using the SEM –EDS indicates these are oxide-rich and sulphate-rich materials respectively (see Figure 3 bottom – SEM image).

The phase assemblages can be understood by distinguishing the “high temperature” phases present in the slag from “lower temperature” phases formed on initial crystallisation from the liquid phase during cooling. From detailed studies of the microstructures it can be deduced that the sequence in which these phases are formed on cooling is as follows; the Ca-As-S-silicate solid solution Ca5As2SiO12-S, then dicalcium silicate, then the “primary” phase spinel, which also constitutes the largest phase fraction in the structure. The copper calcium ferrites can be identified as important group of phases formed at lower temperatures. This group of “lower temperature phases” include Ca-ferrite Ca4Fe9O17 that contains some copper oxide in solid solution, and delafossite Cu2O.Fe2O3 – both having narrow area of lower temperature liquidus in the “Cu2O”-CaO-“Fe2O3” system (see Figure 2). The copper calcium ferrites, Cu2O.CaO.2Fe2O3 and Cu2O.2CaO.3Fe2O3 have been shown [16] to be stable phases formed at sub-solidus conditions at copper metal saturation at 1050o C. The other Cu-Ca-ferrites 2Cu2O.3CaO.5Fe2O3 and Cu2O.4CaO.5Fe2O3 may be stable at other temperatures/conditions or could be metastable phases formed on relatively fast cooling. ### **SUMMARY, INDUSTIRAL APPLICATION AND IMPLEMENTATION** 

A series of investigations have been undertaken to clarify the effects of minor elements on the formation of accretions in copper converter practice when using calcium ferrite based slags. The characterisation of accretions obtained from the KUC converter furnace, combined with targeted experimental studies under controlled conditions in the laboratory, has enabled the phases present in these materials to be identified and the origin of the observed phase assemblages to be explained. 

It has been shown that the accretions formed on the furnace walls and freeze linings can be described by the phase chemistry of the Cu-Ca-Fe-O system. The accretions that appear in the launder, and likely make up the bridges and material floating on the slag surface, are described by the phase chemistry of the Ca-Si-S-As-O system. It has been shown that in both cases the phase assemblages are sensitive to the presence of minor elements silica, arsenic and sulphur. 

The studies have lead to significant changes to operating practice in relation to the control of slag chemistry in particular the practice of adding silica to meet a fixed target silica of 2 wt % in slag has been removed; rather the strategy was changed to control and, where possible, to reduce the silica and arsenic levels in the converter feed. The minimum levels of silica are now targeted and achieved through careful tapping of clean copper matte from the Flash Smelting Furnace (FSF).  Careful upfront blending of copper concentrates aims to control As in the FSF feed within limits.   The abolishment of the unnecessary silica flux addition saved the energy needed for melting and can assist in increasing throughput

of the converter.  Importantly, the lowering silica below 1 wt % eliminated the risk of building “bridge-type” of deposits in case of possible excursion of the slightly increased As concentration in the converter feed.  The removal of the “bridges” in the past took considerable efforts and losses in production.  There were no “bridges” formed in the converter since the fluxing strategy was changed to reduce the silica in the converter slag to the minimum – this resulted in considerable savings due to the increased furnace availability. 

The chemistry of the high-calcium sub-systems has been shown to be complex and sensitive to the minor elements, and even relative proportions of these elements, present in the feed. Although significant progress has been made in understanding the behaviour of the KUC converter there is significant scope for further research to accurately describe the high temperature chemistry of these slag systems and to use this to further optimise slag chemistry to achieve even more stable operation and further increased throughput of the converter.

### **ABSTRACT** 

A physico–chemical/kinetic model is being proposed to explain the formation of bornite, chalcopyrite and magnetite during partial roasting of high–arsenic copper concentrates at 700ºC. The mechanism involves solid state-gas and solid–gas reactions between chalcosite, pyrrhotite and gaseous sulphur, and is thermodynamically consistent with the experimental results obtained in pilot plant.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

High–arsenic copper concentrates with over 0.3 wt-% arsenic can not be processed by conventional smelting-converting, and therefore requires an additional arsenic removal step to reduce its content to manageable levels. 

Partial or “neutral” roasting of these concentrates at 680-720ºC can remove up to 95% of the arsenic as As2S3 (As4S6) which has a high vapour pressure under this conditions, leaving a calcine with low residual arsenic, although also can reduce the sulphur content to 20-22% in the calcines, which require to blend these calcines with high sulphur concentrates for smelting.

In order to explain the composition of the calcines obtained by partial roasting of DMH concentrates, and particularly the formation of bornite, chalcopyrite and magnetite, a reaction mechanism is proposed which involves solid-state reactions between Cu2S and FeS in presence of gaseous sulphur for bornite formation, and oxygen for chalcopyrite and magnetite formation, both in the emulsion phase of the fluidized bed. 

### **PHYSICO – CHEMISTRY OF PARTIAL ROASTING** 

The proposed mechanism considers three kinds of reactions that could takes place during partial roasting of high – arsenic copper concentrates, such as those of DMH: 

- a) Thermal decomposition of enargite, pyrite and covelite. 

- b) Solid–solid–gas and solid–gas reactions to form bornite, chalcopyrite, and magnetite both as stoichiometric and non-stoichiometric compounds. 

- c) Homogeneous gaseous reaction between sulphur and oxygen to form SO2 and oxidation of arsenic trisulphide to trioxide. 

Reactions a) are all endothermic, while reactions b) and reactions c) are exothermic, and provide the heat required to maintain the process at the desired temperature. Reactions and their standard heat and free energy of reaction at 700ºC are as follows<sup>(6):</sup>

The emulsion phase contain virtually of the solids, with a small amount of interstitial gas flowing though under approximately its minimum fluidizing condition, which for the DMH calcines is equivalent to a spatial velocity of near 5 cm/s at 700ºC(*) . The other fraction of the air blown into the bed forms gas bubbles and/or columns of gas bubbles with and equivalent spatial velocity of 60 to 70 cm/s of at 700ºC, which represents over 95% of the total air blown into the fluidized bed. According to the model of Rowe(3) of gas recirculation in bubbles and fast rising columns of gas bubbles the gas recirculation penetrates the emulsion creating an evolving cloud and a lower pressure wake of gas that surrounds them, in which a high degree of mass and heat transfer takes place, as it is schematized in a simplified form in Fig. 4. > (*) The spatial velocity is a reference velocity calculated for the empty reactor. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 549 Clouds of gas bubbles and

The oxidation of sulphur to SO2, which is an irreversible reaction at 700ºC, would takes place mainly in the volume formed by the cloud and wake surrounding the ascending gas bubbles and columns of gas were a high partial pressure of oxygen exists, while the formation of bornite and chalcopyrite by reaction between Cu2S and FeS in presence of gaseous sulphur could takes place

in the emulsion phase of solid–gas where the thermal decomposition of enargite, covelite and pyrite occurs at a fast rate, generating large amount of gaseous sulphur, and also where low partial pressure of oxygen exists due to the low volume of gas flowing through it, and where any oxygen available would react with gaseous sulphur to form SO2. At 700ºC, the partial pressures of As2S3 and S2 are close to 1 atm., while the partial pressure of oxygen is virtually nil. For the fluidized bed pilot reactor with a feed rate of 25 kg/h of DMH concentrate at 700ºC and an average reaction time of 1 hr., at steady state the generation of gaseous sulphur is equivalent to 6.7x10-2 mole/s, while the oxygen (air) available that flows across the emulsion phase under minimum fluidizing conditions is only 2.0x10-3 mole/s. Since the reaction of gaseous sulphur with oxygen requires 2 moles of oxygen per mol of sulphur, there is a deficit of over 95% of oxygen to oxidize the sulphur, which means that in the emulsion there is a high partial pressure of sulphur available to form bornite through reaction (4). Under local non-equilibrium conditions or in absence of gaseous sulphur, also some arsenic trisulphide could be oxidized to arsenic trioxide in the clouds and wake of the gas bubbles and gas columns, but this may occurs in a limited extent, due to its thermodynamic constrain. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 550 The formation of bornite and chalcopyrite is shown in Fig. 5. The formation of bornite and chalcopyrite requires the physical contact between hot particles of chalcosite and pyrrhotite, which takes place in the highly turbulent emulsion phase of the fluidized bed. Once a collision between particles of Cu2S and FeS occurs, the particles forms rapidly a new interface of synthetic mineral (bornite or chalcopyrite) in between of them and the reaction could progress further by solid sta

te diffusion of Cu2S or FeS in apposite directions. Since these reactions requires the presence of gaseous sulphur, this gas may be adsorpted through a gas–solid adsorption mechanism in which the adsorpted sulphur could moves by solid diffusion inside the crystalline structures towards the reactional front. 

Alternatively, the gaseous sulphur could diffuse through the relatively porous Cu2S and FeS formed by decomposition of enargite, covelite and pyrite. Thermal decomposition change the morphology of particles leaving porous particles due to the mass loss, as it was shown by Cauwe et al<sup>5</sup> who used  SEM analysis of thermally decomposed pyrite particles.  In this case, the effective diffusion coefficient of gaseous

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A physico–chemical/kinetic model is being proposed to explain the formation of bornite, chalcopyrite and magnetite during partial roasting of high–arsenic copper concentrates at 700ºC. 

The mechanism involves solid state–solid and solid–gas reactions between chalcosite, pyrrhotite and gaseous sulphur, and is thermodynamically consistent with the experimental results obtained in pilot plant.

The study considers a modeling of a laboratory prototype involving four parameters: the initial oxygen concentration in oxidized copper, the packed bed height, the furnace outlet diameter and, the diameter of spheres. By using a 3D geometry generated with a computational algorithm and a CFD software it was possible to solve the mass and momentum transport equations as well as deoxidation reaction that occurs inside the packed bed furnace. Preliminary computational results allow visualizing the copper flow and oxygen concentration profiles inside the crucible, which represents essential information for future industrial furnace design. It was also possible to verify that oxygen values in reduced copper were below 1500 [ppm] in optimal conditions. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 554 ### **INTRODUCTION** Throughout history, the copper production by pyrometallurgical processes has been carried out mostly in discontinuous or batch systems. In recent decades new continuous technologies have been developed but focused only on Smelting and Converting stages leaving aside the last stage before casting, the Refining. In 2002 a novel technology was proposed by the Department of Mining Engineering of University of Chile [1, 2] which consists of two cylindrical packed bed furnaces in cascade which treat molten blister copper from converting contains around 100 and 5000 [ppm] of dissolved sulfur and oxygen, respectively. The first furnace, containing a refractory packed bed has the function of removing the sulfur until about 25 [ppm] as SO2 using a countercurrent airflow, while the second furnace, containing a coal or coke packed bed that of reducing the oxygen from 10,000 to around 1,500 [ppm] as CO, CO2 and H2O(g). ### **INVESTIGATION OF FREEZE LINING FORMED IN A FLASH CONVERTING SLAG** 

- A. Fallah-Mehrjardi<sup>1</sup> , J. Jansson<sup>2</sup> and P. Taskinen<sup>2</sup> , P.C. Hayes<sup>1</sup> and E. Jak<sup>1</sup>

### **ABSTRACT** 

Slag freeze-linings are increasingly used in industrial coppermaking processes such as, flash smelting and converting reactors to ensure furnace integrity in highly aggressive environments is maintained. In the present study, a cold-finger technique was used to form the deposits in an industrial calcium ferrite slag under controlled conditions. The effects of immersion times on the thickness and microstructures in the freeze-lining deposits have been investigated.  Microstructural and phase analysis show that range of complex oxide solutions and copper-containing phases have been formed in the deposits. Also, it has been experimentally demonstrated that the bath-deposit interface temperature at steady-state conditions can be lower than the liquidus temperature of the bulk liquid. The findings of the study indicate a potential to improve the operation of the converting furnace and the design of freeze linings in metallurgical systems.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Calcium ferrite slags are currently in use in several commercial coppermaking technologies, such as, the Mitsubishi downward lance converter, the Outotec flash converter and the IsaConvert top submerged lance technology.  These processes typically operate between fifteen and twenty wt pct copper in slag and between fourteen to twenty wt pct of lime [1]. Calcium ferrite slags have been selected for these processes due to their low viscosity and ability to absorb solid magnetite forming during the operation, which traditional iron silicate slag cannot absorb. In addition, reduced slag volume and improved impurity removal, such as antimony and arsenic, from the molten copper are other advantages of calcium-ferrite slags over silicate-ferrite slags [2]. 

The principal downside of using calcium ferrite slags is difficulties in containment

and refractory degradation of the reactor lining [3]. In addition, pyrometallurgical coppermaking processes are operated under high process temperatures and vigorous bath convection, to increase the kinetics of reactions and to achieve high reactor throughput. As a result, thermal and chemical attack by aggressive slag may result in increased refractory degradation in the metallurgical reactors. In industrial practice the formation of freeze-linings is deliberately induced through the use of wateror air-cooled jackets or refractories to protect the refractory wall from the harmful effects of thermal and chemical attack by the aggressive slag. In addition, the use of freezelinings rather than traditional hot face refractory linings greatly extends the range of operating conditions, and enables increasing energy efficiencies and productivities to be economically achieved [4-9]. 

The formation of freeze-linings have been widely investigated from heat transfer point of view to predict the thickness of deposits as a function of process conditions such as superheat, capacity of the cooling medium, bath agitation at transient and steady-state conditions. These models have assumed that the interface between the stationary frozen layer and the agitated molten bath at steady-state conditions consists of the primary phase crystals, which are in contact with the bulk liquid at the liquidus temperature, Tliquidus [1013] However, recent-laboratory-scale studies in silicate-based slags [4,5] and in a low temperature physical model system [14] have shown that this assumption may not hold in general. A mechanism has been proposed taking into account the effect of chemistryrelated parameters (e.g. viscosity, thermal and mass diffusivity, nucleation and crystallisation kinetics, phase equilibria and liquidus shape and dissolution kinetics) and flow of liquid in the bath to explain why bath/deposit interface temperature, Tf, is below the liquidus at steady state conditions [5]. The aim of the current study is to investigate the interface temperature between the stagnant deposit and bath at steady-state conditions as well as the characteristics of the deposit in a system that is of significant importance, the industrial calcium ferrite slag used in the copper flash converting furnace (FCF) of Rio Tinto – Kennecott Utah Copper smelter.

### **EXPERIMENTAL METHODS** 

### **Cold Finger Experiments** 

The freeze-lining experiments were carried out using a water-cooled probe technique in a vertical tube furnace (25 kVA, manufactured by Entech Sweden). 2.5 kg of granulated flash converting furnace slag was charged in a MgO crucible. The selected process conditions are summarized in Table 1. The crucible was placed and fixed on a rotating disk and heated up at a rate of 3–4 °C/min to the designated temperature. In addition, nitrogen gas (with flow rate of 4 l min<sup>-1</sup> ) was passed over the surface of the liqui

d slag so that the molten bath was maintained at conditions corresponding to equilibrium with metallic copper. To commence the experiment, the probe is immersed in a molten slag bath and the slag forms a deposit on the surface of the cold finger. The probe with the attached deposit is removed from the bath after selected period of time and rapidly quenched in water to preserve the deposit structure present at the bath. 

The water-cooled probe consists of two concentric AISI 316L tubes, with external diameters of 8 and 14 mm and 1 mm wall thickness. The water was passed in through the central tube and was released by passing through the gap between the central and the outer tube as shown schematically in Figure 1.b. A set of two S-type thermocouples (see Figure 1.b) were placed at distances from the cold probe surface to measure the temperatures across the freeze-lining deposit. The inlet and outlet temperatures of the water flowing inside the probe were measured with six A class PT100 temperature sensors. All measured temperatures by thermocouples and sensors vs. immersion time were recorded continuously during the experiments.

### **RESULTS** 

### **Temperature Measurements** 

The liquidus temperature of the FCF slag was estimated in the ”Cu2O”-“Fe2O3”CaO system at molten metallic copper saturation [15]. The bulk composition measured by EPMA was used (see Table 2) and the description was simplified by adding magnesia and alumina to the iron oxide; also lead was added to lime; and minority components, such as, silica, arsenic and barium were omitted. The concentrations of the modified analyses were then normalised to obtain a total of 100%. The liquidus temperature of the FCF slag was estimated to be 1250 ˚C. 

Figure 2.a shows the change in temperatures in the deposit as a function of immersion time for a given set of process conditions. Analysis of temperature trends indicates that the deposit reached a steady-state thickness approximately 50 min after the probe immersion since no significant changes in temperature were observed after this time. In addition, thickness of the deposit at 60-min immersion time is equal to that at120 min. The temperatures measured by thermocouples at steady-state conditions along with the liquidus temperature were used to interpolate the thermal profile across the deposit as a function of distance from water-cooled probe surface (see Figure 2.b) using a 1-D logarithmic heat transfer equation. Heat transfer through the freeze lining is assumed to be radial; axial and angular heat transfer in the proximity of the freeze lining and the water-cooled probe is neglected.

### **Freeze-Lining Microstructures** 

The focus of the present study is investigation of microstructures, morphologies and compositions of the phases formed at steady-state conditions. As a result, a series of freeze-lining experiments at various immersion times was carried out to find out the steady-state thickness. Systematic analysis of deposit microstructures in the earlier studies [4, 5, 8, 9, 16-18] shows that several layers are present within the deposit and adjacent to the deposit/bath interface at steady-state conditions. These layers were given a generic classification as follows (starting from the material immediately adjacent to the cold probe surface); (1) Homogeneous, single phase glass; (2) Mixed glassy and microcrystalline layer; (3) Closed crystalline layer; (4) Open crystalline layer; (5) Sealing primary phase layer; (4′) A subliquidus layer; and (6) residual bath material where the bulk composition of this layer is identical to that of the bulk bath. 

In the present study on the calcium ferrite slag having low silica concentration, the glassy layer (1) and the open crystalline layer (4) were not observed in the steadystate deposit for the process conditions examined. Figure 6 shows the typical microstructures of the deposit for 120 min-immersion time at steady-state conditions. 

The microcrystalline layer (2) consists of amorphous oxides matrix with very fine microcrystals (see Figure 6.a). The bulk composition of the layer (2), obtained by 100 EPMA measurements, appears to be similar to bulk compositions of the liquid. 

The closed crystalline layer (3) is present from approximately 4 mm (≈710<sup>◦</sup> C) to a distance of 23.7 mm (≈1160<sup>◦</sup> C) from cold-probe surface (see Figure 6.b-e). The phases present in this layer depend on the distance from the cold probe surface. The phases identified by EPMA below the solidus temperature (T<1080<sup>◦</sup> C) at steady-state thickn

ess of the deposit are metallic copper, spinel solid solution, calcium wusto-ferrite solid solution, delafossite, dicalcium silicate, 5CaO.As2O5.SiO2, Cu-Ca-ferrite and cuprite (see Figure 6.c) . Above the solidus temperature (greater than 18.5 mm from the probe surface) up to 1160<sup>◦</sup> C (23.7 mm from the probe surface) all phases mentioned above are retained except for the cuprite phase; liquid is found to be present (see Figure 6.d).

### **DISCUSSION** 

The phase assemblages formed from the industrial calcium ferrite slag in the steady-state deposit are very complex and information on the phase equilibria of the multi-component systems with addition of minor elements may not be available. Subsolidus [19] and sub-liquidus [15] phase equilibria in the Cu-Ca-Fe-O system at metallic copper saturation along with interpolated temperature across the deposit, microstructural changes and compositional trends in the phases (see Figure 4) in the deposit have been used to understand the formation and characteristics of the phases in the steady-state freeze-lining. For example, solidus temperature, Tsolidus, of the FCF slag was estimated to be approximately 1080<sup>◦</sup> C where no liquid was observed in the microstructure of the freeze-lining at steady-state conditions. The concentration of the copper oxide in spinel phase was used as a cross-check to ensure the validity of the solidus temperature estimation. This is consistent with the recent sub-solidus phase equilibria study in the CuCa-Fe-O system [19]. 

In addition, a number of copper calcium ferrite phases (CCF’s) were observed in the deposit (see Figure 5.a). A recent study of sub-solidus phase equilibria in the Cu-CaFe-O system at copper saturation [19] has, however, reported that only the Cu2O.2CaO.3Fe2O3 and Cu2O.CaO.2Fe2O3 calcium ferrite phases are stable at temperatures below 1060<sup>o</sup> C. These phases may in fact be metastable and transformation of the copper calcium ferrite phases (CCF’s) into phase Ass may take place over time. 

Importantly, detailed examination of the subliquidus layer (4′) formed between the stagnant deposit interface and

liquid bath shows that detached crystals of the spinel and calcium arsenic silicate phases are present in the liquid ahead of the sealing layer of the deposit (Figure 6). This observation indicates that the stationary deposit/bath interface must be below the liquidus temperature. This observation is consistent with other recent laboratory-based studies by the authors [4,5] on silicate-based slag systems. It provides further evidence that the position of the deposit interface in freeze linings at steady state is determined by a dynamic process involving crystallization in a subliquidus region of the bath ahead of the interface, convective mass transport of detached crystals to and from the stagnant interface at steady-state conditions.

### **CONCLUSION** 

A water-cooled probe technique has been used to investigate the mechanisms of freeze-lining formation and the effects of chemistry on the microstructure, stability, thickness and morphology of the phases formed in the deposit in an industrial copper converting calcium-ferrite slag in equilibrium with metallic copper. Microstructures of freeze-lining based on distinctive layers across the deposit thickness were classified. Spinel phase was identified as a primary phase. Also, calcium wusto-ferrite solid solution, delafossite, di-calcium silicate, calcium arsenic silicate, copper calcium ferrite phases and cuprite were formed in the deposit. Analysis of the deposit microstructure at steady-state conditions indicates that bath-deposit interface temperature may not be the liquidus temperature of the bulk liquid. This then opens up opportunities for significant improvements in process performance and a deeper understanding of the fundamental mechanisms of deposit formation. It indicates the possibility of selecting process conditions below the liquidus temperature of the bulk bath that could result in significant energy savings and increases in the throughputs of the metallurgical reactors.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Phase-equilibria data make it possible to identify the likely outcomes of reactions and the limits to reactor performance. Although many studies have been carried out on copper slag/matte/gas systems over the past several decades, significant gaps and uncertainties still remain. The descriptions of liquidus temperatures, and major and minor element equilibrium partitioning between phases require further improvements. 

Experimental procedures involving high-temperature-equilibration and quenching followed by electron-probe X-ray microanalysis, developed at PYROSEARCH, have resolved a number of experimental difficulties associated with high temperature phase equilibria determination in these systems. The techniques have enabled systematic investigations to be carried out in the multi-component slag(Cu-Fe-Si-S-O)/matte(Cu-FeS-O) systems at controlled oxygen and sulphur partial pressures and temperatures in the range of interest to copper smelting operations. 

New experimental data have been obtained for slag/matte/gas equilibria at the silica saturation (i.e. in equilibrium iwht tridymite), and for copper and sulphur solubilities in slags, for the range of matte grades from ~30 to 75 wt. % Cu. These data demonstrate the capabilities and accuracy of the improved experimental techniques and how these can be applied to obtain thermodynamic information on the complex chemistry; information which is vital for further process optimisation in copper production.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Slag chemistry plays a key role in copper smelting and converting technologies influencing productivity, process efficiency and stability of operation. These are complex multi-component systems and the task of determining the optimum process conditions and improvements to industrial copper production processes can be greatly assisted with detailed knowledge of high temperature phase equilibria, minor elements partitioning and slag properties. 

Extensive data on the equilibria between the Cu-containing slags and copper metal or matte have been reported over the years [1-12]. However there are sets of conditions that are not well defined, and important gaps remain in fundamental property databases of these systems. Most previous experimental studies have used the equilibration and cooling technique, with large several-gram-sized samples contained in quartz, magnesium oxide or alumina crucibles. Following cooling, the slag and matte (and/or metallic copper) phases were physically separated, and the bulk compositions of the separated phases were analysed by wet chemical techniques. Whilst these represented the best available methodologies for determination o

f this information at the time, the above mentioned techniques for the characterisation of the gas/slag and gas/slag/matte systems have the following limitations: i) the relatively large sizes of the samples meant that the cooling rates were relatively low and changes in microstructure and compositions of phases can occur on cooling. In addition, bulk analysis techniques used in previous studies are not able to detect whether or not the slag was fully liquid under the process conditions investigated, and ii) it is also possible that fine particles of the matte phase are suspended inside the slag. This combination of factors makes it impossible in practice to achieve a complete physical separation of liquid slag from the crystalline oxide(s) and the entrapped matte phases, and therefore to provide accurate analyses of the liquid slag phase using the wet chemical methods. The uncertainties in the data will depend on the proportions and compositions of the solid and matte phases suspended in the slag; these uncertainties can be significant when metal and impurity concentrations in slag are low. ### **EXPERIMENTAL TECHNIQUES AND PROCEDURES** In recent years new experimental procedures have been developed and have been successfully applied to characterise a number of complex industrial slag systems [2, 1315]. These experimental procedures in general involve high temperature equilibration, rapid quenching of the samples, followed by the electron probe X-ray microanalysis (EPMA) using wave-length dispersive detectors (WDD) to determine the compositions of the resulting phases. The experimental technique can be explained with reference to Figure 1. The samples are deliberately equilibrated at sub-liquidus temperatures, typically forming at least one solid phase. On quenching to room temperature, in the case of silicatecontaining slags the liquid phase is converted into glass or amorphous material and crystalline solids present at high temperature remain unaltered. The quenched samples are then mounted, polished for metallographic examination and the compositions of the _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 581 liquid (a) and solid (c) phases are measured by electron probe X-ray microanalysis (EPMA). The approach provides superior accuracy to differential thermal analysis and conventional optical approaches that have previously been used. The ability to control temperature enables liquidus isotherms to be measured rather than interpolated and tie lines between conjugate solid solutions and liquid phases at fixed temperatures to be readily established. Whilst the equilibration/quench/EPMA approach provides superior accuracy and enables the range of systems that can be accurately characterised to be extended, care must be taken in its application. Changing the equilibration time to confirm that no further changes take place as the time is increased. 2). Confirming the chemical homogeneity of each of the phases. 3). To avoid contamination from conventional crucible materials, the open substrate support technique has been developed in which the primary phase that is present under the equilibration conditions is actually used to support the slag. The use of high purity metal and oxide powders is important since impurity elements can partition preferentially to particular phases during equilibration and significantly influence the outcomes of the phase assemblage, particularly when there is a low volume fraction of the contaminated phase. The fact that the compositions of phases are measured directly and after the experiment brings the key advantage of the technique and the final results do not depend on the changes of the bulk composition during equilibration. This is the main important feature that enables the measurement to be done in systems very difficult or impossible for investigation previously. It enabled the substrate container-less approach to be introduced to reduce samples size to less than 0.1g and, therefore, to avoid contamination from crucibles and importantly to achieve high quenching rate. In the case of low- or nosilica slags, molten sulphide and metal phases, even though ultra rapid quenching is achieved, it is still difficult to obtain amorphous quenched material on cooling. It is, _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 582 however, possible for these difficult-to-quench phases to be retained as microcrystalline material so that the grain size is significantly smaller than the take-off volume of the EPMA. Although the presence of microcrystalline material introduce additional uncertainty into the EPMA measurements, it is still possible to obtain relatively accurate quantitative measurements. As demonstrated in the case of calcium ferrite slags [3] to maximise the accuracy of the results and minimise the measured variations in composition, only the areas immediately adjacent to the quenching medium, where the fastest quenching takes place and it is confirmed that microcrystalline material is present, sh

ould be selected for analysis [3]. An example of the differences in quenching rate as a function of distance from the quenching medium is shown in Figure 2. The area distant from the direct contact with the quenching media has a number of high-Cu precipitates – these precipitates are believed to be one of the main reasons for uncertainties in results of previous researchers. Careful analysis of the microstructure and adequate selection of the area for measurements enables previous uncertainties to be eliminated and accurate measurements to be obtained. Matte

Using controlled gas mixtures and the equilibration/quench/EPMA technique, the effects of oxygen partial pressure on phase equilibria and liquidus have now been established for a wide range of oxygen partial pressures from air to iron saturation for the FeO-Fe2O3-SiO2 system [2, 13, 17, 18]. **Liquidus temperatures in converter/direct smelting slags** The system “Cu2O”-FeO-Fe2O3-SiO2 at copper metal saturation characterizes the principal features of direct copper smelting slags. An example of the experimental data and model predictions defining the isothermal section of this system at 1250o C is shown

in Figure 3 [19-21]. The technique has also been applied to the determination of phase equilibria and liquidus in the system Cu2O-CaO-FeO-Fe2O3-SiO2 copper saturation conditions at fixed oxygen partial pressures (Figure 4) [14, 22, 23]. The effects of impurities commonly encountered in smelting operations, such as MgO, Al2O3 [15, 24] on the liquidus temperatures of ferrous silicate have also been determined [24]. ### **Slag/Matte equilibria** This approach has now been extended from slag/solid/metal/gas systems to slag/matte/solid/gas systems through the use of controlled oxygen and sulphur dioxide partial pressures at Cu-Fe-S matte saturation (for example, see recent study [30]). New measurements on the relationship between matte grade and slag composition have been obtained in the present study using the substrate support technique. The Fe/SiO2 ratios in the liquid phase at SiO2 saturation for the Cu-Fe-Si-O slags in equilibrium with a range of Cu-Fe-S matte concentrations are given in Figure 5. It can be seen that the presence of sulphur and copper through the coexistence with the matte phase significantly changes the Fe/SiO2 present in the liquid slag at the tridymite primary phase liquidus. From a practical viewpoint these resulte are important to be able to accurately assess and optimise the fluxing requirements of the processes. Note the present data are for synthetic Cu-Fe-O-Si-S slags; the conditions in industrial slags and the corresponding Fe/SiO2 ratios will be significantly influenced by the presence of minor “slagging” components, such as, CaO, MgO, Al2O3. The important _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 584 point here, however, is that these types of measurements under controlled conditions are now possible, and this opens the way for systematic examination of the effects of minor elements on the equilibria. ### **Copper losses in smelting slags** Matte smelting using ferrous silicate slags is the common first step in the pyrometallurgical processing of primary sulphide concentrates. In all process technologies there are losses of metal values through the presence of dissolved and entrained copper in the discard slag. In a large scale industrial operation even a small difference in copper losses can mean large reductions in revenue. Despite this, the minimum concentrations of copper in slag that can be achieved for a given matte grade and slag composition remain uncertain. These uncertainties arise directly from the experimental techniques that have been used historically to investigate this problem. Examples of the range of copper concentrations in slag as a function of matte grade reported in the literature are illustrated in Figure 7. For example, at a matte grade 65 wt.% Cu the concentration of dissolved copper in slag is reported in some cases to be as low as 0.25 wt.% Cu and in others in excess of 1 wt.% Cu. There are disagreements as to whether the copper in slag increases monotonically with increasing matte grade or has a maximum at intermediate matte grades. As demonstrated in the previous examples the presence of each new chemical component present in the system changes the equilibrium phase boundaries. A review of the literature indicates that minor element partitioning between slag and matte phases is dependent on liquid slag and matte compositions, oxygen and sulphur partial pressures, total impurity concentrations and process temperature. Although the general behaviour of impurities can be deduced from plant measurements the theoretical limits to separations that can be achieved are still not well established. Some examples of

data available for the arsenic distribution between slags and mattes are illustrated in Figure 9 [26-30]. Measurements using EPMA technique for the synthetic and industrial samples are included in this figure. It can be seen that order of magnitude differences in distribution ratios are reported in different studies. Clearly there is a need for accurate data on these properties for the key impurity elements encountered in copper smelting and converting systems, in order to design and optimize plant operations of not just the smelter but the subsequent downstream metal refining capacities and to achieve reduced environmental impacts. It has been shown that the equilibration/quench/EPMA approach can be extended to these complex systems and recent studies [30] have shown good agreement between plant and laboratory data using this approach. New experimental data on the liquidus temperatures in copper smelting slags at matte saturation have been presented. The concentrations of sulphur and copper dissolved in slag under these conditions have been measured. The improved experimental approach demonstrated in this paper now provides the opportunity to accurately characterise the behaviour of minor elements in copper smelting and converting conditions. ### **ABSTRACT** 

The increasingly stringent environmental requirements against the emission of impurities and fugitive gases and the higher energy costs during the converting of copper matte have encouraged the development of continuous and cheaper processes. Thus, a new continuous converting process has been developed based on the oxidation of copper matte with a countercurrent oxygen-enriched air blast into a packed bed reactor. In this study, the oxidation kinetic of copper matte was investigated by experimental tests at laboratory scale in relation to three variables; blast flow rate, oxygen enrichment into the blast and packed bed height. Copper matte oxidation, in terms of desulfurization, follows a first order kinetic, where the sulfur content into the blister copper, [S], depends on the oxygen enrichment, %O2, and the packed bed height [H]: 



_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Continuous converting in a packed bed reactor is based on a countercurrent oxidation between copper matte and oxygen-enriched air blast within a bed of chromemagnesite ceramic grains and the addition of CaO, SiO2 and Al2O3 as main fluxes. Previous researches have shown the technical feasibility of this new technology [1, 2] indicating a faster oxidation kinetic due to the increase of the reaction area given by the higher dispersion of copper matte. Although several and useful researches have been carried out concerning oxidation kinetics of copper matte at laboratory scale [3-6], no further works have been made in a continuous laboratory-scale setup. 

In the present work the experimental technique was carried out, at a fixed temperature of 1250°C, considering the packed bed height as the

main variable in order to establish the oxidation kinetic of the process. Oxygen enrichment and blast flow rate ranges of study were chosen adequately to characterize the copper converting process. 

In this paper, the obtained experimental results are presented in the form of sulphur content in blister copper versus packed bed height, oxygen enrichment and blast flow rate. The results allowed developing a kinetic model for desulfurization as a function of the packed bed height and the oxygen enrichment in order to predict the copper matte oxidation for future works. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

Similarly to Warczok et _al._ [2], the main installation consists in two electric furnaces: The first one used as an auxiliary smelting stage for the solid feed and the second one used for the converting process (Figures 1 and 2). 



Figure 1– Schematic experimental setup for continuous converting in a packed bed reactor 

Solid copper matte (72.5% Cu) from ENAMI’s Hernбn Videla Lira smelter is fed continuously by a vibrating device at a rate of 20 [g/min]. Copper matte is melted inside a silica carbide crucible (OD= 12.7 [cm], H=16.5 [cm]) with a tapping hole at a height of 10.5 [cm]. When the level of molten copper matte reaches the tapping hole, the liquid phase flows gravitationally, allowing the copper matte to flow down through the ceramic packed bed located in the second furnace below the first one. 

A silica carbide crucible (OD= 9 [cm], H=30.5 [cm]) is filled by grains of chromemagnesite from 0.95 to 1.3 [cm] diameter. On its way down to the bottom of the crucible, copper matte reacts with the oxygen-enriched air blast and with the mix of fluxes producing slag and blister copper. The latter one is evacuated in an inclined tapping hole playing a role of siphon at the lower end of the crucible. Blister copper flows through short graphite launder out of the electric furnace into a graphite-clay crucible, where it solidifies instantaneously.

On the other side, the hole for the converting slag allows for continuous tapping out of the slag through another graphite launder out of the furnace. About 1.5 [cm] above the slag tapping hole there are two holes of 6.3 [mm] diameter in which are placed alumina tubes that play the role of tuyeres. Mass flowmeters were used to control precisely the flow of air and technical oxygen.  Table 1 shows the variables considered in the kinetic study and their values at a fixed temperature of 1250°C.

### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper discusses the removal of sulphur and arsenic directly from enargitebearing concentrates by pyro-decomposition in a variety of gaseous atmospheres, including vacuum, to yield a low volume of disposable arsenic/sulphur mixture. Experimental results are presented for various process routes. Treatment in a N2 gasflushed reactor of a 4:1 enargite/metallic iron charge at 700<sup>0</sup> C consistently transformed enargite into bornite and chalcopyrite with less than 0.1% As in the product. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

606 

### **

INTRODUCTION** 

Testwork was undertaken to define conditions for generating a product from enargite (Cu3AsS4) concentrates assaying less than 0.2% As – a concentration currently acceptable for smelting contracts [1]. This testwork was an extension of the reductive testwork reported on for arsenopyrite [2], but also took note of literature which indicated that As could be volatilized from enargite, e.g. [3]. Avoiding oxidation of the As in enargite can be desirable as arsenic sulphides are denser, less soluble and, hence, easier to deal with as waste than arsenic oxides [4]. Various experimental apparatus were designed, built and tested as part of the program. Under certain process conditions the arsenic sulphides could even be collected as a liquid. The process was developed to a point where products well below the target arsenic concentration were generated regularly under laboratory conditions. Potential future production routes are presented. 

Earlier work such as that by Padilla et al. [3, 5] and Bruckard et al. [1] suggests that As can be effectively volatilized from enargite or high-As copper concentrates at temperatures above 650 °C in an inert atmosphere at atmospheric pressure or, as demonstrated by Jiang et al. [6], under vacuum conditions. Padilla et al. [3] achieved over 98% As removal from an enargite concentrate (12.1% As) in 60 min under an inert atmosphere at 650 °C and Bruckard et al. [1] cite 91.2% As removal from a concentrate containing 3.73% As that was held at 700 °C for 60 min in N2. In addition to providing an inert atmosphere, N2 flow was also used by Padilla et al. [5] to continuously purge the reaction chamber and eliminate resistance to mass transfer to the gas phase, effectively creating a low-pressure regime for volatilized species. The sweeping gas could potentially be gaseous sulphur, providing a higher driving force than N2 for the removal of available arsenic as sulphides, as previously proposed by Outokumpu [7]. 

### **TESTWORK** 

In the present work, samples of Peruvian enargite (labeled E1, E2 and E3) were successively obtained from Excalibur Mineral Corp., Peekskill, NY, USA. Duplicate samples of E1 were sent to Activation Laboratories, Ancaster, Canada, for instrumental neutron activation analysis (INAA) and reported 10.3% As. X-Ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of sample E1 identified only enargite as the arsenical mineral present. Samples of E2 and E3 assayed 10.53% As and 11.50% As, respectively. XRD identified the presence of both enargite and tennantite (Cu12As4S13) in E2, while analysis of E3 produced peaks for enargite, marcasite and pyrite. 

Eventually, a larger enargite/quartz/pyrite sample from Montana, USA (E4) was obtained from Minerals Unlimited, Ridgecrest, CA, USA. XRD identified enargite, tennantite, pyrite, quartz,and stibarsen (AsSb). Optical microscopy on a polished section of E4, performed by Dr. Aparup Chattopadhyay of PROrtech [8] as part of mineralogical analysis, showed enargite, te

nnantite/tetrahedrite (Cu12As4S13/Cu12Sb4S13), pyrite, chalcopyrite (CuFeS2), quartz, covellite (CuS), chalcocite (Cu2S), bornite (Cu5FeS4), and 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

607 

trace galena (PbS). INAA on E4 returned an As concentration of 6.61%. Assuming all As in the sample is present as enargite and tennantite, E4 consisted of approximately 34.7% enargite/tennantite. 

It was decided to attempt to de-arsenify the enargite samples by heating under vacuum, conceptually following the Pidgeon process for the production of magnesium. A vacuum chamber was constructed of a ≈ 49 cm length of ½ inch steel pipe with a compression fitting at one end and a solid cap at the other. The pipe was placed in a small tube furnace with ≈ 15 – 17.5 cm of the pipe protruding from the furnace and angled such that the protruding end was lower than the heated end. This arrangement was devised to allow evolved vapours to diffuse away from the hot zone. The inclined tube would also prevent liquid AsxSy condensate flowing back into the hot zone. This is a notable difference to the setup used by Jiang et al. [6] for their vacuum experiments, where the concentrate was positioned at the bottom of a steel retort with the only exhaust exiting from the top of the chamber. That arrangement could allow volatilized material to pool around the sample and impede gas phase mass transfer. 

A water-cooled copper coil was wrapped around a section of the protruding pipe to condense evolved vapours as they moved down the tube from the hot zone. The samples of enargite were charged in clear fused quartz tubes (12 mm outer diameter, 10 mm inner diameter) from Quartz Scientific, Inc., Fairport Harbor, USA. The quartz tubes were cut into approximately 35 cm lengths and one end was sealed. The sealed end of each quartz tube held the enargite sample and was located in the hot zone of the furnace during testing. The quartz tubes extended through the cooled region of the outer steel pipe such that any volatilized compounds would condense on the inside of the quartz tube. The vacuum chamber was connected to a scrubber filled with an aqueous solution of Ca(OH)2 which was, in turn, connected to a vacuum pump. A gauge connected to the system indicated a pressure of 14.9 Torr while under vacuum. The ambient temperature of the area in which the experiments were performed was 18 °C; the vapour pressure of water at 20 °C is reported as 2.3388 kPa (17.54 Torr) [9]. See Figure 1 for a schematic representation of the experimental apparatus. 

A thermocouple placed inside an empty quartz tube was used to investigate the temperature gradient across the wall of the steel vacuum vessel and the wall of the quartz reaction tubes used. At surface temperatures of 600 °C – 700 °C, internal temperatures were found to be 10 °C – 20 °C lower than those at the surface, with the temperature difference across the walls decreasing with increasing surface temperature. In order to facilitate diffusion

of volatilized species away from the enargite sample during processing, a larger vacuum chamber was constructed using a 60 cm length of ¾ inch steel tubing and larger clear fused quartz tubes (18 mm O.D., 16 mm I.D.). There was approximately 20 °C difference between the vacuum chamber surface and the interior of a quartz reaction tube, when the chamber surface was held at 625 °C and approximately 35 °C when the tube surface was at 420 °C. For all tests, timing of the experiment was initiated when the outer pipe’s surface temperature reached its set point (chosen to ensure an internal temperature of ± 5 °C of the nominal testing temperature) – the additional

### **SUMMARY** 

Enargite/pyrite assemblages can be transformed into bornite/chalcopyrite with < 0.2% arsenic content by pyro-decomposition at 650 -700<sup>0</sup> C. Metallic iron, preferably in close contact, and modest volume inert gas flows appear beneficial for achieving high arsenic removal rates, but do not lower the required reactor temperature. ### **ABSTRACT** 

Industrial processes at high temperatures are complex in nature involving many types of compounds, substances and solution phases. Due to this complexity it is sometimes impossible to investigate a specific problem experimentally or even understand in-depth the problem in question without input from reliable models.  The MTDATA software package from UK’s national measurement institute NPL (National Physical Laboratory) and the thermodynamic databases developed by NPL and its collaborators are used to understand these problems faced by industry. This work gives insight into the development of a lead-based database built as a part of NPL’s extensive MTOX (metaloxide-sulphide-fluoride) database. The lead-based database development work has required a critical literature review, new equilibration experiments providing information of the mutual solubilities of the elements, and optimization of interaction parameters for lead-containing systems. A direct-to-blister copper slag cleaning process in an electric furnace has been simulated as an illustrative application of the MTOX database. Additionally MTDATA’s new viscosity and electric conductivity models are validated against experimental data.
