### **INTRODUCTION** 

Phase diagrams provide a graphical presentation of a system’s equilibrium state as a function of different variables, often composition and temperature. They show the mutual solubilities of system components, temperatures of transformation between phase combinations and the thermodynamic data which underpins them can be used to derive microstructures formed during solidification. Although the equilibrium state is not always reached in the timescales relevant to industrial processes, due to kinetic constraints, for example, it is the state to which all the reactions tend. Thus, thermodynamics provides a valuable guide to real states of a system and, in that sense, forms a sound base for understanding materials’ behavior. 

Nowadays the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) method [1,2] is used as a generic tool for materials scientists and engineers to understand industrially related problems and phenomena. The CALPHAD method together with advanced thermodynamic software, such as MTDATA [3], has numerous advantages: Multicomponent systems can be studied with fewer experiments: Extrapolation to experimentally elusive environments (e.g. high temperatures) is possible: Metastable states of a system can be calculated: Many important thermodynamic properties can be derived from the Gibbs energy. However, thermodynamic calculations require internally consistent and reliable thermodynamic databases with reasonable coverage. Currently building these databases is one major task done by the CALPHAD community. The National Physical Laboratory’s (NPL) MTOX (metal-oxide-sulphide-fluoride) thermodynamic database [4,5] covers equilibria data for metallic, oxide, fluoride and sulphide systems related to metal smelting and refining processes. The MTOX database [4,5] is created under the guidance of MIRO (Mineral Industry Research Organization, UK) and mainly funded by industrial partners. 

In this paper the development of a smaller lead alloy database to be a part of the current MTOX database [4,5] is presented. Building a thermodynamic database is a challenging task and even adding one component to an existing database requires a lot of work but is worth the effort. The nature of this kind of work is basic research and has great potential for practical application. For instance a better knowledge of lead alloys’ thermodynamic behavior can help in the development of new alloys such as lead free solders, bearing metals, alloys for use in IVGen Nuclear power plants and also help in recycling and understanding impurity behavior in smelting and refining processes. At the end of this paper, as an illustrative example of the application of the database, an electric furnace slag cleaning process has been simulated using the most recent MTOX database [4,5] and MTDATA [3] software. Additionally MTDATA’s new viscosity and electric conductivity models are validated against experimental data.

### **CALPHAD METHOD** 

In the CALPHAD method [1,2], phase equilibria and thermodynamic properties in multi-component systems are calculated based upon models developed for the Gibbs energy, _G_ , of phases in smaller systems as a function of temperature, pressure and composition, starting from unaries and binaries. The models describe the Gibbs energy of each phase in a system, not just within the stable range but covering metastable temperature and composition ranges. The model parameters are optimised by fitting critically evaluated and selected experimental data during the assessment procedure. These experimental data can be phase diagram information, thermodynamic measurements and nowadays, increasingly, the results of first principle calculations [2]. The optimized thermodynamic model parameters are stored in a database (e.g. MTOX) for later retrieval as a basis for predictive calculations in multicomponent systems. 

Accurate experiments are needed as an important part of database creation and validation, as a thermodynamic assessment is only as reliable as the experimental data used as its foundation. When lower-order systems are known it is possible to interpolate to predict behavior in higher-order systems. In practice, this enables detailed visual and numerical examination of the thermodynamic properties and phase equilibria for a specific system. In addition, it is possible to calculate thermodynamic properties and simulate transformations of multicomponent systems using the modelled Gibbs energies and their derivatives. Besides the calculation of phase equilibria the CALPHAD method is used in dynamic applications such as diffusion simulation and simulation of solidification and the evolution of microstructures [2]. 

### **MTOX DATABASE** 

### **Models and experimental data** 

MTDATA [3] is a stand-alone package able to perform calculations appropriate to large multi-component systems containing many different types of phases, such as slags, mattes, alloys, gases and aqueous solutions, with exceptional reliability. Facilities are provided for the generation, manipulation, storage and retrieval of thermodynamic data, for plotting results in a variety of different ways including binary, ternary, multicomponent and predominance area diagrams and for linking to other process modelling software. Non-equilibrium calculations can be undertaken by omitting phases or placing restrictions on the distribution or behavior of components. 

The liquid oxide (‘slag’) phase in the MTOX database is modelled in terms of a series of non-ideally interacting species, either pure oxides, such as CaO and SiO2, or associated species, such as CaSiO3 and Ca2SiO4, used to take account of sharp changes in the thermodynamic properties of the liquid phase at particular compositions. The “associate” model [6] is conceptually simple, flexible and, unlike other models, which were tested at NPL, has no trouble representing amphoteric oxides and no tendency

Crystalline solution phases, such as those with the spinel, halite, olivine and pyroxene structures are represented in MTOX using the compound energy model in which ionic species are assumed to mix independently on a series of separate sublattices [8].

### **DEVELOPMENT OF THE LEAD ALLOY DATABASE** 

The chosen coverage of the lead alloy database development work was the binaries and ternaries of the Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni-Pb system. At an early stage of work it was noticed that although some of the le

ad binaries are rather well-known for some of them only a very limited amount of experimental information is available. It was necessary to make equilibration experiments of our own for some systems in order to achieve a more reliable thermodynamic description. 

### **Equilibration experiments** 

In the selected technique, liquid lead was equilibrated with solid metallic foil in specially formed quartz ampoules. Quartz ampoules were chosen due to the high vapor pressure of lead, as they prevented lead loss. Another benefit was that the samples could be stirred during the experiments by turning the ampoules upside down. This helped to 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

628 

accelerate diffusion and homogenize the alloys. A neck was made in the middle of the ampoule to permit separation of the liquid and solid material in the end of the experiment. The test materials used in the experiments were pure metallic granules and foils. This method enabled two solubility limit points from the ends of the phase diagram (a tie line) to be obtained in one experiment. 

Initially a chamber furnace was used but during the course of the experiments some development ideas led to a vertical tube furnace being built. After 48 h equilibration time the ampoules were quenched in ice water. The lead matrices with dissolved metal were analyzed using an Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) spectrometer at the companies involved in the project. The metallic foil saturated with lead was prepared for electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) at Geological Survey of Finland (GTK). The experimental method has been reported in detail elsewhere [14-18].

### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** 

Multi-component systems can be examined through predictive thermodynamic calculations, obtaining information even if unattainable experimentally. The MTOX (metal-oxide-sulphide-fluoride) from NPL is a thermodynamic database developed for systems related to metal smelting and refining. The MTOX database is under constant development work being able to serve better industrial partners. New components are added, such as lead, which is reported in this work, but even adding one component to the database requires a lot of work. As the approach is semi-empirical, the thermodynamic assessments are as reliable as the experimental data used as its foundation. Thus, accurate experimental data are essential in order to create a reliable thermodynamic database. Also new features are added to the MTOX database, e.g. new viscosity and electrical conductivity models. Thermodynamic databases assessed using the CALPHAD method can help in solving industrial scale problems. As an illustrative example, in this paper is given a direct-to-blister copper slag cleaning process, where copper slag is reduced in an electric furnace by adding carbon. According to the calculations copper oxide reduces exponentially. About 20 – 25 wt.% of lead reduces to liquid metal and thus tends to circulate internally when returned back to the smelting. Within this work the MTDATA’s new viscosity and electrical conductivity models were tested against experimental data, resulting that the new viscosity model has been improved and shows better agreement with the experimental data than the old viscosity model. The electrical conductivity model showed excellent agreement with the experimental data.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Chilean mining is facing high and rising levels of arsenic and antimony contents in copper sulphide ores and therefore their smelters have had to treat complex concentrates rich in these impurities under stricter environmental regulations. Concerning the study of the continuous converting of copper matte to blister in a packed bed reactor, the distribution of detrimental impurities of As, Sb, Pb and Zn were investigated by experimental laboratory scale tests at 1523K in relation to four variables; matte grade, packed bed height, blast flow rate and oxygen enrichment into the blast. 

The results indicated that the removal of impurities towards the slag and gas phases is strongly dependent on oxygen enrichment and packed bed height. Since the liquid matte flows gravitationally through the packed bed, an increase of this, contributes to prolong the residence time of the impurities improving contact with the blast, while higher oxygen enrichment enhanced their oxidation and subsequent slagging and volatilization. Compared to the conventional processes, As and Sb removals were similar, whereas those for Pb and Zn were higher. This study corresponds to the first reference of impurity behaviour in a packed bed reactor and indicates a concrete and promising use of this novel technology as a replacement to the traditional ones.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Continuous converting in a packed bed reactor has been extensively developed in previous works [1-3]. It consists on a countercurrent oxidation between copper matte and oxygen-enriched air through a ceramic packed bed of chrome-magnesite grains, were it is observed that the oxidation kinetic is faster compared to other technologies due to the higher dispersion of copper matte within the furnace. 

Quality standards for copper marketing require systematic monitoring of trace elements contained in it during the course of processing. The behavior of certain impurities in copper pyrometallurgy is critical for the success of the operation, particularly, levels of As, Sb, Pb and Zn have to be reduced under the limits specified by the refinery due to the detrimental effects of these impurities on the physical and mechanical properties on the manufactured copper products. 

Previous works have studied the thermodynamics of impurities involved in copper converting [4-11], giving an understanding of the behaviour for several minor elements typically related to the pyrometallurgical processes. In the present work an experimental technique was carried out in a packed bed reactor at a fixed temperature of 1250°C considering four variables; matte grade, packed bed height, oxygen enrichment and blast flow rate. The ranges of study were chosen adequately to characterize the copper converting process. 

The obtained experimental results are

presented in the form of As, Sb, Pb and Zn elimination regarding to the main variables considered in this study as well as their calculated distribution amongst gas and condensed phases. These results corresponds the first reference for impurities distribution in a packed bed reactor, which give useful information for future works.

### **Arsenic and antimony elimination**

Regardless of the variable studied, antimony elimination was higher than arsenic. In every copper grade range, activity coefficient at infinite dilution, γ<sup>0</sup> , of arsenic is always smaller than the corresponding coefficient for antimony [5]. Therefore, affinity of

will be always more difficult to remove this impurity. 

Removal of these impurities increase with an increasing bed height, ascribable to an increased residence time of condensed phases in the process, which also allows more contact between the impurities and oxygen in the blast. A similar result was observed regarding blast flow rate. Higher values produce more volume of exhaust gas which promotes the volatilization of these impurities which are definitely controlled by a drive mechanism to the gas phase. 

It is also observed that the removal of both impurities decreases slightly as a function of the matter grade. This behavior is explained, first, for higher matte grades copper, the activity coefficients of the impurities decreases [5], increasing their affinities with copper and therefore reducing the distribution of arsenic and antimony to slag and gas phases, and second, for higher copper content, sulfur content in this phase is lower reducing the volume of SO2 produced and therefore their contact with the impurities. 

### **Lead elimination** 

Lead elimination is significantly higher compared to arsenic and antimony due to the high value of their activity coefficient in infinite dilution [12, 13] (Figure 6). However, the behaviour of this impurity for each variable can be explained in the same way as for arsenic and antimony.

Because of the lower contents of zinc in blister (<20 ppm), no clear trends were found in order to establish their behaviour. Despite the above, calculations regarding zinc elimination were almost perfect, achieving an average value of 98%. 

### **Fractional distribution of impurities** 

Considering slag samples, fractional distribution diagrams of all impurities were made using packed bed height as independent variable (Figure 7). 

Arsenic and antimony have a very similar behaviour. As bed height increases, it was observed that both removals are mainly through a slagging mechanism at the expense of volatilization. At lower bed heights, and for the same blast flow, there is a greater volume of gas per copper matte volume, allowing a comparatively greater contact between both impurities and gas phase.

### **CONLUSIONS** 

1. Higher packed bed height gives a longer residence time and an increase in the removal of arsenic, antimony and lead due to prolonged contact of the impurities with the blast within the furnace. 

2. Impurity removal was strongly influenced by the oxygen enrichment rather than blast flow rate. Comparatively, elimination rates were higher for this first variable, indicating that there is preferably a removal of their oxidized compounds instead of their elemental compounds. 

3. Elimination levels were consistent with thermodynamic information. In increasing order, the average removal of these impurities was: 

As <Sb <Pb <Zn 

4. Elimination of arsenic and antimony was relatively low given the strong affinity of both elements in copper solutions. In some cases elimination levels were smaller than those reported in thermodynamic works, mainly due to the short residence time inherent to the packed bed technology. 

5. Lead showed a strong affinity for slag and gas phases reaching values even higher than 90%. Volatilization of this metal becomes important with increasing bed height due to the high value of its vapor pressure generated in the technology. 

6. Zinc removal showed the highest levels in this study, averaging 99%. Fractional distribution confirms that volatilization of this impurity is high on this technology, which reached values up to 75%. It was not possible to make an accurate analysis for the behavior of zinc as a function of the operational variables given the very low concentrations in the blister phase.

Zhi Sun<sup>a</sup> , Masanori Suzuki<sup>b</sup> , Peter Hayes<sup>a</sup> , Evgueni Jak<sup>a*</sup>

### **ABSTRACT** 

Slag viscosity is one of the key properties particularly important for high metal recovery and overall productivity in pyrometallurgical copper-making processes. The quasi-chemical viscosity (QCV) model has been developed and recently modified to allow the viscosities of multi-component fully-liquid oxide slags to be predicted within experimental uncertainties over wide ranges of compositions and temperatures. This model takes into accou

nt the complex internal slag structure providing advantages in accurate predictions of multi-component liquid slag viscosities, especially in slags having high SiO2 concentrations. The present research extends the QCV model to the SiO2 - Al2O3 - CaO - MgO - ‘FeO’ - Fe2O3 – “Cu2O” liquid slags directly relevant to various copper smelting and converting operations by incorporating new experimental data and a new optimised thermodynamic model of copper-containing oxide slags. Critical analysis of the available experimental viscosity measurements and their uncertainties, as well as analysis of common trends, has enabled the model parameters to be developed so as to give reliable viscosity predictions. Examples of the applications of the model are presented for conditions where the control of viscosity of the multi-component complex slag systems is important for the copper smelting, converting and recycling operations.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Slag viscosity is a key property during pyrometallurgical copper-making processes. A better understanding of the physical chemistry in relation to viscosity and successful prediction of the viscosities of multi-component copper-containing slags can play an important role in improving metal recovery and overall copper production. There are, however, very few reliable viscosity measurements of copper oxide containing slags available due to the physico-chemical properties of these systems. The aggressive slags react with oxide ceramics, and molten metallic copper reacts with noble metals (e.g. Pt, Rh), so that the combination of the slag and molten copper makes it very difficult to find suitable materials for the crucibles and spindles used in viscosity measurements. With this in mind, significant efforts have recently been made in the authors’ laboratory to obtain viscosity measurements of copper-containing slags [1] as well as to develop a model that can be used for interpolation and extrapolation. Using these data, it becomes possible to optimise the current viscosity model and extend its application to coppercontaining liquid slags. In the present paper, the quasi-chemical viscosity model is optimised and modified based on these recent measurements and is further extended to estimate viscosities of copper-containing slags during copper smelting and converting operations.

One view of silicate slag structures is that they consist of the silicate tetrahedra _SiO_ 44  and that the different metal cations distribute throughout to maintain electroneutrality. A silicate slag may also be considered as a nearly close-packed arrangement of larger oxygen anions with smaller metal cations that occupy the interstices and interact with each other. Experimental data are critically analysed before use in the optimisation to distinguish the level of uncertainties in the viscosity measurements. The model parameters as well as the experimental data needs to be further evaluated to ensure that they are consistent with trends and compositional/temperature dependences exhibited by other silicate slag systems. During the model optimisation, a number of key principles were followed, it was assumed that: - The viscosity/activation energy increases with silica content in the liquid slag; - The charge compensation effect from Al3+ needs to be considered; - The viscosity decreases with increasing temperature; - The Parameters can be evaluated by considering both the experimental data and estimation based on the physico-chemical properties of the liquid slag. Additionally, there should be no unexplained deviation in trends or abrupt transitions in the calculated composition-dependent profiles of viscosity. These principles enable systematic approach to developing the optimised parameters to be taken and provide a rational basis for judgements to be made over the relative weight given viscosity measurements and the estimated energy terms and parameters. ### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A structurally based viscosity model has been developed for copper–containing silicate slags taking into account the localised interactions between Cu-Si-Fe-Ca-Al-O species in liquid slags.The concentrations of structural units used in the model are obtained from predictions using a quasi-chemical thermodynamic model of the slags. New model parameters have been evaluated based on limited experimental data available in copper containing slags and the observed trends in related chemical systems. 

The model fills a gap in the current suite of predictive tools in that it can be applied to systems containing high copper concentrations, such as those encountered in copper making and copper pyro-recycling processes.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Research on slags involved in smelting-converting-refining operations to produce blister copper at the Atlantic Copper smelter in Huelva (Spain) has been carried out by quantitative electron microprobe analysis, X-ray diffraction and digital-imaging techniques. 

The results showed that mechanically-entrapped matte particles account for the biggest losses of copper in the slags. The largest proportion of Cu-bearing particles is present in the magnetite-rich converter slags, due to the negative effect of viscosity on coalescence and the precipitation of copper matte during conversion. 

The mechanical entrainment (the entrapment of copper matte by slags from both the flash and electric furnaces) resulted in copper losses mostly occurring as tiny particles with a stoichiometric composition similar to that of bornite. 

The Cu-bearing particle distribution has been analyzed and the effect on settling time in the slag cleaning furnace calculated.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The increase in production at the Flash Smelter Furnace (FSF) installed in 1975, from the original 40 tph design to the current 180 tph, reflects the upgrade of the whole smelter that has taken place.The sulfide ore concentrate (ca. 25-30 wt % Cu) is treated for copper extraction using a two-stage pyrometallurgical process: 1) smelting concentrates in flash furnace to matte, in which the average copper content is raised to 62 wt %; and 2) converting matte to blister copper with an average content of 99.5 wt % Cu). The silicate slags produced from both the flash furnace and the converters are treated in an electric furnace to reduce the contained copper from 1.4 and 5 wt % respectively to less than 1 wt %. After thermal refining,

The continuing increase of the feed in the FSF and the high variability of copper concentrates make it difficult to maintain a low copper content in slags. ### **Copper losses in slags** 

A number of papers have revealed that slag composition has a strong influence on copper losses to slag [10,11]. In fact, an increase in the iron concentration in the slag leads to a separation of magnetite crystals, which causes the heterogenisation of the silicate melt and a sudden rise in its viscosity [12], thus inhibiting the slag-matte separation and so increasing the mechanical losses of copper to the slag. This could explain the greater abundance of copper-bearing particles found in the magnetite-rich slag samples from the converter. 

The copper losses in the converter slag samples were mainly in the form of mechanically-entrained matte prills due to the effect of slag viscosity. The matte particles can be seen scattered throughout the slag matrix mostly occupying the gaps between the large elongated skeletal crystals of fayalite (Fig. 4A) although, more rarely, they were also observed as inclusions within the magnetite crystals. The copper matte particles often exhibit a distinct compositional zoning (Fig. 4B) and vary widely in size and shape (Fig. 5), even within the same slag sample, because of the occurrence of sporadic large matte granules (up to about 300 µm in length).

ite (Cu2S). 

The compositional variation of the entrained matte phases is far greater in the slag samples from the FSF than from the Converter slag samples. They can be described as iron-copper sulfides with a wide range of compositions, from chalcocite to cubanite. The EPMA results showed that most particles have concentrations of around 65 wt % Cu, 24 wt % S and 10 wt % Fe, with a stoichiometric relationship that approximates to bornite (Cu5FeS4), a sulfur-deficient phase in which chalcopyrite tends to be transformed when it loses its labile sulfur [12]. The concentration of copper in fayalite crystals was almost negligible (mean 0.05 wt % CuO), however, the rims of skeletal magnetite surrounding the matte particles housed appreciable amounts of copper (up to 0.43 wt % CuO). 

Likewise, the copper matte particles analyzed in the slag samples from the Electric Furnace were compositionally complex. The majority of particles had a chemical composition similar to the theoretical composition of bornite, with concentrations in the range of 61.5-69.3 wt % Cu. The EPMA results also showed low CuO content (mean 0.10 wt %) in the crystal structure of both fayalite and magnetite. 

Finally, the copper losses in the granulated slag sample are consistent with highgrade matte particles (64-72 wt % Cu, and 68.82 wt % Cu on average), showing intermediate compositions along the chalcocite-bornite join. In this slag, copper was also found not to be enriched by fayalite (mean 0.14 wt % CuO) and magnetite (mean 0.04 wt % CuO) as solid solution. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The copper slags resulting from the pyrometallurgical processing of chalcopyrite concentrates by Atlantic Copper at the Huelva smelter are spinifex-textured materials composed basically of fayalite and magnetite, with minor amounts of copper matte particles, and with amorphous or short-range phases. The Converter slags contain the largest proportions of magnetite and high-grade copper matte particles, suggesting that the slag composition and copper grade of the matte play an important role in the copper losses.

The copper losses in the slags appear mainly as mechanically-entrapped matte particles varying in size from a few to several hundred microns occupying the gaps between the skeletal and dendritic fayalitecrystals. However, copper sequestration by the crystal lattices of fayalite and magnetite was negligible, as indicated by the very low concentration of CuO detected in such metallurgical phases.

### **INVESTIGATION OF FREEZE-LININGS IN COPPER-CONTAINING SLAG SYSTEMS: EFFECTS OF BATH AGITATIONS** 

A. Fallah-Mehrjardi, P.C. Hayes, and E. Jak _PYROSEARCH, The University of Queensland Brisbane, Australia a.fallahmehrjardi@uq.edu.au_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

In heat transfer modelling of the freeze-lining deposit in high temperature reaction systems, it has been widely assumed that the interface temperature between the deposit and bath at steady state conditions is the liquidus of the bulk bath. There is, however, significant evidence which shows that the interface temperature may be lower than that of the liquidus. A general conceptual model has been developed that explains the factors influencing the steady state deposit interface temperature and thickness in chemical reaction systems in a positive temperature gradient. The findings demonstrate the basis for, and potential benefits that may follow from, operating the reactor at temperatures below the liquidus te

mperature, i.e. with solids present, without a catastrophic build-up of solids. This change in design concept could result in significant decreases in operating temperature, energy and operating cost savings. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

678 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Slag freeze-lining reactor wall protection is in use in a number of pyrometallurgical applications, such as, copper flash smelters, copper electric furnaces, ilmenite smelting processes, zinc slag fuming systems and Hall-Hйroult aluminium production cells [1-3]. To date the designs of freeze-linings for pyrometallurgical reactors have been based almost exclusively on heat transfer considerations, such as, bath convection, superheat, heat conductivity of deposit, and the heat-removing capacity of the coolant from the interface of the deposit and bath [4-8]. It has been widely assumed that the interface between the stationary frozen layer and the agitated molten bath at steady-state consists of the primary phase crystals, in contact with the bulk liquid at the liquidus temperature, Tliquidus. However, only a few studies have been carried out on the effects of bath composition and phase chemistry on the deposit formation.[1-3, 7-9, 9- 13]. There is increasing evidence that deposit/bath interface temperature may be below liquidus of the bulk bath. The recent laboratory-based study by the authors [1, 2] has shown, that the phase assemblage formed at the stagnant interface of deposit/bath at steady-state conditions is not necessarily solely that of the primary phase. The microstructural examinations and temperature measurements of deposits formed at steady-state conditions have clearly demonstrated that the temperature of the steady-state deposit/ bath interface, Tf, can be lower than the liquidus temperature of the bulk liquid, Tliquidus. 

A new conceptual model has been proposed [2] to explain this unexpected phenomenon (see Figure 1); this model assumes that crystal growth can occur not only at the existing deposit interface but on the detached crystals in the multi-phase liquid – solid(s) volume close to the interface. The steady-state deposit thickness and interface temperature is attained at a condition at which there is a balance between crystallisation on detached from the deposit interface crystals and their dissolution processes. This highlights the need for identification of the chemically-related parameters that may affect the interface temperature of the stagnant deposit and thus the freeze-lining thickness in steady-state conditions. The aim of the current study is to examine the effects of various convective flow patterns on the microstructures, morphology of phases and interface temperature of the bath/deposit at steady-state conditions.

### **Preliminary Considerations** 

The proposed conceptual model [2] suggests that the phase assemblage and temperature of the stationary interface at steady-state conditions is determined by a combination of factors, for example, 1) the fluid flow pattern within the liquid bath, 2) the extent of achievement of chemical and thermal equilibrium between the deposit and the liquid phase at the stationary deposit-bath interface, 3) the mass transfer rate close to and at the stagnant deposit interface, 4) the chemical and physico-chemical properties of the melt, such as, the change in the liquidus surface as a function o

f temperature and composition, the phase equilibria, mass and thermal diffusivity, viscosity, and 5) the rates of reaction phenomena, such as, crystal nucleation and growth rate and the dissolution of unattached solids. To identify how these factors influence the freeze lining deposit, a number of scenarios are examined with further focus on the elementary reactions and mechanisms.

### **Model Development** 

### <u>Equilibrium Crystallization</u> 

For the chemistry defined by the phase diagram in Figure 5.a a hypothetical case in which convective mass transfer in the liquid, and the local equilibrium between solid and liquid achieved within the moving cell at each moment in time, is analysed first. The achievement of local equilibrium is assisted by rapid local mass transfer / crystallisation within the moving cell and the presence of the heterogeneous nuclei in the liquid in the cell. Following the path of the cell, natural and forced convection moves the cell with bulk bath composition (Xbath) from the bulk bath at temperature Tbulk towards the interface of the freeze lining deposit, which is a

t a lower temperature Tf. In doing so the cell passes into a layer of material that is below the liquidus temperature, Tliquidus. In this sub-liquidus layer the cell temperature T is between Tliquidus at time t0 and Tf at time tf (i.e. Tf < T < Tliquidus). At temperatures below Tliquidus there is the potential for crystal growth. If the rate at which the cell approaches the deposit interface is slow compared to the rate of crystal growth and mass transfer within the cell, then local equilibrium is achieved within the cell. The compositions of the solids and liquids within the cell in this subliquidus layer will follow the solidus and liquidus lines of the phase diagram respectively (see Figure 5.a). 

It can be seen then that all of the solid primary phase A is formed before the interface of the freeze lining deposit is reached (illustrated in Figure 5.c). The proportion of the solid phase present in a cell and the composition of the remaining liquid at each moment in time are determined by the bulk cell composition, the temperature of the cell, and the liquidus in the primary phase field. On this basis the cells arriving at the interface of the freeze lining deposit at temperature Tf contain liquid of composition that is already in equilibrium with the solid phase under these conditions; there is then no net driving force for further deposition of solid at the stagnant interface. The crystals floating in the sub-liquidus layer do not become attached to the deposit surface, are washed away by the convective fluid flow into the bulk liquid, and are redissolved as the cells move into areas with higher temperatures. This process is continuously repeated at steady-state conditions. For this special case, where chemical equilibrium between solid and liquid is achieved within the moving cell at steady state conditions, it is argued that the limiting deposit interface temperature, Tf, is the solidus temperature of the system, Tsolidus. 

### <u>General Case</u> 

This analysis is now further extended to determine the interface temperature for general conditions under which incomplete crystallisation within the moving cell occurs. Again, consider the case of a cell of material approaching the interface of the freeze lining deposit across the subliquidus layer (see Figure 5.b). On this occasion the combination of the chemical properties of the system and the convective fluid flow pattern is such that only partial crystallisation within the cell takes place at each stage of movement across the sub-liquidus layer; the composition of the liquid at temperature T is

685 

illustrated in Figure 5.d. The cell then arrives at the interface partially supersaturated relative to the average local temperature Tf, that is, for some of the cells the thermodynamic driving force for the deposition of A on the stagnant deposit interface is now non-zero. 

In addition, in the systems with Tf  < Tliquidus a compositional gradi

ent (Xf – Xbath) > 0 will always be present resulting in a diffusive component of the mass transfer from the bath to the freeze lining interface across the subliquidus layer. It is assumed that some of the diffusive flux can be captured by and incorporated into crystallisation within the individual cells moving through the subliquidus layer by convective flow. Fresh material available for crystallisation on the stagnant deposit surface may or may not arrive to the interface through a combination of convective and diffusive mechanisms at various stages of the deposit formation depending on the crystallisation rate on the detached crystals. 

In this dynamic system there will always be compositional and temperature fluctuations in the liquid in the vicinity of the stagnant interface due to turbulent flow or eddy diffusion. As a result of perturbations in the shape of the surface of the solid, formed by crystal deposition and crystal growth will be selectively melted by interaction with local eddies of superheated liquid thus maintaining the dynamic steady state. This is similar to the formation of the smooth stable interface in the case of directional solidification [15]. As a result, a dynamic steady state interface with average Tf and Xf corresponding to the equilibrium liquidus would form; the position of the interface is determined by the balanced between the local periodic undercooling/superheating and under/over saturation present in the liquid eddies recirculating in the vicinity of the interface. 

If the formation of and crystallisation on the detached A crystals in the subliquidus layer did not occur then fresh solid A would crystallize directly on the deposit interface and the deposit would grow till the steady state is established; the absence of crystallisation on the detached crystals in the limiting case would then result in the temperature of the interface approaching the bath liquidus, TLiquidus. 

This initial analysis of the system behaviour indicates that the steady state interface temperature of the freeze lining, Tf **,** can be between Tliquidus and Tsolidus depending on the degree of crystallisation of the material that takes place in the subliquidus layer, and may be characterized in terms of the process parameters, such as, the rate of crystal growth (crystallization) within the cell, the rate of mass transfer in the liquid within the cell and also the velocity of the mobile cell induced by the bath agitation (i.e. the rate of convective mass transfer).

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Experimental laboratory study has been undertaken to investigate the effect of convective flow on the stability, thickness and interface temperature of the freeze lining deposits at steady state conditions. A general conceptual model has been developed that explains the factors influencing the steady state deposit interface temperature and thickness in ch

emical reaction systems in a positive temperature gradient. The proposed model assumes that nucleation and growth of the solid phase occurs in a subliquidus layer in the fluid phase ahead of the deposit, and that crystalline material is transported to and from the interface by turbulent eddies. The position of the interface is determined by the balance between crystallisation, attachment and removal of material from the interface within the temperature gradient. The conceptual model is significantly different from that used in the current engineering design practice, which assumes that the deposit interface is always at the liquidus temperature of the bulk liquid.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The final refining step in copper making is fire refining. Fire refining consists of several stages, but the most important are oxidation and reduction. These operations results from the interaction between an injected gas and the melt. In this paper, we present a mass transfer model that represents the reduction stage. It has been found that two mechanisms control the deoxidation of copper: i) Transport of the reducing gas from the gas bubbles towards the melt/bubble interface and ii) Transport of dissolved oxygen from the melt towards the melt/bubble interface. The former occurs in the early stages of deoxidation, while the latter controls towards the end of the reduction of copper. Fluid flow of the gases in the refining furnace has a strong effect on the dissolved oxygen transport.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Gas injection into melts is widely used in metal refining. In the particular case of copper, converting and fire refining are conducted by blowing a reactive gas into a melt to either remove sulphur and iron or oxygen from the metal. 

Copper fire refining consists of a couple of operations: _i_ ) oxidation of impurities and _ii_ ) reduction of the copper oxide that formed as a consequence of impurities oxidation. 

Oxidation is conducted by blowing air and adding fluxes. During oxidation, dissolved gases are expelled from the melt and some impurities are volatilized (Zn, Pb, Sb, As, S) or captured in the slag as oxides (Fe, Zn, Mg, Pb, Al, Mn, Ni, Co, Bi). As oxidation proceeds, copper also bec

omes oxidized and a fraction of this oxide is captured by the slag. The oxidation process stops when slag formation ceases; at this point, the metal may contain up to 1 wt% oxygen [1]. Once the slagging ends reduction of the melt is necessary to lower the oxygen content in the copper. 

Copper de-oxidation used to be conducted by “poling”, which consisted in throwing lumber to the molten copper to reduce the oxygen (dissolved) content. Brantley and Shack [2] conducted several reduction tests on molten copper (blister) using different gases and gaseous mixtures to reduce the oxygen content in the melts they tested. The experiments were carried out between 1125 and 1325 °C using various gas flowrates and processing times. They lowered the oxygen content from 0.3 wt% to as little as 0.1 wt%; additionally, they realized that gaseous reduction of copper is labor intensive and cheaper than the traditional poling operation. In terms of the gases used, Brantley & Shack noted that butane yielded better results than any of the other gases tried. Propane and methane gases were almost as efficient as butane, whereas reduction of copper with CO, CO-H2 mixtures and reformed gases only offered results similar to those obtained with butane when high flowrates were used. 

In a different study, Henych et al, [3] blew ammonia into a copper blister melt both at laboratory and pilot scale tests. They found that ammonia gas is able to reduce oxygen contents in copper to values below 300 ppm. 

Andreini et al. [4], reported experimental results on the de-oxidation of copper using CO under different sulphur contents. After testing melts with sulphur concentrations from as low as 10 ppm to 200 ppm and from 1113 to 1173 °C; they found that oxygen transport is the rate limiting step in copper reduction. Chitta and Geiger [5] confirmed Andreini´s findings. 

On a different investigation, Themelis and Schmidt [6] found that the dispersion and rate of reaction of CO jets depend on the diameter of the tuyeres used as well as to the depth of the injection point in the melt and the gas flowrate used for reduction.

Soltanieh & Karimi [7] compared the de-oxidation efficiency of gaseous and liquid reductants. They results show that natural gas reacts more readily than the liquid agent used. They also found that the early stages of gaseous de-oxidation are controlled by a diffusion mechanism, more likely that of dissolved oxygen in liquid copper. 

Marнn et al [8] reduced molten copper with graphite rods. They continuously measured the off gases by means of an infrared gas analyzer. It was found that depending upon the dissolved oxygen content, the overall reduction kinetics change. Gas evolution from the graphite rods is believed to have a effect on the rate of reduction of copper.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The new technology of continuous copper converting, developed by Universidad de Chile with ENAMI, generates a series of questions about the mechanisms of a liquid copper matte oxidation, formation of the slag, affecting the rate and efficiency of converting process. 

The CFD, mass and heat transfer modeling together with detailed analysis of phenomena taking place at the copper matte/gas , matte/slag , slag/gas and blister copper/gas interfaces allowed for determination of key factors affecting the rate of oxidation. The process requires specific self-melting fluxes being able to infiltrate the porosity of ceramic, packed bed and dissolve iron oxides as the product of oxidation, forming the slag, which properties permit for the flow inside the bed, separation from blister copper and continuous tapping out. 

It was found that the rate of sulphides oxidation is controlled by mass transfer and formation of iron oxide film separating sulphides and oxygen containing gas phase. Therefore, slag formation affects the rate of iron sulphide oxidation

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Continuous copper matte converting is a goal of metallurgist for long time, It has been achieved partly by Mitsubishi process, Noranda c

onverting to semi-blister and KennecottOutokumpu flash converting of pulverized matte. Direct to copper smelting processes, such as Noranda and Outokumpu flash smelting direct to copper, (GLOGOW and OLYMPIC DAM),include continuous converting. 

The classical copper smelting process consists of concentrate smelting furnace, such as flash smelter, Teniente Converter, shaft furnace and electric furnace, The smelting processes are fully continuous. The smelting slag is cleaned in an electric furnace or other reactor, as Teniente HLE. Off-gases are sent after separation of flue dust to sulphuric acid plant. Next, the produced copper matte is converted in Pierce-Smith or Hoboken converters. Converting as classical batch process produces blister copper and converting slag, which is recycled into smelting or slag cleaning process. Blister copper is directed into anode furnaces for fire refining, a typical batch process, consisting of two stages: oxidation with slagging and reduction. 

The proposed continuous converting process can be carried out in two reactors with classical “iron blowing” and “copper blowing  stages, or in one reactor producing classical blister copper or even over-oxidized blister, corresponding to the first stage of copper fire refining. 

Continuous oxidation of copper matte in a ceramic, packed bed with countercurrent flow of injected air or air enriched in oxygen, with continuous tapping out of blister copper and converting slag make full process continuity. 

The aim of this research is the analysis of very complex phenomena taking place in the reactors and factors determining the rate of matte converting. 

### **PRINCIPLE OF COPPER MATTE CONVERTING IN A CERAMIC PACKED BED** 

The principle of packed bed reactor is used in engineering chemistry, The major goal is a dispersion of a liquid phase and the increase the reaction surface, permitting for very high production capacity in a small reactors. Generally, the rate of heterogeneous reactions can be increased by temperature and reaction surface. The temperature is limited due to properties and service time of refractory, but the surface area can be enlarged by the dispersion of a liquid phase. In comparison to classical blowing of air into a liquid matte the reaction surface are orders of magnitude bigger during matte dispersion in a packed bed. 

The sketch in Figure 1 shows schematic cross-section of two reactors, corresponding to stages of “iron blowing” and “copper blowing.

### **DISCUSSION** 

The converting of a copper matte in a ceramic, packed bed characterizes a set of complex phenomena, very difficult for systematic analysis. Presented mechanisms of chemical reactions at the matte/air, iron oxides/slag, slag/ air interfaces is a simplification of very dynamic processes. 

The understanding of the complex phenomena of matte converting in a packed bed needs long and extensive fundamental research. 

It seems that the major factor affecting the very high rate of sulphides oxidation is the development of surface area of a liquid matte and its continuous motion. Comparing the reaction area in classical converting as air bubbles/matte area with very short residence time the reaction surface of a liquid matte in a packed bed is orders of magnitude greater. 

Next, key factor of the process is the slag formation. The fluxes are added onto the packed bed surface and the iron oxides are formed inside the bed. Self-melted fluxes, accessible and cheap, is the one of major achievement in the development of the process. Additionally, hypothetical advantage of the process is the use of the scrap of chromomagnesite bricks. The formed converting slag will be saturated by MgO and Cr2O3 due to large contact area, and will not attack chromo-magnesite refractory lining of the reactor or reactors. 

The refractory wear in classical Peirce-Smith or Hoboken converters is in tuyeres zone due to liquid motion. Proposed new technology basis on injection of the air through the tuyeres into packed bed, what ensure long tuyeres service time. 

The important invention inside a new process is a tapping block with inc

lined tapping hole, playing a role of siphon and stabilizing the level of white metal or blister in on the reactor hearth. This solution was previously applied in continuous copper fire refining. The pilot industrial scale tests demonstrated the perfect operation of this siphon [4].

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

1. Continuous converting of copper matte in a ceramic, packed bed allows for very high velocities of chemical reactions due to matte dispersion and the increase of the reaction surface. Thus, compact reactor has very high production capacity. 

2. The process can be carried out in two reactors, in which classical stages iron sulphide oxidation and iron oxide slagging, and copper sulphide oxidation to blister copper, take place. The process carried out in the one reactor produces directly over-oxidized blister copper and rich in copper converting slag. 

3. The countercurrent flow of the matte and air oxidizes iron sulphide, and iron oxides creates with the mix of fluxes (silica, limestone and clay) converting slag. When the concentration of FeS in the matte decreases the oxidation of Cu2S produces blister copper. Local oxygen saturation in oxygen causes precipitation of Cu2O, which dissolves in the converting slag. 

4. The products of matte oxidation depend on the matte/oxygen (air) ratio and utilization of the oxygen in the process. The oxygen utilization is a complex function of reactor geometry, grain size and porosity, matte grade and enrichment of air in oxygen. 

5. The converting in a packed bed is more suitable for high grade matte. Low grade matte produces more converting slag, which dynamically cover the matte surface slowing down the rate of sulphides oxidation. 

6. Air blown through tuyeres into ceramic packed bed ensures the long tuyeres service time in comparison to classical blowing into a liquid matte. 

7. Developed surface area of contact between converting slag and chromo-magnesite packed bed results in saturation of the slag with MgO and Cr2O3 and slow corrosion of reactors walls. 

8. Continuity of the process and low residence time of reactants and small dimensions of reactors results in low unitary heat losses, what means high energy efficiency of matte converting. 

9. The understanding of complex phenomenology of the copper matte converting in a packed bed requires extensive research.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Limited data are available on the phase chemistry of the copper smelting slag system used in the copper smelting and slag cleaning processes. The measurement of liquidus temperature of silicate slag systems relevant to copper smelting was carried out at controlled oxygen partial pressures in equilibrium with metallic copper by the procedures, which involve equilibration of mixtures, rapid quenching of resulting phases, and measurement of phase compositions using electron probe X-ray microanalyses (EPMA), developed at the Pyrometallurgy Research Centre (PYROSEARCH), the University of Queensland. The measurement of viscosities was also carried out by using the rotating cylinder viscometer techniques which developed at the Kyushu University from 1423K to 1573K at oxygen partial pressure of 10<sup>-9</sup> atm as a function of CaO%, Al2O3%, and Fe/SiO2 weight ratio. 

In the spinel side, increasing CaO%, Al2O3%, MgO% and Fe/SiO2 increases the liquidus temperature in the measurement range. The decreases of viscosity were obtained with the increase of CaO% and the increase of Fe/SiO2 without relation to the liquidus temperature change.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Optimal control of the slag chemistry in the copper smelting is one of the important issues. The slag properties, particularly liquidus temperature and viscosity (η) play an important role in the copper smelting, especially with the object of copper recovery from slag. However limited data are available on the phase chemistry of the slag system used in the copper smelting and slag cleaning processes. 

The aim of this study is to determine the liquidus temperature and viscosities of synthetic slags in FeO-SiO2-CaO-MgO-Al2O3 system in the range of temperature corresponding to the actual copper smelting operation.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The smelting processes units of the Chuquicamata smelter, i.e., the Flash Smelting Furnace and the Teniente Converter are based on the maximization of the energy value of the sulfide concentrates which are smelted by using oxygen enriched air in both the flash smelting and in the bath smelting technologies. Thus, since 1986 the FSF has been affected by several improvements in the design of the feed system, concentrate burner, and furnace cooling elements, process control and dust sulfating techniques. On the other hand the Teniente Converter smelting unit had improved extensively its concentrates feeding system. 

The thermodynamic conditions for the copper matte smelting is usually expressed by the phase relation in the Cu-Fe-S-O-SiO2 system, and can be understood intensively based on the phase equilibrium of the copper matte and the slag under high partial pressures of SO2. For these oxygen-smelting processes as the FSF and TC are of the practical importance. 

In the present work, the fundamental data of solubility of copper in the FeOXSiO2-MgO slag with the matte or high grade matte is evaluated for both the FSF and TC for a 13-months period of the Chuquicamata smelter operation.

It is well known that the viscosity of the slag is rapidly increased when magnetite saturation is reached and the solid magnetite crystals are separated in the fayalite melt. Assuming that the variation of the densities of slag and matte on composition is negligibly small the main factor to influence the rate of matte settling is the slag viscosity. This physical effect dependent on the oxygen potential or matte grade is responsible for the mechanical entrapment of the copper drops in the slag. For instance, for a copper content in the matte of 70-75 % (TC) the slag is nearly saturated with magnetite and the mechanically entrapped matte particles form are the predominant copper losses in the slag phase. Usually the copper losses are approximately 80% in the form of dissolved Cu2S and 20% in the form of dissolved as Cu2O. From these results it could be concluded, that higher _pO2_ in the TC enhance the saturation of magnetite in slag which increases the mechanical copper losses. 

### **CONCLUSION** 

The thermodynamic analysis showed a notable dependency of the copper solubility in the FeOX-SiO2 base slag which depends mainly on the oxygen potential or matte grade. 

Industrial data confirmed the thermodynamic analysis and showed that smelting furnace slag typically contains an average of 2% Cu for the FSF and 8% Cu for the TC. Copper is present in molten slags as entrained droplets of matte or white metal and dissolved Cu. The Cu content in slag increases as the matte grade increases.

### **PHASE EQUILIBRIA STUDIES FOR COPPER SMELTING/CONVERTING SLAGS** 

Baojun Zhao _School of Chemical Engineering The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia baojun@uq.edu.au_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Phase equilibria of silicate slags relevant to the copper smelting/converting operations have been systemically investigated in the temperature range 1200 to 1300<sup>o</sup> C and oxygen partial pressures between 10<sup>-5</sup> and 10<sup>-9</sup> atm. The experimental procedures include high temperature equilibration, quenching and accurate measurements of phase compositions using electron probe X-ray microanalysis (EPMA). The effects of CaO, Al2O3, MgO and Po2 on the phase equilibria of the fayalite slags have been systematically investigated. 

It was found that spinel and tridymite (SiO2) are major primary phases in the composition range related to copper smelting/converting slags. In addition, olivine, diopside and pyroxene may also appear at certain conditions. The presence of up to 20 wt% CaO, up to 10 wt% MgO and 10 wt% Al2O3 in the slag increases the spinel liquidus and decreases the tridymite liquidus. Liquidus temperatures in tridymite primary phase field are not sensitive to Po2; Liquidus temperatures in spinel primary phase field increase significantly with increasing Po2. Addition of the same weight of Al2O3 or MgO in slag shows the same effect on the liquidus temperatures in spinel and tridymite primary phase fields. The trends in the effects of Al2O3 or MgO on liquidus temperatura are similar for both copper smelting an

d converting slags.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

One of the important objectives of copper smelting/converting process is to remove impurities from matte or metal through the formation of the slag phase. Knowledge of the phase equilibria information of these slag systems are required to determine the optimum operating temperature. An optimum operating temperature should be close to the liquidus temperature of the slag to enable the slag to be tapped smoothly and required freeze lining can be formed to protect the refractory. The major components of copper smelting and converting slags are iron oxide and SiO2. The liquidus temperatures (conditions when the system is completely liquid) have been determined for the system FeO-Fe2O3-SiO2 for a range of oxygen pressures [1-2]. Other components can also present in the slags, such as CaO, Al2O3 and MgO. Phase equilibria of ferrous silicate slags in the system “FeO”-SiO2-CaO have been investigated by different researchers at oxygen pressures relevant to copper smelting/converting slags [3-7]. Phase equilibria in the systems “FeO”-SiO2-CaO-Al2O3 [8] and “FeO”-SiO2-CaO-MgO [9] at iron saturation have been investigated in the composition ranges related to copper smelting slags. However, copper smelting/converting processes operate at intermediate oxygen partial pressures between 10<sup>-5</sup> and 10<sup>-9</sup> atm. Information of the phase equilibria of ferrous silicate slags in air or at iron saturation is not sufficient to accurately describe the commercial copper smelting/converting processes. It is important to obtain the information of phase equilibria and liquidus temperatures at the intermediate oxygen partial pressures directly relevant to copper smelting and converting slags for the improvement of existing and development of new technologies. Limited information is available on the complex system “FeO”-SiO2-CaO-MgO-Al2O3 on phase equilibria and liquidus temperatures at the intermediate oxygen partial pressures relevant to copper smelting and converting slags. 

The aim of the present study is to demonstrate that the gaps in fundamental information, encompassing the conditions of copper production operations, can be filled through careful and systematic laboratory-based studies. Examples of new phase equilibrium information are provided in the system “FeO”-SiO2-CaO-MgO-Al2O3 at intermediate oxygen partial pressures between 10<sup>-5</sup> and 10<sup>-9</sup> atm. 

### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

### **Sample Preparation** 

High purity oxide and metal powders were used as starting materials, i.e. CaO (calcined at 1000<sup>o</sup> C from 99.0 wt% CaCO3), SiO2 (99.99 wt%), Fe2O3 (99.99 wt%), MgO (99.95 wt%), Al2O3 (99.99 wt%) and Fe powder (99.9 wt%). Mixtures of various compositions were prepared by accurately weighing the oxide/metal powders and mixing them thoroughly using an agate mortar and pestle. Each mixture was pressed to a pellet approximately 0.2

grams. Envelopes made from 0.025 mm-thick platinum foil were used in most of the experiments. Iron was found to be dissolved in the platinum under the conditions investigated. This would change the bulk composition of the slag. However, the compositions 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

739 

of the phases at equilibrium would not be affected and they were directly measured by EPMA after the experiments. 

At 1300<sup>o</sup> C and Po2 = 10<sup>-9</sup> atm the SiO2 concentration in the liquid phase of the wustite primary phase field is relatively low, which results in very high fluidity of the slag. On cooling the crystallisation rates are very high and the liquid phase in this system is therefore difficult to be quenched. New experimental procedures have been developed to overcome this difficulty [10-11]. The new technique, the primary phase substrate suspension technique used in the present study, involves preparation of substrate materials that are known, from preliminary experiments, to crystallise first during solidification of the melt. The iron oxide substrate used in this project was prepared from iron foil (99.5 % Fe, 0.1 mm thickness) supplied by Goodfellow Ltd. The substrate was first made to the shape required in the final experiment and then treated at required temperature and Po2 to form wustite. The slag mixture less than 0.1 gram was placed on the outside of the substrate and raised to temperature in a controlled gas atmosphere with PO2 controlled by CO2/CO gas mixture. As the slag melted the mixture was held on the surface of the substrate by surface tension forces, forming a thin film. Following equilibration the substrate and sample were released and quenched directly into water. The direct contact of the liquid slag with the quenching medium and the thin slag film lead to rapid quenching rates, much greater than can be achieved with the use of larger samples contained in metal foil or in crucibles. 

### **Equilibration** 

To monitor the actual temperature surrounding the sample, a calibrated working thermocouple was placed immediately adjacent to the sample in a re-crystallised alumina sheath. The temperature was controlled within 2<sup>o</sup> C of the target temperature. It is estimated that the overall absolute temperature accuracy of all experiments is within 3<sup>o</sup> C. 

The oxygen partial pressure inside the reaction tube was controlled by introducing gas mixture with a specific CO/CO2 ratio for a given temperature. In this study, equilibrations were carried out at oxygen partial pressures between 10<sup>-5</sup> and 10<sup>-9</sup> atm. These oxygen partial pressures required very low CO/CO2 ratios, thus premixed CO and Ar gases were used to achieve the target CO/CO2 ratios. 5% and 20% CO diluted in high purity Ar (Beta standards, 0.02% uncertainty) mixtures were supplied by BOC and high purity CO2 (99.995 % pure) was supplied by Coregas. The proportion of each gas was controlled using pressure di

fferential type flow-meter. The total flow-rate of the gas inside the furnace was between 400-600 ml/min and the fluctuation of the gas flow-rate was found less than 1% of the total flow-rate. 

A DS-type oxygen probe supplied by Australian Oxygen Fabricators (AOF, Melbourne, Australia) was used to confirm the oxygen partial pressures during the experiments. This was done by directing the output gas from the equilibration furnace into a separate vertical tube furnace held at the same temperature equipped with the DS-type oxygen probe. By this arrangement, direct monitoring of the oxygen partial pressure during the equilibration was possible. The results of the measurements in the present study are within the accuracy of the DS-type oxygen probe, i.e. ± 0.1 Log (Po2) units. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

740 

Equilibration experiments were carried out using a vertical tube furnace. The specimen with suitable container material was introduced from the bottom of the furnace and suspended by platinum wire. Before the specimen was raised into the hot zone, the reaction tube was preconditioned for 30 minutes to the required temperature and oxygen partial pressure. The specimen was then raised into the hot zone of the furnace and pre-melting of the sample was carried out by increasing the temperature 25<sup>o</sup> C above the target temperature. After 30 minutes of pre-melting, the temperature of the furnace was adjusted back to the target temperature. Equilibration was then carried out for 24 hours at the target temperature and oxygen partial pressure. After the equilibration the bottom end of the furnace was immersed in water and the lid was removed. The specimen was rapidly quenched into the water by pulling the sample holder upward. The quenched sample was dried on a hot plate, sectioned into smaller pieces and mounted in epoxy resin. The mounted sample was then polished for metallographic and EPMA examinations. 

### **Examination** 

The polished samples were initially examined using an optical microscope to identify the phases present. Then the sample was coated with carbon film using a JEOL (Japan Electron Optics Ltd) Carbon Coater for electron microscopic examination. A JXA 8200 Electron Probe X-ray Microanalyser was used for further analysis. Quantitative analysis was performed at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a probe current of 15 nA. The DuncumbPhilibert ZAF correction procedure supplied with the EPMA was applied. The standards used for analysis were from Charles M. Taylor Co. (Stanford, California): Al2O3 for Al, CaSiO3 for Ca and Si, Fe2O3 for Fe and MgO for Mg. The average accuracy of the EPMA measurements was estimated to be within ± 1 weight percent of the element concentration. Iron was present in the slag in both Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> forms. EPMA cannot measure Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> separately. All iron is calculated as “FeO” in this article for presentation purpose. 

### **RESULT

S** Iron oxide (spinel or wustite) and tridymite were determined to be the major primary phase fields in the composition ranges investigated. Typical microstructures of the quenched samples are presented in Figures 1a and 1b, showing well-quenched liquid slag in equilibrium with primary phases. Figure 1a shows a typical microstructure of liquid in equilibrium with spinel [(Fe2+ ,Mg)O·(Al,Fe3+ )2O3] and olivine [(Fe,Mg)2SiO4]; Figure 1b shows a typical microstructure of liquid in equilibrium with tridymite (SiO2) and diopside [(Fe,Mg)CaSi2O6]. Phase diagrams in the multi-component systems “FeO”-SiO2-CaO-MgO-Al2O3, for convenience of use, are often presented in a form of pseudo-ternary sections “FeO”-SiO2-CaO at fixed Al2O3 or MgO concentrations. For these multi-component systems it is difficult to experimentally obtain the exact target concentrations of all components in the liquid phase (for example, MgO = 4.0 wt %) due to the precipitation of solid phases from the melt and interaction of the liquid with the container/substrate. An optimisation procedure has therefore been used to analyse and interpolate all experimental data having a range of concentrations of the minor components Al2O3 or MgO in the liquid at a given primary phase field, temperature _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 741 and oxygen partial pressure. The basis of the optimization is that at a given CaO concentration in liquid the “FeO”/SiO2 ratio in liquid is function of Al2O3 and MgO concentrations. The interpolation procedure has been described in a previous paper in details [12] and it introduces a number of advantages. Experiments were planned so that the whole range of concentrations of interest can be described with one set of interpolation coefficients rather than focusing on exact fixed compositions. All experiments at a given temperature and oxygen partial pressure were used simultaneously for a fixed concentration of “FeO”, CaO, SiO2, Al2O3 and MgO. Isotherms at any required fixed concentration within the investigated range can then be constructed using this set of interpolation coefficients. glass

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The liquidus temperatures of copper smelting/converting slags have been determined by equilibration/quenching/EPMA technique. It has been demonstrated that MgO has significant effect on primary phase fields and liquidus temperatures of copper smelting slags. The isotherms in both spinel and tridymite primary phase fields move towards SiO2 direction with increasing Al2O3 or MgO concentration in liquid. This indicates that the liquidus temperatures increase in the spinel primary phase field and decrease in the tridymite primary phase field with increasing Al2O3 or MgO concentration. Al2O3 and MgO have the same effect on the liquidus temperatures in spinel and tridymite primary phase fields. The trends in the effects of Al2O3 or MgO on liquidus temperatura are similar for both copper smelting and converting slags. Liquidus temperatures in tridymite primary phase field are not sensitive to Po2; Liquidus temperatures in spinel primary phase field increase significantly with increasing

Po2. The information will be used to improve the industrial operations and for the optimisation of thermodynamic databases.

### **ABSTRACT** 

A major cause of metal losses in slags is the mechanical entrainment of metal droplets. One important factor is the attachment to solid spinel particles in the slag phase. Consequently, these particles hinder the settling of the metal droplets. In order to improve phase separation it is important to identify the fundamental mechanisms governing this attachment. Two complementary methodologies have been developed to study the tendency of metal droplets to attach to solid spinel particles. In one methodology, the interaction between Cu-alloys and spinel is studied by high temperature contact angle measurements. In the other, the entrainment is studied using a synthetic slag containing spinel solids.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Slags play an essential role in pyrometallurgical processes acting as collectors for specific groups of metals and for the elimination of unwanted impurities. Decantation is often the last step in pyrometallurgical processes, allowing the phase separation between slag and matte/metal. However, industrial Cu smelters still suffer from metal rich droplet losses in slags due to insufficient phase separation. In order to realize an improvement of copper smelting and recycling processes and to minimize these metal losses, it is essential to gain fundamental knowledge concerning the form and origin of these losses. 

Based on extensive research, it is currently well accepted that metal losses in slags are mainly caused by chemical dissolution in oxidized form and mechanical entrainment [1-3]. Chemical dissolution of copper is intrinsic to pyrometallurgical processes as its occurrence is determined by the thermodynamic equilibrium of the system such as the chemical activity of the metal [1], slag/matte phase [1, 4-6], the partial oxygen pressure [1, 4-6], the temperature of the system [1;6] and the reaction time. Mechanically entrained metal droplets can arise from a variety of sources like charging or tapping [7-8], metal precipitation from slag due to temperature fluctuations [9], gas producing reactions dispersing metal into the slag [9-11] or attachment to solid particles in the slag [9]. The first three main sources have be

en studied extensively in literature. Concerning the latter, available literature and fundamental knowledge is scarce; nevertheless this phenomenon is industrially relevant as the attachment of Cu-alloy droplets to spinel particles is found to cause metal losses in the slag. The specific and complex nature of the mechanisms responsible for this phenomenon, warrant a fundamental and systematic investigation. 

The present study aims to develop a methodology to study the interaction between Cu droplets and spinel particles in industrial systems. To our knowledge, no systematic evaluation on the specific interactions responsible for this attachment phenomenon has been performed in literature so far. In order to gather the desired knowhow on this interaction, two complementary methodologies have been developed, as represented in figure 1 [12]. On one hand, the interaction of Cu with spinel particles present in the synthetic slag system PbO-Cu2O-CaO-SiO2-Al2O3-ZnO-FeO is examined. The experimental methodology for the melting experiments is based on the decantation of one bigger Cu droplet through the slag system with a well-chosen synthetic composition in the ( ) single-phase region of the slag system. In order to increase the possible interaction, the slag is saturated with alumina, leading to a spinel layer at the interface between the slag system and the alumina crucible. In a first series of experiments, the methodology to study the metal droplet-solid-slag interaction has been developed, which has been described extensively by De Wilde [12]. 

Additional a methodology for high temperature contact angle measurements has been developed in order to study the interaction between Cu-droplets with spinel substrates in the absence of a slag system, using contact angle measurements at high temperature. First steps in the development of this methodology have been described by

### **EXPERIMENTAL SECTION** 

A conventional method to investigate interfacial interaction between a substrate and a liquid is observing the wetting behaviour of the liquid on the substrate, quantified by the contact angle. Analogously contact angle measurements between spinel substrates and Cu-alloys under varying atmosphere could yield the important influencing factors on the interfacial interactions between spinel and Cu-alloys. However, contact angle measurements are not evident for the current system. High temperatures have to be obtained in order to melt Cu and Cu-alloys (TM Cu = 1083°C). Moreover, Cu-smelters work at temperatures of 1100°C-1300°C. Consequently standard contact angle measurement equipment cannot be used. 

In order to be able to perform high temperature contact

angle measurements with comparable results, measurements have to be executed using a repeatable and reproducible methodology. A suitable setup has to be developed and spinel substrates have to be produced. Furthermore the presence of surface active species such as oxygen and sulphur has to be fully controlled in order to avoid unknown and unwanted effects.

### **Optimization Experimental procedure Contact angle measurements** 

### <u>Production spinel substrates</u> 

Contact angle measurements demand good substrates. More specific substrates for contact angle measurements should be dense, with minimal porosity, chemical homogeneous, free of thermal stresses and produced in a reproducible way. For the production of spinel substrates, a powder metallurgical process was chosen. Two commercially available spinel powders were selected as the starting material: MgAl2O4 and ZnFe2O4. 

For the production of MgAl2O4 spinel substrates, the spark plasma sintering equipment is used as described by Vanmeensel and co-workers [13], based on previous experiments from Wang, Morita and Frage [14-16]. The MgAl2O4 powder (<50 nm particle size, Sigma Aldrich) was sintered under a load of 60 MPa at a temperature of 1300°C. The MgAl2O4 plates were subsequently annealed at 1000°C for 3 hours. The sintered and annealed MgAl2O4 samples were polished using a 1-3-9 µm diamond paste, while a finishing step using colloidal silica was applied. More details concerning the sintering process are described by De Wilde [12]. 

ZnFe2O4 substrates were produced using a ‘free sintering’ approach. ZnFe2O4 powder (<100 nm particle size, Sigma Aldrich) was first compressed in pellets (1.2 cm diameter) using a cold press, using a pressure of 5N. The pellets were subsequently isostatically pressed with 2500 bar (= 33 kN). These compressed plates were then sintered in air in a tubular furnace at 1200°C for 3 hours. Finally an annealing step was performed during 2h at 1000°C. The sintered and annealed ZnFe2O4 samples were polished using a 1-3-9 µm diamond paste, while a finishing step using colloidal silica was applied. An XRD diffractometer (Siemens diffractometer D 5000) was used for identifying the spinel phase in the ‘free sintered’ substrate. The XRD pattern is shown in figure 3. All the diffraction peaks can be indexed to the cubic spinel structure of ZnFe2O4 (International centre for diffraction data, No 01-070-6394). This indicates that the free sintering does not have any influence on the chemical composition of the ZnFe2O4. Representative optical micrographs of the polished substrate can be seen in figure 2. An average Vickers harness of HV-3 of 524.4 ± 11.8 was obtained, the density of the ZnFe2O4 substrate is 4.91 g/cm³.

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The methodology of the contact angle measurements at high temperature has been further optimized, in order to study the interaction between Cu-droplets and spinel substrates in the absence of a slag system. The combination of this methodology with the melting experiments could be very useful to reveal fundamental information considering the interaction between Cu-alloys and spinel particles in industrial Cu-smelters.

### **ABSTRACT** 

AVA is a system capable of determining the copper content of white metal or matte samples based on visual clues such as color tone and texture. Empirically, it relates the intensity of color with the copper content, which is the foundation of the Chilean patent No. 47,109, `Integrated System for the Determination of Copper Content in a White Metal Sample and its Associated Procedure’. This technology reinforces the operators’ visual ability to determine the quality of the product by identifying distinguishing and quantifiable physical characteristics of the sample. AVA captures an image of the sample employing a diffusive illumination system, and through image processing algorithms it quantifies hue and texture, which are then correlated with its copper composition. The main advantages of our method is that it does not require a dedicated room for sample preparation, it analyzes very quickly and accurately the white metal grades, and it allows the operator to correct the input variables to control the monitoring process in a timely manner.
