### **INTRODUCTION** 

The good performance of process's control in a copper smelter depends on experience of their operators, and its capacity to detect through view, its operation of furnaces and the quality of intermediate and final products. The temperature of matte and slag are estimated by its color in the discharge from tap-hole or launder, the matte grade can be estimated with the accretions shapes solidified in the launder or measurement of matte level the drag of copper in the slag is observed by emission of SO2 in the slag discharged, etc. In summary, there are some characteristics of process that the operator can identify through observation that allows process's control and questioning a determined measurement on line, in fact usually wrong sensed due to the hard work conditions of sensors in pyrometallurgical processes. Only sensors based on vision or radiation allow an operational continuity because they are not in contact with smelted liquids and for these reasons the measurements of temperature are carried out with optic

pyrometers or laser based on emitted radiation. According to the experience of the operators we have designed a system and a procedure to determine copper's content on samples of white metal or matte in the launders for fusion reactors of copper concentrates. Actually, the empiric experience indicates that when copper content increase in the white metal its hue changes from dark gray to light gray, furthermore this is the main attribute to quantify and correlate with the copper analytical assays. There are additional attributes such as texture and metallic copper that also are considerate through their gray equivalent. 

Currently, copper content in white metal or matte is determined by X-Rays Diffraction (XRD). The analysis requires a physical treatment of cooling, crushing and milling in the special room. The pulverized sample is introduced to the XRD equipment for its analysis. This method of analysis is "dirty" because requires pulverizing the sample which implies a preparation room, cleaning of sieve to avoid sample´s pollution and handling of dust generated storage and final disposal. The analysis proposal using artificial vision, AVA system, is a clean analysis; the sample is partitioned and introduced in the analyzer for its digital treatment to determine the gray hue and its correlation with content of copper. Once the analysis is finished, the sample can be retired and returned to the process. In addition, digital records are stored for revision or export. Not requiring a sampling preparation room; the equipment can be installed in the reactor control room, simple procedure with less steps that decrease the handling mistakes. The analysis is fast, delivering timely information for process control. Figure 1 shows a comparison of steps between XDR and AVA System.

### **DISCUSSION** 

In this paper is presented a study to determine the copper content through the imaging treatment for samples of white metal or matte. The discriminant characteristics of samples are: the gray hue, texture and metallic copper present in them. Each furnace has its own calibration curve due to the different aspect the samples show. 

When the white metal is low (70-72 wt% Cu) the samples have more texture and dark gray hue. In addition, when the white metal is high (74-77 wt% Cu) they have less texture, light gray hue and metallic copper presence. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

773 

When the matte is low (58-61 wt% Cu) there are less texture and presence of fine particles of copper and dark gray hue. In contrast, when the matte is high (63-65 wt% Cu) there are more texture, more particles of copper and dark gray hue. The presence of copper particles along the matte range indicates there is

copper conversion in the shaft of SFS. The phenomenology in the SFS is different to TC. The presence of copper in TC appears only when white metal composition is higher than 75% Cu. 

The accuracy of AVA analysis is expressed by the difference between its value and the chemical assays performed by CESMEC and it is ±0.6wt% Cu. The AVA accuracy is greater than XRD accuracy. For Hernбn Videla Lira Smelter, the XRD accuracy was ±2.5w% Cu and for Chagres Smelter was ±1.26 wt% Cu. The precision of AVA analysis was determined with measurements repeated and the result was ±0.22 wt% Cu. 

During validation tests in Hernбn Videla Lira Smelter, we made measurements with samples cooled to air with different times to observe if the temperature of sample has some effect associated to the infrared radiation. This was not observed, and the dispersion of the values measured was 0.02 wt% Cu. Additionally, we made measurements with samples air cooled and water cooled. These tests establish that it is possible to obtain results with a response time less than 10 minutes after that the molten is discharged from tap-hole. The current analysis requires of: cooling, transfer, preparation and analysis, which involves times upper to 25 minutes. 

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The AVA System is an efficient technology to determine the content of copper on white metal samples from Teniente Converter, white metal from Electric Furnace and matte from Smelting Flash Furnace. The accuracy of AVA analysis is ±0.6wt% and its precision was ±0.25wt%. 

Response time is at maximum 10 minutes and current analysis´s time is at least 25 minutes. The AVA System is more sustainable than XRD because it does not require a preparation room of samples, which involves acoustic contamination, production of dusts, solids handling. It has fewer steps implicating a reducing of mistakes by samples handling.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Iron nickel alloy containing platinum group metals (PGM) which is produced in South Africa with reduction of a high chromium content ore, contains the valuable metals such as iron, nickel, copper, silver and PGM. This PGM content iron nickel alloy is treated with a copper smelting process, and copper and PGM are recovered, however, nickel is lost to slag. Demand of the nickel is increasing as raw materials of the stainless steel, and recovery process for nickel and PGM is required in nonferrous smelting process. It is necessary to remove iron from the iron nickel alloy to recover the value metals by a hydro process economically because the PGM content iron nickel alloy contains 75-85% of iron. 

In this study, fundamental research of the oxidation process was carried to recover the value metals of nickel, platinum and palladium from PGM content iron nickel alloy. We assumed that a copper added to the PGM content iron nickel alloy to lower the melting point of the alloy, and a Fe-Ni-Cu alloy was produced. Distribution ratio of iron, nickel, platinum and palladium between the iron oxide slag and molten copper is measured the range of log pO2 between -9 and -5 at 1573 K.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The chemical composition and dust formation during the oxidation of copper concentrate particles under suspension-smelting conditions were investigated. The effects of initial particle size and oxygen concentration in the process gas on the particle composition, morphology, and mineralogy of the reacted particles along a laminar-flow reactor were tested. The chemical composition of the reacted particles was determined by atomic absorption spectroscopy. The mineralogy was determined by X-ray diffraction and QEMSCAN® techniques, the latter of which involves scanning electron microscopy combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The experimental data indicated that the smaller the size fraction in the feed, the higher the extent of oxidation. The QEMSCAN® micrographs in general agree with a reaction mechanism involving expansion and further fragmentation of the particles during flight. The extent at which both phenomena occurred was dependent upon the initial particle size and residence time of the particles in the reactor.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Since its invention [1], the flash smelting process has been adopted as the major primary copper production technology around the world. Because of its productivity and rapid application at commercial scale, the process has been continuously studied to improve its efficiency and decrease its environmental impact. A major area of research concerns the reaction path followed by the copper concentrate particles during their flight in the reaction chamber of the flash smelting furnace. Despite the evident progress so far made in this direction [2-13], a number of uncertainties still remain. Also, experimental data to validate the mathematical formulations so far developed in the literature [14] are scarce. 

The most accepted model for the reaction path of sulfide particles in the reaction shaft of a flash

smelting reactor was developed by Kim and Themelis [10] and further modified by Jokilaakso et al. [11]. In this model, the initial particles are first heated up by the reactor walls by radiation and the process gas by convection until they reach its ignition temperature. At this stage, oxidation occurs at the particle surface forming a porous crust of copper and iron oxides surrounding the core of unreacted sulfides. As the oxidation reactions proceed and the heat of reaction is released, the particle temperature increases rapidly and the core of sulfides eventually melts. The gas evolved by the oxidation reactions accumulate inside the molten core and increases the pressure within the particle, thus causing the particle to bloat. When the pressure inside the particle overcomes the interfacial tension of the surrounding oxide layer, the particle undergoes fragmentation. Particle fragmentation produces a large number of fine particles, droplets, and empty shells which continue their flight throughout the reaction chamber. Fragmentation is also responsible for the generation of dust particles which are undesirable in the industrial operation. It has long been recognized that the rate of oxidation of sulfide particles at high temperatures is strongly dependent upon the size and chemical composition of the initial particles and the operating conditions prevailing in the reactor. The present work is part of an ongoing research aimed at characterizing the most relevant phenomena occurring in the particles along their trajectories in the reaction chamber of a flash smelting reactor. For that purpose, extensive experimentation is being conducted in a laboratory furnace under suspension-smelting conditions. The goal of this investigation was to test the effect of particle size and oxygen concentration in the process gas on the chemical characteristics, morphology and mineralogy of copper concentrate particles during oxidation in a laboratory-scale laminar-flow furnace. In a complementary paper [15], the evolution of the size distribution of the particle population is discussed. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 787 ### **EXPERIMENTAL WORK** The experimental set-up is shown in Figure 1. ### **CONCLUDING REMARKS** 

An experimental study was conducted to track the history of the oxidation reactions of copper concentr

ate particles under suspended-smelting conditions. The results showed that particle composition was strongly dependent on particle size in the feed material. Overall, the reaction path followed by the particles suggests that particles experienced expansion followed by violent fragmentation with generation of dust. Small particles in the feed were more reactive than large particles, and pyrite was more reactive than chalcopyrite along the trajectory of the particle cloud. Magnetite and ferrites were found to be the predominant phases in the oxidized particles, whereas copper vaporization was negligible during particle flight.

### **VISCOSITY MEASUREMENTS FOR COPPER SMELTING SLAGS** 

Mao Chen and Baojun Zhao _School of Chemical Engineering The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia baojun@uq.edu.au_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Understanding a metallurgical process requires accurate data on physiochemical properties of the slag. Viscosity is one of the key properties of the slag required for optimisation and improvement of copper smelting operations. In the present study, the viscosities of the synthetic slags relevant to copper smelting process have been investigated systematically by rotation technique. Molybdenum crucible and spindle sets were used in the study and metallic iron saturation of the slag was maintained during all measurements to control the oxygen partial pressure. The apparatus has a system of quenching the sample after the viscosity measurement, which enables the phase assemblages and compositions of the phases present in the slag at temperature to be me

asured by electron probe X-ray microanalysis (EPMA). The viscosities of the slag systems SiO2-“FeO”, SiO2-“FeO”-Al2O3, SiO2-“FeO”-MgO, SiO2-“FeO”-CaO, SiO2“FeO”-CaO-MgO and SiO2-“FeO”-Al2O3-CaO-MgO have been measured at temperatures up to 1500<sup>o</sup> C in equilibrium with metallic Fe. Effects of Al2O3, MgO, CaO and “FeO” and their combinations on viscosity of copper smelting slags have been discussed and experimental data are also used for development of the viscosity model. Activation energies of these slag systems have been derived from the experimental data.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Fayalite slag “FeO”-SiO2 is the base of the copper smelting slags. In addition, Al2O3, CaO and MgO are also present in the slags in relatively low concentrations. Understanding the viscosity of fayalite slag and the effects of Al2O3, CaO and MgO on the viscosity is crucial to optimise the smelting process. Slag tapping, separation of matte from the slag and formation of protection lining are all related to the viscosities of the slags. In particular, the viscosity appears to be more important when the copper smelting tends to be operated at lower temperature. 

The viscosity data on fayalite slag are not consistent due to the difficulties associated with the high temperature viscosity measurements. The study of this fundamental system is not only important in practical aspect, but also essential for the viscosity modelling development. High temperature viscosity measurements are timeand cost-consuming process. Viscosity model is an effective way to predict the viscosities of the complex slags at high temperature. However, comprehensive viscosity models can only be developed on the base of accurate experimental data on low order systems. The aim of the present study is to provide accurate viscosity data on the “FeO”SiO2-CaO-MgO-Al2O3 system in equilibrium with Fe to resolve the large discrepancies of the measurements in this system. With an improved viscosity model, the viscosities of Cu smelting, converting and cleaning slags over a wide range of compositions and temperatures can be predicted and later can be applied in the process control and modelling. 

### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

A high-temperature viscosity measurement apparatus was developed at The University of Queensland, Australia [1, 2]. A Brookfield digital rotational rheometer (model LVDV III Ultra) controlled by a PC was used in the present study. A Pyrox furnace with lanthanum chromite heating elements (maximum temperature 1923 K) was employed. A Pt-6Rh/Pt-30Rh (B type) thermocouple was bound to the suspension tube platform, the tip of which remained adjacent to the crucible at the level where the spindle rotated. This enabled accurate temperature of the slag to be measured during the viscosity experiments. 

The main feature of the current experimental setup with top suspension provides a possibility of quenching the slag sample immediately after th

e viscosity measurement. After the viscosity measurement, the Pt suspension wires were sheared by alumina tube placed inside the suspension tube to enable the crucible to drop directly into a water bucket beneath the furnace. The ability to quench the slag sample is important since this enables the microstructure of the slag and compositions of the phases present in the slag at the temperature to be retained and characterised directly after the viscosity measurement. In this way the uncertainty associated with the changes of the slag composition during the measurements can be minimised. In addition, presence of crystals, if any, during the experiment can be identified.

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Viscosities of fayalite slag with different combinations of replacement of “FeO” by MgO, CaO or Al2O3 have been systematically investigated in equilibrium with metallic iron. The comparisons of the viscosity and activation energy data between the present and previous results in the system “FeO”-SiO2 demonstrate that accurate measurements are important to obtain the clear trend for further analyses. The slag viscosity can be decreased by the additions of oxides other than SiO2 and the order of the decrement at high SiO2 (> 40 mol pct) is CaO (up to ~ 12 mol pct) > “FeO” > MgO > Al2O3. However, at low SiO2 (~ 33 mol pct), “FeO” is a stronger network modifier than CaO to decrease the viscosity. The parameters in Modified Quasi-chemical Viscosity (QCV) model have been optimised based on the new viscosity data. The tendencies in the higher order systems were discussed with the assist of the model predictions. The effect of solid fraction on the viscosity of the slag was also discussed based on the Einstein-Roscoe equation.

### **APPLICATION OF SPECIALIZED NON-DESTRUCTIVE TESTING (NTD) FOR OPERATING COPPER PROCESS VESSELS*

* 

Afshin Sadri, Wai Lai Ying and Pawel Gebski 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Monitoring refractory condition in process vessels allows plant owners and operators to proactively identify problem areas in the linings. Short and long term maintenance planning can then be implemented to prolong vessel campaign life and minimize the possibility of catastrophic failures such as molten metal run-outs. The refractory lining of copper process vessels such as flash and slag cleaning furnaces, reactors, converters, and absorption acid towers is known to ultimately fail, resulting in a shorter campaign life. Refractory wear, refractory hydration, refractory lining failure, and hearth lifting are well known failure mechanisms of process vessels. 

In this paper specialized Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) techniques available for monitoring operating copper process vessels will be discussed.  We will demonstrate how the application of such techniques has been used to identify deterioration, ultimately allowing plant owners and operators to prolong the service life of process vessels through proactive maintenance planning and action. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

814 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Broadly, primary copper smelting can be divided into two general categories: Flash Smelting and Bath Smelting.  Among the Flash Smelting vessels are Outokumpu flash furnaces and Inco flash furnaces.  All others, such as, Teniente and Noranda reactors, Pierce Smith, Anode Converters, Reverberatory furnace, ISASMELT and Ausmelt furnaces, Mitsubishi Process, Electric, Vanyukov and Blast furnaces are considered as bath smelting process. 

Globally there are about 70 large smelting plants operating. Thirty of these plants are based on Flash Smelting and 40 are based on Bath Smelting process.  Regardless of the type of process, refractory lining is one of the most crucial structural elements affecting the campaign life of a copper process vessel.  Structural health monitoring and integrity evaluation of the refractory lining is a continuous task and crucial in preventing costly run-outs and disastrous campaign failures. 

In addition to traditional process vessel monitoring systems such as thermal readings and physical measurements, new methodologies based on applied physics principles have been developed. These NDT techniques have been successfully applied on numerous copper smelting vessels for the past decade by Hatch.  In this paper we discuss application of two of these techniques that have been applied on copper smelting vessels and relevant acid towers.   The two are Acousto Ultrasonic-Echo (AU-E) and Acoustic Emission (AE) techniques. Both techniques are based on stress or elastic wave propagation in to the materials.  AU-E is an “active” technique, while AE monitoring is a “passive” NDT technique.  Both techniques are sensitive to refractory material and structural changes. 

To demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the AU-E technique we are including a p

aragraph from a paper presented and published by Kennecott Utah Copper Corporation at Copper 2007: 

_“Starting in fall of 2004 and leading up to the shutdown, Hatch Associates, Ltd. was contracted to conduct five non-destructive acoustic testing (NDT) surveys to determine FSF hearth condition.  This test work was utilized to establish a level of risk around the timing of the shutdown and allowed KUCC to confidently push the shutdown out from the originally planned 2005 date.  The capability of the method to detect unusual melt penetration into the hearth and between the hearth refractory layers was validated during the shutdown.”_ [1]

In the following sections we briefly introduce the two techniques and discuss their relevance and application in copper smelting vessels. 

### **AU-E Methodology** 

The Acousto Ultrasonic-Echo (AU-E) is a stress wave propagation technique that uses time and frequency data analysis to determine coarse-grained material thicknesses, such as refractory and castable materials in operating furnaces. A mechanical impact on the surface of the structure (via a hammer or a mechanical impactor) generates a stress pulse, propagating into the furnace layers. The wave is partially reflected by the change in refractory layer properties, but the main portion of energy propagates through the solid refractory layers until it dissipates. The signal is mainly reflected by the refractory/molten metal or gases interface, or alternatively by the build up/air or molten metal interfaces that are formed between internal layers or at external boundaries. 

A receiver placed beside the impactor detects surface displacements caused by reflections from internal and external interfaces. The signals are analyzed both in time and frequency domains, where the controlling factors include changes in thickness, temperature, dimensions, and wave speed. 

With this methodology, the principal stress wave captured and analyzed for quality assessment is the Primary wave (P-wave), or the compressive wave. The compressive wave speed is affected by the density, thermal gradients, shape and dimension factors, and elastic properties. A drastic change in density and/or in elastic properties of the material will result in partial or total reflection of the wave. In addition, stress free zones, such as cracks and discontinuities, will result in partial or full reflections. 

### **AU-E Applications on Copper Smelting Furnaces** 

AU-E technique has been used to inspect furnace hearths, sidewalls and endwalls, reaction shaft roofs and sidewalls, build-up thickness measurements on uptake shaft walls and taphole thickness measurements. In the following sections we discuss a number of selective applications. 

### **Furnace Hearths** 

For the purpose of AU-E inspection the area under the hearth is typically subdivided into a number of panels to form a regular measurement grid. If required the measurements are fo

cused on specific locations, such as areas under uptake shafts or reaction shafts. The number of measurements is also driven by the accessibility of the test locations. Depending on the hearth cooling type there may be a need to remove the plenum plates to provide access to the bottom plate. Typically, the spacing between each two

measurement points is approximately 200mm. AU-E measurements are repeated at least 3 times to assure repeatability and accuracy of each data set. 

Primary objectives for hearth inspection are to identify: 

1. Refractory wear or impregnation 

2. Metal penetration between the hearth layers 

3. Hearth lifting or delaminations 

Secondary objectives for hearth inspection are: 

1. Detecting refractory failure due to hydration 

2. Detecting cracking and fracturing in hearth layers 

### **Hearth Impregnation** 

Our experience in measuring copper Flash Converting Furnaces (FCF) is limited to one case study.  After the end of the campaign and visually checking the hearth lining, it was confirmed that 100% of AU-E results matched the physically measured refractory thicknesses in the hearth.  One important observation was presence of metal impregnation into the refractory matrix.  After the furnace campaign was finalized and we could drain and enter the furnace, the Working lining looked intact (Figure 1). However, examining the individual bricks revealed 30% increase in magnesia-chrome bricks mass density.  After cutting the magnesia-chrome refractory samples and analyzing them for the chemical composition, it was revealed that the bricks were highly impregnated by copper.  A maximum impregnation of 210 mm for a full thickness of 460 mm (almost half of the original length) refractory was recorded (Figure 1).  Thanks to the early “baseline” inspection, the AU-E data was corrected to compensate for the wave speed changes that influence the hearth thickness measurements.  The AU-E signals were used to identify the highest concentration of copper penetration into the Working layer. These results could be used to correct the hearth thermal gradient results that were affected by the copper penetration into the Working lining and altering the refractory thermal behaviour.

### **Sidewalls and Endwalls** 

Wearing and deterioration of the sidewalls and endwalls are common in most copper smelting furnaces including slag cleaning furnaces.  For the sidewalls and endwalls, cross-sectional profiles are prepared by connecting the AU-E thickness measurements at different elevations along the height of the furnace walls.  Figure 8 shows a schematic drawing, produced based on the AU-E thickness measurements.  AU-E measurements can be conducted on the sidewalls with or without cooling blocks.  AU-E readings can be taken on the cooling blocks or on the refractories between the cooling blocks. In case of spray cooling, because of wet environment the connection between the sensor and the cable is changed to the waterproof type. Copper furnace walls are usually lined with 1 to 3 layers of Magnesia or Alumina brick.  Typically, between the refractory and the shell a granular material is used to act as a heat conductor and fill the gap between the shell and the refractory.  Due to frequent thermal cycling of furnaces (shutdowns and startups), which cause expansions and contractions of the furnace hearth and the wall movement, the granular infill subsides to the bottom resulting in formation of gaps and discontinuities between the refractory and the shell, reducing the cooling effect from the spray cooling.  Because of lack of cooling, wall refractories undergo more rapid and more severe deterioration particularly at the tidal zone, where slag and metal levels vary frequently.  Periodic inspection of the same testing stations is used to determine the wearing and deterioration rate for the walls. 

Build-up or skull can also be measured by the AU-E system.  Skull or build-up should be solid, thick and have acoustic impedance higher than the refractory to be detected by AU-E signals.  Because of the material’s heterogeneity and lack of known wave speed,

### **AE Monitoring Technique** 

### **Taphole Acoustic Monitoring** 

Tapblock refractory is vulnerable to damage and wear due to drilling, lancing and tapping operations. In 2007, Hatch developed a Taphole Acoustic Monitoring (TAM) technique to monitor the deterioration of the tapblock refractory [2]. This method is based on acoustic emission (AE) monitoring principles. We applied this technique at the tapblock of a flash converting furnace. This is a water-cooled tapblock with cast-in Monel pipes that served as cooling circuits, which enabled the flow of cooling water within the copper tapblock. A set of four AE transducers was attached on the cooling pipes inlets and outlets, and the Monel pipe acted as wave guide for the AE propagation. Any AE signals related to the deterioration of refractory were transmitted through three types of material, i.e. refractory lining, copper tapblock, and Monel pipe, before they reach the transducers. Based on the difference in P-wave arrival times at each transducer, the AE source locations were then assigned to twelve different zones surrounding the tapping channel. When the detected AE rate exceeds the preset threshold limit at any particular zone (location), an alarm is issued to warn the operator about the off-centre drilling or lancing that is causing extensive damage to the taphole bricks and may also affect the copper block integrity. Figure 12 shows a schematic diagram of the TAM system, indicating an alarm was issued when the lancing direction was skewed.

### **Leak Detection at Absorption Towers** 

The production of copper requires smelting of sulfide based ores which results in gases such as SO2 and SO3. These gases are often transferred to absorption tower for conversion into sulphuric acid. The condensed high concentration acids can chemically react with the refractory lining of the tower, particularly with the castable/mortar and through the gaps between bricks. As a result, castable failure leading to acid leaks typically occurs at absorption towers. Since 2009, Hatch has adopted acoustic emission monitoring as a means to detect acid leak [3]. This acoustic emission monitoring has been used for leak detection for many years and is well established in ASTM standards [4]. Prior to the absorption tower leak detection, the AE transducers are affixed on the steel shell of the tower at regular intervals of less than 3 m by 3 m to cover the area of interest (Figure 13). The baseline acoustic signals are detected. This provides the basis for the threshold limits for the signature acoustic signals of acid leaks. Each section is then monitored for a period of one hour.

The location of an AE event is determined when several transducers record a voltage, which exceeded the threshold limits, from the same AE event. The source location problem is illustrated in Figure 14. For an array on i transducers the coordinates are:  (x1, y1), (x2, y2), …, (xi, yi). The first arrival times of the P-waves are used for the location of the AE event. By the Pythagorean Theorem, the i-th sensor located at xi, yi will detect the signal when Equation 1 is satisfied (where ti is the time required to reach the i-th sensor, c is the wave velocity). 



The AE source location can be determined by solving for the three unknowns x, y and t0 (Figure 14).

### **ABSTRACT** 

Experiments were conducted to investigate the effects of the initial particle size and oxygen concentration in the process gas on the size distribution of copper concentrate particles oxidized under suspension-smelting conditions. The size distribution was determined by both QEMSCAN® and laser diffraction techniques from samples of reacted particles collected along the reactor length of a laminar-flow reactor. The experimental data indicate that the change in particle size of the particle population was strongly dependent upon the particle size of the feed material, whereas the oxygen concentration in the process gas did not play a significant role in the range of 40-70 vol. %. Particle expansion was the predominant phenomenon in the early stag

es of oxidation, whereas fragmentation started to occur at further stages of oxidation down the reactor length. The amount of dust, i.e., particles with size smaller than 20  m, is discussed as a function of the operating conditions tested in the experiments.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Since the commercial implementation of the flash smelting process in the middle eighties, the process has been the subject of continuous scientific research. This is because a number of phenomena occurring in the reaction shaft of the flash smelting furnace are yet not well understood. A fundamental knowledge of this process is relevant because it may allow the optimization of the furnace operation in terms of energy requirements, the quality of the molten products, and the generation of dust, among other issues. Over the last decades, extensive experimentation [1-12] has been conducted to elucidate the relevant features of this process. Despite the evident progress so far made in this direction, the current models used to represent the reaction path of concentrate particles in the reaction shaft [9, 10] remain essentially qualitative. Quantitative aspects such as particle oxidation rate, particle composition, and size changes experienced by the particles are strongly dependent upon particle size in the feed, particle mineralogy, and the local conditions prevailing in the furnace. 

The present work is part of an ongoing research aimed at clarifying from a quantitative standpoint the most relevant phenomena occurring along the reaction path of copper concentrate particles in a flash smelting reactor. For that purpose, extensive experimentation in a laboratory furnace is being conducted under suspension-smelting conditions. Also, mathematical models based as much as possible on basic principles are being developed to describe both the reaction kinetics and size changes experienced by the particles. In an accompanying paper [13], the experimental observations concerning particle characteristics associated with the reaction kinetics are discussed. This includes the chemical composition, morphology, and mineralogy of the reacted particles. In the present paper, the evolution of the size distribution of the particle population as it travels through the reaction chamber is presented. 

Size changes experienced by the particles during flash smelting are relevant because they are related to particle fragmentation, which is known to be the major responsible for dust generation. The generation of dust particles in flash smelting reactors is undesirable because they cause a number of operational problems, such as plugging of the transport system and a decrease of the waste heat boiler efficiency, among other problems. The goal of this investigation was to determine the evolution of the size distribution of the particle population and to correlate such observations with the reaction path followed by the individual particles d

linder was surrounded by a compact 0.1 m-thick layer of ceramic fiber acting as thermal insulator. The bottom of the reaction chamber was attached to a stainless steel watercooled receptacle. The lower portion of the receptacle was detachable and fixed to the shaft body by bolts. The goal of the receptacle was to quench the particles falling from the shaft, thus interrupting the oxidation reactions, and collect them for further analysis. The upper portion of the receptacle had a sidestream 0.025 m diameter opening for the exhaust gas. The off-gas was taken out of the reactor by means of a vacuum pump and bubbled into a 20 L plastic vessel containing 1.6 M NaOH aqueous solution for the absorption of the SO2 gas produced by the oxidation reactions. 

In this study, La Caridad copper concentrate provided by Mexicana de Cobre, S.A. was used as a raw material. The concentrate was wet-sieved into six size fractions, the compositions of which are shown in Table 1. The composition of the unsieved material is also shown as a reference. Based on X-ray diffraction analyses of the samples and mineralogy calculations performed with the HSC software [14], it was concluded that the small particles contained chalcopyrite as the major component, whereas large particles mostly contained pyrite. Because a large fraction of the copper concentrate is made up of fine particles, the overall composition of the unsieved material resembles that of the finest particles in the population. 

The oxidation tests were conducted with both the sieved fractions and the unsieved material. Prior to the experiments, extensive calibrations of the vibratory feeder and the gas rotameters were made. In a typical experiment, the furnace was first heated up while the SFA was maintained at the corresponding position for the experiment. The oxygen and nitrogen flow rates were adjusted to achieve the oxygen concentration to be tested (40 and 70% by volume). The process gas was allowed to flow through the reactor until the temperature readings stabilized at 900  C, upon which the vacuum pump and the vibratory feeder were turned on.

upon which the reacted particles were taken out of the system. Depending on the operating conditions, about 100-300 g of reacted particles were collected. Similar trends are observed in Figure 3(b) regarding the size fraction 74-106 µm. In this case, the expansion-dominated stage is signaled at z = 0.3 m by the increase in the amount of particles with sizes greater than 90 µm, which is accompanied by a decrease in the amount of most particles below this size. By the time the particle cloud reached the position at z=0.9 m, a significant increase in the amount of particles with sizes smaller than 30 µm was observed. Thus, at z = 0.9 m, significant fragmentation occurred which dominated the overall behavior of the particle population. 

The trends discussed in Figures 3(a) and 3(b) agree with the qualitative model of Jokilaakso et al. [10] on the reaction path of single particles in a flash reactor. However, it should be emphasized that the population of particles entering the reactor consisted of a distribution of sizes, even though the concentrate was sieved. If two initial particles with different sizes enter the reactor at the same time, at a given location one of them may be expanding while the other is fragmenting. From the information provided by Figures 3(a) and 3(b), it is not possible to establish the specific sizes in the population that were either expanding or fragmenting at a given location. Similarly, it is not possible to identify the specific position along the reactor at which fragmentation started to occur. Because expansion and fragmentation of particles occurred simultaneously along the trajectory of the particle cloud, the changes in the size distribution shown in Figures 3(a) and 3(b) may be seen as an overall indicator of the predominance of either phenomenon on the population of particles as a whole. 

The implications of the above considerations become most relevant when the behavior of the unsieved concentrate is analyzed. This is shown in Figure 3(c). It is expected that the expansion-followed-by-fragmentation sequence discussed in Figures 3(a) and 3(b) also occurred in this case. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that the amount of particles in the range of 0-13 µm increased at the final location: z = 0.9 m. However, it is not clear whether expansion or fragmentation prevailed in the population of particles.

### **ABSTRACT** 

One of the stages of copper production process based on direct-to-blister flash furnace is decoppering of a sl

ag containing <mark>considerable amounts</mark> of copper (12-15 wt%). At the KGHM Glogow Copper Smelter this stage is performed under reducing conditions in an electric slag-cleaning furnace with <mark>the</mark> addition of coke and limestone. During the implementation of a process, there are changes of the slags viscosity subjected of decoppering process. In this work, viscosity of the industrial flash smelting slag with different degree of reduction and variable contents of the oxides was investigated in the temperature range from 1100 to 1400<sup>0</sup> C. The viscosity was measured using a viscometer equipped with a rotating spindle using a concentric cylinder. The increase of CaO contents leads to viscosity decreasing as long as the slags remain fully liquid. However, upon reaching the liquidus temperature, a sharp inverse in viscosity is observed. This is clearly illustrated by change in the slope of the viscosity logarithm vs. the temperature. The activation energy above the critical temperature has been determined.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The process of coppermaking from sulfide concentrates <mark>consist of two</mark> major steps: smelting and converting, which are a part of the same chemical process; oxidation of Fe and S from Cu-Fe-S phase. It has long been the goal of metallurgical and chemical engineers to combine these two steps into one continuous direct-to copper smelting copper.

### **ELECTRIC FURNACE Cu-FROM SLAG RECOVERY** 

One of the stages of copper production process based on direct-to-blister flash furnace is decoppering of a slag containing considerable amounts of copper (12-15 wt% at the  KGHM Glogow and 23-28% at the Olympic Dam [2]). All direct to copper smelters recover Cu from their slag in an electric slag –cleaning furnace. The slag flows from the direct-to-blister furnace into an electric furnace. The purpose of electric furnace slags cleaning is to reduce oxidized copper to metallic copper and trivalent iron to divalent iron and to settle the metallic copper droplets from the slag. During the reduction of a blister smelting slag, the trivalent iron is reduced from the slag simultaneously with the copper. The resulting Fe joins the newly reduced copper. This is an important factor, because the copper in the slag or Cu2O is an important fluxing agent. Now as the copper in the slag decreases, the trivalent iron and <mark>thus</mark> magnetite decreases and magnetite precipitation is avoided. 

Industrial practice as well as theoretical evaluations has shown the importance of mass transfer in electric furnace slag cleaning. Mixing of the slag intensifies the reduction reactions. The reactions are most intense when FSF slag is being tapped into the electric furnace as the jet of incoming slag causes mixing in the slag bath. Also the electrodes cause mixing in the slag because the slag around the electrodes is hotter and because of MHD (magneto-hydrodynamic) flows.

### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

At the KGHM Glogow Copper Smelter stage of slag cleaning is also performed under reducing conditions in an electric slag-cleaning furnace with the addition of coke and limestone. The condition for conducting this process result in essential changes in viscosity of the slag subjected to decoppering, which in turn influences transfer rate of both the substrate mass and the product of the reduction process as well as the possibility of tapping decoppering slag with sufficient speed. 

In this work viscosity of the flash smelting slag with different degree of reduction obtained from an electric

slag cleaning furnace was investigated at variables temperatures. The samples were taken during conducting industrial process of slag decoppering (from filling up furnace to slag tapping). 

The viscosity was measured by rotating cylinder method which has been previous described in [3]. The slag sample was melted in an alumina crucible 55 mm diameter and 120 mm height and placed in a vertical electric furnace. The rotating stainless steel (H23J5- 23% Cr, 5% Al) inner cylinder was 19 mm diameter, with a height of 25 mm and with a supporting rod 5 mm diameter <mark>. The high chromium stainless steel rotor finally selected for these measurements corroded very slowly and could be reused several times.</mark> The axis <mark>was</mark> rotated by a synchronous motor through a 12-gear transmission allowing for a variation in the rotation speed from 0.3 to 243 rpm. The torque on the suspended rotating cylinder is measured by an electromechanical transducer. The optimal rotation rate was found to be 23 rpm for slag viscosities from 0.5 to 18 Pas. 

The temperature was measured by a Pt/Pt-Rhl0 thermocouple that touched the crucible from outside. Calibration experiments showed that the actual slag temperature did not vary more than ±5<sup>0</sup> C from that measured by the thermocouple on the outside of the crucible. All measurements were carried out in a purified argon atmosphere. 

Powdered <mark>slags were</mark> melted in an alumina crucible at about 1357 to 1387<sup>0</sup> C under an argon atmosphere. After temperature stabilization, the rotating cylinder was immersed. Each measurement was performed during the cooling cycle. Temperature and viscosity readings were made at 5-minute intervals during the equilibration period and then for another 30 to 60 minutes after temperature and viscosity stabilization. Then the furnace temperature was lowered from 5 to 10<sup>0</sup> C and the procedure was repeated. This procedure was continued until the slag temperature approached the liquidus temperature.

Chunlin Chen*, Ling Zhang* and Sharif Jahanshahi**

### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper losses in slag vary from process to process during pyrometallurgical production of copper, depending on the slag chemistry and operating conditions. Minimize copper losses is one of major focuses in considering the optimal operating condition for copper smelting/converting processes. At the same time, the deportment of minor elements between various phases during copper smelting is of great interest by the smelters. This interest is driven by the gradual depletion of high-grade ore with low levels of minor elements such as arsenic, the requirements to manage the emission of toxic elements to the biosphere, and a growing need to produce highpurity saleable products. 

The Multi-Phase Equilibrium (MPE) is a thermodynamic package developed by CSIRO for simulating reactions between phases in multi-component and multiphase systems. Over the years the capability of the MPE model has been extended to cover the behavior of a large number of elements in high temperature system. The sulphide smelting module of the MPE, which covers the minor elements such as As, Bi, Sb, Pb, Se, Te, Sn, Co and Zn, is capable of modeling the deportment of major and minor elements between various phases during the smelting of complex ores/concentrates. 

In the present paper validation of the MPE model and databases against published experimental data on multi-component and multiphase systems are presented.  Results obtained from application of the model in predicting the copper losses in slag, direct recovery of copper to blister in direct-to-blister sm

elting process, as well as the arsenic deportment between matte, slag and gas phases of various commercial copper smelting processes will be presented.  These results should allow process metallurgists in developing practices for improved management of copper losses and minor elements during smelting of feed materials.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper losses in slag vary from furnace to furnace during pyrometallurgical production of copper, depending on the slag chemistry and operating conditions. Minimize copper losses is one of major focuses in considering the optimal operating condition for copper smelting/converting processes. The direct recovery of copper to blister and the cost required for slag cleaning determine the economic performance of a process. At the same time, the deportment of minor elements between various phases during the copper smelting/converting is of great interest by the smelters.   In particular, the performance of different smelting technologies such as Top Submerged Lance (TSL) smelting, flash smelting/converting and other bath smelting processes with respect to departure from equilibrium and effectiveness in removing such impurities has not been well investigated.  This interest is driven by the gradual depletion of high-grade ore with low levels of minor elements such as arsenic, the requirements to manage the emission of toxic elements to the biosphere, and a growing need to produce high-purity saleable products. 

To assist the process metallurgists in assessing the impact of smelting copper concentrates with various Cu/S ratio and high levels of minor elements, one needs to use an advanced model of the base metals smelting process which is based on the process fundamentals and allows quantifying the deportment of major/minor elements in the smelter under various operating conditions. Since the early 1990’s, CSIRO has been involved in development and application of thermodynamic models of melts and solid solutions. Over the years the capability of the CSIRO’s Multi-Phase Equilibrium (MPE) model has been extended to cover the behavior of a large number of elements in high temperature system [1]. The copper smelting module of the MPE, which covers the minor elements such as As, Bi, Sb, Pb, Se, Te, Co, Sn and Zn, as well as some naturally occurring radio-nuclide elements, is capable of modeling the deportment of major/minor elements in the smelter.  Our previous published work has provided some details of the assessment carried out as well as application of the model to predict deportment of some minor elements during the smelting of sulphide concentrates [2,3]. 

In the present paper a series of plots covering the validation of the model and databases against published experimental data on multi-component and multiphase systems are presented.  Application of the model in predicting the copper losses in slag, direct recovery of copper to blister in direct-to-blister s

melting process, as well as the arsenic deportment between matte, slag and gas phases of various commercial copper smelting processes will be demonstrated. Solid line is the 1:1 line, dashed lines are the  30% [29]. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 864 ### **APPLICATIONS** ### **Direct-to-blister flash smelting** It has been demonstrated in 1960’s at Outokumpo Research Centre that copper concentrate could be smelted directly to blister in one single stage in a flash furnace. There are currently three commercial s

cale direct-to-blister flash furnaces in the world. Producing copper continuously in a single sealed furnace gives improved emission control. One obstacle in direct-to-blister smelting is the high solubility of copper in slag. 

The correlation between sulphur and oxygen in blister, shown in Figure 5, suggests that the sulphur content in blister is a good and practical way to describe the oxidation degree of the smelting system and define the copper losses in slag. 

Jorgensen and Collins [30] carried out an experimental study on copper solubility in iron-silicate based slag in contact with blister copper at temperatures close to 1300 °C.  Their starting slag and blister were obtained from samples taken from the Olympic Dam flash furnace. They used a flowing N2-SO2 gas mixture to simulate the atmosphere inside a flash furnace and after 1-3 hrs of reaction between the phases the melts were air cooled to room temperature and the metal and slag samples characterized. While they were hoping to reach metal-slag equilibrium between phases during the reaction period, their data suggests significant departure from equilibrium with very high copper oxide levels is the slag (as high as 42 wt%) which decreased to about 13% as the sulphur content of the blister phase increased to about 0.66%.  Their own comparison of laboratory data with plant data suggested significant reduction in copper content of flash furnace slag could be achieved by allowing more reaction time.   However, Jorgensen and Collins did not present strong evidence in favor of reaching equilibrium between condensed phases.  In fact the oxygen and sulphur potentials of their system were varying with time as they only controlled the SO2 partial pressure.  It is of some interest to examine their data together with data from commercial flash smelters with respect equilibrium between metal and slag at different partial pressures of SO2. 

Figure 7 shows the calculated correlations between the copper losses in slag and sulphur contents in blister under various conditions and comparison to the observed data in pilot plant tests and laboratory study [30-32]. For the Peirce-Smith converting, both calculation and plant observation show that a large portion of As in the matte can be removed into the gas at the slagmaking stage before liquid copper appears in converter. The batch operating nature of PeirceSmith converter ensures that the As eliminated into the gas phase would not be absorbed back to the matte/copper phase due to decreasing of As activity coefficient with increasing of matte grade. ### **SUMMARY** Thermodynamic models and databases have been developed for slag, matte and liquid copper phases, in which the behavior of minor elements usually present in base metal ore such as As, Bi, Sb, Pb, Se, Te, Sn, Co and Zn are covered. These databases have been developed through critical evaluation of various available thermodynamic and phase diagram data. Through application of the thermodynamic model MPE, the Cu and S solubility in smelting slags and the S activities in matte under various matte grade were calculated and compared with published experimental data. These comparisons show good the predicted values by the model to be in good agreement and within experimental uncertainty. The validated model was

used to predict the copper solubility in slag and the direct copper recovery to blister in direct-to-blister smelting with various copper concentrates. It was found that industrial slag has a higher copper content than expected from the equilibrium calculation. It is clear that the copper recovery decreased rapidly with decreasing Cu/S ratio in the concentrate. 

The arsenic deportment in various commercial copper smelting processes were also analyzed by the MPE model. The results obtained show strong dependence of the deportment of arsenic with copper matte grade, particularly at high matte grade.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The Oxygen Bottom-blowing Copper Smelting Technology is a new copper smelting process developed by China ENFI Engineering Corporation. This paper describes the characteristics of this technology, summarizes production of the oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace, analyzes problems occurring in the production and proposes countermeasures for coping with these problems. The paper also discusses the future development orientation of the oxygen bottom-blowing copper smelting technology. By continuous exploring, development and improvement, advantages and potentiality of the technology will be brought into full play.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

China is not only a big copper producer but also a big copper smelting country. Most technologies are introduced from abroad. Weak technological innovation ability of China has become the key factor restricting the non-ferrous industry development in China. 

From 1960s, the former Hunan Shuikoushan Mining Administration and China ENFI Engineering Corporation, together with several universities and research institutes in China developed the bottom-blowing bath smelting technology. The first industrial application if this technology was in 1998. Since then, it has been developed into a mature technology [1]. So far, there are 29 production lines for bottom-blowing lead smelting, and 4 production lines under construction. 

Over the past 20 years, flash smelting, ISA smelting, Ausmelt smelting and Noranda smelting for copper smelting have been introduced into China. In 2008, the oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting technology developed by China ENFI Engineering Corporation was industrialized and achieved very good technical and economical results after one year’s production operation. Especially, the technology has shown obvious advantages like simple process, good tightness, sound environmental conditions, low noise and easy operation, etc. The carbon-free smelting makes the technology a broader development perspective. 



### **CHARACTERISTICS OF OXYGEN BOTTOM-BLOWN COPPER SMELTING TECHNOLOGY** 

In terms of chemistry, copper smelting actually is a process of desulphurization and deferrization which occur in all kinds of Cu smelting processes. In case of the flash smelting, the chemical reaction of desulphurization and deferrization takes place by heat transfer, mass transfer and fluid flowing among three phases of gas, solid and melt of

charges in the reaction tower. The reaction speed of furnace charges depends on heat and mass transfer rates between concentrate particles and gas as well as oxidization rate of sulfide, etc. In case of the bath smelting, the heat and mass transfer and fluid flowing of charges take place in the liquid

bath and so do the desulphurization and deferrization reactions; the reaction speed of charges depends upon the heat and mass transfer rates in the bath, or in other words, the agitating and mixing conditions in the bath. 

The modern non-ferrous metal bath smelting technology can be divided into three types as per different air blowing ways, i.e. top-blowing smelting, side-blowing smelting and bottom-blown bath smelting. The smelting results are slightly different among each other due to different positions of air supply. The oxygen bottom-blown smelting has following characteristics:

### **High Oxygen-Enrichment Percentage and High Degree of Autogenous Smelting** 

The autogenous smelting in the pilot test of the oxygen bottom-blown smelting technology conducted in a small furnace (10m<sup>3</sup> only) with an hourly throughput of two tons shows that this method has high heat efficiency but low heat loss. The furnace is a tightly enclosed vessel with low air infiltration, high oxygen-enrichment percentage, low off-gas volume and low loss of heat carried away by air. The above mentioned is critical to the fully autogenous smelting which requires that all heat inputs come from reaction heat of furnace charges (the sensible heat brought by charges is very small and can  be neglected). For charges with a given composition, the heat input can be considered as a

constant. Under the prerequisite of being impossible to increase heat input, the only method to realize heat balance is to reduce heat expense. 

Heat expense = heat entrapped by copper matte + heat entrapped by furnace slag +

heat for decomposition reaction + heat for moisture evaporation + heat loss in water jacket and furnace wall + heat entrapped by off-gas. As for furnace charges, copper matte and furnace slag with equivalent mass, the former four items are constant, and the latter two items are closely related to production capacity and oxygen-enrichment percentage. Therefore, to improve production capacity, increasing the oxygen-enrichment percentage and reducing volume of off-gas would be an important way for realizing fully autogenous smelting. 

That the oxygen-enrichment percentage is more than 70% can greatly increase the smelting speed and decrease the off-gas volume. The oxygen-enrichment percentage can only reach 40% to 50% in case of the top-blowing smelting or side-blowing smelting due to restriction from the material of tuyere. High oxygen-enrichment percentage can reduce the volume of off-gas, thereby reducing the heat loss. 

According to the production experience of oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace in Dongying and Humon, as long as copper concentrate contains more than 40% of iron and sulfide, the autogenous smelting can be realized without concurrent heating by oil or coal burning. 

### **Long Service Life of Furnace and Oxygen Lance** 

The oxygen lance area is the quick-wear area at the bottom of the oxygen bottomblowing smelting furnace. This is because that the air stream injected towards the melt in the bath will generate non-continuous counter-impact (i.e. blowback of air bubbles). The counter-impact of such air stream may destroy refractory material of the lance area seriously. Studies show that the impact frequency depends upon the pressure of bottom blowing. The impact frequency decreases significantly with increase of the bottom blowing pressure. The oxygen pressure applied in the bottom-blowing smelting is about 0.4-0.6Mpa, under which the blowback of air bubbles can be basically eliminated. In addition, the air blown toward the melt will be dispersed into the bath, so that the furnace life can be greatly extended.  The first bottom-blowing smelting furnace in Dongying and Humon is 3 years and 2.5 years respectively. After 6 month of operation, brick wearing in Dongying is about 40mm, and the brick wearing in Humon is about 60mm, since the diameter of lances in Humon is larger. 

The double-sleeve lance is adopted for the oxygen bottom-blown smelting. Oxygen is blown into the furnace from the inner sleeve and the air is from the outer sleeve. Because the air from the outer sleeve is injected towards the melt at a higher speed, the strongly injected air will absorb a large amount of heat. Consequentially, a quenching area around the lance tip is formed which makes the melt solidified to form a “mushroom tip” in the lance, thereby protecting the lance. The service life of a single lance for the

oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting can be more than 5000h [3]. According to the prod

uction conditions of oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace in Dongying, when the oxygen concentration is 70%~71%, a larger mushroom tip with a diameter of 30~40mm will be formed; when the oxygen lance structure is changed and oxygen concentration is increased to 74%, a mushroom tip with a diameter of 100mm and a height of 60mm will be formed; as a result, wearing of lance will be reduced and its service life will be over half a year. 

### **Sound Operation Conditions and Low Labor Intensity** 

In case of the oxygen bottom-blown smelting, the lance is inserted to the furnace from the bottom. The air flowing into the furnace contacts firstly with the melt at very bottom of the furnace. Most of the air dynamics is consumed in the bath. However, in the top-blowing smelting and side-blowing smelting, plenty of air is injected at a higher speed in the furnace heath and dynamics of the air consumed in the space of the heath, which produces loud noise. The noise produced by oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace is lower than 80dB; also, the negative pressure of the furnace heath is stably controlled and only the charge door left open, thus showing a good operation environment. 

The oxygen bottom-blown smelting process can be controlled in fully automatic mode by DCS. Slag is tapped by way of overflowing, thus reducing labor intensity. 

### **Low Fe3O4 in Slag & Safe Operation.** 

In the oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace, the oxygen-enriched air is directly blown into the copper matte layer from the furnace bottom and reacts firstly with sulfides to form oxides of copper and iron. The oxides formed are turned over to upper layer of the melt by bubbling force resulted from bottom blowing and contact with furnace charges, then Fe3O4 in the smelting is reduced by furnace charges. In addition, the blown oxygen-enriched air does not directy contact with slag layer, so there is almost no probability that the slag layer is directly formed into magnetite. In case of top-blown smelting and side-blown smelting, FeO in the slag layer is easily oxidized into Fe3O4 because the air blown contacts directly with the slag layer; so in production practice, splattering that may easily occur in top-blown and bottom-blown smelting is related to a large amount of magnetite formed. 

The oxygen bottom-blown smelting can avoid generation of foaming slag due to low content of Fe3O4 in slag, thus making it safer in operation. 

### **Simple in Furnace Charge Preparation and Good Adaptability to Feeds** 

The oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace is not so strict in connection with moisture content of concentrate. It can treat the concentrate with moisture of 8%~10% without drying or pelletizing, and its dust yield is about 2.0%. In addition, the furnace is

### **Oxygen lance** 

The lance for the oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace is transplanted from that of the bottom-blown steel-making converter; it is a double-sleeve lance with the outer sleeve protected by oxygen-enriched air. The oxygen-enriched air flows through the sleeve at high speed to cool the sleeve wall, thus achieving a good protection effect. As the air flows at high velocity, high flow and small specific surface area inside the lance, this type of flow can be regarded as an adiabatic flow to which the differential equation<sup>[4]</sup> for adiabatic air flow can be applied:

According to the equation above, the change of temperature depends on the change of flowrate. Increasing the flowrate will inevitably cause the decreasing of temperature. When the medium velocity inside the lance reaches a certain value, the medium will have strong cooling effect on the lance. In normal smelting practice, all sleeve walls of the lance is at the room temperature or below the room temperature. 

The outer sleeve of lance for oxygen bottom-blown lead smelting is cooled by N2 while that for copper smelting cooled by compressed air. The increasing of oxygen concentration in the mixed air improves the SO2 concentration in the off-gas and reduces the heat carried away by the off-gas. The actual production shows there is no apparent difference between compressed air and nitrogen in terms of the protection effect for oxygen lance.

### **PROBLEMS IN PRODUCTION AND COUNTERMEASURES** 

The oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting is a newly developed technology. There are some problems encountered during the operation of the oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace already put into operation, which need to be solved so as to make this technology more perfect： 

### **Long “Mushroom Tip” Easily Formed At Lance Outlet** 

After Dongying’s oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace was put into operation for a period of time, the formation of very long “mushroom tip” was observed at the lance outlet, and the longest “mushroom tip” was longer than 1m, as shown in Fig. 2. The advantage of the formation of “mushroom tip” is that it can better protect the oxygen lance. However, it can easily make the inlet oxygen-enriched air dash out of the bath and cause the splashing at the furnace top and serious sticking at the feeding port. According to the study, the external air injected at high speed may cause forced cooling of melt in surroundings and make the surrounding melt solidified, which leads to the formation of very long “mushroom tip” at the oxygen lance outlet; the “mushroom tip” forms a channel in which the oxygen-enriched air can dash out of the bath very easily to cause the splashing on the bath surface. The lengths of the “mushroom tip” are different for the 9 lances. The lower of the slag temperature, the quicker the formation of the “mushroom tip”. The furnace often needs to be rotated so as to knock off the “mushroom tip” from the feeding port.

It is not possible to carry out melt probing in the course of production. As the melt height shown on the probing rod is 2.5m and the designed bath depth is 1.4m, the boundary between slag layer and matte layer cannot be distinguished. The slag tapping and copper matte tapping based on the production experience may make copper matte tapped out with the slag. The position of probing rod needs to be moved from the current smelting area to the settling area at the slag tapping end; in addition, the bath surging should be controlled.

The pressure of oxygen at outlet of the compressor in the oxygen-making station is 0.75MPa and there is an oxygen pressure relief valve station arranged in front of the furnace. Increasing lance diameter could lower its oxygen pressure to 0.3~0.4MPa. Cancelling the oxygen pressure relief valve station, providing only the flow regulating and check valves, could greatly reduce oxygen supply pressure. 

### **Relatively High Copper Content in the Slag** 

For the oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace, the copper content in the slag is 3%~5% currently and high-iron slag will be mainly produced. After slow cooling, the furnace slag will go through the slag concentration. Based on the production practice of oxygen bottom-blown smelting furnace, the settling effect of the settling area inside the furnace is not ideal and the bath stirring is very intense. ### **FUTURE DEVELOPMENT** 

The oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting technology is a developing advanced technology. China ENFI Engineering Corporation is confident that this technology would be widely applied in smelting projects; and, of course, there are still a number of topics for future development and study in this field. 

### **Development of Low-Pressure Oxygen Lance** 

The pressure of oxygen used by the lance currently for the oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting is 0.4-0.6MPa and the pressure of oxygen at outlet of the compressor is 0.75MPa. Now, a new l ance with an oxygen pressure of 0.2-0.3MPa is under testing, then the outlet pressure of oxygen compressor can be reduced to 0.3-0.4MPa (equivalent to the pressure of oxygen supplied to the top-blown smelting furnace), thus reducing significantly the energy consumption. The development of low-pressure oxygen lance requires the simulation of bath melt bubbling, hydraulic test of lance as well as the verification with the lance installed on the furnace, which is a topic for extensive study. 

### **Copper Matte Tapping By Siphon** 

Since the oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting furnace is provided with doublerow oxygen lances, where intermittent copper matte tapping and intense bath stirring are practiced, it is hard to probe the thickness of the copper matte layer. If single-row oxygen lance arrangement is adopted and copper matte tapping by siphon is developed, the thickness of copper matte layer can be stabilized; with relatively stable oxygen pressure of the lance, the bath surface will be relatively calm. 

### **Slag Cleaning** 

Bottom-blowing furnace slag is treated with cooled slag floatation method, with long process flow and high capital cost, but could obtain high metal recovery rate. It could be a future development direction to develop deep cleaning of furnace slag to reduce Cu in slag to 0.5% or even less than 0.4%.

### **CONCLUSIONS** 

According to current production conditions, the industrialization of the oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting technology is relatively ideal. Compared with other advanced copper smelting technologies, the oxygen bottom-blown copper smelting technology has the advantages of simple process, high adaptability to feed, less investment, lower noise and labor intensity, easy operation and good operation conditions. Operators describe this furnace as a point-and-shoot camera. In particular, it produces high-Fe slag, with less slag amount. And after slag floatation, Cu recovery rate is as high as 98.5%. The whole smelting process is autogenous without adding coals, thus energy consumption is low. Currently, the bottom-blowing furnace in Dongying has realized the capacity of 120,000t/a blister. Through further improvement, it is possible to increase the throughput capacity to over 1,000,000t/a-1,500,000t/a Cu concentrates and lower energy consumption to less than 150kgce/t of blister. This Technology has its unique advantages in terms of environment, energy consumption and capital cost compared with flash smelting furnace, top-blowing furnace, Teniente furnace, Noranda furnace and Mitsubishi furnace.

### **ABSTRACT** 

This Paper describes the continuous bottom-blowing matte converting process, as well as the pilot plant test conducted for this process from May to June, 2012. The pilot plant test shows that under three-phase co

nditions in the bath, sulfur in blister is 0.7%-1.0%, and Cu in slag is 8-12%; while under two-phase conditions, sulfur in blister is 0.2%, and Cu in slag is around 20%. ### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper matte converting, more than 80% of such converting in the world applies PS converter with a history over 100 years to intermittent operation, however, PS converter has been out of date for meeting the requirements of current smelting industry on environmental protection, production operation automation and others, because of low altitude serious pollution of SO2 fume, high unit consumption of refractory materials due to alternative cold and heat of intermittent converting furnace, more difficult acid making due to large fluctuation of fume quantity, large construction investment and low production operation automation. In order to solve the problems of PS converter, metallurgical researchers started to study continuous copper smelting in 1950s and 1960s, and the development of continuous copper smelting has become the common goal of the copper smelting industry. 

### **OVERVIEW OF CHINESE STUDIES** 

In 1960s and 1970s, copper matte continuous converting techniques were widely studied in China, e.g. Northeast University, Shenyang Smelter, Baiyin Nonferrous Metals Company Smelting Factory, Chenzhou Smelting Factory, Fuchunjiang Smelting Factory and other units made great efforts to conduct R&D of copper matte continuous converting techniques<sup>[1-5]</sup> . 

In 1969, Shenyang Smelter built up one copper matte continuous converting furnace to raise and stabilize SO2 concentration in fume. However the original purpose was changed to copper concentrate treatment due to the problem of temperature control after only 17 tests. 

Continuous converting tests of Baiyin Nonferrous Metals Company Smelting Factory in its early stage and those of Chenzhou Smelting Factory applied vortex furnace-reverberatory furnace to continuous copper smelting test, but failed to obtain satisfactory results. 

In 1965, Fuchunjiang Smelting Factory developed a kind of fixed continuous converting furnace<sup>[6]</sup> . Such converting furnace solves the problem of copper matte dump and transport, and has higher blowing time ratio and SO2 concentration in fume than PS converter. The process had been applied in a number of small smelter in china. Nowadays, fixed continuous converting furnaces are still used in Smelting Factory of Yantai Penghui Copper Industry Co., Ltd. and other small and medium copper smelting enterprises. Nevertheless, fixed continuous converting furnace has the defects as

follows: 

(1) Continuous converting furnace is fixed and has large labor intensity of furnace clinker removal, especially its vent hole may be fully blocked by molten mass if no emergency measures are taken after the occurrence of sudden power outage and off blast, and it’s very hard to remove such molten mass.

(2) Converting process includes slag forming stage and copper making stage, thereof copper making stage needs artificial judgment of end point, so the production is semicontinuous and has low level automation. 

(3) Fixed continuous converting furnace has small hearth area and small production capacity, so it can be used for small scale production only. 

Just because of such defects, fixed continuous converting furnace hasn’t been widely popularized yet. 

China R&D of continuous copper smelting were mainly conducted in 1960s and 1970s, thereof Fuchunjiang fixed continuous converting furnace succeeded to some extent, while the findings of other studies weren’t put into industrialized application. 

### **OVERVIEW OF INTERNATIONAL STUDIES** 

International studies of continuous copper smelting began in 1950s, and the continuous copper smelting methods in related references include Vokla smelting-converting method<sup>[7]</sup> , Q-S continuous copper smelting method<sup>[8-9]</sup> , Noranda continuous copper converting method, Mitsubishi continuous copper smelting method, double flash continuous copper smelting method (involved in flash smelting and flash converting), etc. 

Vokla smelting-converting method and Q-S continuous copper smelting method directly generate blister copper by copper concentrate in a furnace, and requires waste slag. However, neither of them has been put into industrial application yet for their shortcomings, e.g. complex atmosphere in furnace and diffi cult process control. 

underwent the R&D of one-stage continuous copper smelting and copper matte continuous converting in sequence, later copper matte continuous converting technology was put into industrial application in Canadian Horne Smelter in 1997. But Noranda continuous copper converting method is obviously deficient, e.g. molten mass dump and transport, overhigh<sup>[10-15]</sup> sulfur content in blister copper generated by converting adopting three-phase molten pool (blister copper, white copper matte and slag) operation. At present, Noranda continuous copper converting method hasn’t been popularized yet for its unsolvable shortcomings above. 

Two continuous converting techniques already in service during industrial production well solve in-plant copper matte dump and transport and other problems, raise sulfur catching rate to more than 99.8% and well avoid the low altitude pollution of copper matte converting. One method is Japanese Mitsubishi method<sup>[16]</sup> . In this method, top blast furnace is used for smelting, electric furnace is used for copper matte sedimentation, slags are leaned, a

nd then top blast furnace continuously converts copper matte into blister copper, finally blister copper enters anode furnace via flute for refining. Its flow chart is shown in Fig. 1.

### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper introduces various types of smelting and converting technologies adopted for Copper Pyrometallurgical Process, and describes in particular the development of Continuous Bottom-blowing Cu Smelting Technology, coming to the conclusion that Copper Continuous Smelting Technology has become the trend for Greenfield or Brownfield copper smelters.
