### **INTRODUCTION*

* 

Relative to the situation today, high grade, clean copper deposits were preferentially exploited during most of the 20<sup>th</sup> century. More challenging ore bodies are now becoming of economic interest. These include polymetallic deposits, ore bodies in challenging locations and ores containing high levels of deleterious impurities such as As, Hg, Sb, Pb, Bi, Cl and F. At the smelter, volatile elements such as Hg, Cl and F for the most part deport to the off-gas and are handled in the gas cleaning section of the acid plant. The deportment of other troublesome minor elements (such as As, Sb, Pb, Bi, etc.) is influenced by several factors, including the technology in use and the specific practices at a given smelter. 

There are several key features involved in selecting a smelter flow sheet for handling high impurity feeds, some of these are listed below: 

- Low dust generation in the smelting unit (low concentrate entrainment) 

- Batch converting allows for lower minor element deportment to copper compared to continuous converting 

- Dust treatment plant required to separately process smelting and converting flue dust 

- Fluxing in anode furnaces is required in some cases where high levels of impurities are present in the feed, or if no dust treatment plant is installed at a given site 

This paper discusses one specific technology which could be used for removing and controlling the arsenic content in copper anode. This technology can be applied in the Peirce-Smith converters on the copper blow, but preferably in the anode furnace, prior to the anode reduction stage. 

Fire refining of blister copper containing high arsenic or lead has been practiced in copper smelters for more than a century and a number of relevant publications are available describing the use of Na2CO3, CaO, CaCO3 and SiO2 as fluxes to control these minor elements in blister copper [1-10]. At the anode furnace stage, As and Pb are most commonly controlled using respectively Na2CO3 and SiO2 fluxes. While de-leading is relatively simple in that a silicate slag is produced along with minimum emissions of gaseous lead, the use of soda ash/soda slag to removal arsenic is somewhat more challenging (arsenic gaseous emissions, refractory corrosion, slag quality, operating costs, etc.). It is also known that the arsenic level needs to be at a certain level in anode copper to ensure that Bi and Sb are precipitated as (Bi,Sb)AsO4 in the electrorefining stage [11]. In this respect, the molar ratio, [As/(Bi+Sb)] in copper is normally controlled to a pre-determined value. Related to this requirement, an ideal technology would

### **DEVELOPMENT OF NEW COPPER REFINING TECHNOLOGIES AT THE FORMER NORANDA TECHNOLOGY CENTRE** 

Considerable R&D was performed on fire refining by the former Noranda Inc in the period 2000 to 2001. Patents and publications by the Company have been reviewed as part of the present paper. Treatment of complex Cu/Au concentrates at the Company’s plants at the time, containing high levels of arsenic and antimony warranted the evaluation of different refining slags. During the years 2000 and 2001, an ambitious fire refining development program was led by Dr. Manuel Zamalloa at the former Noranda Technology Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada and one of the authors of the present study. Initially, it was realised that little was known of about phase diagrams relevant to fire refining. The oxygen potential in blister copper was certainly known to be one of the drivers for impurity elimination during the fire refining stage, nevertheless, not much was known about the solid phases which could form under fire refining conditions. 

During this period, as reported in various publications [12-15], nearly one hundred trials were performed at a bench scale (with a ~10 kg impure copper charge) using different recipes. Phase diagrams were also developed to better understand the temperature and conditions that could be employed industrially to obtain minor element eliminations with good slag quality with minimal slag volumes.

While great success was obtained by conducting fire refining trials in the laboratory with different fluxes, there was a lack in fundamental data needed to help commercialize the work, hence further studies were required. Since calcium and sodium arsenates/antimonates were produced during the fir

e refining stage (see next section), finding a salt/slag with the proper solubility for these compounds was essential to the success of this project. This was a significant challenge, since there were literally no data available on this subject. It appeared that for decades, plants had typically operated essentially on a trial and error basis to obtain a fluid slag, which at the same time, was highly corrosive for the anode furnace refractory lining. 

An ambitious program was therefore performed over a 2-3 year period, including phase diagram determination, bench scale trials (about 100 trials) and industrial trials (+100 anode furnace or converter charges). This work ultimately led to a patent being awarded to Zamalloa et al. in 2002 [13].  The original concept was based on refining blister copper while allowing for the “in-situ” scrubbing of SO2 and As4O4 vapours that had been produced. A number of technical papers discussing the fundamental data, as well descriptions of the technology, were published between 2002 and 2005, nearly 10 years ago [15-21].

The main strengths of the technology were the low slag corrosion and the low arsenic emissions compared to soda fluxing; in addition, the slag had the capacity to “buffer” the arsenic in copper to an appropriate level. Given this, it is suggested that a copper smelter with high level of arsenic and a moderate level of antimony in blister copper should therefore consider this approach for both reducing arsenic emissions and controlling the arsenic content in copper prior to electrorefining. One of the limitations of the proposed process is the generally low selectivity for antimony over arsenic, which would have been ideal. The molten sulphate also exhibits low solubility for antimony salts and the slag quality deteriorates rapidly when the antimony level is over 1-2 wt.%. 

### **PROCESS CHEMISTRY-SULPHATE REFINING** 

When blister copper containing arsenic and oxygen is contacted with a solution of calcium and sodium sulphate, they tend to react according to reaction (1).  If free lime is present in the molten salt, it can also react according to reaction (2); the main advantage of using CaO is the absence of SO2 as a product of reaction that occurs in reaction 1. 



CaSO4 and Ca3(AsO4)2 have melting points in excess of 1400<sup>0</sup> C and it is desirable to add some excess CaO or Na2SO4 as a flux to reduce the melting point to the 1150-1250<sup>0</sup> C range. To illustrate the impact of such additions, the CaO-CaSO4Ca3(AsO4)2 and the Na2SO4-CaSO4-Ca3(AsO4)2 phase diagrams are presented in Figures 3 and 4 [17-19].

The conventional soda fluxing process presently in use in industry to remove arsenic and antimony from blister copper utilizes soda ash and lime as reagents. This process is found to emit small but measurable amounts of arsenic during the refining operation, presumably due to volatilization of gaseous NaAsO3 as discussed by Mangwire and Jeffes [22] and Coursol et al. [12]. From our interpretation, Reactions (3), (4) or (5) are examples by which NaAsO3 would be potentially emitted. Although the Free Energy of reaction for these chemical reactions may be positive (hence not favored thermodynamically), the equilibrium partial pressure of NaAsO3, calculated by accounting for activities of all components, is sufficiently high to volatize some arsenic (square brackets indicate a component is in solution in a given phase (slag or salt)). 



In order to attenuate/eliminate the presence of gaseous NaAsO3 associated with soda fluxing, the process described here uses CaO and CaSO4 as reagents to form calcium arsenate and the sodium present in the salt (as Na2SO4) is employed only as a flux; it is too stable to react with arsenic in copper and hence emit any NaAsO3. 

Reactions (1) and (2) indicate a complex relationship between the residual arsenic content in blister copper and other variables. Essentially, the salt composition, the partial pressure of SO2 and the oxygen content of the blister copper are the main factors influencing the final level of arsenic in blister copper. Generally, a level of arsenic between 300-600 ppm is desirable for typical levels of bismuth and antimony found in anode copper (under 100 ppm for Bi and under 200 for Sb); if high levels of bismuth or antimony are present, more arsenic would be required to precipitate the Bi and Sb as (Bi, Sb)AsO4 in the tankhouse electrolyte. 

It is to be noted that when arsenic is removed according to reaction (1), SO2 was found to be “bubbling” from the salt bath and a partial pressure of SO2 near atmospheric pressure is obtained in the salt (that is, the effective p(SO2) value). This effective partial pressure can potentially be lowered by tuyere or porous plug gas stirring/mixing. If sufficient lime is added as a reagent, the SO2 partial pressure will be strongly depressed and the residual level of arsenic could be reduced to undesirably low levels.  From author’s experience, it can easily drop under 50 ppm [12]. In the next section thermodynamic models developed in previous studies [17-20] were used to evaluate the best conditions to refine blister copper with the sulphate flux. The goals were to produce a fully molten slag, with the highest concentration of soluble arsenic possible, and to produce a blister copper with arsenic content between 300 and 1,000 ppm, while maintaining the oxygen level under 7,000 ppm.

Potential issues/challenges related to this fire refining technique discussed in the paper include: 

- i. The unit cost of the required flux components (e.g. the blend as follows:  30% Na2SO4, 35% CaO and 45% CaSO4) may be higher than that for soda ash alone (Na2CO3); 

- ii. Requires the expense of a dedicated flux injection system at the anode furnace if the fluxes are not pre-mixed; 

- iii. Careful slag skimming would be required at the converter to minimize carryover of converter slag which can be deleterious to good fire refining slag quality; 

- iv. Hygiene and environmental issues due to slag handling would need to be addressed. 

It is suggested that a techno-economical evaluation of this technique would be warranted to evaluate the net economical/environmental benefits associated with this technology for a given plant. ### **_ABSTRACT_** 

A new process is being developed which permit to recover up to 98% of copper, 76% molybdenum and 98% zinc from copper smelter slags, generating a solid residue of red hematite that can be used in paints and ceramics. The process consist of two consecutive step:  an initial total sulphation of the slag at 150-180ºC with sulphuric acid followed by a thermal decomposition at 700ºC – 750ºC of the sulphated slag to form copper and zinc sulphates, copper molybdate and hematite. The acid used in the first step of sulphation is re-synthtetical in the seconds step of thermal decomposition and recirculated back to the sulphation step. The process is being developed at pilot scale in a plant that will be commissioned by the end of 2013.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper smelting slags contain from 2 up to 8 wt-% copper, and in some cases molybdenum (0.05-0.3 wt-%) and zinc (0.5-1 wt-%), in addition to 30 to 40 wt-% of iron, generally as fayalite.  These slags are processed generally either by flotation or reduction in molten phase, recovering from 60 up to 85% of the contained copper. No others metals are recovered, in spite that the value of this metals in the slags could be even higher than that of the copper. 

Although a number of process has been proposed to recover some of this metals, no one has succeeded in recovering molybdenum, which is associated to magnetite forming a complex spinell in the slag, either to recover zinc or iron as a commercial product such as hematite. 

This new technology, which is being developed jointly by the University of Concepcion and CODELCO´s ECOMETALES Division, would permit to recover virtually all of the metals contained in the slag in a true “zero waste process”, and transforming copper smelting slags in a valuable source of metals. 

### **THE SULPHATION – THERMAL DESCOMPOSITION PROCESS** 

The Sulphation – Thermal Decomposition (S-TD) Process consists of two main steps for processing copper smelting slags: 

- Sulphation of the -65 mesh grinded slag at 150-180ºC with 96 wt-% sulphuric acid in a weight ratio slag/acid of 1/1 to 1/1.1 to generate a semi-solid sulphated mass. 

- Thermal decomposition of the sulphated material at 700-750ºC to form copper and zinc sulphates, copper molybdate and to fix the iron as hematite, recovering the sulphuric acid which is recirculated back to the process. 

### **a) Sulphation step** 

The sulphation of the -65 mesh slag is done at 150-180ºC at atmospheric pressure with a slag/acid weight ratio of 1/1 to 1/1.1 and a reaction time of 1 to 1.5 h to generate a mass of iron sulphates, iron silicate, copper and zinc sulphates and molybdic oxide and/or coppe

r molibdate. Main reactions are as follows: - Fayalite sulphation: _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1025 - Sulphation of copper oxide and sulphide and zinc oxide: - Molybdenum – iron spinell sulphation: At the end of the sulphation step, the sulphated mass contains only FeSO4, Fe2(SO4)3, SiO2, MoO3/CuMoO4, ZnSO4 and CuSO4. The iron, in a weight ratio Fe+2 /Fe+3  3/1 contains near one mole H2O per mole of FeSO4 and it’s the only water remaining in the sulphated mass, as it was determined by thermogravimetry. ### **b) Thermal decomposition** The sulphated material, which is left to complete the formation of the hydrated FeSO4  H2O for 24 h and to become solidified, its decomposed at 700750ºC in order to fix the iron as hematite and iron silicate; silica as crystalline silica; copper and zinc as sulphates and/or basic sulphates and molybdenum as copper molybdate. Reaction time is 1 to 1.5 h., depending of the decomposition temperature. Reactions are as follows: - Decomposition of iron sulphates: - Formation of molybdenum compounds: Although there is scant information in the literature, molybdenum trioxide could form a volatile compound as hydrated MoO3  nH2O, which appears to be the case in the thermal decomposition step where water vapour is present. The gases from the thermal decomposition reactor contain SO3, some SO2 and volatilized molybdenum hydrate, in addition to dust. This gases are cooled below 150-160ºC in a condenser to re-synthetize sulphuric acid according to: _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1026 The acid, containing also dust and dissolved molybdenum, is recirculated back into the sulphation step, therefore the net consumption of acid for the all process is only 80 to 90 kg/ton of slag. The calcine, after cooling to 80-100ºC, its leached with 50 gpl acid at 60ºC for 30 min to get copper, zinc and molybdenum in solution. After liquid – solid separation and washing the residue with hot water, the solution can be processed in conventional form to recover the metals contained, for example by IX or SX for molybdenum and SX-EW for copper and zinc. In Fig. 1 it is shown a general process flow diagram of the process projected to commercial scale. The final residue consist mostly of red hematite, some iron silicate and silica, with a particle size below 10 microns. This product could be used either as red pigment due to its intense red color, or as an additive to high-quality ceramics. The traces of copper that still contains the residue (<0.02 wt-%) also can acts as an antifouling agent in paints or ceramics. This residue could be also upgraded by reverse flotation of the silica. ### **ABSTRACT** 

Oxygen Bottom-blowing Cu Smelting Technology is a modern and clean technology featured with low capital cost, low comprehensive energy consumption, high metal and sulfur recovery rate, low operating cost and a good operational environment. The core equipment of this technology is the bottom-blowing smelting furnace. This paper summarizes the development history of bottom-blowing Cu smelting technology, and the structural features and applications of a bottom-blowing smelting furnace. It then compares it with other bath smelting technologies, coming to the conclusion that oxygen bottom-blowing smelting furnace could ensure higher smelting strength, longer furnace life and higher operational efficiency and that this technology has broad development prospect.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The traditional technologies for copper smelting mainly include the blast furnace process, the reverberatory furnace process and the electric furnace process before 1970s. However, these processes have many fatal defects, such as low melting strength, high energy consumption, low utilization of sulfur, serious environmental pollution, low productivity etc. With the increasing pressure of environmental protection and energy conservation, the traditional technologies have gradually being replaced by flash smelting and bath smelting technologies in half a century. 

In the recent ten years, China ENFI Engineering Corporation, in collaboration with its partners, developed a new kind of bath smelting technology: oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting technology, which has been successfully applied to copper smelting and solved the pollution problem of sulfur dioxide effectively. 

The new technology has the advantages o

f low energy consumption, better raw material suitability, high work rate, easy in control and operation, high automation level, large processing capacity, investment effective and better kinetics condition, which attracts more and more attention in the metallurgy industry. 

### **DEVELOPMENT OF OXYGEN BOTTOM-BLOWING CU SMELTING TECHNOLOGY** 

The idea of oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting technology comes from the SKS lead smelting process. The pilot plant of SKS lead smelting process was modified to process low grade gold copper concentrate, and a copper smelting experimental study (namely matte making and gold collecting) was carried out. The results obtained from the study were encouraging. 

### **Development history of oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting technology** 

In the early 1980s, to solve the pollution problems in the traditional lead smelting process, the Chinese National Ministry of Science and Technology decided to study a new lead smelting technology. 

Due to experimental results and relevant experiences, Beijing Central Engineering & research Institute for Nonferrous metallurgical Industry (the predecessor of China ENFI Engineering Corporation) focused on oxygen bottom-blowing smelting-blast furnace lead reducing technology, and contacted Shuikoushan Bureau of

The industrial test was finished during 1998, receiving consistent high praise during an expert appraisal. The technology was advanced, environmentally beneficial and the main indicators could be used as the basis of an industrial design. Subsequently, two lead smelters were completed and the new technology was placed into operation at the Chizhou Anhui and Yuguang Henan in China. This symbolizes that the research and development of bottom-blowing copper smelting technology has realized industrial application. 

During the intermediate stage of the oxygen bottom-blowing lead smelting test, the China ENFI Engineering Corporation conducted a copper smelting test using the oxygen bottom-blowing pilot plant and subsequently also achieved success. Following the positive results obtained two industrial oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting plants were constructed in Vietnam and China (Dongying, Shandong province), which marked the first industrial applications of the Cu oxygen bottom-blowing technology. 

### **The comparison between oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting technology and other smelting technologies** 

The operating temperature of the pyrometallurgical copper smelting process is above 1000 ℃, and the liquid metal density in the molten pool is thousands or even tens of thousands of times more than that of the gas. When the gas at room temperature is injected into the molten pool, it expands suddenly, leading to even bigger

density differences between the gas and liquid metal. According to investigations, stirring power of the Vanyukov smelting furnace is 10~100 kW/m3 , and that of a Pierce Smith Converter furnace and Noranda furnace are 60~120 kW/m3 and 60 kW/m3 , respectively. However, the stirring power of the oxygen bottom-blowing furnace is up to 180 kW/m3 based on rough calculations. This high stirring power is beneficial to the heat and mass transfer between the melt and the charge, so that the concentrates can melt rapidly, and the chemical reaction rate is accelerated [1-3]. The molten pool has good flow and mass transfer performance due to its strong stirring effect. Studies show that Nu numbers of the Noranda furnace is 38.7. The Nu number for the bottom-blowing smelting furnace is 168, aproximately four times that of the Noranda furnace. The mass transfer rate of the Noranda furnace is 1.59 Nm3 O2/m3 ∙s, whilst the mass transfer rate of the bottom-blowing furnace is 3.77 Nm3 O2/m3 ∙s, two times than that of the Noranda furnace [4]. ### **THE STRUCTURE AND DESIGN OF OXYGEN BOTTOM-BLOWING CU SMELTING FURNACE** 

During the bottom-blowing smelting process, mixed ore materials are fed into the furnace to smelt via a belt conveyor without being dried or grinded. Oxygen and air are continuously injected into the copper matte through oxygen lances at the bottom of the furnace. The exhaust gas, following waste heat recovery via the waste heat boiler and dust collection via an electrostatic precipitator, is sent to an acid plant for further processing. The slag is tapped regularly, and then transported to the slow cooling area by a slag transporting car or a crane. The slag is processed to recover Cu . Containing matte is tapped regularly from the matte taphole on the side of the furnace, and is transported to Pierce Smith converters by a matte ladle for further converting. 

### **The main structure of the oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting furnace** 

The oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting furnace is a kind of cylindrical, horizontal furnace, which mainly consists of a furnace body and a series of oxygen lances. The furnace body generally includes the furnace shell, refractory materials etc. The feeding inlet, exhaust vent, temperature and pressure measuring ports are arranged on the top of the furnace. The oxygen lance holes and slag taphole are arranged at the bottom and the end of the furnace respectively.Matte taphole can be set either on the end wall, or on the side wall, depending on the technology requirement. 

The oxygen lance system is the core component of the oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting furnace, which needs a special design according to the required furnace used in the specified process. The basic structure of an oxygen lance is a multi-layer casing pipe, with oxygen channel in the inner casing and central pipe, and also protective gas channel in the outer layer. One of the most vulnerable parts is the outer casing which is made of heat resisting stainless steel. Oxygen injected through the oxygen lance is the most important characteristic of the furnace, which can not only enhance oxidation reaction rate, but also reduce the amount of exhaust gas, so that heat taken away by the gas is reduced, leading to the increase of heat efficiency and the decrease of energy consumption. ### **Design of the oxygen bottom-blowing Cu smelting furnace** 

### <u>The size of the furnace</u> 

The size and shape of the furnace must meet the requirement of the processing material. Thermal intensity in the furnace should be high enough to ensure a high melting rate of the furnace charge. The furnace size is also determined depending on the process conditions. 

### 1. Furnace volume

me, m<sup>3</sup> ; Q is the capacity of dry concentrates processed per day; q is the smelting intensity, t/(m³.d), which is about 10 t/(m<sup>3</sup> .d) according to experimental and practical production experience. 

### 2. Furnace diameter 

Two factors should be considered when determining the diameter of the furnace. One is the depth of the molten pool, which is determined based on the power of the oxygen lancing and the kinetic energy conversion of the gas injected into the furnace to make the melt fully stirred whilst avoiding splashing. The thickness of the slag layer is commonly 200-400 mm, and slag level should be controlled at 200-400 mm below the center line of the furnace. Another factor is the gas velocity in the furnace, which can't be too fast to avoid dust carry-over and subsequent offgas accretion formation restricting the

1041 

gas flow through the offgas system. 

### 3. The Length of the furnace 

The length of the furnace is determined by many factors. One is the length of the required smelting zone, which depends on the number of oxygen lances and the spacing between them. The second factor is the sedimentation area required prior to slag and matte tapping. In addition, the location and the length of the offgas vent should be taken into account when determining the length of the furnace. 

### <u>The structure of the furnace</u> 

### 1. Furnace shell 

The cylindrical furnace shell consists of welded steel plates and is supported on rollers by two tyres. The oxygen lance hole, feed inlet, tapholes , and exhaust/offgas vent are set on the wall of the furnace body. Hundreds of tons of high temperature melt can be contained inside the furnace. To ensure structural integrity during times of bad operating conditions, high quality steel plate material Q345R is used. 

### 2. Refractory lining 

The refractory lining consists of high quality magnesium chromium bricks. Water jackets are utilized in high wear areas such as the matte and slag tapholes and the exhaust/offgas vent. The structure of the oxygen lance hole zone is specially designed by using higher quality bricks to extend the service life of both the oxygen lances and the bricks used in the oxygen lance holes. 

### <u>Design for the oxygen lance</u> 

Protective gas (compressed air) flows through the outer channel, whilst oxygen or oxygen-enriched air passes through the inner channel of the oxygen lance. The different types of oxygen lances that can be used include a cartridge type, spiral groove type etc. which can be selected according to the requirement of use. 

When the oxygen lance is eroded up to a set critical length, it must be replaced by a new one. ### **ABSTRACT** 

The paper describes the "Bottom Blowing Copper Converting" BBCCS, a continuous converting process with high oxygen enrichment of the Dongying Fangyuan Nonferrous Metal Company (DF), as a new step applying of the continuous improvement in research and innovation to increase the efficiency and effectiveness in copper production of our company. 

Based on this process, tests were carried out to process a high matte grade metal, called "White Metal" (WM), both solid and liquid, with different conditions in order to quantify the effects of different parameters including slag type, blowing intensity, oxygen level, end point in copper blowing and others. Also the arrangement of tuyeres or lances and the life of refractory lining were investigated. 

This paper showed the series of tests have empowered us to develop and show in this world conference, this continuous copper smelting process including the reactor and its ancillary equipment to produce anodic copper directly.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

At present maybe the 95% of the copper smelter world or more are using the Peirce Smith (PS) furnace in converting process in an intermittent and batch operation. The reality of PS is it has the need to "turn up" the furnace to blow and "turn down" it to pour the molten material into ladles, make a really difficult, expensive, inefficient and ineffective to make complete gas sealing and, finally, it is almost impossible. 

This is a worldwide common problem for PS, and it has been taking much efforts and sacrifice of many companies and smelters trying to do it, putting primary, secondary and tertiary hoods to seal plus some blowing control improvements and putting cold material through some lateral feeders to avoid the "turn up/turn down" movement of reactor and its consequence, the high level of fugitive gases. 

The Continuous Copper Smelting technology started as an industrial application in the years '70, almost 40 years ago, with the Mitsubishi Process for direct copper production in Japan; another alternative is the Double-Flash process applied by Kennecott and Outokunpu in USA, as an extension of flash smelter for concentrates with high copper grade and low iron content used in Poland and Australia.  Both technologies are examples used at the present industrial operation, but they are not so expanded around the world<sup>[1]</sup> . 

The process flow of Mitsubishi used 3 furnaces, first in a smelting furnace with top lances to blow enrichment air and feeding of concentrate, after a settler to separate the matte and slag in an electric furnace, plus a continuous converting furnace to blister with top blowing lances with air oxygen enrichment, in which the furnaces are linked by channels to make continuous transferring of the molten

materials between them. The high construction cost is the main problem, plus a fine tuning to work in a stationary regimen of equilibrium between the 3 furnaces, giving a not so high flexibility and, finally, the need than the first furnace must be put in a higher position. These facts explain why this process is not so extended in the industry. 

The process flow of Double-Flash includes a Flash smelting furnace (FS) with water quenching of matte, which needs grinding and drying to put into the Flash converting furnace (FC) is an expensive investment process. In this conversion alternative, the cold matte mixed with flux is injected into the flash burner at FC. Obviously some heat is wasted during water quenching, while some extra heat or fuel are needed to dry and smelt the solid matted feeding into FC, and this is a paradox in heat efficiency. Additionally, the extra processing steps including the water quenching, milling to dust size, drying to zero and smashing increase the converting cost because these steps consume much labor and energy, that we believe are the reason of limited popularity of FC.

Others are the Noranda and the INCO processes, but they are not available in industrial application. 

This paper main covers a new industrial development of Bottom Blowing Continuous Copper Smelting technology (BBCCS) including the phenomena and result of test with both, solid and liquid WM from bottom blowing smelting furnace (BBF). It also gives description of the research in Dongying Fangyuan Nonferrous Metals Co., Ltd (DF) to produce anode Copper directly by half continuous converting based on the characteristics of WM from BBF. 

### **BBCCS. RESEARCH TESTING AND RESULTS** 

### `—` **BBCCS solid WM Test.** 

It was definitely a new direction of development, and there were no experience, neither papers nor lectures or anything to consult. So we started the test from relative simple decision, start with cold WM to increase and accumulate new knowledge. 

Aiming at finding out the feasibility of BBCCS processing, the test was carried out on a test in a BBF with a capacity of 5.000 tons blister/year, composed by tuyeres or lance life under enriched oxygen condition and possibility of “mushroom head”, trying to make an accretion to protect the end of tuyere to increase the life of it, testing the lance life, the burning of refractory lining and the effect of different conditions on distribution of sulfur content in blister, copper content in slag and impurities as principal focus of the tests. 

Cold matte test is different from molten matte test because we can accurately measure the feed matte and accessories obtaining an easily adjust of process indexes like temperature. At the beginning, there were four phases: gas/slag/matte/blister. As the barrier effect of low blister degree, just 96-97,6%Cu and a relative large and variable sulfur content in blister from 0,03% to 0,98%S, the copper

content in slag was very low, but parameters were not sufficiently good enough to meet the refining process. Thus we changed the ratio of oxygen over feed to keep only three phases in furnace "off gas/slag/blister". The furnace got gradually a stable condition, and the blister quality was improved, became higher than 98,5%Cu and sulfur content lower than 0,25%S, obtaining parameters absolutely satisfactory for copper refining process. But there was a new emerging problem to solve, the slag viscosity increase, and its subsequent effect in the copper content in slag, which increased to levels of 10-15%Cu, too much.

### <u>Devices decision</u> 

It is a fact that small size’s furnaces enlarged operational problems and cause a great volatility in results. Thus the liquid WM test was carried out in a bigger enough size of BBF of 3.6<sup>Φ</sup> Ч8.1 m with a designed capacity of 50,000 tons blister per year; a PS converter of the same size could produce 100,000 tons blister per year.. 

The furnace was lined with magnesia-chrome brick with 5 bottom special tuyeres with a casing protective, inserts in the structure of the furnace, using high oxygen through tuyere to react and a flow of nitrogen/air under 0,45-0,6MPa in the external casing to protect the lance. The tuyeres were arranged in two lines in the same side at angles of 7° and 20° respectively; the off gas hole was in the middle above. The liquid WM was charged continuously into the furnace chamber through a chute while flux and other solids were charged continuously through the furnace mouth after they were been measured. Slag and metal tapping hole were on the end wall being distant enough from blowing area; slag was skimmed out by overflow and metal using a siphon.

### **ABSTRACT** 

Today, pyrometallurgy is the most widely applied industrial practice for copper recovery in Kazakhstan.  More than one half of copper in Kasakhstan is produced through Vanyukov smelting. Ores occurring in Kazakhstan differ for their various compositions. Moreover, high zinc, lead and arsenic sulphides content and low contents of iron sulphide in the copper concentrates shall be noted. Reduced concentrations of iron sulphides lead to shifting the heat balance of the autogenous smelting process that requires increased levels of desulfuration which, in its turn, results in different slag compositions, altered mechanical properties and increased copper losses. One way to solve this problem could be using additional fuel; another way is increasing oxygen content blowing in a gas mix.

### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS** 

Strict compliance of technological parameters is required to provide relevant operational efficiency in Vanyukov furnaces (VF). Altered ore mineralogy resulted in decreased iron sulphide contents in the feed to the extent that they are lower than what is required for an autogenic process, and a decreased smelting temperature, impairing matteslag separation efficiency and increased copper losses with additional discarded slag. 

<mark>A high copper concentration in the slag may be due to several factors. In general, they can be conventionally classified in three groups. The first factor is related to the</mark> _<mark>chemical compositions of the slag</mark>_ <mark>. The second factor consists on temperature conditions in the smelting furnace and slag mixer. The third factor includes the lack of compliance of the technological smelting process and slag mixer operating conditions.</mark> 

<mark>The long-term experience in the operation of fuel-oil furnaces (OF) and Vanyukov furnaces (VF) as well as theoretical research data proved that the

least copper losses with discarded slag are at concentrations of 35-37% silicon dioxide, 5-7% calcium oxide and with a magnetite content of not more than 3-4%.</mark>

### **SULFIDES ELECTROLYSIS** 

### **Changing paradigm?** 

From an extraction perspective, the objective of copper smelting is the separation and reduction of copper cations from sulfides ore, which after concentration by grinding/flotation can reach a high grade in sulfide phase (>85%). A new paradigm could therefore arise from an innovative extraction step that operates with such concentrate feedstock. In that scope, and to reduce emissions, the key component to reconsider is the reductant, which could potentially be chosen among carbon, hydrogen or electrons. 

Sulfides chemical metallurgy teaches that carbon is not appropriate because of the lack of chemical stability of CS and CS2. Hydrogen is at the present time not readily available, what leads to consider the third alternative, using electricity. Indeed, similar to what has been proposed for oxide feedstock [6], one could envision the direct decomposition of sulfides compounds into elemental copper and sulfur, e.g. 



The three key potential advantages of such approach are the following: 

- direct production of high purity copper, ideally in a liquid phase 

- production of a low volume and high value sulfur by-product 

- drastic mitigation of SO2 emissions along with a simplification of copper extraction flow-sheet 

### **Previous examples** 

The review by Prof. Fathi Habashi published by the Bureau of Mines in 1966 [7] reveals that the concept of recovering elemental sulfur from sulfide ores is not a mere dream and that numerous approaches are possible. In particular, direct electrolytic approaches have been proposed as early as 1906 [8, 9]. At that time, a chloride/alkali chloride mixture is used as a supporting electrolyte, with the limitation that the sulfides solubility in such melts is low. However, the concept appears technically feasible and allows the production of high purity lead from galena (PbS, [9]) or copper from copper sulfide (Cu2S, [10]). One development of the direct electrolysis of sulfides in chloride melts by Hoar and Ward [10] consists in using the sulfide feedstock as cathode and anode, taking benefit of the high electronic condu

ctivity of these compounds. 

Recently, a regain of interest for the electrolysis of sulfide compounds in chloride melts has been noticed, for example to win aluminium [11], tungsten [12], molybdenum [13] or to refine copper [14]. 

As a summary, it appears that several difficulties are inherited from the use of chloride melts: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

1068 

- a limited temperature of operation i.e. the metal product is often solid, therefore porous and requiring a rinsing step, 

- a limited anodic faradaic efficiency for the production of sulfur, partly because of the presence of oxygen and the possible competition of chlorine evolution, 

- a difficulty in maintaining  high cathodic efficiency for the production of copper 

Moving forward, it is envisioned to develop an electrolytic route that will not rely on the use of halides-based electrolyte. The foreseen process would operate with a multicomponent sulfides melt at a temperature above the metal product melting point (i.e. above 1085°C for copper) and allows the selective decomposition of copper sulfide from a concentrate into liquid metallic copper and sulfur gas. 

### **High temperature sulfides electrolysis** 

Despite the original patents, there are very few reports that are relevant in the scope of the direct electrolysis of a sulfide melt because of the experimental difficulties in mastering such systems at the laboratory scale. As a matter of fact, previous reports faced the challenge of high vapor pressure of the selected electrolyte [15], contamination by oxide impurities [15] or incompatibility with the container material [16]. 

Those reports however point to the relevant scientific questioning, encompassing: 

- What is the range of thermodynamic stability of a multicomponent sulfides mixture, i.e. does the community have sufficient experimental data to provide the phase diagrams for such systems? 

- What is the corresponding solubility of sulfides feedstock (e.g. Cu2S) and their relative stability with respect to impurities, i.e. what is the electrochemical series for molten sulfides? 

- What is the nature of the electrical conductivity properties of molten sulfides? Is it possible to obtain satisfactory ionic conductivity with such systems? 

- Is the selectivity obtained by electrolysis acceptable for practical application? 

Despite these questions, the proof of concept has been achieved with production of molten copper and sulfur in energetically promising conditions [13MJ/kg to win liquid copper at less than 0.001wt% sulfur from concentrate, reference 10], dissolution of a sulfide feed in a sulfide mixture [15] and generation of high purity sulfur gas [10].

### **CONCLUSION** 

The promises of the direct electrolysis of sulfide concentration for copper production are very appealing. Such a process would offer a reduction of the energy consumption, the SOx emissions and the number of unit o

perations while reducing the volume of sulfur by-product from the industry. Past results are promising though not directly obtained with sulfide melts. The direct electrolysis of sulfides therefore requires a more fundamental understanding of matte thermochemical as well as electrical properties to allow the design and operation of laboratory scale demonstration cells. Innovation in this field would be beneficial beyond the scope of electrolysis, for example to design innovative sensors for matte processing or new recycling processes.

### **ABSTRACT** 

WorleyParsons has used Discrete Event Simulation (DES) methods in conjunction with more traditional process models to assess the performance of copper smelting operations. The DES model allows for a more complete and realistic picture of an operation to be developed based on the plant capacities and accounting for breakdowns and shutdowns. This paper outlines methods used to identify the opportunities to de-constrain existing operations and demonstrate that other constraints will not impact the overall improvement to the production. Examples of aisle and typical smelting operations are covered.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Traditionally for debottlenecking studies of smelters and other process plants, a mass balance is performed based on continuous operating rates and expected operating hours. Smelters have several points of failure that will restrict, if not take the entire plant offline. By using a more detailed model than simple spreadsheets, validated against plant experience, bottlenecks can be demonstrated and strategies to remove them can be modeled to increase plant availability and economics. These models are also ideally suited to production planning and for studies examining feed changes and sensitivities. 

The modeling simulates the plant performance in real time, and by performing enough simulation the expected long run performance of the plant can be estimated. Although there are a number of commercially available packages, ExtendSim which is a powerful Discrete Event Simulation software package that is ideally suited to the batch and semi-batch processes and events that occur within smelter operating environments has been used in these examples. The value of performing this work is that the operational performance of the plant can be assessed ensuring production targets are met, without using excessive capital outlay.

### **THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS** 

Common steps to any optimization process are to identify the limits/constraints within your smelter, and then to look at ways to remove or ease this restriction on your plant. Other changes to the plant, operating practices and expansions can also be simulated. 

WorleyParsons has completed a number of debottlenecking projects with various clients.  The approach involves spending time at the operation: 

- Collecting plant data 

- Interviewing a cross section of personnel to determine individual though

ts on the process bottleneck 

- Assessing plant data to determine in particular if this supports the individual ideas on the process bottleneck 

- Reviewing future plans with regards to concentrate supply and current development plans 

With this data collected and correlated the modeling of ‘future’ operations can begin.  The modeling process includes mass and energy balancing, typically using Metsim, however some clients prefer to run either site developed models using specific packages or Excel based models.  In some cases the client is also keen for an independent review of their model. 

The next step is to utilize outputs from the steady state peak modeling assessment to develop the DES model.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

Among various converting technologies that produce blister copper a special case is the one that processes copper-nickel-containing feeds such as matte and concentrates. The principal difficulty of such converting processes is the removal of nickel, which, in oxidizing conditions forms solid spinel with high nickel oxide content. 

The Gipronickel Institute is developing a new technology of continuous converting of granulated copper-nickel-containing matte in a two-zone converter Vaniukov furnace in cooperation with the Canadian company “Flogen Technologies Inc” and the Ural Institute of Metallurgy.  This furnace is schematically shown in Figure 1. 



Figure 1 – Two-zone converter Vaniukov furnace, a schematic view 

The process of continuous converting in a two-zone Vaniukov furnace can be presented as follows. Copper and nickel containing matte after granulation is fed along with fluxes and coal into the oxidizing zone of the furnace. Quartzite and limestone are usually used as fluxes. A mixture of air and oxygen and hydrocarbon fuels are injected though lances. The use of hydrocarbon fuels or coal is required to maintain the heat balance of the furnace and to control the oxidation degree of sulphide feed. The high copper-oxidecontaining slag produced in the oxidizing zone flow in the reduction zone of the furnace where it is reduced in a reduction atmosphere obtained as a result of burning of hydrocarbon fuel under the conditions of oxygen deficiency. The goal of the reduction zone is to reduce the copper oxide in the slag. The metallic beads formed in the reduction 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

1083 

zone settle into the bottom of the furnace and get mixed with the blister copper produced in the oxidation stage. The slag from the reduction zone is continuously discharged from the furnace through a siphon. 

Generally the smelting in a Vaniukov furnace can be referred as a bubbling process whose effectiveness in many respects depends on the slag properties. As a result the choice of the optimal composition of the slag that lies in the Cu2O-NiO-FeOx-SiO2-CaOAl2O3 system is important to achieve the process stability with high productivity of a high-grade blister copper. 

The choice of the optimal composition of the slag is complicated by extremely limited information on the structure and properties of slags in the Cu2O-NiO-FeOx-SiO2-CaOAl2O3 system in a wide range of compositions. In this regard new complex investigations of the structure and properties of the slags of the abovementioned system have been undertaken. Based on the results of these investigations recommendations for an optimal slag composition for t

he two zone Vanuikov Furnace are given in the present work. It is however appropriate at first to overview the principal results of our thermodynamic and experimental work on the structure and properties of slags containing significant amount of copper, nickel and iron oxides. ### **Slag Temperature** One of the requirements for the slag composition in the Vaniukov furnace is the low level of of crystallized magnetite (spinel). In this regard several tests were performed in the temperature range of 1225-14000 С. Some of these results are presented in Figure 2. As it can be seen from the graph the slag remains homogeneous until temperature reaches around 1330o C. If temperature decreases a sharp increase of magnetite content is observed. This magnetite/spinel is a trevorite (NiFe2O4)-based one and has the following average composition in % (weight.): 18-19 Ni; 49-51 Fe; 0,2-0,4 Со; 2,1-3,1 Аl; 0,150,2 Мg; 28-29 О. It is known from the practice of Vaniukov furnace operations that high amount of magnetite or spinel should be avoided. The spinel content of 10% can be considered as a critical point and this approximately corresponds to the temperature of 13000 С. As a result the oxidation stage needs to be carried out at temperatures higher than 13500 С and the slag liquidus temperature should not exceed 13300 С. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1084 Figure 2 –Spinel concentration in the slag (wt. %) versus slag temperature ### **Flux Consumption** The slags of continuous converting that lie within Cu2O-NiO-FeOx-SiO2-CaO-Al2O3 system are inclined to saturation of trevorite (NiFe2O4)-based spinel and the concentration of the latter to a great extend depends on the flux consumption and, as a result, on the changing of (Fe+Ni) and (SiO2+CaO) total concentrations in the slag [1]. Taking into account the fact that slag liquidus temperature should be lower than 1330о С, it is not recommended to process matte with copper content lower than 60%. ### **Density and Surface Tension** One of the important factors that affect the separation of smelting products is the difference in the density of produced melts [5]. In the current case the melts are blister copper (its density is 8,9-8,94 g/cm3 ) and slag. To achieve a good separation it is necessary to aim at lower density of the latter, as blister copper density is already determined by its conditional composition while slag density can change depending of the choice of its chemical composition. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1088 Among other important slag properties, in particular for bubbling-type processes, is the surface tension [6, 7]. According to previous data [8], the surface tension of 240-270 mN/m does not cause any problem in the smelting process although the above mentioned range is already close to a boundary value. In any case, for the purpose of further discussion the surface tension of 240 mN/m has been accepted as a boundary value. Using the method of maximal pressure in a gas bubble [9] several measurements of density and surface tension for slags in the Cu2O-FeOx-SiO2, Cu2O-NiO-FeOx-SiO2 and Cu2O-NiO-FeOx-SiO2-CaO-Al2O3 systems have been performed. It was determined that in the slags within the Cu2O-NiO-FeOx-SiO2-CaO-Al2O3 system a decrease of fluxing components content and, as a result, an increase of travorite-based spinel content in the slag to 55 % causes an increase of its density from 3.6 to 4.0 gr/cm3 , and a sharp fall of surface tension from 320 to 50 mN/m. The increase of SiO2/CaO ratio in the homogenous slag from 0.3 to 4 results in a decrease of slag density from 3.8 to 3.4 g/cm

up>3</sup> and of the surface tension from 350 to 270 mN/m. Improvement of the quality of coppernickel-containing feed supplied to continuous converting and, as a result, the reduction of (Fe)/(Cu+Ni) ratio in the slag from 1.6 to 0.4 gives rise to the growth of the slag density from 3.5 to 3.8 g/cm<sup>3</sup> and decreases its surface tension from 300 to 270 mN/m. In the recommended range of SiO2/CaO (1.8-2.3) ratio in the slag of continuous converting density falls within 3.6-3.5 g/cm<sup>3</sup> , and surface tension within 320-300 mN/m. 

### **Viscosity** 

Slag viscosity is an important property having influence on the smelting process as excessively free-running slag results in saturation of the furnace refractory lining and the decrease of its lifetime [10-12]. On the other hand, slag with high viscosity slows down diffusion and kinetic processes and results in formation of dead zones of the furnace and also promotes slag melt foaming which is typical for bubbling type processes [5,13,14]. 

Abundant literature sources related to the slag viscosity lack the clear definition of viscosity limit values, above which slag cannot be used for the smelting process in a commercial scale. However, according to indirect definitions, this value is somewhere in the range of 30-50 Poise [15-17]. Therefore, for the purpose of further discussions slag melt viscosity equal to 30 P has been accepted as a boundary value. 

Using a vibration method [18], measurement of slag melts viscosity in the Cu2O-NiOFeOx-SiO2-CaO-Al2O3 system has been carried out in a wide range of compositions. The results have shown that in the temperature range of 1250-1450<sup>о</sup> С viscosity of homogenous slags in the oxidation zone of continuous converting process is in the limits of 0.5-3.5 Poise in a wide range of their compositions and this corresponds to property requirements of bubbling processes slags. Regularities of viscosity change as a function of temperature changes have been determined and they comply with modern conception of slag structure.  The effect of spinel (trevorite) content on the slag viscosity was

### **EMISSIONS REDUCTION AND PROCESS IMPROVEMENTS ACHIEVED WITH THE NEW ANODE FURNACE OFF-GAS SYSTEM AT ASARCO HAYDEN**

### **ABSTRACT** 

The ASARCO smelter in Hayden, Arizona operates three anode furnaces to firerefine blister copper for casting to anodes. The furnaces use natural gas with steam for reduction and natural gas burners for temperature control. Previously, anode furnace offgas discharged directly to the building with no gas collection, and burner gas consumption was high. 

ASARCO engaged GCT, LLC to provide preliminary and detail engineering and EPCM services for a new off-gas system to reduce anode furnace emissions. The baghouse-based system was installed and successfully started up in February 2012. Following startup of the new off-gas system, ASARCO and GCT worked together to optimize the tuyere and burner practices in order to improve reduction efficiency and processing time, to reduce gas consumption and soot formation, and to optimize the offgas system operation. The process improvements resulted in significantly reduced natural gas consumption and improved gas capture performance of the new hoods. 

This paper outlines the challenges faced in designing the new off-gas system and the process improvements and energy savings achieved through the collaborative optimization effort.

### **INTRODUCTION** 

The ASARCO smelter in Hayden, Arizona operates two of three anode furnaces to fire-refine blister copper for casting to anodes. The furnaces use natural gas with steam

for reduction and natural gas burners for temperature control. Previously, anode furnace off-gas discharged directly to the building with no gas collection, and burner gas consumption was high. ASARCO engaged Gas Cleaning Technologies, LLC (GCT) to provide preliminary and detail engineering and EPCM services for a new off-gas system to reduce anode furnace emissions. The baghouse-based system was installed and successfully started up in February 2012. Following startup of the new off-gas system, ASARCO and GCT worked together to optimize the tuyere and burner practices in order to improve reduction efficiency and processing time, to reduce gas consumption and soot formation, and to optimize the off-gas system operation. The process improvements resulted in significantly reduced natural gas consumption and improved gas capture performance of the new hoods. This paper outlines the challenges faced in designing the new off-gas system and the process improvements and energy savings achieved through the collaborative optimization effort. ### **FURNACE OPERATIONS BEFORE NEW SYSTEM IMPLEMENTATION** Figure 1 – Anode Furnace Operation before Off-Gas System Installation _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1097 The anode furnace shells at ASARCO Hayden are 13’ diameter x 35’ long. Each vessel also has a separate skimming port and casting port. Off-Gas from the anode furnace was vented directly into the anode building and out to atmosphere with no gas or dust treatment. However, wet scrubbers are not effective at removing carbon soot from anode furnace off-gas because the carbon particles are not easily wetted for effective scrubbing. A baghouse is quite capable of removing carbon soot and other dust and is therefore the standard treatment technology for anode furnace offgas. In most anode furnace applications, SO2 scrubbing is not warranted due to the low concentration of SO2 in the off-gas and the short periods of operation when SO2 is _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1099 actually generated in the furnace. When SO2 treatment is required, it is generally done with a wet scrubber using lime or caustic downstream of a baghouse. Continuous converting and direct to blister operations are more likely to use SO2 scrubbing due to the higher sulfur content in the blister from these operations compared to conventional Peirce-Smith batch converting. Some smelters send the anode furnace off-gas to a concentrate dryer first for heat recovery. This option was evaluated for ASARCO but found to economically unfeasible at Hayden. #### **NEW OFF-GAS SYSTEM CONFIGURATION** After completing the benchmarking analysis, the project team finalized the new off-gas system configuration. Each anode furnace was modified to install a new smaller off-gas mouth on the barrel between the existing charging mouth and the end wall on the burner side (away from the tuyeres). A pneumatically-operated charging mouth cover was installed to cover the existing charging mouth when not charging the vessel. A fixed wrap-around refractory-lined hood was installed over the new off-gas mouth that would cover the off-gas mouth throughout the full operating range of vessel rotation. #### **PROCESS OPTIMIZATION** 

After successfully commissioning the new off-gas system, it was agreed that the anode furnace process could be further optimized. Reduction time was longer than expected, and burner inputs were still relatively high. Therefore, a series of trials were performed to optimize the anode furnace process. 

The first optimization trial was to set the burner and hood draft setpoints to optimize the anode furnace process. New instrumentation was added to monitor the tuyere and burner air and gas inputs, and the burner air-to-gas ratio was reduced to 10:1. The burner gas flow rate setpoint was reduced in order to find the minimum input that would maintain the acceptable bath temperature. ### **THE SAVARD-LEE SHROUDED INJECTOR: A REVIEW OF ITS ADOPTION AND ADAPTATION FROM FERROUS TO NON-FERROUS PYROMETALLURGY** 

J.P. Kapusta _BBA Inc. 630, Renй-Lйvesque Blvd. West, Suite 1900 Montrйal, Quйbec, Canada H3B 4V5 Joel.Kapusta@bba.ca_ 

R.G.H. Lee _Air Liquide (retired) Calgary, Canada_ 

### **ABSTRACT** 

Pyrometallurgical processes for iron and base metals present major similarities since they occur at high temperatures and in molten state. Pyrometallurgists, therefore, have long believed that some technologies from ferrous metallurgy could be beneficially adapted (and transferred) to non-ferrous metallurgy, and vice versa. The Savard-Lee shrouded injector is one such technology. Developed for steelmaking, the concept has inspired non-ferrous pyrometallurgists for decades and is now receiving renewed interest in light of recent commercial successes in high intensity smelting, particularly in Asia. This paper provides a review of key non-ferrous pyrometallurgical processes that have innovatively adapted and implemented the shrouded injector concept. Such processes include bath smelting of lead and copper (QSL, SKS), bath converting of copper and nickel (Hoboken and SMC with ALSI Technology, SKS), copper pyro-refining (O2/N2/H2 injectors) and lead-silver cupellation (BBOC). The authors highlight how the Savard-Lee injector was adapted from its original steel refining design for oxygen bottom metallurgy (OBM) into new designs for non-ferrous applications. The authors also offer their views on the future of bath smelting and converting with high oxygen submerged injection, especially at times when energy conservation and efficiency, lower quality concentrate, and environmental footprint awareness are at the forefront of the industry preoccupations. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

1116 

### **INTRODUCTION** 

In their 1992 paper, Mackey and Brimacombe [1] reported how Guy Savard and Robert Lee of Canadian Liquid Air have transformed the metallurgical landscape in 1966 with their invention of the high oxygen shrouded injector, commonly known as the Savard-Lee injector. That invention became the enabling oxygen injection technology for the advent of the Oxygen Bottom Metallurgy (OBM) process that revolutionized the steel industry in the 70s. The Savard-Lee injector has also had a significant impact on nonfer

rous pyrometallurgy: all oxygen bottom blowing processes currently developed for non-ferrous matte smelting and converting have adopted Savard-Lee type injectors as a critical and integral part of their process reactors. After receiving comments on a manuscript he was preparing on the pioneering developments of sonic injection in Canada [2], one of the authors (JK) felt compelled to expand the story to developments made outside Canada and provide a more thorough review of the adoption and adaptation of the Savard-Lee shrouded injector from ferrous to non-ferrous pyrometallurgy. Private communications and access to the archives of one of the inventors of the injector and coauthor of this paper (RL) provided insightful information to recount the story. 

This paper begins with a brief historical perspective on the development of the Savard-Lee injector and provides details of its typical design for oxygen bottom metallurgy (OBM) in steelmaking. The authors then present key milestones for the first Savard-Lee injector implementation in non-ferrous pyrometallurgy in what is now known as the QSL Process (Queneau-Schumann-Lurgi process). 

The next three sections briefly reviews how shrouded injection has been adapted and applied in bath converting of copper and nickel with the Air Liquide Shrouded Injection (ALSI) Technology, in secondary copper pyro-refining with concentric-pipe injectors for desulfurization (oxidation) and deoxidation with O2/N2 and H2/N2 gas mixtures, respectively, and in lead-silver cupellation with the Bottom Blown Oxygen Converter (BBOC) Technology. 

The authors complete their historical perspective with their assessment of the development of the Oxygen Bottom Blown smelting process, also known as SKS Process. With a focus on shrouded injection implementation, the technical and metallurgical details of the processes reviewed are out of the scope of this paper. The readers are referred to the references provided for each process. 

In their conclusions, the authors discuss their views on the future of bath smelting and converting that will inevitably use high oxygen submerged injection as an integral part of the process, as exemplified by the development of the high intensity, low off-gas volume SKS process for new smelters. As for existing smelters, they also discuss a brownfield retrofit alternative using Savard-Lee type shrouded injectors for matte smelting with Noranda Reactors or Teniente Converters, or matte converting with PeirceSmith or Hoboken converters.

### **BRIEF HISTORY OF THE SAVARD-LEE SHROUDED INJECTOR INVENTION (DEVELOPMENT)** 

The research and development efforts leading to the invention of the Savard-Lee concentric injector lasted almost two decades from 1947 to 1966. Mackey and Brimacombe [1] provided a well-documented and detailed account of that Canadian metallurgy story in their paper titled “Savard and Lee – Transforming the Metallurgical Landscape”

, presented during the Savard-Lee International Symposium on Bath Smelting. In the symposium honoring them, the inventors themselves gave their own anecdotal recount of the vision and perseverance needed during their journey to find a way to inject pure oxygen into molten steel [3]. This paper only provides a brief summary of the key milestones of the quest for oxygen bottom injection. 

The journey started in 1947 when a young Robert G.H. Lee, fresh from McGill University in Montreal, joined the headquarters of Canadian Liquid Air (CLA), as the company was known at the time. That same year, during a visit to a steel plant, he witnessed the process commonly used at the time to homogenize steel for temperature and composition when a ladle full of molten steel was repeatedly plunged with an ingot. He left the plant thinking there had to be a better method though the idea did not materialize until months later, when soaking in his bath. Could an inert gas such as argon be injected from the bottom of the ladle to homogenize the steel? After a few years of research in collaboration with Etienne Spire of L’Air Liquide France and some support from the former Canadian Bureau of Mines (now CANMET) facilities in Ottawa, the porous plug was invented, and with it, Ladle Metallurgy. 

Also in the late 1940s, CLA was pursuing research on oxygen injection. The first trials, run in 1947 at the DOSCO steel mill in Sydney, Nova Scotia, were aimed at desiliconizing molten iron via supersonic top lancing of oxygen in a ladle. The tests were not successful as the jet did not penetrate the bath deeply enough. New trials were conducted at DOSCO in 1951-52, this time via submerged top lancing with a refractory coated pipe submersed 40 cm into the molten iron bath with oxygen pressures up to 700 kPag (100 psig). Although successful in lowering the silicon content to levels around 0.25%, the technique was abandoned due to the excessive volumes of iron oxide fumes. 

The next logical step was to inject the oxygen from the bottom of the bath at high pressure to benefit from the Joule-Thompson cooling effect of an expanding jet. Between 1951 and 1956, top submerged lancing and bottom injection trials at various steel mills and foundries were conducted with oxygen pressures ranging from 2 750 kPag (400 psig) to 4 825 kPag (700 psig) and heats ranging from 500 kg to 35 tonnes. A first major breakthrough was achieved when, in 1954-55, a protective accretion – or mushroom – was discovered to form at the tip of a bottom injector at an oxygen pressure of 4 825 kPag (700 psig). Following water-steam physical modeling at the National Research Council in Ottawa, Canada in 1955, a first bottom blown vessel – a modified 18-tonne ladle – was equipped with a set of 4 to 6 bottom injectors and operated at DOSCO in 1956. The drive was to focus on developing an injector that could operate at commercially and commonly available oxygen pressures (much lower than the pressures used up until then). The new challenge was then to find an alternative to the JouleThompson cooling effect. The new concept was to shield the oxygen jet with a gas inert with the bath, or better yet, an oxygen “getter” gas that would displace the highly exothermic metal oxidation reaction away from the tip of the injectors. The early tests of the shrouded injector started in 1964 at the Freeman Corporation foundry in the town of Cap-de-la-Madeleine, some 150 km east of Montreal. The trials were first run as top- _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 1119 submerged shrouded lancing and then, after some confidence was gained from successes, via bottom injection with a simple, effective and safe injector design, as shown on Figure 3. Readily available methane and propane were selected as shroud gas and oxygen getter allowing the generation and control of protective accretions (mushrooms) at the injector tips. Bustos contributed significantly to the understanding of submerged gas injection phenomena, particularly when he was a member of the Brimacombe group at the University of British Columbia, as exemplified by some of the publications he authored or co-authored [13-18]. After joining Air Liquide in 1989, he applied his experience in converting and expertise in sonic injection to the development of the Air Liquide Shrouded Injector – ALSI Te

chnology – for high oxygen injection into nonferrous bath converting vessels and its patenting in 1995 [19]. This Savard-Lee type injector takes advantage of the benefits of operating at enrichment levels above 28% oxygen without increasing the rate of refractory wear. This is achieved by forming a protective accretion at the injector tips (chemical protection) and by eliminating the need for punching (no mechanical damage), as shown in Figure 18. The shrouded injector has an inner pipe through which oxygen enriched air is injected. The inner pipe is surrounded by an annulus through which nitrogen (or other inert gases or hydrocarbon) flows. Both the oxygen enriched air and the nitrogen streams are injected at pressures such that the flow through the inner pipe and the annular space is choked [20]. 2

Drawings from the 1976 patent are shown on Figure 29. The main issue with shrouded injection is the control of the protective accretion. Too small an accretion will not provide sufficient protection, while too large an accretion will hinder the flow of reactive gas. Tuyeres or injectors have been developed to remedy this issue, including a three concentric pipe design as shown on Figure 30 where oxygen is injected into the inner annulus while natural gas is injected into the central bore and outer annulus. The inventors claim a better control of the accretion formation by controlling the flows of oxygen and natural gas.

In the secondary copper refining, however, Savard-Lee type injectors have been implemented in their simplest design for oxidation (desulfurization) and deoxidation. Unfortunately, very limited publications are available and, to the best of the author’s knowledge, none provide operating details. From personal experience with producers in Europe and North America, secondary copper refiners make one of the most elegant uses of the shrouded injector concept. The same shrouded injectors are used for both steps of oxidation and deoxidation by alternating injection of oxygen and hydrogen as reactive gas, and nitrogen as shrouding for tuyere protection and diluent for bath stirring. In the oxidation step, high oxygen-enriched air (typically ~ 80% O2) is injected into the central bore at sonic velocity and nitrogen into the annulus for shrouding, also at sonic velocity.

For the deoxidation stage, hydrogen diluted with nitrogen (typically ~ 75% H2) is injected into the central bore at sonic velocity, while nitrogen is injected into the annulus for shrouding. A key safety feature of the valve train and flow control system is a short step (1-2 min.) for purging the central bore with nitrogen. This purge eliminates any explosion risks due to residual oxygen in the piping system and central pipe of the tuyeres when switching from oxidation to deoxidation and to hydrogen injection. A similar purge is done prior to a new oxidation refining cycle and oxygen injection. A 25tonne secondary copper refining furnace is shown on Figure 31. ### **SKS PROCESS FOR COPPER AND LEAD SMELTING** 

The early research on high intensity bath smelting in China was conducted by Shuikoushan Mining Corporation in the 80s with pilot tests completed in 1991 on a 3 000 tonnes per day pilot furnace [38]. The technology was, however, not commercially developed at the time. Shuikoushan Nonferrous Metal Co. Ltd. and China Nonferrous Engineering and Research Institute (ENFI) continued their research, developed and patented the oxygen bottom blowing copper process in 1994 [39], which is now known as the Shuikoushan or more commonly the SKS process. 

As recently described in a brochure jointly prepared by China Nonferrous Metal Industry’s Foreign Engineering and Construction Co. Ltd. (NFC) and China ENFI Engineering Corporation (ENFI), the SKS lead smelting technology was first piloted in 1999 at the Shuikoushan lead smelter in Hunan Province, commercially engineered and constructed in 2001, and successfully commissioned in 2002. The SKS lead process was, therefore, the first commercial implementation of the technology. Since then, more than 30 lead smelters in China and elsewhere have been or are being constructed using the SKS lead process. 

The SKS copper process was first adopted in 2001 and commissioned at the Sin Quyen Copper Complex in Vietnam in 2008, marking the first commercial implementation in copper. The second (and larger) implementation of the technology – the first in China – took place in 2008 at the Dongying Fangyuan Nonferrous Metals Co., Ltd. (Dongying Fangyuan) smelter when production was expanded from a 3 000 tpa scrap re-melting plant to a 100 000 tpa copper concentrate smelting operation [40-41]. 

R. Stephens [42] reported in 2005 that the SKS lead furnace was described “as the smelting section of a QSL reactor.” Kaixi Jiang _et al._ [40] described the SKS copper furnace as similar in design to the Noranda Reactor, though contrasting by the fact that the blast is blown from the bottom via high oxygen ‘guns’, which are essentially Sav

ardLee type shrouded injectors with the particularity (peculiarity) of blowing high pressure air as shrouding gas. Figure 36 presents an illustration drawing of the SKS lead furnace.

A key future development reported by Jiang Jimu was the necessity, according to the Ministry of Science and Technology in China, to “[…] _develop low-pressure, high-capacity gas gun and adopt single-row distribution to improve the circular mode of fused mass, avoid surge of fused mass and lengthen the area of slag setting to reduce copper content in slag_ .” An interesting point is that the double row of injectors for bottom blowing, which appeared as one of the major differences compared to the QSL reactor oxidation zone, seemed to be more detrimental than beneficial. ### **DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS** 

Gao Chang-Chun _et al._ [44] indicated in their conclusions that further improvements to the shrouded injectors were needed to increase life span. They also suggested that once such improvements are achieved, the shrouded injectors could be used to increase the smelting intensity of side-blown furnaces such the Noranda Reactor, the Teniente Converter, or even the Peirce-Smith converter. We certainly share the view that high oxygen, high intensity bath smelting and converting is one of the avenues for copper and nickel smelters to address some of the industry concerns and preoccupations. Savard-Lee type injectors offer great potential for energy conservation and efficiency due to their ability to operate at high oxygen enrichment levels. At a time of greater environmental awareness and regulations, reducing off-gas volumes and controlling volatile impurities such as arsenic have become major drivers for process modernisation and intensification. 

The authors also believe that retrofitting shrouded injection in brownfield operations currently using single-pipe tuyeres is one of the intensification options that should be considered. Such shrouded injectors could be s

imple pipe-in-a-pipe design such as ALSI Technology, or more complex multi-pipe designs with rings of injection grooves such as QSL-type injectors. Selecting the continuous annular space or ring of grooves primarily depends on the metallurgical process requirements, particularly in terms of injection gas flow rates and oxygen enrichment to achieve a desired process 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

1145 

intensity within a specific bath chemistry. Designing the injectors – particularly the size of either their annulus gap or their grooves – is however key to their performance in terms of splashing and life span. Competence in compressible fluid flow, knowledge of gas injection phenomena in molten metals, and experience in injector design and commissioning are therefore major assets for an engineering firm or technical solution provider interested in deploying high intensity injection. Having been in a close business relationship with one of the inventors of the shrouded injector and being provided access to the inventor’s archives, one of the authors (JK) feels particularly privileged in this domain. 

Designing shrouded injectors must ensure the right balance of cooling: enough to ensure the formation of protective accretions, though not in excess to avoid the formation of oversized, lower porosity accretions. A higher oxygen enrichment per injector and a lower number of injectors per vessel is the optimum approach with shrouded injection. One of the most persistent myths about high oxygen shrouded injection is the belief that high enrichment per injector, say above 40-50% O2, is tantamount to overblowing of the converter charge and out-of-control heat generation. A detailed heat and mass balance would correct that perception. In fact, if properly designed, a small number of shrouded injectors could inject less oxygen than a conventional converter with 48 to 60 tuyeres blowing oxygen enriched air, and yet be much more efficient as the heat losses through the off-gases would be significantly reduced. A controlled excess of heat in the bath also becomes an opportunity to reprocess scrap or reverts. Retaining full control of the heat balance, even with larger excess heat, can be achieved when cold dope is delivered to the converters without cranes, typically via a chute. The Glencore Xstrata nickel smelter in Sudbury has mastered the practice, even using submerged sonic injection of nitrogen under the chute to provide appropriate stirring of the solid additions [24-25]. Operating the high oxygen SMC vessel in a green blow mode allows custom feed additions together with reverts and dusts. This custom feed provides a source of added revenues, while giving operators the needed flexibility to control the heat balance. 

For bath smelting, a higher overall oxygen enrichment has always translated into a higher smelting rate. The example of the Noranda Reactor at the Horne smelter in Canada is a testament to the practice. Originally designe

d in 1973 to operate with air, its capacity was about 720 tonnes of feed per day. By the time the enrichment levels reached 40% oxygen, the capacity exceeded 2 800 tonnes/day. Further intensification of matte smelting furnaces beyond 50% oxygen, as achieved with the SKS process, are bound to be the norm in the future modern smelters. We just cannot wait to witness these upcoming developments of shrouded injection in bath smelting and converting and soon have the opportunity to visit one of the new high intensity vessels.

G. Damm and L.Voisin

### **ABSTRACT** 

In order to develop a new pyrometallurgical process for the elimination of detrimental arsenic and the recovery of precious elements such as silver, gold and platinum from arsenicrich copper-lead scraps, the phase relations in the Cu-Fe-Pb-As system saturated with carbon and the distribution of minor elements between the condensed phases generated during the equilibrium at high temperature were studied.
